en: First Chapter: The Vision of the Reality of Vajrayāna; The Turning of the Fourth Wheel of Dharma. Regarding the subject matter of the words taught by the Buddha—from the attainment of awakening until the final great nirvāṇa—there is no consensus among scholars of the various different scriptures. Should those complete instructions be gathered within a single turning of the wheel of dharma, or rather in more than that?

Regarding this matter, some scholars cite this word of the Buddha from the *Guṇavyūharājasūtra*: "I have not prescribed any specific philosophical system (*darśana-viśeṣa*), yet sentient beings have understood it in various ways according to their own respective inclinations.

Based on this, those who maintain that the teaching of the Dharma occurs all at once rightly say: "The Buddha imparted his instruction all at once, and that instruction was [perceived] by sentient beings according to their own respective modes of thought."
The excellence of the Buddha’s speech is that he reveals the teaching of the entire cycle of Dharma with a single utterance.
Thus, the Tathāgata’s teaching is like rain:
does rain not moisten trees without making distinctions?
Even trees and plants grow by taking up water according to their own capacity;
likewise, the truth taught by the Buddha is also one and the same,
yet it is understood and explained by sentient beings according to their own respective intellects.
For this very reason, there has arisen a proliferation of distinct branches and sub-branches, as well as a multiplicity of commentaries on those teachings.
Some, however, consider the Buddha to be like a physician;

just as a physician administers treatment to patients by providing medicine according to their specific ailments, so too does the Buddha provide instruction according to the disposition and capacity of each individual.
As it is said in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra: "Just as a physician administers medicine according to each specific illness, so indeed do the Buddhas teach 'mind-only' (cittamātra) to sentient beings."

(2.123) Some scholars, viewing time and the subject matter to be expressed, accept the account of the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma and state: First of all, beginning with the four noble truths and accepting the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena, the Buddha turned the first wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park in Ṛṣipattana (Sārnāth) for the group of five monks, as well as for the gods and goddesses of the infinite realms of desire and form.
And where the Tripitakas of the Hīnayāna are compiled;

thereafter, on Vulture Peak Mountain, beginning from the aggregate of form up to omniscience, he established the emptiness of all phenomena and demonstrated the vision of the absence of defining characteristics,
which is designated as the turning of the second wheel of Dharma.

Wherein the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras* and other scriptures occurred; and because, in realms such as Vaiśālī and Padmagarbha, he distinguished all phenomena according to the three natures known as the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), clarifying the distinction between the existence of intrinsic nature and the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena— that which was taught to ordinary beings and bodhisattvas is precisely what is called the "turning of the wheel of Dharma of excellent analysis."

And all the scriptural compositions connected with this teaching of the *tathāgatagarbha*— including those that set forth the views of both the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and others— are gathered here. Here, a question arises:
Whose *tantra* is to be included within the turning of the wheel of Dharma?

It is only when the Blessed Buddha is the author of its teaching that these *tantra* treatises possess the status of being the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*); otherwise, how could they be considered Buddhist tantras? In this context, modern scholars have sought the distinction between the Pāramitāyāna and Mantrayāna within the Śrāvakayāna (or Hīnayāna).
In the treatises— meaning those such as the *Pālitripiṭaka* and others—
it is established that one should strive to obtain the seeds of both the Mahāyāna and the Mantra systems from those very texts.

What kind of contradiction is this, that when the followers of the Hīnayāna lack the intellectual capacity to accept the status of the Mahāyāna scriptures as the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*), what then can be said regarding the Mantra system and the like?
Furthermore, this question must be investigated: how appropriate is it to seek the seeds of one's own existence among those very things that are opposed to it?
Why does this question arise? Is it not the case that the Tripitakas available today were actually uttered directly from the mouth of the Buddha himself?
If one should think thus...
If that is so, how can it be maintained that nothing other than this was taught by the Buddha?
For there exist their own respective views, philosophical systems, paths, and treatises for the Hīnayāna, Mahāyāna, and Mantrayāna.
It is only with reference to these that a definitive determination of the Dharma teachings is appropriate.

Regarding the subject matter of the teachings of the Mantra system, it is stated in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*— a single, most significant work of the Vajrayāna— that the teaching of the tantric scriptures was performed by past Buddhas and will likewise be performed by future Buddhas. Those scriptures whose teaching is here attributed to future Buddhas are considered to be the very same tantric texts existing in the present.
Just as it was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, and will indeed be spoken by those of the future,
and that which the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the present speak again and again.

(Eleventh Verse) It was set forth by Naḍapāda in his *Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā*: "When the Buddha was engaged in teaching the Mahāyāna *Prajñāpāramitā* on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), at that time the *Guhyasamāja*, *Kālacakra*, and other [tantras] were being taught by him in Dhānyakaṭaka—
just as the Teacher [taught] the system of the *Prajñāpāramitā* on Vulture Peak."
Likewise, the teaching of the Dharma was proclaimed in the Śrīdhānya [Kalpa] according to the Mantra system.
Thus it is said in the *Sekoddeśaṭīkā* (p.

3): The master Śākyamitra stated that when the Tathāgata was performing austerities on the bank of the Nairañjanā River, his gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) reached the Akaniṣṭha realm and performed the teaching of the Yoga Tantra.

Furthermore, in many works of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttara-tantra*), it has been established that the Tathāgata himself is the teacher, he himself is the Dharma, and he himself is also the listener. As it is said: "I am the expounder, I am the Dharma;
I am the listener, possessing the qualities of heaven and earth."
I am the one to be realized, the teacher of the world;
I am the world, and I am also that which pertains to the world. I am the nature of innate bliss, the ultimate limit, beginning with the stage of cessation.

(Hevajra Tantra 2.2.39–40) Beyond this, the Blessed One’s teaching of the *tantra* scriptures— such as those on ritual action (*kriyā*), conduct (*caryā*), and yoga— was imparted to various disciples in diverse locations and circumstances throughout the worlds of the nāgas, gods, asuras, and humans. Indeed, there is a profound diversity among the *Kriyā*, *Caryā*, *Yoga*, and *Anuttarayoga* tantras, owing to their respective adherence to the principles of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and philosophical view (*darśana*).
The primary subject of this treatise is precisely the presentation of these distinctions along with their authoritative proofs.

Therefore, it remains to be investigated to which category the teaching of the *Tantra* belongs, just as the other three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma are considered according to whether phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatā*) or lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), and through their correct classification.

Just as there is the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, so too might there be a fourth turning of the Wheel of Dharma pertaining to its essential nature (*svarūpa*); yet even that is not perceived as being logically consistent, because the vision of the Tantric scriptures and the procedure for their practice attain their full development through distinct and secret dimensions. Furthermore, these cannot be designated by the name "the fourth turning of the Wheel of Dharma" either on the basis of some single category or from the perspective of time.

Since the Blessed Buddha taught certain mantras for the sake of Ānanda and other monks long ago, while for others he did so after a considerable lapse of time, the conclusion is this: it is possible that the Buddha was able to provide teachings to those to be trained (vineya-jana) at any time and in whatever form suited their specific desires and dispositions. In such a case, what is appropriate regarding a particular sequence or a specific number? What is the point of such a calculation?

That is indeed inconceivable; the Lord taught it in the *Mahāyānottaratantra*: "With respect to the realm of those to be trained, the means of training them, the act of training the realm of those to be trained, and the movement to the appropriate place and time—the activity of the All-pervading One occurs always through effortless spontaneity."
In that very same [text], this is also stated: "Having displayed the persistence of existence within impure fields...
(Mahāyānottaratantra 2.56).
As long as there is existence and saṃsāra, so long does he provide teaching in whatever form is necessary;
this alone is the great task of the Buddhas. What is the nature of the Buddha’s word? What is the Buddha’s word?
And how many divisions does it have?

This is the answer: speech that is endowed with the three higher trainings of ethical discipline, free from faults of expression, examined by the three means of valid cognition, consistent with reasoning, and joined with wholesome action at its beginning and end—this alone is the word of the Buddha.

In the *Mahāyānottaratantra*, the Protector Maitreya said: "Speech that is meaningful, endowed with the words of the Dharma, which eradicates the afflictions of the three realms, and which demonstrates the ultimate benefit—that is the word of the Sage; anything otherwise is its opposite."
(5-18) That which is bound by the essential Dharma, which brings about the abandonment of all afflictions of the three realms,
and which is taught for the sake of the state of supreme peace— that alone is the Dharma, the word of the Great Sage.
According to the Tibetan tradition, the word of the Buddha is divided into five categories based on the condition of the authoritative master.
1. Directly taught from the mouth;
2–4. Empowered by body, speech, and mind; and 5. Spoken by way of authorization.

And just as the Mahāyāna sūtras and other texts were taught from the mouth of the Buddha: 2. when the Buddha placed his hand upon the head of Vajragarbha, who was empowered by his body, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* was thereby explained; 3.
when the Buddha spoke to Mañjuśrī in order to dispel the grief of Ajātaśatru, the explanation of the Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Ajātaśatrukaukṛtyavinodana*, prompted by him, was composed by Mañjuśrī.

4. O Śāriputra, when Avalokiteśvara and [Mañjuśrī] are impelled by their enlightened mind (*buddhicitta*), and once that mind has bestowed its empowerment (*adhiṣṭhita*) upon them, the two of them mutually investigate the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
It is precisely within the flow of that investigation and discernment that the Sūtras flash forth and the Śāstras arise.
This very [process], empowered by the mind, is designated as the "Word of the Buddha" (*buddhavacana*).

Immediately after the Parinirvāṇa of the Blessed Buddha, he spoke to those who were to compile his words regarding the commencement of the treatise, so that they might say at the beginning, “Thus have I heard,” deposit separate sections in the middle,
and proclaim approval at the end, saying, “Excellent, excellent!
That which is thus declared is known as the authorized word of the Buddha.
The subject of exposition will be explained in detail in the subsequent chapters. What is the name of this *tantra*?
The word *tantra* is employed in many senses; this explanation was provided by the late Dr. P.V. Kane in the first chapter of his work, *A History of Dharmaśāstra*.

The word *tantra* is considered to be derived from the two verbal roots *tanu* (to expand) and *tri* (to protect). That in which various subjects converge, or in which reality (*tattva*), mantras, and so forth, are combined, is called *tantra* because it expands and protects them;
therefore, this is termed *tantra*.

In Buddhist Tantric literature as well, the word *tantra* is employed in this very sense: "Tantra is that by which knowledge (*jñāna*) is extended (*tanyate*) or expanded (*vistāryate*). The definition and classifications of *tantra* are described in the *Guhyasamāja-uttaratantra*: "A continuous composition (*prabandha*) is called *tantra*; that composition is threefold:
the basis (*ādhāra*), the nature (*prakṛti*), and..."
By way of its indivisibility from that which cannot be taken away.
The source, the cause of form, the fruit that cannot be destroyed,
the support, and its means— by these three, the summary of the meaning of the Tantra is comprised.
In this statement from the *Guhyasamāja*, the continuous discourse is declared to be the "tantra" (*tantra*);
for the intended meaning of "tantra" is continuity (*nairantarya*). Continuity is that very thing which is devoid of beginning and end.
There can be no continuity for that which has a beginning, because it must originate from that point;
nor can there be continuity for that which has an end, because such continuity is impossible.
Therefore, for the eternal consciousness, the very state devoid of beginning and end is the *tantra*.
In this context, from the perspective of the subject matter (*abhidheya*), there are three divisions of the *tantra*: the cause (*hetu*), the means (*upāya*), and the fruit (*phala*).
From the perspective of the expression (*abhidhāna*), those treatises that elucidate the aforementioned subjects are called *tantras*.

Regarding the number of this scripture as it exists in the vast collection found in the land of Tibet, Darathaṅ Rinpoché stated in the preface to his own publication of the Kangyur and Tengyur (*Derge Kanjur and Tanjur*, Content Analysis, p.
35): "The number of tantric texts within the Word of the Buddha is 4,710 sections and 41,500 verses; the number of tantric texts composed by Indian paṇḍitas is 2,630 sections..."
There are 3,575 verses, 103,000 [lines], as well as numerous other Nyingma tantras (*rgyud 'bum*) and collections of *dhāraṇīs*.
[Regarding] the *hetu* (basis/cause)...

In this tantra, from the perspective of its subject matter, the nature of our own mind and so forth— which is the very essence of a Buddha— is present yet obscured by artificial (adventitious) stains;
it is like a seed.
And that which, having attained a state of association with conditions, possesses the capacity for the attainment of the fruit—
when the adventitious (āgantuka) impurity is destroyed, the sattva-mind becomes stainless, and that is called the Buddha.
Therefore, from the perspective of what is to be expressed, it is this very mind that is designated as the "supporting continuum.

In its defiled state, this mind becomes the cause of the six worldly realms of rebirth; yet, when matured and refined upon the path, it manifests in the form of a Buddha. Apart from the destruction of artificial and adventitious stains, there is nothing else to be performed by the practitioner, because no modification or transformation whatsoever occurs within its own intrinsic nature.
Therefore, he abides in a single, uninterrupted stream of his own essential nature.
As it is taught in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "Sentient beings are indeed Buddhas, but they are veiled by adventitious impurities.
Through the removal of those [impurities], sentient beings are undoubtedly Buddhas."
(2/4/69) A Buddha is not found anywhere else in other world-systems;
for the perfectly awakened one is indeed the mind itself—the Buddha is not shown to exist elsewhere.
(2/4/70) Thus, the mind of the *sattva* alone is the substratum for both impurity (*mālinya*) and purity (*nairmalya*).
For this very reason, this is here called the *āśrayatantra* (substratum-tantra) or the *hetutantra* (cause-tantra).

Regarding the *upāyatantra*: indeed, the mental state (*cittavṛtti*) of the cause which bestows the nature of the fruit according to the intention of the means—that is, that which is an auxiliary in the manifestation of the fruit and resembles a condition (*pratyaya*)—is precisely what is termed the "means" (*upāya*).

Just as water, light, and so forth are considered the means for obtaining a harvest from a rice seed, in the same way, the status of efforts as means for the ripening and refinement of the mind is stated in the *Sampuṭatantra*: "The Buddhas have shown the means for the increase of the wisdom of sentient beings;
merit should be abandoned from the perspective of ultimate reality—what need is there to mention the grasping of non-merit?"
(Nepalese manuscript, folio no.

133) Even the lineage of realization (*ānubhava-upāya*) is called *tantra*, because the lineage of experience belonging to a practitioner who is devoted to the practice and to the unbroken succession of oral instructions and empowerments continuously attains expansion in the form of a means (*upāya*).
Taking this extensively, it is stated that these very means (*upāya*) also constitute the nature of tantra.
As it says in the *Hevajratantra*: "Like the flow of a river’s current, like the continuity of a lamp’s flame."
One should remain constantly, day and night, through the yoga of reality.
(1/8/56) For a beginner, an uninterrupted stream of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is impossible;
however, through gradual practice, the state of uninterrupted absorption is eventually attained.
As stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "Uninterrupted streams of merit flow forth, equal to the expanse of space."
(1-19) This samādhi, which consists of an uninterrupted stream of merit and serves as the means for the purification of the mind, is also merely a single state of the mind;
therefore, this is the Upāyatantra.

Regarding Phalatantra: the intended meaning of Phalatantra is the manifestation of the fruit—which exists in an indestructible form within the cause—as the mind remains in the causal state, with its pure mental functions contained within.
The *phalatantra* is explained as follows:

Just as a fruit that exists within the flowers of a tree in an inseparable form (*avinābhāva*) ripens in the course of time, in the very same way, the mind— having been refined into the form of enlightenment through the assistance of the *upāyatantra*— is born as the fruit.
Even the *phalatantra* (result-tantra) possesses the nature of a tantra because it exists as something delimited [by the causal path].
As stated in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "The collection of the bodies of the Buddhas is to be understood by means of three bodies."
That which constitutes the welfare of oneself and others, together with its basis, is demonstrated by means of the three bodies.
They are considered equal in terms of their basis, their intention, and their action;
their permanence is established through their intrinsic nature, their non-interruption, and their continuity.

(9/65-66) The *dharmakāya* is eternal by its very nature because it is unchanging; the *saṃbhogakāya* is characterized by constant enjoyment of the Dharma; and the *nirmāṇakāya* incessantly brings about the welfare of living beings. Thus, even with respect to the body of fruition (*phalakāya*), continuity is established.
Therefore, this is called the *Phalatantra*.
And as it is also established in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*: "Just as worldly activities are seen to proceed without interruption in space,
even so the activities of the Victors proceed without interruption in the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*)."

The intended meaning is as follows: the *tantra* is said to be the process of the path and so forth for a practitioner whose mind regarding sentient beings is without beginning or end and whose continuum is uninterrupted; or else, it is the basis or support for the discourse on the descent [of the teachings].

Among the various Buddhist philosophical systems, this has been explained under such names as *gotra*, *tathāgatagarbha*, *sugatagarbha*, *mahāmudrā*, *bodhicitta*, *nijacitta*, *samantabhadra*, and so forth.

In the opinion of the Bhadvaṣikas, the noble lineage (*āryagotra*) is exclusively a mental factor (*caitasika*), consisting of a state of mind that is unattached to existence, its causes, and its requisites;
for it is from such an unattached mind and mental factor that untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) arises.
As it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "Non-attachment is the noble lineages; three of them consist of contentment."
Livelihood is established by three [of the factors] through right action; the arising of craving is the adverse side.

(6/7) Here, by the word *bhava* (existence), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are to be understood; and by the "requisites of existence" (*bhavopakaraṇa*), the religious robes (*dharmakāṣāya*) and so forth are to be taken. In the Vinaya Piṭaka as well, contentment with the religious robes, alms-food, common bedding, and so on, is declared to be the practice belonging to the lineage of wealth (*arthagotrīyā*). Likewise, that person who cultivates a taste for renunciation and meditative concentration, [is established in the lineage].
He, too, abides in the noble lineage (*āryagotra*).
Here, in the first [section], three things— [the dharma-robe, alms-food, and common lodgings]—
are said to be the antidotes to worldly existence (*bhava*).
The engagement in the cultivation of renunciation and meditative concentration is declared to be the antidote to the cycle of existence (*bhavakrama*).
According to the Sautrāntikas, a specific mental continuum (*cittāyatana*) characterized by an uninterrupted flow is accepted as the lineage (*gotra*).

Among the Vijñānavādins of the Mahāyāna, the lineage is described as the uncontaminated seed (*anāsrava-bīja*) obtained from the *dharmadhātu*, which has been functioning in an uninterrupted form since beginningless time.
This very lineage (*gotra*) is the support for the qualities of a bodhisattva, as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "In that regard, what is the support?

Here, the bodhisattva’s own lineage, the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*), and all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are called the support."
For what reason?
Because here a bodhisattva, relying upon the lineage (gotra),
must be established as one capable of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, by way of homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), the lineage (*gotra*) is called the "basis" (*ādhāra*).

According to the view of the Madhyamaka Mahāyāna, the lineage is said to be the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) or the luminosity (*prabhāsvaratva*) of the mind that is possessed of stains.
Because all the qualities of a Buddha are contained within this,

even in the case of the *avataṃsaka* (the crest-jewel), the lineage (*gotra*) of the Bodhisattvas is said to consist of the *dharmadhātu*, to be like space, extensive, and by nature luminous. Thus, the reality of the Tathāgata endowed with these qualities is called the Buddha-lineage.
This very same subject is also found in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "The suchness of all things, though distinguished, has attained purity;
therefore, it is the state of a Tathāgata, and for that reason all embodied beings possess its embryo."
(9/37) Also in the *Mahāyānottaratantra*: "That which is the nature of the mind is luminous; it never undergoes transformation, just like the sky.
However, through adventitious stains such as passion, born of unreal conceptualization, it undergoes defilement."
In the *Samādhirāja-sūtra*, it is established that the entire world is pervaded by the *sugatagarbha*; this is also stated as follows: "This whole world is the maker of a Buddha.

Just as oil is contained within sesame seeds and butter within milk, even so does this [nature] abide in every living being, having the luminous, unceasing, and untainted (*anāsrava*) as its intrinsic nature."
Demonstrating this cause, it is stated in the *Uttaratantra*: "Because the body of the Perfect Buddha pervades [all], because suchness is undifferentiated,
and because the lineage exists always, all embodied beings possess the Buddha-essence."
(1/28) Hereafter, in the Vajrayāna, the *āśrayatantra* is accepted by its very nature as the effortless maṇḍala.
Unchanging great bliss and emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects—
their non-duality— is itself the lineage (*gotra*) or the tantra, which is the great maṇḍala indivisible and indestructible by the three bodies (*trikāya*).
This is also understood by the names Mahāmudrā and Bodhicitta,
as follows: "Just as the seed of fire resides depending upon fuel,
or as oil is conceived in sesame seeds, or as juice is found in sugarcane."
Just as fragrance exists in flowers, or butter in curd,
so does it exist everywhere— in all sentient beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Furthermore, Mahāmudrā is established as both form and that which has entered into form;
thus, bodhicitta is also manifested by way of its basis.
As stated in the *Śrīsamājottaratantra*: "Without beginning or end, peaceful, the indestructible of existence and non-existence, the all-pervading Lord."
The indivisibility of emptiness and compassion is known as bodhicitta.

(18/37) Here, it is not merely the desire for all living beings to attain Buddhahood that is called *bodhicitta*; rather, the nature of *bodhicitta* is explained as belonging exclusively to the luminous mind-vajra (*prabhāsvara-cittavajra*), and its cultivation has also been taught. This was delineated in the *Jñānasiddhi* within the commentary on the aforementioned verse: "This is what is meant: the yogin who knows the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is mutually [pervaded] by all the Tathāgatas."

The meaning of "Vajra" is that which always abides as the pervasive nature, performing the activities of a Buddha; it is great compassion toward all sentient beings and the bodhicitta that conforms to the immeasurables.
By this, it is shown that one should likewise perform meditative cultivation.
"It is known as *bodhicitta*," thus it is intended in all the Yoga Tantras without exception.
For beginners and others, however, *bodhicitta* is merely the thought: "I shall establish all sentient beings in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment" (p.

135). In the *Guṇavatī* commentary on the *Mahāmāyā Tantra*, *bodhicitta* is also described by way of cause, means, and fruit—the threefold tantra consisting of the causal tantra (*hetutantro*), [the means tantra, and the resultant tantra].
The tantra of fruition and the tantra of means.
In that regard, the mind that is naturally luminous and without beginning or end is the bodhicitta.
That seed has a cause.
Of what is it the seed? It is the seed of awakening; perfect enlightenment is its fruit.
Because they possess unsurpassed results... these treatises of instruction concerning these causes, results, and methods are, respectively, the *hetutantra*, the *phalatantra*, or the *upāyatantra*.

By this demonstration, it is made perfectly clear that just as there are three divisions of the *tantra* from the perspective of the subject matter (*abhidheya*)—centering on the mind (*citta*)—likewise, from the perspective of the expression (*abhidhāna*), the *tantra* scriptures that elucidate the three aforementioned states of the mind are also threefold.

Through the analysis of the nature of the aforementioned tantras, it is quite clear that various qualities have been attributed to the nature of the mind—whether in the mind itself, its continuum, or its flow—by followers of different Buddhist schools according to their own intellectual capacities, or observed in relation to various objects. In brief, this must be accepted: the state of the mind is uninterrupted.
In the absence of that, nothing can be done, nor can anything come into being.
Saraha says: "O mind, in your absence, who could explain the Dharma?
If the seeker searches for all appearances within the mind and the Dharma, they shall not find them, for they were never there from the beginning."
Non-existence throughout the three times, unborn and unceasing. (Rāhula Dohākośa)
(Hindi Chayā, p. 253): Synonyms for Mantrayāna are Vajrayāna, which is also designated as Phalayāna or Upāyayāna.
The causal system is that of the *pāramitās*, and the resultant system is that of the *mantras*.
By virtue of cause and result—namely, wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*)—there exists the indivisibility of the two, which is the *vajra*.
By "vajra," emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is expressed.
Through existence, there is the state of pure consciousness;
the identity of these two is established as the very nature of Vajrasattva.
(Advayavajrasaṃgraha, p. 24) The distinction between emptiness and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light;
[yet] there is the unity of emptiness and compassion.
Like that of a lamp and its light.
Emptiness is not other than phenomena,
nor do phenomena exist without it;
this is an inseparable relationship, just like that between the produced and the impermanent.
(Relying on this statement of Advayavajra, *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, p. 24: The path that leads to Vajra or Vajrasattva, or the vehicle itself, is called the Vajrayāna.
Furthermore, the treatise that demonstrates the non-difference between cause and fruit is designated as the Vajrayāna.
It is also stated in the *Guhyasamāja*: "The Vajrayāna is the scripture that purifies attachment, aversion, and delusion;
or else, the Vajrayāna is the scripture that purifies body, speech, and mind.
It is called the Vajrayāna precisely because it establishes the indivisibility of body, speech, and mind."

This Secret Mantra Vehicle is taught as a secret for those who are unfit vessels; yet, by means of the mantras and mudrās taught herein by qualified practitioners, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained.
And it is said in the *Guhyasamāja*: "Whatever arises dependently through the senses, objects, and the mind—that mind is known as 'conceptualization' (*manana*)."
Because its purpose is the protection of the agent.
That which is called the commitment-vow (samayasamvara), free from worldly conduct,
and its preservation by all Vajras, is described as "mantra-conduct" (mantracaryā).
(18.69–71) By implication, the mind (*manas*) is said to be precisely that cognition produced by the eye-consciousness and so forth, which arises from objects and sense faculties.
This has been defined in exactly the same way in the *Abhidharmakośa* as well:
the mind, when attached to the various qualities and categories of objects, becomes the cause of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).
That mind can be protected by means of the method taught in the Mantra-naya.
Because it protects by destroying the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) through the act of contemplating (*manana*), it is for that very reason called "mantra."
All the worlds of the vessel, the celestial palaces of the chosen deity,
all the worlds of sentient beings, the chosen deities themselves, and all sounds whatsoever are the mantras of the chosen deity.
All conceptualizations, reasonings, deliberations, and the fluctuations of the mind of the chosen deity are [the path].
Having thus established the path that demonstrates the supramundane convention, the vehicle that leads one toward it is indeed the Mantra Vehicle.

Even though the reality inherent in manifest phenomena is accomplished, the description of this subject is as follows: all these various types of mudrās and even those diversions of speech are the various types of mantra.
Also in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*: "Because it is impossible to transgress, it is indestructible and indeed secret;
since the state of secret accomplishment is conveyed [therein], it is therefore defined as 'mantra'."

(p. 206) This is also called the *phalayāna* (vehicle of the fruit), because just as this fruit is perceived in various states such as the body, objects of enjoyment, place, and action, so too does the establishment of its cultivation persist even during the state of the path.
And this is also called the *upāyayāna* (vehicle of means).
For, in comparison with the Pāramitāyāna, many skillful means and easy paths have been delineated herein;
and from this, the state of Vajradhara is attained with rapid progress.
Thus, in the *Vinayapradīpa*, there is the statement of the master Tripiṭakamala: "Even though the goal is one and the same, because of the absence of confusion..."
Because it possesses many methods and is not difficult to practice,
and because it is intended for those with sharp faculties,
the science of mantras is superior.

The Classification of Tantras: Scholars have established numerous distinct categories for the practice of tantra, and a brief exposition of these is now provided. In his *Āmnāyamañjarī*, a commentary on the *Sampuṭatantra*, Abhayākaragupta divided tantra into two sections based on the distinction between external and internal: he designated *Kriyātantra* and *Caryātantra* as external tantras, while identifying *Yogatantra* and *Anuttarayogatantra* as internal tantras.

The Tibetan scholar known as Koṅ-sprul Rin-po-che, having extracted the words from the *Pradīpoddyotana*, designated those treatises that explain either the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) or the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) as "inner tantras," while those treatises that explain the generation stage were designated as "outer tantras. In his commentary on the *Ārya-trailokyavijaya*, he stated: "Kriyātantra is for those with many conceptual constructions, and Yogatantra is for those whose minds are one-pointed."
Those who accept both systems [as distinct] commit an error,
because even in the two systems, no deities other than those of Kriyātantra are found;
therefore, only two divisions of Tantra are possible, not three or four.
In the *Vajragarbhālaṃkāra*, the Buddha taught three divisions of tantra named Kriyātantra, Caryātantra (also known as Ubhayatantra), and Yogatantra.
In the commentary on the *Vajrāmṛtatantra*, three divisions named Kriyātantra, Yogatantra, and Guhyatantra were described.

In the *Vajrapañjara* as well, the Pratyekabuddha taught the Kriyā-tantra for those of inferior capacity, the Caryā and Uttama [Yoga] tantras for those of middling capacity, and the Anuttarayoga-tantra for those of the highest capacity, each according to their respective intellectual levels.
In the *Sampuṭa-tantra*: "Laughter, gazing, and the grasping of hands—this is established in the Tantra."
Both passion and dispassion— having chewed these up, the wood-worm remains.

(6/3/49) Following these four systems of passion (*rāga*), the fourfold division of the *tantra* has been established. Śraddhākaravarman, in his *Anuttarayogāvatāra*, explained Yogatantra as being twofold, through the distinction between internal meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and external conduct (*caryā*).
Thus, five divisions of the *tantra* are delineated therein: Kriyā, Caryā, Ubhayayoga, Yogatantra, and Anuttarayogatantra.
Śāntipāda also divided this system of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) into five sections known as Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Mahāyoga, and Anuttarayoga.
In the *Ḍākārṇava-tantra* as well, there are exactly five divisions, namely:
Kriyā-tantra, Caryā-tantra, Mahāyoga-tantra, Yoga-tantra, and Mahānuttara-tantra.

In the *Vajrajñānasamuccaya-tantra* as well, a fivefold enumeration is stated, namely: Kriyātantra, Caryātantra, Ubhayatantra, Kalpatantra, and Yogatantra. Kāṇhapāda also, in his *Yogaratnamālā*, having declared that the accomplishment of the entire Mantranaya is fivefold—distinguished as Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Yogottara, and Anuttarayoga—establishes these five divisions. Tripaṭakamala likewise included this within six sections: Kriyā, Mūla-caryā, Yoga, Yogaguhyā, and Anuttarayoga.

The scholar Alaṃkalaśa also asserted that the entire tantra taught by the Blessed Buddha is divided into five sections, and their names are: Kriyātantra, Caryātantra, Yogatantra, Anuttaratantra, and Anuttaramātṛyogatantra.
Furthermore, in his own commentary on the *Bodhipathapradīpa*, Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna also divided it into seven sections, naming them: Kriyā, Caryā, Kalpa, Ubhaya, Yoga, Mahāyoga, and Anuttarayogatantra.

In the Nyiṅma tradition of Tibet as well, after establishing the fourfold division known as Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Anuttara, and further specifying the threefold division of the Anuttarayoga Tantra known as Anuyoga, Atiyoga, and Mahāyoga— these seven divisions being considered the independent vehicle (svatantrayāna)— they further establish nine vehicles by including these together with the Śrāvakayāna and the Pāramitāyāna.

The great scholar Buston categorized the texts of the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Anuttarayoga Tantras into three divisions: Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), and Non-dual Tantra (*advayatantra*). Having thus divided the entire corpus of tantric literature into seven sections, he compiled a catalog.
Regarding the purpose of teaching the Tantras: the Blessed Buddha desired the welfare and upliftment not only of the human race, but of all living beings.

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, there is an address to the Buddhist monks: “Go forth, O Bhikṣus, on a journey for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. (1-21) Following this, the founders of the Buddhist schools (*bauddhavidhvadbhiḥ*) adopted this very activity for the sake of gathering sentient beings and showing them the path; they established various philosophical systems (*nānāmatāni*) and practiced them accordingly. In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*: “Generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds [are the means of conversion]. (1-7)
Its teaching is held to consist in undertaking [the practice] and following it oneself.

The means [of conversion] should be known as fourfold: that which bestows favor, that which causes grasping, that which sets [the recipient] in motion, and likewise that which conforms [to their needs]. These constitute the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*).

(16-72/72) That is to say, in order to favor those to be trained (*vineyajana*), one should practice generosity; thereafter, instruction that delights the disciples should be bestowed through exceedingly sweet words.
Furthermore, one must personally follow that very same path according to the nature of the trainees who arrive;
for the teaching of the Dharma is carried out through such means, as it cannot otherwise be possible for us to favor them.
It is also stated in the *Catuḥśataka*: "Just as a barbarian cannot be made to understand by means of another language,
so the world cannot be made to understand without recourse to worldly conventions."

(8.19) The primary objective of instruction should be nothing other than setting the disciples upon the correct path. The rules for language and formal procedures, however, are merely means (*upāya*) for attaining what is to be accomplished; they are not the ultimate goal.
As it is stated in the *Kālacakravimalaprabhā-ṭīkā*: "By whatever means possible, the ripening of sentient beings [should be achieved]."
In each and every such manner, one should perform the teaching of the Dharma.
The yogi diligently grasps the Dharma through both correct and incorrect words;
when the meaning has been obtained, it is by means of the regional dialect.
In that context, what is meant by the word "treatise" (śāstra)?
(Lokadhātupaṭala, pṛ.

24) Regarding the superiority of the means taught in the Mantra system in comparison to the Pāramitā system, the *Advayavajra* has described it as follows: "Even though the goal is the same, [the Mantra system] is superior because it is free from confusion, possesses many means, is not difficult to practice, and is intended for those with sharp faculties."
The science of mantras is preeminent.
(Leaf 21) Regarding the purposes for the divisions of the tantras: instruction on the tantras is given in four ways according to the varying levels of intelligence of those to be trained (*vineya*).
For instance, although there is no difference in the result—Buddhahood—among the fourfold set of tantras beginning with *Kriyā*, [the distinctions are made for the sake of the trainees].

In the stage of the path, there is no difference whatsoever between the generation of the bodhicitta, the practice of the ten perfections, the vision of emptiness, and the cultivation of deity yoga and so forth; moreover, [this involves] the purification of the four kinds of passion, the four types of birth, the four afflictions, and the four types of persons.
Based on the fourfold nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the fourfold consecration of the watches and ages (*yāma-yuga*), the learned have divided the Tantras into four sections.
1. There are four levels of passion (*rāga*), and the path of passion is established in four ways; therefore, the Tantra was divided into four parts.
And as it was declared by the Buddha in the Sampuṭatantra: "Laughter, the sight [of the consort], and the joining of hands—these are established in that tantra;
likewise passion and dispassion, having been chewed up, remain like woodworms."

In the *Abhidharmakośa* as well, this very same point is demonstrated by the statement: "Sexual union consists of coupling, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing" (3.69). This very truth is proclaimed by the Buddha in the *Vajrajñānasamuccaya* as the causal basis for the fourfold classification of the tantras.
2. Contemplating the purification of the four castes and their mental dispositions, the Buddha divided that [teaching] into four parts and established its instruction.

As it is stated in the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*, through the gradual practice of the conduct of secret mantras, the practitioner becomes liberated from the afflictions (*kleśa*). The Brahmin caste especially encourages the pursuit of such external practices and prescribes the abandonment of asceticism and difficult austerities; thus, they consider this very path to be the way to liberation and release.
For the sake of favoring other practitioners and those of such castes who adopt these types of conduct, the Buddha taught the Kriyātantra.

(b) To those disciples belonging to the merchant class—who neither desire to perform difficult austerities nor wish to engage in conduct that is loathed by the world—the Buddha taught the Caryātantra.
These individuals do not reach the spiritual path according to the system of Yogatantra, yet they remain far removed from the external rituals of Kriyātantra.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the Caryātantra to these [practitioners], in which the instruction of both tantras is found.

These practitioners, who perform the practice and application of the Yoga Tantra in terms of contemplation and the Kriyā Tantra in terms of conduct, are called "practitioners of both tantras" (ubhayatantrin).
(ga) Furthermore, for those kṣatriyas or other men who do not wish to engage in difficult practices such as asceticism— meaning, those who desire attachment to the qualities of desire and so forth—
the Buddha taught the Yoga Tantra after prescribing for them the ritual procedures for consecration and the like that are appropriate to their high status.
Thus, it has been explained in detail in the commentary on the *Āryatrailokyavijaya* titled *Tattvasaṃgraha*.

(Gha) Furthermore, those men who—even if they be Śūdras—who, being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), do not make distinctions between what is drinkable and undrinkable, what is approachable and unapproachable, or what is auspicious and inauspicious, are fit to consume the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five great meats (*pañcamahāmāṃsa*).
And generally, those practitioners (*sādhakas*) who are able to take excrement, urine, and so forth, without hesitation, as if they were milk;
For such practitioners, the Buddha taught the Anuttarayoga Tantra in the language of the Saṅgha;
for them, there exists no bondage whatsoever,
as has been extensively established in the Hevajra Tantra, the Sampuṭa Tantra, and other works.
3. Among those to be trained, there is a predominance of four afflictions; for their destruction, the tantras are divided into four sections.
For those who are extremely deluded, there is the Action Tantra (Kriyā-tantra).

He taught Caryātantra to those who were extremely dull-witted; Yogatantra to those characterized by hatred, delusion, and so forth; and Anuttarayogatantra to those disciples endowed with passion and delusion.
4. There exists a teaching of the four classes of tantra that conforms to the varying degrees of intelligence of sentient beings:
namely, the Kriyātantra for those of inferior intellect, and the Caryātantra for those superior to them.
The Buddha taught Yoga Tantra to superior individuals, and Anuttarayoga Tantra to those disciples with extremely sharp faculties.

For those individuals who possess dull faculties and desire external practices such as ritual bathing, he taught the meditation upon and worship of the deity through a painted image or a statue fashioned from material substances in Kriyā Tantra.
It has been taught:
for individuals of middling faculties, there is the *Caryātantra*, which consists in practicing the deity meditation (*devatābhāvanā*) by means of external forms;

for superior practitioners, there is the *Yogatantra* for the sake of deity-yoga meditation, wherein [the deity] is first summoned through gnosis (*jñāna*) alone and subsequently dissolved into the visualized *samaya*-deity.

Indeed, the Unsurpassed Yoga Tantra (*anuttarayogatantra*) was taught for the sake of the most excellent of persons; that in which the teachings on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*utpannakrama*) are found is called the Unsurpassed Yoga Tantra.

Furthermore, the fourfold tantras were taught for the sake of exhausting the four types of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), as it is said in the *Kālacakratantra*: "The Wisdom Tantra (*prajñātantra*) indeed proceeds from the front, and furthermore, from the back [of the face], it is permeated by yoga."
The Lord of Jinas proclaims the Yoga Tantra from his right face; from his left face, the Kriyā and other [tantras];
indeed, the Yogācāra from the eastern face; and again, from the western face, the entire Madhyamaka; from his right face he proclaims the Sūtrānta, and from his white face, the pure Vaibhāṣika.

(5/48) When sleep is interrupted, through the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of disparagement, there arises an attachment to the external world; to abandon this, there is *Kriyātantra* by means of the left face.

When the mind is manifested through the latent impression of one's own [worldly] conduct (*svapravāsanā*) by means of the right face, there is attachment to mere appearances (*ābhāsamātra*); to abandon this, there is *Caryātantra* by means of the front face. By means of the latent impression of excessive sleep, one becomes distanced from external conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); to abandon the manifest attachments, there is *Yogatantra*.

Furthermore, for the sake of abandoning the adherence to phenomena produced by the latencies of all subtle conceptualizations and attachments—which arise through the power of latencies directed toward the back [of reality]—the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*) was taught for the purpose of such abandonment.

6. That tantra in which there is merely the procedure for the water-pot consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) is the Action Tantra (*kriyātantra*); that in which there is the procedure for the consecrations of the vajra-bell, mirror, teaching of the Dharma, and permission (*anujñā*) is the Conduct Tantra (*caryātantra*);
and that which prescribes the eleven consecrations connected with the vase of the Vajrācārya and so forth is indeed the Yoga Tantra (*yogatantra*).
That which contains the procedure for the secret, wisdom, and fourth empowerments is called Anuttarayogatantra.
Furthermore, it is maintained that the teaching of the four classes of tantra follows the sequence of the four ages (*yuga*).
Just as the Blessed One established the teaching of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Anuttarayoga tantras respectively during the Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages.

8. Furthermore, the fourfold set of tantras beginning with Kriyātantra was taught for the purpose of taking the fourfold extension of passion (*rāga*) as the path. Specifically, Kriyātantra is for taking laughter as the path, and Caryātantra is for the sake of vision (*darśana*).
The Yoga Tantra was taught for the sake of attaining union through the hands, and the Anuttarayoga Tantra was taught for the purpose of making embracing the path.
Furthermore, four divisions of the Tantras were established in order to favor the Buddhists who uphold the four philosophical systems, beginning with the Vaibhāṣika.

Just as among the Vaibhāṣikas the existence of external objects is maintained, in order to favor them, Jñānadeva is invoked upon a cloth painting placed before one's eyes; having deposited the mantra in his heart and having purified oneself through rituals such as bathing, accomplishment is sought. Therefore, the Kriyātantra exists for their sake. By the Sautrāntikas, the momentariness and atomicity of both the apprehended object and the apprehending subject are accepted.

Therefore, in order to favor them, the Caryātantra was established; therein, the procedure was set forth for attaining accomplishment by meditating upon oneself as the Samayadeva, invoking the Jñānasattva before one's own eyes, placing the mantra within his heart, and regarding the chosen deity as equal to a friend.
The Vijñānavādins, not accepting external objects, accept as the ultimate reality an internal, non-dual self-awareness consisting of the grasped and the grasper.

Having meditated upon that self-aware deity in accordance with their philosophical view and reflection, they dissolve the deity of knowledge (jñānadeva) into that [self-awareness] and, following the repetition of the mantra, dismiss the deity of knowledge; this is what is called the procedure of Yoga Tantra.

The Mādhyamikas, while accepting the conventional existence of the duality of object and subject, do not acknowledge any kind of ultimate reality whatsoever. Therefore, having personally visualized the deity of the ritual occasion (*samayadeva*) as the object of meditation, they dissolve the deity of gnosis (*jñānadeva*) into that [visualized form] and remain without even performing the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*). This is the procedure declared for the Anuttarayogatantra.
Furthermore, the tantric scripture is divided into four sections according to the four distinct types of deity visualization (*devabhāvanā*).
Thus it is accepted by the hosts of accomplished masters such as Nāgārjuna;
this alone is also the position favored by Tibetan scholars.
Regarding the investigation into whether the *tantra* scriptures constitute the *Tripiṭaka*: are all the words taught by the Blessed Buddha included within the *Tripiṭaka*?
In the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, this answer is stated as follows: "The three baskets, or the two [baskets], are held to be subsumed by nine reasons;
through perfuming, awakening, pacification, and penetration, they bring about liberation."

(11/1) That is to say, all twelve branches of the teaching (*pravacana*)— namely, *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and so forth— are subsumed within the three baskets (*piṭakatraya*),
and their establishment is effected through nine reasons.
But are the *tantras* also included within the *Tripiṭaka*?

Regarding this matter, there is a divergence of opinion among scholars, as Vasubandhu stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "The eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma which the Sage proclaimed—these are either speech or names; thus, they are included within the [aggregate of] form (*rūpa*) and the [aggregate of] formations (*saṃskāra*)."
Some say that the measure of a "dharma-aggregate" (dharmaskandha) is the extent of the treatise; others say it is each individual discourse concerning the aggregates and so forth.
However, the dharma-aggregate is described as being the antidote to specific types of conduct.
(1/25–26) Eighty thousand sections of the Dharma were taught by the Buddha.
However, their specific nature is not determined here;
for what is a "section of the Dharma"?

This will be examined so that there may be an understanding of the intention behind the teaching of the eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (dharmaskandha) established by the Buddha, and the arrangement of the Piṭakas shall also be described;
this truth has been clarified in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*:
"What is the measure of a dharmaskandha?"
The view of some is that whatever is the measure of the *Śāstra* is itself the measure of this [work].
Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*, which is designated as a "mass of dharma" (*dharmaskandha*), its measure consists of six thousand verses.
Furthermore, each individual verse concerning the aggregates (*skandha*) constitutes one single "mass of dharma."

Others, however, maintain that each individual exposition—such as those on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), noble truths (*āryasatya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), vows (*praṇidhi*), and the knowledge resulting from vows (*praṇidhijñāna*)—constitutes a single *dharmaskandha*. In presenting his own view, Vasubandhu states: "Each *dharmaskandha* was described as an antidote for each specific type of conduct among those to be trained."
Therefore, according to the differences in the conduct of sentient beings, their number is calculated as eighty thousand.
Some have a temperament dominated by passion (*rāga*), others by hatred (*dveṣa*), some by delusion (*moha*), and some by pride (*māna*).
For this reason, the Blessed One taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) as antidotes for the afflictions of sentient beings.

The followers of the Mahāyāna consider that there are eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*), and they believe these were taught for the sake of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*). In the Chinese translation of the *Kṛtārṇava* Sūtra, this report is related that the Mahāyānists possessed infinite aggregates of Dharma;
furthermore, it is said that Devadatta had committed to memory sūtra texts as voluminous as five thousand elephants carrying loads.
By this it is established: in the Pāramitāyāna, the number of sūtras was immeasurable.

In the Vajrayāna as well, for the sake of subduing passion (*rāga*), there were twenty-one thousand Vinaya Piṭakas; for the sake of subduing hatred (*dveṣa*), twenty-one thousand Sūtra Piṭakas; as an antidote to delusion (*moha*), twenty-one thousand Abhidharma Piṭakas;
and generally, for the destruction of all obscurations, twenty-one thousand Fourth Piṭakas—which, in effect, constitute eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
They consider that it was taught by the Buddha.
The tantric texts are called the Fourth Piṭaka or the Sūtrānta.
Also, in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*: "For he who [upholds] this supreme, principal sūtra, the treasury of Dharma empowered by the Victor..."
Those mortals on earth who reject [the teaching] shall go to the Avīci hell until the end.
(54/75) Furthermore, in that very same place: "Wherever a person of base intellect goes, there he is reborn;
by rejecting this sūtra, he is born in those very places."
(54/81) This means that the *tantra* is considered to be included within the *sūtra* and the *Sūtrāntapiṭaka*.
As it says in the *Guhyasiddhi*: "By way of the divisions of Kriyā, Caryā, and so forth, [it is included] within the *Sūtrāntapiṭaka* and the rest."
It is one alone, supremely pure, not established in a single form.

(1/29) It is also stated in the *Prajñopāyasiddhi*: "Likewise, by the perfectly awakened ones of the three times, who bring joy to the world, [this] has been proclaimed in succession within numerous sūtras, tantras, and manuals of conduct."

(2/4) Therefore, it is possible for the fourth *piṭaka* to be the *Sūtrānta*, since other scholars as well consider the *Tantra* to be the conclusion (*anta*) of both the *Sūtrānta-piṭaka* and the *Vidyādhara-piṭaka*. Śraddhāvarman also included the Mantra Vehicle within the *Tripiṭaka*;
however, this is called the *Vidyādhara-piṭaka* because this Mahāyāna *Piṭaka* occupies a distinguished position and contains numerous methods for attaining the state of a *Vidyādhara*.
Therefore, the fourth Piṭaka is called the Vidyādhara-piṭaka.

Just as one who upholds the Vinaya-piṭaka is called a Vinayadhara, and those who uphold the Sūtra-piṭaka are called Sūtradharas and so forth, in the same way, one who upholds the Tantra-piṭaka is considered a Vidyādhara.
Furthermore, it has been stated by Buddhaguhya that this tantra establishes the non-differentiation between deities and mantras.

While Abhayākaragupta was extracting the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*, he stated that for the benefit of gods and asuras, secret mantras (*guhyamantra*) were taught; among the many divisions and subdivisions such as *vidyā-mantras* and so forth, more than five hundred thousand *Vidyādharapiṭakas* were imparted, and thus this is called the Fourth Piṭaka.
Śāntipāda considers them to be included within the Sūtra Piṭaka by virtue of their being instructions on *tantra* within the *Vaipulya-sūtras*.
And he says that these *sūtras* exist because they have been taught among the dharmas of the twelvefold scriptural tradition (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

Also, in the *Yogaratnamālā*, it is stated: "The *Avadānaśataka*, the *Tridaṇḍakamālā*, and so forth are *sūtrāntas*; likewise, the *sūtras* that are not profound are the *sūtrāntas*, such as the *Ekagāthā*, the *Caturgāthā*, the *Upadhāriṇī*, the *Ṣaṇmukhī*, the *Bhadracaryā*, the *Lalitavistara*, the *Daśabhūmika*, and others. Thus it is said.

Śāntipāda states that generally we explain the Buddha’s teachings by dividing them into the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) according to the three aggregates known as ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*); in that case, even the tantras are included within the three baskets from the perspective of their subject matter. And just as in the tantras, wherever there is an instruction on pledges (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*), it belongs to the basket of discipline (*vinayapiṭaka*).
The Abhidharma Piṭaka is that in which the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of phenomena are expounded;
it contains [teachings on] such matters as the hidden meaning of meditative concentration (samādhi).
That which is established therein is considered to be included within the Sūtra Piṭaka.
Raṅ ’byuṅ rdo rje considers this to be the fourth Piṭaka because the objects of the three Piṭakas are subsumed within it.
Therefore, since the Vidyādhara Piṭaka establishes ethical discipline (*śīla*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), its status as the fourth Piṭaka is asserted.

Furthermore, since the profound meaning has been described in brief in the *Buddhaguhya-mata*, it can also be included within the Sūtra Piṭaka. Regarding the classification of tantras by way of their subject matter (*abhidheya*), scholars have categorized the tantras as follows: the great scholar Butön divided the tantras into seven classes based on their titles: the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*), the Subsequent Tantra (*uttaratantra*), the Further Subsequent Tantra (*uttarottaratantra*), the Compendium Tantra (*saṃgrahatantra*), the Tantra Following the Subsequent Tantra (*uttarikatantra*), the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*), and the Related Tantra (*sabhāgīyatantra*).
As examples: the root tantra text of the *Cakrasaṃvara*, consisting of one hundred thousand chapters; the subsequent tantra (*uttaratantra*) consisting of one hundred thousand verses;
the subsequent tantra consisting of fifty-one chapters;
and the *Yoginīsaṃcaryāsaṃgraha* tantra.
There exist the *Vajraḍākārṇavavyākhyātantra*, the *Buddhakapālottarikatantra*, and the *Sampuṭodbhavasabhgīyatantra*.

According to the divisions of entry into the tantra, Padmakarpo [identifies] the tantras by the names: Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*), Examination Tantra (*parīkṣātantra*), Subsequent Tantra (*uttaratantra*), Further Subsequent Tantra (*uttarottaratantra*), Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*), Womb Tantra (*garbhatantra*), Fruition Tantra (*phalatantra*), and Extraordinary Tantra (*atyadbhutatantra*)—thus [categorizing them] into eight.
These were divided into sections.

That which was composed as the fivefold division consisting of the *Mūlatantra*, *Saṃgrahatantra*, *Vyākhyātantra*, *Uttaratantra*, and the *Uttarottaratantra* and so forth by the Śākya Śuddhodana— this is the *Mūlatantra*.
That which is taken as the root and taught in the form of an exposition is called the *vyākhyātantra* (explanatory tantra).
And for each of these two, there are two subdivisions.
For example: the Root Extensive Tantra (*mūlavistāratantra*) and the Root Compendium Tantra (*mūlasaṃgrahatantra*);
the General Explanatory Tantra (*sāmānyavyākhyātantra*) and the Uncommon Tantra (*asāmānyatantra*).
(a) The Root Extensive Tantra is said to be that tantra which was composed as an instruction by the Buddha himself for the benefit of those to be trained.
That which was taught for the purpose of Viṣṇu’s disciples is called the *Saṃgraha-mūlatantra*. A tantra that clarifies the intent of various distinct tantras is called a *Sāmānya-vyākhyātantra*.
And that which clarifies the specific intent of a particular *Mūlatantra* is an *Asāmānya-vyākhyātantra*.
(kha) A commentary tantra (*vyākhyātantra*) is said to be defined by six causes: 1. it clarifies the hidden intent of the root tantra;
2. it completes subjects that were incomplete;
3. it establishes diverse ritual procedures.
4. He expands upon concise subjects; 5. he makes the essential meaning understood; 6. he explains the true meaning with great clarity.
These divisions are found exclusively in the texts of the Unsurpassed Tantra (Anuttara-tantra), and all such divisions are not found in the Action (Kriyā) and other tantras.

For instance, in the Action Tantra, four divisions are found, known as the Root Tantra (Mūla-tantra), the Subsequent Tantra (Uttara-tantra), the Further Subsequent Tantra (Uttarottara-tantra), and the Explanatory Tantra (Vyākhyā-tantra).
In Caryātantra, there exist divisions known as the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*), the Subsequent Tantra (*uttaratantra*), and the Further Subsequent Tantra (*uttarottaratantra*).
In Yogatantra, three divisions are found: the Root Tantra, the Subsequent Tantra, and the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*).
By the term *khasaḍubaja*, the *sabhāgatantra* is counted in place of the *uttaratantra* within the Yogatantra.
There are many internal divisions among the Itthanta-tantras,

and all of these are included within the Sūtra-piṭaka. Regarding the various paths for attaining Buddhahood, the Blessed Buddha taught diverse Dharmas through various skillful means to disciples of different dispositions, according to their respective inclinations and capacities.

They were taught as follows: whatever means and path the Buddha himself taught to his disciples, he himself attained Buddhahood by following that very same path, so that those to be trained might practice that path with steadfastness and a spirit of total dedication.

There is not even a trace of doubt here that followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna, Mahāyāna, and Vajrayāna each accept Buddhahood precisely according to their own respective paths and thus establish an independent, singular system.
Even within the Śrāvaka-yāna, the establishment of the three vehicles (yānatraya) is found.

As it is stated in the Abhidharmakośa regarding the appearance of Pratyekabuddhas and Samyaksambuddhas: "The state of Buddhahood arises during the period of decline down to [a lifespan of] one hundred years;
Pratyekabuddhas appear during two such periods, while the Rhinoceros-like [Pratyekabuddha] has been a practitioner for a hundred eons."
(3.94) The rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha] strives for the equipment of awakening—namely, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—for up to one hundred aeons.
In his final birth, he attains awakening independently, without recourse to the oral tradition of the scriptures.
Because he has personally realized the principle of liberation and does not teach the Dharma to others, he is called a *pratyekabuddha*.

The clarification of that path is as stated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "The independence from instruction by others due to self-awakening, and the profundity of knowledge—these are declared for the Pratyekabuddhas."
For whomever, for whatever purpose, in whatever place, and in whatever manner service is performed,
that very purpose— though it may lack renown— becomes manifest for each of them in that very same way.
The summary of the rhinoceros-like path is to be understood through the abandonment of the conceptualization of the apprehended object, the non-abandonment of the apprehending subject, and its basis.

(2.6–8) In the section on the Bodhisattva within the fourth chapter of the Abhidharmakośa, the Exposition of Karma, it is said: "From what point until when is one a Bodhisattva? From the time he performs the karma for the marks [of a Great Man]. He is born in a happy realm, of noble birth, with unimpaired faculties, male, remembering his former births, and irreversible."
(4.108) As the performer of those deeds, he brings forth the thirty-two marks.
That Bodhisattva, being thus destined, subsequently assumes a male form in Jambudvīpa.
Contemplating awakening, he accumulates the equipment of merit for the duration of three incalculable eons.

Seated upon a single seat, having realized all knowledges from the path of preparation up to the end of the path of no-more-learning, one becomes a Buddha. Thus, according to the Abhidharmakośa of the Śrāvakayāna, this is the accepted view: that a Buddha does not attain enlightenment only after many previous eons, but rather [attains it] through Siddhārtha’s subsequent birth in cyclic existence, his departure from home, his renunciation, his asceticism, and his attainment of enlightenment.

According to the Mahāyāna-Madhyamaka perspective, this is not accepted as being merely a display (*līlā*); rather, it is held that after accumulating the two provisions over countless eons, he directly realized the paths of preparation, seeing, and meditation during the four watches on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, and attained Buddhahood at dawn. 2. Regarding the Mahāyāna, the followers of the Mahāyāna consider the attainment of enlightenment by the Buddha at Bodh Gaya, as taught in the *Mahāyānottaratantra*, to be merely of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).

Regarding the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the Buddha is considered by them to have already attained awakening long ago. However, he is not regarded as being without cause like the *Ādibuddha* as propounded by the followers of the Vajrayāna in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*. Likewise, he is not described in that way even by the followers of the Pāramitāyāna; rather, they maintain that after generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and gradually training in the Mahāyāna for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyakalpa*), one subsequently attains Buddhahood.

It is held that awakening is attained by the followers of the Śrāvaka vehicle through their own path of training, and by the followers of the Mahāyāna through training in their own path. As stated in the *Viśeṣastava*, the Buddha declared that the very same path by which Buddhahood is attained is also taught to one's own disciples. Regarding the divisions of the Tantric teachings, the Mahāyāna is divided into two parts known as the Pāramitāyāna and the Mantranaya; furthermore, the Mantranaya is further subdivided into four classes, beginning with Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Anuttarayoga Tantra.
There are distinctions.

Within these four divisions of the Mantra Vehicle (*mantrayāna*), there likewise exists a difference in the method for attaining the awakening (*bodhi*) of a Buddha and in the method for the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). According to the Action Tantra (*kriyātantra*), Śākyamuni, having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) in the presence of the Tathāgata Sarvapuṣpanirdeśa, practiced the conduct of mantra (*mantracaryā*).

Throughout infinite eons, the Tathāgata, having pursued the mantras and accumulated merit and wisdom, gathered merit until he attained the status of a preceptor to the son of a brahmin at the time of his meeting with Pūrṇakaśyapa in the world. Subsequently, having met death from that very cause, he descended into the Tuṣita heaven in the form of Śvetaketu and taught the Dharma to those born in the divine realm.
Thereafter, being born in the human world, he pointed out the path for the welfare of those born in the human realm.
This subject has been described in detail in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*.
In the accounts of the Buddha’s playful deeds (*buddhalīlā*), a general similarity is observed across almost all traditions: Māra employed many kinds of obstacles in various forms;
yet, with his army shattered, he turned back and returned once more to his own abode.

(53.33) According to the Anuttara Tantra, at the time when the Blessed One was about to attain perfect enlightenment at Buddhagayā, a portentous disturbance was produced by the forces of Māra in order to create obstacles.

At that moment, the Blessed One, absorbed in the samādhi called "Defeat of Māra," generated the Great Wrathful King Mahāyamāri from his own body, speech, and mind, and commanded: "Vajrapāṇi! Assuming a terrifying form, destroy the Māras, nāgas, asuras, and others!"

According to the Kriyātantra, immediately after the Blessed One’s first turning of the wheel of Dharma, he went from Kāśī to Śrāvastī and there displayed a miraculous feat; this same event is recorded in the Āṭānāṭīya Sūtra.
Following that miracle, the Blessed Buddha proceeded from Śrāvastī to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven in order to give instruction to his own mother.

Having remained there for three months, he observed the *upoṣadha* at the appropriate time; thereafter, having ascended to Akaniṣṭha, Tuṣita, Brahmāloka, and other realms, he taught the Tantra. Then, after those three months, returning to the world of earth, he taught the *Kriyātantra* in Magadha, Śrāvastī, and other places.

For example: the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* was taught on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*); the *Tathāgatagarbha* on the seashore; and the one bearing the name *Sarvadharmaguṇavyūharāja* in the Bamboo Grove (*Veṇuvana*).

In this manner, the Buddha taught the *dhāraṇīs*, *kalpas*, *mantra-sūtras*, and explanatory tantras (*vyākhyā-tantras*) of Action Tantra (*kriyā-tantra*) in the worlds of gods and humans according to the capacity of those worthy of them; likewise, the teaching of the various tantras associated with the different families (*kula*) and deities was extensively established therein.

Just as the Tathāgata [taught] the Tathāgata family in the Akaniṣṭha realm, Avalokiteśvara [taught] the Lotus family at Potalaka, Vajrapāṇi [taught] the Vajra family in Alakāvatī, and [the Teacher taught] the tantra associated with the Jewel family—

In Alakāvatī, Maṇibhadra and Vaiśravaṇa, together with the two sages Pañcaka and Harita, [established] the family of nourishment; likewise, in Kapilavastu, the bhūtas and piśācas who were devoted to the Tathāgata offered a spell (vidyā-mantra) and its ritual procedure to the Tathāgata.
Subsequently, they were empowered by him, and thus this family of the world was propagated in the world.
This account has been described in detail in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*.

Regarding the *Caryātantra*: in accordance with the *Caryātantra*, the Buddha first generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) in the presence of the Tathāgata Puṣpābhāsa in order to perform the practice of the Mantra system. Having received a prophecy from the Tathāgata, he accumulated the equipment of merit and wisdom by following the path of Mantra.

And in that very place where, within the *Kriyātantra*, he performed the practice and recitation of the many sādhanas of the Blessed One’s eighteen dhāraṇīs, there, following the *Caryātantra*—in the work titled the *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-vyākṛtādhiṣṭhāna-vaipulya-sūtrendrarāja-nāma-dharmaparyāya*—Vajrapāṇi asks the Blessed One Vairocana regarding the fundamental and ultimate points for the sake of wisdom and enlightenment; then he says: “The cause is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and the root is compassion.”

The culmination of the method is found in that very place; clarifying the *bodhicitta*, he declares: "Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is precisely the correct and authentic knowledge of one's own mind, and this alone is also the *bodhicitta*.

Therefore, O Vajrapāṇi, "examine your own mind completely for the sake of enlightenment and for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)"—by teaching in this way, he strongly impels one toward the direct realization of the *bodhicitta*.

Likewise, it is stated in the *Vajraśekhara-mahāguhyayogatantra*: "In former times, the Blessed Buddha, having taken up the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), became a bodhisattva. Thereafter, having accumulated the two provisions (*saṃbhāra*) and attained the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpūrṇatā*), he received the initiation of the cloth (*paṭalābhiṣeka*). Abiding in the Akanistha realm of the mind-made body, he attained Buddhahood through the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*). And in the world of Akanistha, he taught the *Vairocana-sāmānya-mahāyāna-tantra*, the *Caryātantra*, and the root mantra for the initiation of Vajrapāṇi."
Furthermore, he taught the ritual manual (*kalpa*) named *Ārya-acalamahākrodharāja-sarvatathāgatabalāparimitavīravinaya-svavyākhyāta* while exercising mastery over the supreme nirvāṇa.
Subsequently, having appeared in the human world, he set the wheel of Dharma in motion in sacred fields such as Sāranātha and others, like a Mahāyānist.
Thus do the practitioners of the Carya-tantras maintain.

In the Caryātantras, the procedure for generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is considered similar to that of the Kriyātantras, while the attainment of awakening follows the method of the Yogatantras. Therefore, some scholars state that the Caryātantra is indeed designated as "both" (Ubhayatantra). Due to the high esteem accorded to the Caryātantras, they remain eternally in the realm of Akaniṣṭha, and within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they shall endure until the end of the Buddha's teaching.

In the Yoga Tantra, specifically in the first chapter of the *Tathāgataguhyaka* (the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*), within the ritual for the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala, the attainment of Buddhahood is described in detail through such words as: "Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvārthasiddhi, being impelled by all the Tathāgatas, having arisen from that very Āsphāna Samādhi... and so forth.

And in that very place, immediately after attaining Buddhahood through the five types of perfect enlightenment, he was authorized by all the Tathāgatas through both consecration and the proclamation of the Dharma. His *nirmāṇakāya* then went to Mount Sumeru and taught the Yoga Tantras, such as the *Mūlatantra*, the *Uttaratantra*, and the *Trilokavijaya*.
Following that, he taught the *Paramādya-tantra* at Paranirvāṇavaśavartin, and having taught the *Caryātantra* in Ānandavana, he took up residence for his *nirmāṇakāya* in the Akaniṣṭha realm.

The Tathāgata remained absorbed in the meditative equipoise of Vairocana; then, manifesting the twelve deeds in Jambudvīpa for the sake of those to be guided (*neyārtha*), he appeared and taught the various vehicles.

Relying on this truth, the master Śākyamitra stated that Siddhārtha, the son of Śuddhodana, while practicing austerities on the bank of the river Uruvelā, thereupon cast off his *vipākakāya* (maturation body).

Having perceived the Akaniṣṭha realm from his subtle body, he attained awakening right there through the five types of perfect enlightenment; after teaching the Yoga Tantra on Mount Sumeru, he re-entered the ripening body (*vipākakāya*) and attained Buddhahood at Bodh Gaya. Later Tibetan scholars such as Ratnabhadra, the translator, and the commentators on the *Hevajra*, also accept this as a fact.

According to Ānandagarbha, the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) an incalculable number of eons ago; for this very reason, Ānandagarbha does not regard Siddhārtha—who was born into the Śākya clan—as being in the form of a Bodhisattva, and he also refutes the opinion of Śākyamitra.

This master maintains that "the Buddha first attained enlightenment in the Akaniṣṭha realm," and that the subsequent attainment of Buddhahood by one born into the Śākya clan is merely the play (*līlā*) of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
And the *neyārtha* [interpretation] is accepted.
Regarding the *Anuttaratantra*: the *Anuttaratantra* is divided into three sections known as the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), and Non-dual Tantra (*advayatantra*).
There exists a diversity of opinions concerning the subject matter of the teachings for these three categories.
Furthermore, regarding the attainment of Buddhahood, we can generally present the position of the common Unsurpassed Tantra (Anuttarayoga) by following the *Saṃpuṭa Tantra*.

According to this, the Buddha is seen at one and the same time in various places: in one place generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), in another descending from the celestial realm, and elsewhere turning the wheel of Dharma and emerging from meditative equipoise.

Therefore, it is not possible to clarify how all of this is included within a somewhat distinct sequence of arrangement. Regarding the Pitṛtantra—the teaching of the *Guhyasamāja*—several different opinions and alternative views are observed. Among those, one or two views are presented here: in the *Guhyasamāja-pañjikā*, Ānandagarbha states that the Buddha teaches the Great Passion (mahārāga) to those such as the Vaiṣṇavas; this is the great [view] of the Tibetans.
