The accomplished master Buston also maintains that the Buddha taught the *Guhyasamāja* in the world governed by supreme nirvāṇa in order to favor those who were attached even to Vaiṣṇavism.

In the *Gambhīrārthadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Śrīvajramālā-mahāyogatantra*, the scholar Alaṃkalaśa states: "When Siddhārtha, on the bank of the Nairañjanā River, [attained] the meditative absorption named 'Pervasion of Space'..."

Perceiving that he had attained enlightenment while in a state of meditative absorption, the Tathāgatas arrived from pure realms such as Akaniṣṭha, Ratnasaṃbhava’s field, Sukhāvatī, and others; having seen him, they clarified his misconception regarding meditation. Then, when he uttered, “Oṃ, with prostration to the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, I perform the vajra-binding,” the Tathāgatas consecrated him and taught the three meditations, the hundred families, the five stages, and so forth.
Consequently, they each departed for their own respective fields.

Siddhārtha, following the path thus taught by that Tathāgata, attained awakening; thereafter, having reached the Tuṣita realm with a subtle body, he fashioned a jeweled celestial palace from the great elements of his own body.

Furthermore, having transformed his own five aggregates into the five Tathāgatas, he taught the *Guhyasamāja-mahātantra* in two hundred and fifty verses in order to set the path for the passion of those who desire sensual pleasure. And so it was.
By instructing his followers concerning the five degenerations— namely, those of lifespan, views, afflictions, time, and the path—

he taught the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*, which consists of eighteen chapters; and this [tantra] subsequently spread throughout Jambudvīpa through the lineage of Vajrapāṇi, Mañjuśrī, and others, who were the compilers of the *Guhyasamāja*.
According to the Tibetan tradition, it is held that the Buddha himself taught the *Guhyasamāja* to Indrabhūti, the king of Oḍḍiyāna.

It is said that upon seeing the Blessed Buddha traveling through the sky, the king inquired of his ministers regarding him; they informed him that this was a disciple of Śākyamuni. Struck by this, the king invited the Blessed One and his disciples for a meal. When they had arrived, the king requested the Buddha to grant him his grace.

Addressed by the Buddha regarding the renunciation of the householder’s stage of life, the king replied: "Having abandoned the qualities of sensual pleasure and the like, I do not desire liberation; if this person may be favored while remaining within this very worldly existence," then, in accordance with the king's words, the Buddha perceived that the king was a worthy vessel for the Tantric system. Thereupon, the Śrāvakas vanished, and the Buddha himself appeared in the *Guhyasamāja* [Tantra], where Indrabhūti was ordained as a monk.
By the mere act of consecration, he attained perfect awakening.

Subsequently, on the preeminent mountain, at the principal center of residence for the gods and goddesses—the palace of Alakāvatī—he heard from Vajrapāṇi that the *Guhyasamāja* had been committed to writing by the Bodhisattvas.

Having established it in Gandholā within the Svayambhū Palace and having instructed Ḍākiṇīśvarābhiratī and others following the consecration, [the teaching was entrusted] thereafter to the visiting siddhas and those who would preserve it.
The names have been proclaimed.

Regarding the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), it is set forth in the *Ācāryakāmadhenu*’s commentary titled *Hevajrapadoddhāraṇanāmaṭīkā* that the teaching of the *Hevajratantra*, which is the principal [text] within the Mother Tantras,
was delivered by the Tathāgata through his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for a period of thirty-two years.
During his residence in Jambudvīpa, [the Hevajra Tantra] was composed for the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, the compiler of the Hevajra, in Magadha.

And in that very place, in the commentary on the passage "At one time I heard," it was written very clearly: "The instruction of this was not received through any lineage, but was given by the Buddha himself to Vajragarbha."

But Bu ston, citing passages from the *Vyākhyātantra Vajramālā*—a great commentary (*bṛhaṭṭīkā*) on the *Hevajra*—within his general tantric system, stated that following the teaching of the *Cakrasaṃvara*, the teaching of the *Hevajratantra* occurred in Jambudvīpa at Māgadha through the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) at the time of destroying the four māras.
In almost all the commentaries and explanatory treatises (*ṭīkā*) on the *Hevajratantra*, [it is asked: where was the teaching performed?
A very clear explanation of this is not found [elsewhere].
Regarding the *Advayatantra*—in the *Advayatantra* as well, many tantras such as the *Kālacakra* and the *Māyājāla* are included.

Among those, concerning the subject matter of the teaching of the *Kālacakra*, it is established in the *Paramādya-tantra* as follows: "Just as it was taught in the system of the *Prajñāpāramitā* at Gṛdhrakūṭa according to the scriptures, so too has it been proclaimed in the system of Mantra."
The teaching of the Dharma took place at Śrīdhānya.
Nāḍapāda also stated in his *Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā* that the teaching of the Kālacakra occurred at Dhānyakaṭaka (Amarāvatī) in this manner: *(Source: Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā, p. 3)*

It is also stated in the *Amṛtakaṇikā*, a commentary on the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "In this very place, the great shrine of Śrī Dhānyakaṭaka, the Blessed Buddha named Śrī Śākyasiṃha, being entreated by those desiring to hear various tantras, on the full moon day of Caitra, having manifested the mandala of the glorious Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara and above that the glorious mandala of the constellations—the *Ādibuddha*—on that very day bestowed the consecration of a Buddha."

Having bestowed [the teachings] upon the gods and others, he taught them according to the various divisions of all the *mantra-nīti* and the great *bhūta-tantras*. His intention was as follows: having attained Buddhahood on the full moon of Vaiśākha, according to the Mahāyāna view, twelve years after the first turning of the wheel of Dharma at Ṛṣipattana in the Deer Park, on the full moon of Māgha, the Blessed Buddha taught the Pāramitāyāna at Gṛdhrakūṭa.

At that very time, for the sake of those with extremely sharp faculties, he manifested himself in the form of Kālacakra at Dhānyakaṭaka and taught the twelve hundred verses of the Root Tantra (*mūla-tantra*).
King Sucandra of the land of Śambhala, having requested the teaching of the *Mūlakālacakra Tantra* with due humility, compiled the tantra and explained it in sixty thousand verses.

Subsequently, within that lineage, this was propagated by the six Dharma Kings who ruled for a period of one hundred years. Thereafter, for the sake of its condensation, following Mañjuśrīkīrti, the sages and seers [composed it] six hundred years after the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha (600).
Having condensed the Root Tantra (mūlatantra) into thirty thousand verses in the meter named Puṣpamālā, it was brought forth by the former Master.

Regarding the teaching of the Tantra according to the divisions of the Vinaya, Mañjuśrī established it in the *Māyājāla-vyākhyātantra*: "The primary locations for mantras are three narrative bases: the Akaniṣṭha realm, Mount Sumeru, and Jambūdvīpa."
Among those to be trained, there exist three types of persons belonging to the divine lineage of Bodhisattvas: [gods, humans, and mānavas].

The Teacher as well—Śākyamuni, the emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Vajradhara—manifests in his own threefold form and teaches. When we examine the subject matter of this tantra’s teaching, it becomes clear that the vision of the reality of the tantra and its method of practice are extremely profound and secret in nature.
It prevails extensively. Just as in the Yoga Śāstra, there exists a secret method for entering another's body by controlling the subtle vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth;
likewise, there exists a secret method for entering another's body by controlling the subtle vital breath, mind, and so forth of the entire universe.
The entire universe exists as nothing more than the expansion of one's own mind, and as nothing more than the very nature of the mind itself.
As it is stated in the *Acintyakramopadeśa*:
"Just as everything is seen within the reflections in a mirror or in light."
In the same way, within this non-dual gnosis, the awakening of a Buddha is inconceivable. 82.
Within all the three realms, by means of the causes of arising and abiding, all those things are non-dual gnosis; all sentient beings have emerged from that. (83)
The oceans, mountains, trees, and whatever grasses, shrubs, and creepers there are—all have emerged from non-dual gnosis;
no delusion exists herein. (84)
(Guhyādyaṣṭasiddhi, verses 82–84, p.

203) If, in reality, there were a separation among all phenomena by virtue of their independence, then how could the knowledge of others' minds, the entry into another's body, and so forth, be possible?
Furthermore, regarding that very subject of the Tantra teachings, Padmavajra also stated therein: "The creator of the Tantra is Hṛdvajra; he himself is the speaker and the teacher. (25)
(From *Guhyādyaṣṭasiddhi*, 2–5, p.
12) That is to say, the compiler, the teacher, and the subject matter are all of one and the same nature.
This is also established in the *Cakrasaṃvara-mūlatantra*: "I am the speaker, and I alone am the listener."

Therefore, the historian Buston also writes: "In this way, during the Buddha’s exposition and explanation of the Dharma, he made separate designations for the teacher, the listener, and those who gather them, specifically for those who are attached to or satisfied with such a formal arrangement. In this manner, the Teacher [performed] his own miraculous display (or sport)."

He manifested in the form of the Teacher, his attendant, and the compiler, and thus imparted [the teachings]; otherwise, the distinct authority of the various lineages (*santati*) and tantras could not be conceived.

It is also stated in the *Pradīpodyotana*: “By this method, he is the compiler (*saṅgītakāra*). This Buddhist drama was displayed for the sake of introducing beginner beings” (*Pradīpodyotana*, p. 12).
This has also been stated in that very same place: "The Buddha never attains final nirvāṇa, nor does there come an end to the Dharma.

The essential point is this: by not observing the facts related to the aforementioned proclamations of the Dharma, it becomes perfectly clear that it is impossible to establish a direct connection between Śākyamuni and the lineage of the complete turning of the wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) as represented by the Tantra, while at the same time providing an explanation [of its origins].
The teaching of the extensive tantras occurred in celestial realms, beginning with the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
while the teaching of a single tantra in Jambudvīpa was performed by manifesting in various forms of chosen deities.
This fact is accepted by all accomplished masters (*siddhācāryas*) of India and Tibet.

This same conviction holds even for those who possess such contemplation on the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and by whom all kinds of common and uncommon attainments (*siddhi*) have been achieved.
Therefore, it is impossible to establish the invalidity of this secret reality through mere fragmentary knowledge, intellectual speculation, or dry logical reasoning.
Furthermore, such secret accounts are found not only in the Tantras, but also in the treatises of the Pāramitā system.
And as Candrakīrti established in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*: having attained the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), the practitioner proceeds from one buddha-field to another field,
directly perceives many Tathāgatas, hears their Dharma, recollects former births, understands the minds of others, and so forth— thus there is the attainment of twelve qualities.

Discussions regarding the display of miraculous feats (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) through the gateway of the Buddha and his journeys to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and other realms occur even in the *Pāramitā* [literature], not only in the texts of the Śrāvaka vehicle; such accounts are still found today in the *Dīrghanikāya*.
Therefore, it can be stated briefly that the Buddha would have been imparting the teachings of the later Tantras to qualified practitioners.
Furthermore, for this very reason, it is impossible to establish a distinct historical sequence for the *tantra*.

This is because even today, those who maintain the eligibility (*pātratā*) for *Kriyātantra* are able to transmit it by repeatedly hearing it from Bodhisattvas. Thus, the view held by modern scholars—that there was first the mantra, then the *dhāraṇī*, the worship of deities, ritual action (*kriyā*), wonder (*carya*), yoga, and finally *Anuttarayoga*—cannot be accepted.
And subsequently, the literature of the Siddhas attained its full development.
Regarding the vision of reality, a question arises here: how can there be realization of this truth?
Concerning this matter, the Buddha said in the Hevajra Tantra: "First the *poṣadha* is given, and thereafter the ten points of training (*śikṣāpada*)."
Therein one should teach the Vaibhāṣya, and likewise the Sūtrānta.
Thereafter, one should teach the Yogācāra, and following that, the Madhyamaka.
Having understood all the systems of Mantra, one should then begin with Hevajra.
The disciple should receive it with reverence; he will attain accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.

And the underlying intention is as follows: having undertaken the three training rules (*śikṣāpada*) beginning with the *upoṣadha* fast and having practiced them in succession, one enters the systems of the Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, and Mādhyamika; then, entering the way of Mantra (*mantranaya*), one reflects upon the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and so forth.
Finally, having entered the unsurpassed *Hevajra-tantra*, non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) is to be attained.
This is precisely the reason why the ultimate goal of the Buddhist vision is the attainment of non-dual gnosis and the state of union (*yuganaddha*).

This alone is the essence of the Buddha’s words; for as it is stated in the commentary on the *Caryāgītikośa*, having cited the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*: "Among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage, those who do not understand the reality..."
All of those indeed result in fruitlessness.
(Page 22) That is to say, the teaching of the eighty-four thousand aggregates was intended solely for the sake of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
But what is that reality?
Regarding this, Kuḍālapāda states in the *Acintyakramopadeśa*: "That whose nature is seen neither to arise nor to perish."
That knowledge is called non-dual, being devoid of all conceptual constructions.

(Guhyasiddhi, p. 196) A person of the Vaibhāṣika or Sautrāntika lineage who is to be trained, following the path set forth in the *Bodhipathapradīpa*— one who abstains from evil deeds and turns away from the pleasures of existence,
seeking only his own peace— is called a person of middling capacity.

(Śloka-kārikā 4) Having become a person of middle capacity, one cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*) endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and analytical reflection (*vitarka*), solely for the sake of attaining personal nirvāṇa.
In reality, however, the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas maintain that external objects exist.

As it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "That which, when broken, no longer produces the cognition of itself, and that which [no longer produces the cognition] when other [factors] are excluded by the mind..."
That which exists conventionally is like a jar or water; that which exists ultimately is otherwise.
(6/4) This very point is also stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "That which is capable of causal efficiency is here the ultimately real;
the other is declared to be conventionally real. These two are your particular and universal characteristics."

(Pratyakṣapariccheda, Verse 3) That alone which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is real and ultimate; conceptual constructions, other universals (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and so forth, are false and merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtika*).

Having accepted this, even the Sautrāntikas admit the existence of external and internal phenomena. However, the Vijñānavādins and Mādhyamikas [hold that]: "He who desires the total destruction of all suffering—his own as well as that of others—is indeed a supreme person."

Following this well-spoken statement, the Vijñānavādins—who investigate for the benefit of all living beings—regard reality as follows: “O Sons of the Victorious One, the triple world is mind-only” (*Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, p.
32). In accordance with this teaching, they accept that there is only mind and do not believe in the existence of external objects.

The Mādhyamikas do not even accept the existence of the mind in the ultimate sense; rather, they maintain that all things are empty of intrinsic nature (*dharma-śūnya-niḥsvabhāva*) and dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*). As Nāgārjuna says: "Since no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not dependently originated, therefore no phenomenon whatsoever exists that is not empty."

Consequently, when the Vajrayāna is examined, it becomes known that the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the Madhyamikas and the "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) of the Vijñānavādins arise as the non-dual reality consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), which is free from the four extremes and devoid of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

This state is expressed in the tantric scriptures through such terms as the emptiness of appearance (*ābhāsa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of gnosis (*vidyā-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of great bliss (*mahāsukha-śūnyatā*).
In the *Pratipattisāraśataka*, the noble Āryadeva stated: "The distinction between wisdom and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light;
the unity of wisdom and compassion is like that between a lamp and its light."
(Nepalese manuscript) Like the lamp and its light, the luminosity (*prabhāsvaratā*) and the manifestation (*ābhāsa*) of the mind,
as well as its non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*), are both distinct and yet not distinct.
This alone is the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*).
Herein, the Vijñānavādins accept that mind-only (*cittamātra*) possesses ultimate existence (*paramārthataḥ sattā*);
however, in the Madhyamaka view, even the mind exists as a phenomenon (*dharma*).
Therefore, even though it is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), it is still required in this context.
And as it was explained by Ratnākaraśāntipāda in the *Guṇavatī*, a commentary on the *Mahāmāyātantra*: "It is 'mind-and-non-mind' (*cittācitta*); that is, mind which is non-mind.
Why is it non-mind?"
Because when there is an absence of the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), there is also an absence of the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*).
If it is "non-mind" (*acitta*) due to being dissociated from the characteristic of mind as the subject of apprehension,
then by association with what characteristic of mind is that [state] "mind" (*citta*)?
The meaning is that it is "mind" because of its connection with the characteristic of mind;
and that [mind] has the nature of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
By this, the ultimate characteristic of bodhicitta—the essential nature of being non-conceptual gnosis—is directly stated as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In his commentary, having explained the non-dual reality (*advaya-tattva*) as taught in the Vajrayāna, he maintains that it is unarisen and unceasing throughout the three times.
This very point is understood to be the philosophical position of the Vajrayāna.
Regarding practice—generally speaking, the terms *sādhana* and *yāna* are synonymous.
In Buddhist scriptures, three vehicles are described, namely the Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Bodhisattvayāna (Mahāyāna).
If there is no goal to be accomplished, the means of accomplishment are purposeless.
Or rather, [are they] impossible to achieve?
Therefore, followers of the Hīnayāna accept three independent goals to be accomplished:
1. Arhatship, 2. Pratyekabuddhahood, and 3. Buddhahood; whereas followers of the Mahāyāna accept the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), which leads to the attainment of Buddhahood.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as well: "The manifestation of the three vehicles is merely my own form of skillful means;
for there is indeed only one vehicle, one method, and this is the single teaching of the Leaders."

(2/69) Thus, by means of his own skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), the Buddha gave teachings according to the dispositions of those who had become suitable vessels, each in accordance with their capacity. Also, in the *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*: "In order to lead beginner beings to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this means was fashioned by the Perfect Buddhas like a staircase."
(p. 21) The Buddha’s intention was directed toward the method for the direct realization of non-dual gnosis by all sentient beings.
As it is said in the *Caryāgīti-koṣa*: "Among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma of the Great Sage, those who do not understand the reality..."
All of them indeed become fruitless.

Thus, the one who has accomplished his task and attained extinction goes neither to the earth nor to the atmosphere;
he goes to no direction, nor to any intermediate direction; through the destruction of the afflictions, he attains only absolute peace.
(ŚauNda 6.28–29) Some consider this to be the state of ultimate peace and cessation,
while the followers of the Mahāyāna maintain that it is not the true meaning.

And as it is said in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*: "In the same way, when all the śrāvakas have attained what they perceive to be nirvāṇa, the Jina then teaches them: 'This is merely a place of rest, not final liberation.'"
(5/74) This is the skillful means of the Buddhas, which they proclaim as this method:
there is no nirvāṇa apart from omniscience; therefore, apply yourselves to that.
(5/74-75) Thus, that supreme state which is realized by those of the Śrāvaka vehicle is not the final goal; it is merely a state of rest.
Therefore, the Tathāgata urges them toward great awakening beyond the cessation of that [state].
Furthermore, it is stated in that very same place: "The knowledge of omniscience, the six perfections, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and so forth, must be accomplished by you.
Again, in that same place: "The infinite knowledge of the three times, the six auspicious perfections, emptiness, signlessness, and that which is devoid of wishfulness."

(5/76) Therefore, Śrāvakas and Arhats, by means of the power of the cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*), the latencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*), uncontaminated karma (*anāsravakarma*), and the transition at death (*mṛtyusaṃkramaṇa*), take up a new birth, enter the Mahāyāna, and attain Buddhahood. Regarding the question of by which path one should enter the Mahāyāna in this regard, the views of the Tibetan masters are as follows: 1. Some scholars maintain that entry is possible through the path of accumulation (*saṃbhāramārga*).

Their intention is as follows: in order to attain Buddhahood, it is necessary to follow the five paths, beginning with the accumulations, of the Mahāyāna. 2. Other masters say: by means of Arhatship, through the total eradication of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one need not take rebirth again in saṃsāra.
Therefore, having been born in a Buddha-field such as Sukhāvatī, one may then gradually train in the practices of a Bodhisattva and thereby attain Buddhahood.

3. Other teachers maintain that, through the Arhat’s gateway, by means of the destruction of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one enters the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), in the Mahāyāna; and then, by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), through the gradual destruction of the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the attainment of Buddhahood is secured.
4. Still other teachers [hold that] among Bodhisattvas, up until the seventh stage, there remains the subtle habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of the obscuration of afflictions.
The Arhats maintain that for those [who hold such views], there is a destruction by the roots, and they teach the entry of Bodhisattvas from the seventh bhūmi onwards.
This view and the details of other positions were set forth by Tibetan scholars in the first chapter of the *Madhyamakāvatāra*,
where the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is discussed that, immediately after attaining the *dūraṃgamā* bhūmi, Bodhisattvas would— by virtue of their wisdom— become attractors of Śrāvakas.
Even among some scholars of the Mahāyāna, this view is held: that even according to the Pāramitānaya, one must ultimately rely upon the Mantranaya (Vajrayāna);
otherwise, the obscurations of āloka, ālokābhāsa, ālokopalabdhi, and samāvaraṇa cannot be purified, and the attainment of perfect enlightenment would be impossible.
Although these two systems are indeed included within the Mahāyāna itself—as stated in the *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*: "The Mahāyāna is twofold: the Pāramitānaya and the Mantranaya" (p.
14)—one should now consider what the distinction is between the Pāramitānaya and the Mantranaya.
Furthermore, what is that reality?
It is that in the absence of which the attainment of the goal is not established even for those following the Pāramitāyāna, nor for those relying upon the Mantrayāna and Vajrayāna.
By investigating and reflecting upon this, one may consider: what is the nature of the method of practice in these two systems?
That too will become very clear.

While elucidating the distinction between the two systems, the great accomplished master of Tibet, Sumatikīrti Coṅkhāpā, stated in the *Mahāmantrakrama*: 1. "Therefore, the ultimate goal of the two systems is [the subject matter] of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* (1.19)."
Following this statement, both [the conventional and the ultimate] seek the reality of awakening for the benefit of all living beings.
Therefore, it is impossible to draw a line of distinction between the two aspects of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

2. Since one accepts the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena, there is no difference even within emptiness (*śūnyatā*); thus, emptiness itself cannot serve as a line of distinction between those two.
3. Even by practicing and training in the six perfections according to both systems, it is impossible to establish a boundary line [between them].

4. It is impossible to make a distinction based on the sequence of inferior, middling, and superior capacities among those who are fit vessels (*pātra*), because these two distinctions are both conceivable within both systems.

5. It is impossible to maintain that the *pāramitānaya* was taught for the benefit of those devoid of passion (*rāga*), while the *tantranaya* was taught for the benefit of those possessing passion; for even in the *pāramitānaya*, there is such a rule, as stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "Having understood this, one should always be intent upon the welfare of others.
Even what is forbidden is permitted for a compassionate person who perceives the [greater] purpose."
(5/84) Beyond this, many householders are also capable of being followers of the Pāramitāyāna; it is not only [monastics] who can do so.
For instance, even the brahmin’s son Bhikṣunakṣatra engaged in sexual intercourse for the welfare of living beings through skillful means (*upāyakauśala*).
Many such accounts are found in the Sūtra texts.
In that very same Mantra system (*mantranaya*), there were likewise many such great beings who were not only monks but also accomplished masters (*siddhapuruṣa*).

Here, indeed, it must be considered that while the transformation of passion (*rāga*) into the path is explained in the *tantra*, in the Vehicle of Perfections (*pāramitānaya*), passion and the like are taught for the benefit of living beings.
Between these two systems, this great distinction exists.
And that which remains to be considered:

6. Having circulated the great bliss (*mahāsukha*), because of the attainment of firmness within the emptiness of objects, even the boundary line cannot be maintained; for even in the Pāramitā system, the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) is restrained through the attainment of firmness in calm abiding (*śamatha*).

Since, having attained physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*), bliss circulates throughout the body, and through the meditative attainment of mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*), one is able to attain stability within one's own object of focus as desired;
therefore, it must be considered how much possibility there is for marking a boundary line by means of the experience of bliss in both [body and mind].
Some speak regarding this in the context of immutability and non-conceptual bliss (*anakṣarasukha*) within the Tantra.
In the Pāramitā system, however, this state remains characterized by a period of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and is replete with exertion and the like.

Furthermore, if one were to grasp it here through the intention of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), by means of the moistening of the red and white bodhicitta and the processes of the channels, winds, and *tilaka*s, resulting in spontaneously arisen bliss, then this would be a unique distinction of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*Anuttara-tantra*) alone, and not of the other general tantras such as Kriyā and so forth.
Thus, when the goal is attained through these two systems, there is no difference;

for in attaining that goal and on the path thereto, it is impossible to establish any distinction between the vision of emptiness, the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the accumulation of the perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth. Furthermore, the essential point to be considered here is this: the primary objective of both systems is the accomplishment of the welfare of others.
And when one reflects upon the sphere of the welfare of others, this task is conceivable through the form body (*rūpakāya*) but inconceivable through the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
In the treatises, the attainment of the dharma body is described as the perfection of one's own welfare, while the attainment of the form body is described as the perfection of the welfare of others.
This too is true: that in the absence of one, the attainment of the other is impossible.

The Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas of the Śrāvakayāna, however, consider the Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) to be the maturation of karma (*karma-vipāka*), and they also divide *nirvāṇa* into two parts.

Even after the attainment of Buddhahood, the state in which the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantati*) exists in an uninterrupted form is called *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*), while the state in which the continuum of the aggregates (the five aggregates) has ceased is called *nirvāṇa without remainder* (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
Thus, following the cessation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*), it is not conceivable that the welfare of living beings could be directly realized.

Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna perspective, it is not even accepted that at such a time those [Buddhas] would cease from their excellence, or that their accomplishment of the welfare of others would be exhausted.

In the view of the Śrāvakayāna, the Buddha’s very teaching itself is considered to be the Dharmakāya, for it is that which accomplishes the welfare of others immediately after his nirvāṇa without remainder.

And just as during the state of the Great Parinirvāṇa, when Ānanda and other disciples manifested the experience of extreme suffering upon the Buddha’s attainment of Great Parinirvāṇa, the Buddha spoke in the form of his final instruction:
"I have not withheld any truth from you regarding my own life."
Your very conduct, free from intoxication and obscuration, is that which reveals the path of the Teacher; that alone is the Dharmakāya.
Therefore, O Master, kindle the lamp of knowledge within yourself.
This was the instruction of the Blessed Buddha, even today, two thousand five hundred years after his passing.

It impels the hearts of people toward truth, non-violence, and the principles of awakening. That very uninterrupted lineage of study and teaching of the Buddhist religion and philosophy is itself [the legacy] of that [Buddha].
The maturation of merit exists. Thus,

according to the perspective of the Śrāvakayāna, although it is not possible for the Buddha to descend in human form and provide manifest benefit to sentient beings, nevertheless, through his Dharma-body in the form of the teachings (*pravacana*), he continues even today to lead people onto the true path for the sake of liberation from suffering.
Followers of the Śrāvakayāna do not consider the attainment of the goal to be through the form body (*rūpakāya*), and they regard the Buddha’s form body as the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Although followers of the Śrāvakayāna accept the Buddha’s body as a mass of suffering and as something subject to outflows (*āsrava*), they nevertheless hold it to be beautifully adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs;
they consider this to be the fruit of the accumulation of merit on the path of causes.

Just as the handsome appearance of ordinary beings is considered the fruit of their meritorious karma, that same principle applies to the Buddha as well. However, in the case of those established in the Mahāyāna, a reversal is observed.

In the context of explaining the *gotra* (spiritual lineage), this point is very clear: according to this system, even after his Great Parinirvāṇa, the Buddha continues to manifest in the forms of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, constantly working for the welfare of sentient beings.
Therefore, it must be investigated how its attainment is possible.

It is observed that while there is a complete exposition of the side of wisdom even in the Pāramitāyāna, nevertheless, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, [it proceeds] for as long as existence lasts for the benefit of all living beings.
What could be the substantial cause (*upādānakāraka*) of the existing form body (*rūpakāya*)?

There exists the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is beautifully adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs and resides in the Akaniṣṭha realm, as well as the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Just as we, considering wisdom that makes emptiness known to be the substantial cause of the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), investigate and meditate upon it, so too [should one do] for the celestial body that serves as the cause of the Form Body.
The method of cultivation (*bhāvanā-vidhi*) is not even mentioned in the *pāramitānaya*.
Whether one considers the cultivation or non-cultivation of the method for taking the form-body (*rūpakāya*), which bestows the accomplishment of the welfare of others,
as the path— it is possible to draw a boundary line between these two systems (*nayadvaya*).

When this has been accepted, the question arises again: what result is to be attained, and how might a corresponding result be cultivated? If it is to be cultivated, should one cultivate a human form for the sake of a human birth?
Should this pervasion be accepted as extending in the same way down to animals and birds?

It is not so; for according to the Pāramitā-naya, although the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) are accomplished through the accumulation of merit such as generosity, a long period of time is required.
In the Vajrayāna, however, the form body (*rūpakāya*) is swiftly accomplished through the meditation on the result.
In the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, it is held that the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) possesses a uniform nature, is restricted to five aspects, and is endowed with enjoyments.
They are considered equal in terms of their basis, intention, and activity;
and their permanence is established by way of their intrinsic nature, non-interruption, and continuity.

(10/65) Thus, for the sake of manifesting the Form Body (*rūpakāya*) directly before sentient beings who are limited [by their perceptions], one must certainly rely upon an uninterrupted basis and a material cause (*upādāna*).

Therefore, the necessity of cultivating its essential nature is established; for in the Pāramitā system, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cause of the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), whereas merit (*puṇya*) is the cause of the Form Body.
As Ārya Nāgārjuna states in the *Ratnāvalī*: "The Form Body of the Buddhas arises from the accumulation of merit."
In brief, O King, the Dharmakāya is born from the accumulation of gnosis.

(3/13) In accordance with this, the accumulation of gnosis (*jñāna-sambhāra*) is the cause of the *dharmakāya*, and the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*) is the cause of the *rūpakāya*. Although almost everyone accepts this view, nevertheless, in the system of the *pāramitās*, the accumulation of gnosis is presented in its complete form.
Furthermore, as explained above, the vision [of reality] cannot possibly be anything other than the non-proliferation of the four alternatives.

Moreover, regarding the connection with the cause of the form body (*rūpakāya*) in the *pāramitā* system: "Whatever cause here establishes each particular mark, by fulfilling that very cause, this [body] is characterized by its full attainment."
(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.18) Following after one's gurus and so forth, firmness regarding the vow,
attending upon those who gather [disciples], and the giving of excellent things.
(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 8.19) Thus,
it has been described how the visiting of the Guru and the ritual of going out to meet him constitute the cause for the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
as well as the practice of the perfections such as generosity, and so forth.

Beyond that, in order to attain the most excellent state, the purification of the buddha-field was established. As it is said in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "The knowledge of the minds of all sentient beings, sporting with the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the purity [of conduct] constitute the perfection of the buddha-field through the service and examination of the Buddhas."
(1/67) Imperishable gnosis, the purification of the Victor’s field, an illusion-like abiding,
and the intentional assumption of existence— this karma is declared to be eightfold.
While explaining this, Haribhadra said: "In such a pure field, the realm of form (*rūpabhūmi*) is fashioned from gold;
the trees, sprouts, and so forth are inlaid with jewels, and even the waters and other elements possess the eight qualities.
Here, the Bodhisattvas manifest in the forms of gods and goddesses, and likewise, they regard all phenomena as being like an illusion."

Furthermore, according to the Vajrayāna system, as long as a practitioner does not cultivate during the very stage of the path the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—which possesses the characteristics and secondary characteristics and consists of the fruit endowed with the thirteen articles of enjoyment within a celestial palace (*vimāna*) joined with a maṇḍala—it is impossible to attain the form body (*rūpakāya*) through mere generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth. Now, it must be considered: what is the process for taking the actual nature of the body of the Vajrayāna as the path?

In the investigation of the distinction between the Pāramitā-naya and the Mantra-naya, this is quite clear: for the attainment of the *devakāya* (divine body), there must be a specific material cause for the *rūpakāya* (form body).

Just as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is cultivated as the material cause of the *dharmakāya*, so too the commencement of the subtle Mantra-yāna serves as the material cause for the *rūpakāya*. This arises through these two [mantras]: “Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature;
I am pure by nature,” and likewise, “Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.”

That is to say, having meditated upon the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), through that meditation on emptiness, a state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) is accomplished by means of one's own consciousness— which is free from the conceptual proliferation of the four extremes— or by means of the subtle vital breath and mind;
just as it is impossible to separate a lamp from its light, or a flower from its fragrance, so too there is no separation between the mind and the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*).
They are mutually of a single essence.
Even in the tantras, it is taught that the subtle wind possesses the nature of the fivefold light of the vital energy (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, the mind is luminous and its intrinsic nature is non-dual.
From that very [source], the form of the deity manifests.

Here, one should oneself meditate upon the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), Vajradhara, endowed with the seven limbs; and subsequently, one should meditate upon emptiness, which by its very nature is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca). For this is what is designated in the Vajrayāna as the meditation on the stages of generation (utpattikrama) and completion (niṣpannakrama).

In brief, this means that in the Vajrayāna, the mind (*citta*) exists as the state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*) and single form (*ekākāratā*) of the three vajra-bodies known as body, speech, and mind.
It is held that the mind itself is the body and speech itself is the mind.
As stated in the *Guhyasamāja Tantra*: "By means of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, because their nature is both divisible and indivisible."
Also in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, without causal succession;
the stainless single eye of gnosis, the embodiment of gnosis, the Tathāgata.
(100) As far as the Buddha’s wisdom is limitless, so too is the Buddha’s form; to whatever extent the Buddha’s wisdom pervades, to that same extent his body also pervades.
Without taking hold of the subtle vital energies (*prāṇa*), the mind, or one's own mind, our objective—which is for the benefit of all sentient beings—will not be accomplished.

In the *Pāramitā*, the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all phenomena is established; yet, in that state, by means of such explanations as "there is neither the grasped nor the grasper," nothing at all comes into one's grasp. Thus it is experienced that we are situated somewhere within the void of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyākāśa*).
Upon investigating the conditions of that which is to be countered, one experiences this: we are situated somewhere in the midst of a sandy expanse (a *registān*) extending as far as the empty sky.
What is there? Where is it?
From where have you come?
Where are you to go? And where do you abide?
"What is to be done?
What is to be done?"— answers to these questions are not found.

Although both the Vijñānavādins and the Mādhyamikas abide in non-duality—in the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) consisting of the absence of the singular form of subject and object—nevertheless, the Vijñānavādins accept the existence of the mind along with an adherence to its reality, whereas for the Mādhyamikas, this is discarded through the moment-by-moment investigation of the aggregates, the Tathāgata, movement, and so forth.

Thus, it is said in the *Gatāgataparīkṣā* (Examination of What Has Been Traversed and What Has Not) of the *Mādhyamakakārikā*: "That which has been traversed is not being traversed; likewise, that which has not yet been traversed is not being traversed."
That which is presently being traversed is not being traversed, as it is devoid of both what has been traversed and what has not yet been traversed.

(2/1) However, in accordance with this, one does not perceive any coming or going and so forth, and a state of functional incapacity is experienced; therefore, for the sake of the great objective which is the welfare of others, and for the purpose of attaining divine powers, the eye of knowledge, and so on, meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is understood to be necessary within the *mahāmudrā*—that is, within the perfected mind which is free from the conceptual proliferation of the four alternatives, and which is, in essence, the non-dual form of appearance and emptiness, within one's own vital breath and mind, or within the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

In this context, regarding the meaning of the emptiness of appearance (*ābhāsa-śūnyatā*), it is not merely the emptiness of cognition; rather, it refers to the ultimate clear light (*paramārtha-prabhāsvara*) symbolized at the time of the fourth empowerment. By implication, this is Vajradhara endowed with seven limbs, who is indeed the *saṃbhogakāya* as Mahāmudrā; or else, he exists as the emptiness of appearance.
This alone is the vision of the Vajrayāna and the primary reality of its practice.
In the Vajrayāna, there exist various methods of meditation that take as their objects the seed-syllables, characteristics, weapons, and so forth, for the purpose of generating oneself as a deity.
This is because the divisions of the tantras arise, such as Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Anuttara, and others.
These methods of meditation will be explained later.
The non-dual nature described here as taught in the Vajrayāna is indeed connected specifically to the Anuttara Tantras.
The various divisions and sub-divisions of these tantras, as well as their methods of practice (*sādhanāpaddhati*), will be explained further below.

Regarding the nature of the practice of the Vajrayāna, the Bodhisattvayāna consists of two divisions—the Pāramitānaya and the Guhyamantranaya—which constitute, in effect, the two streams of the Mahāyāna.
In the *Advayavajrasaṃgraha* as well, it is established in this very way:

prior to understanding the true nature of the Mantra system, it is essential that one comprehend both the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) and the side of the means of accomplishment (*sādhanapakṣa*).
Here, in the first chapter, the matter of the vision of reality has been described in brief.

In connection with the *sādhana*, certain intermediate points that serve as the foundation for the *pāramitānaya* will be presented here, so that the procedure for the *sādhana* of the general tantra may be discerned.
Regarding the object of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is no difference whatsoever between the *pāramitānaya* and the *mantranaya*.
As the Tibetan Mahāsiddha Ācārya Śākyapaṇḍita stated: "Emptiness can be free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)."

If emptiness were to deviate from being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it would fall into the extremes of either existence or non-existence, or eternalism or nihilism. Here, this must be understood: emptiness is indeed free from conceptual proliferation; moreover, precisely where emptiness is merely free from conceptual proliferation, there—in the Mantra system—it exists as this non-duality of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyādvaya*), as in the *Hevajra*: "There is no meditator, nor is there an object of meditation."
There is no mantra, nor is there a deity;
yet mantra and deity abide together,
by virtue of having a nature free from conceptual proliferation.
(1.5–11) Through the practice of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the practitioner desires to directly realize the state of non-dual reality according to his own intellectual capacity.
This subject will be examined in detail within the *sādhana* manuals of the four classes of tantra.
Regarding the four classes of tantra, it is held that the conduct (*caryā*) of the Pāramitāyāna is [the basis for] the *sādhana*.
In the Pāramitā-naya, having contemplated what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, [the path] is practiced;

however, in the Mantra-naya, through the cultivation of pure equality, one regards all gods and goddesses, as well as heroes and heroines, as being like an illusion, and performs various acts of worship and adoration.

Wherein in the Pāramitā-naya śamatha and vipaśyanā are cultivated with effort, therein in the Mantra-naya they are cultivated together with skillful means (upāyakauśalya) along with signs—the generation stage (utpattikrama)—and so forth.
By means of the signless (*animitta*) [meditation] or through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the wind is restrained, and the straightforward procedure beginning with *vajrajāpa* is practiced.

In the Pāramitā system, meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the state attained subsequent to it (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-sthiti*) are cultivated gradually; therein, through non-dual gnosis, because all phenomena are equal in nature, various merits are cultivated simultaneously.
Accumulation [of merit] is performed.

In the Pāramitā system, the attainment of the goal is sought through the means of spiritual practice (*sādhana*). Here, however, in the Mantra system, by means of skillful methods (*upāyakauśalya*), through the practice of yoga with signs (*sanimitta*) and without signs (*nirnimitta*), and by controlling the vital breath (*prāṇa*) via breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the straightforward procedure of the vajra-recitation (*vajrajapa*) and so forth is adopted.
In the Pāramitā system, the attainment of the goal is achieved through practice; however, in the Mantra system, there is the non-dual reality of both the goal and the means.
For this very reason, this is called the "Vehicle of the Fruit" (*phalayāna*).
In the Pāramitā system, arduous asceticism is practiced for as long as an infinite number of eons.
In that very system, this practitioner aspires to the attainment of enlightenment on a single seat and is indeed able to attain it;
for the sake of ordinary beings, the means in the Pāramitā-naya are limited in number.

In the Mantra system, there are numerous methods such as the ritual for bringing rain, the pacification of diseases, and rites for peace (*śānti*), wrath (*raudra*), prosperity (*puṣṭi*), and subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Trinayapradīpa* that the Mantra Vehicle is distinguished from the Pāramitā Vehicle by four types of excellence:
1. non-delusion, 2. abundance of skillful means, 3. practice that is not difficult, and 4. sharpness of the faculties.
1. Non-delusion (*asaṃmoha*)—which accomplishes the perfections (*pāramitā*)—is that by which one gives away hands, feet, and even the body for the welfare of living beings.
Moreover, it is impossible to accomplish the benefit of countless beings without this;
herein there are many means, such as the sword, collyrium, rain, and so forth, by which the welfare of living beings can be established.

2. Abundance of skillful means (*upāyabahulatā*): Wherein in the *pāramitānaya* there are many difficult observances such as commitments (*samaya*), vows (*saṃvara*), asceticism (*tapas*), and fasting (*upavāsa*), in this very tantra one is able to employ the assistance of various skillful means—such as the peaceful, wrathful, loathsome, and terrifying—to accord with the diverse inclinations, tastes, and capacities [of practitioners].

3. Practice that is not difficult (*aduṣkaracaryā*): Wherein in the *pāramitānaya* the afflictions (*kleśa*) are to be abandoned, in this very tantra, without abandoning the afflictions, they are taken as the path for the sake of awakening.

And as it is said in the Hevajra Tantra: "By whatever fierce actions sentient beings are bound, by that very same means, when employed with skillful method, they are liberated from the bonds of existence."
(2.2.50) Also in the *Pañcakrama*: "By that very mind through which fools have fallen into bondage in saṃsāra,
by that same mind the yogins [attain liberation]."
They have gone to the destination of the Sugatas.

(4/16) 4. Sharp Faculties (*tīkṣṇendriyatā*)—Only one who is endowed with prior predispositions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) and possesses an intense intellect in understanding the actual state of things is capable of knowing that very non-dual reality (*advayatattva*). Although the specific nature of an intense intellect varies across numerous fields of knowledge, here it is considered supreme specifically as the intensity of understanding the reality of things. Because the proponents of the *Pāramitā* [system] are unable to understand the state of totality, an analysis of the non-dual reality of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) is not found within their various paths.

And where the practitioner of the *pāramitās* cultivates each one of the six or ten *pāramitās*, right there for the practitioner of the *tantra*, the complete maṇḍala of the universe exists as the dual deity and the *bodhicitta*.
All that is present within oneself and resides in oneself; one’s own body is indeed one’s innate maṇḍala.

This alone is the method of practice for the Tantra. Anaṅgavajra explains: "Even those other [methods] which were shown by the glorious Vajrasattva, some of which are based on the power of individual inclination—what use are they for one who knows reality?"

(5/35) The nature of the fourfold tantra beginning with Kriyā: (ka) That practitioner who, through the performance of external physical mudrās, attains the perfection of body; or through the recitation of mantras by way of speech, attains the perfection of speech; and through the mental cultivation of the deity, attains the qualities of the mind—and who thus, in preference to internal meditation and contemplation, performs external acts of purification and virtuous conduct with great emphasis—is called a follower of Kriyātantra.

The venerable Seratoga Pāma has clarified the nature of the four classes of tantra (*tantra-catuṣṭaya*) in succession as follows: (kha) "The very process of bringing passion into the path by generating it upon seeing an available goddess or a consort (*mudrā*), while remaining established in the meditation on reality (*tattva*), is the essential nature of Kriyātantra.

(ga) Performing acts such as laughing together with the gazing at an available goddess, one effects the practice of the non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*) nature through the experience of bliss; this is the internal mental yoga (*cittayoga*) arising from the purification of body, speech, and conduct."
Furthermore, one who practices and accomplishes through a form similar [to the deity] is said to possess the Carya-tantra.

(Ga) A yogi who, having performed the ritual marriage with the goddess to be attained, circulates bliss and strives for the direct realization of the emptiness of objects through the knowledge of objects as being of the nature of bliss, is called one who possesses the Yoga-tantra.

(gha) Having abided in the yoga of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and directly realized the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*), the practitioner who performs the conduct (*caryā*) without the preparation of external things such as what is drinkable or undrinkable, what is approachable or unapproachable, or what is pure or impure, is called one who possesses the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*).
In the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*, Anaṅgavajra states: "One should never entertain conceptual constructions regarding what is approachable or unapproachable and so forth."
Indeed, everything whatsoever should be enjoyed by means of the yoga of the illusion-like and so forth.
(5/29) Since nothing arises apart from the dharmadhātu, there are no obstacles whatsoever;
one should enjoy [all things] according to one's desire with a mind free from doubt.

(5/31) Even the later Tibetan scholar Paṇḍita Dharmaśrī Mahodaya, while elucidating the nature of the *saṃvara* (initiation) for the four mantras, stated: "Having established a single pleasure as the path through [the acts of] seeing, laughing, and holding hands, and having cultivated the knowledge of specific wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) in order to purify the passion corresponding to that [pleasure],
[one should proceed] with respect to the three doors [of body, speech, and mind]..."

The vow and ethical discipline (*śīla*) obtained through the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the *Kriyā*, *Caryā*, and other tantras—which possess causes that counteract the conceptual mind for the sake of purifying latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)—constitute the essential nature of the vow for the *Kriyā* and other tantras.

Regarding the drawing of the mandalas of the four classes of tantra, the Tathāgata spoke as follows: In the *Kriyātantra* mandala, one should visualize and depict the goddess Tārā on the right in the gesture of passion (*rāgamudrā*), and on the left, Amoghapāśa of the Lotus Family in the gesture of the gift of Dharma (*dharmadānamudrā*). It is also stated in the *Kriyātantravajroṣṇīṣa*: "The father-god [should look] toward the mother-goddess, and the mother-goddess [toward him]."

And one should depict [the deity] looking toward the Pitṛdeva on a white-colored [background]. In the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, while clarifying the ritual procedure for the Carya-tantras, it was written: "To the right stands Buddha [Lokeśvara] in the smiling mudrā, his entire body radiant with splendor; and to the left stands this wife of Śākyamuni."
Regarding the connection with the mandala of Yoga Tantra, the *Vajraśekhara* states: "One should depict the Vajra Goddess making the sound 'vajra' while embracing the hand of the Blessed One.
In the mandala of Anuttara Tantra, one should depict the Father and Mother in the form of the union of the yuganaddha.
This is because it is through the yoga of such union alone that the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*) is accomplished.
And so it is said in the Guhyasamāja: "One should visualize Locanā, who is the great radiance of the Tathāgata;
through the union of the two organs, one shall attain the accomplishment of wisdom."
(7/13) By this it is made very clear that in the four tantras, practitioners who transform passion (*rāga*) into the path desire to directly realize the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*).
Also, in the *Sampuṭatantra*: "Laughter, gazing, and the grasping of hands—that is established in the tantra; as well as passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*virāga*)."
Having gnawed [it], the woodworm remains.

(16-3-49) While explaining this, Buston wrote: "In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types of passion (*rāga*): [passion] below the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyaṃstriṃśa*) by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); in the Yāma heaven by embracing; and in Tuṣita by holding hands."

In the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), satisfaction and bliss are experienced by those to be trained through laughter; and in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmitavaśavartin), they are experienced merely by the sight of a consort.

Since there is no passion for the desire realm within the form realm, the Buddha teaches the method of the perfections (pāramitānaya) for the sake of liberating those beings to be trained from their attachment to the form realm.

This tantra was taught for those practitioners who could not be subdued by the path of detachment (*vairāgya*). By observing this [tantra], there occurs the transformation of one whose passion (*rāga*) is fixed into a spiritual path. Furthermore, for such a person, the practice of relying upon a beautiful consort (*mudrā*) is indeed indispensable; for man and woman consist of both semen and blood, and because cause and effect are of a single continuum.
In this tantric scripture, the meaning of the term "evam" (thus) is clearly established through its exposition.
It is described in various senses;

furthermore, by igniting the *lalanā*—the channel that carries blood—the *rasanā*—the channel that carries semen—and the *melana*, which is the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), one is able to effect the flow of semen.
In this system, numerous objects of the senses are fully described;
and by means of this single conceptual path, passion is transformed into the path and the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*) is directly realized.
In the initial stage, this alone appears to be the most appropriate path for the practitioner.

Having cultivated the seal (mudrā) of a beautiful woman through meditative absorption (samāpatti) in order to realize the non-dual reality (advayatattva), it is indispensable that one first internally cognize the emptiness of phenomena (dharmaśūnyatā) in the form of a mental body, remaining uncontracted until it is known through subtle internal consciousness;
and when the mind becomes one with emptiness, only then should one perform the practice of the great bliss of the extremely subtle, non-dual reality of emptiness.
Due to the practitioner's lack of maturity, this practice becomes an object of contempt in the world, and through it, a disregard for this supreme divine path arises within society.
However, when the practitioner has reached a state of maturity, no one can obstruct its truth or reality if they should practice it.
The practitioner ought to manifest wondrous and marvelous feats.
Some unqualified persons claim that the disciples are unfit vessels for the display of such marvels;
even a guru established in a high station does not demonstrate them.
Furthermore, if those very same individuals, having indulged in the mudrās and so forth, perform the conduct (*caryā*), then they too commit a transgression.
Through this transgression, a sense of inferiority toward the Tantra arose among people; for this is indeed a great fault for those who rely upon the Dharma.

Regarding the consideration of *kula*: In his work on the history of Dharmaśāstra, the illustrious P.V. Kane, who was adorned with the title "Jewel of India," provided a description of both Buddhist and non-Buddhist lineages (*kula*) in relation to the general concept of lineage.
He noted that in Buddhist scriptures, except for the Mantrayāna, the term *gotra* was generally employed in place of the word *kula*.
This is because the term *kula* is used in the Tantras with the same meaning as the word *gotra* found in the texts of the Pāramitānaya and Śrāvakayāna.
In the *Mahāyānottaratantra*, the Protector Maitreya said: "The lineage (*gotra*) or family (*kula*) is that power which leads to the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Therefore it is said: 'On the same day, all living beings will surely attain nirvāṇa, because the lineage exists within all living beings.
Just as it is said: 'Because the body of the Perfect Buddha pervades [all], and because suchness is indivisible.'"
And by virtue of their lineage, all embodied beings are always possessed of the Buddha-essence.
(MA 31/28) Only when the lineage exists can a living being become a Buddha, and not otherwise.
There are two principal divisions of the lineage: 1. the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), and 2. the developed lineage (*paripuṣṭi-gotra*).
For example: "That lineage should be known as twofold, like a treasure and a fruit-bearing tree:
that which abides in its primordial nature from beginningless time, and that which is further developed through cultivation."
The lineage (*gotra*) is like a tree, fully endowed with its root and fruit.

It exists as something pure from the beginning, due to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and it abides with the form of space. This luminous nature of the mind never undergoes transformation, just like the sky.
However, it undergoes defilement through adventitious stains such as passion, which are born of unreal conceptualization.
The accumulation of the waters of karma and afflictions does not cause this [Self] to turn back;
nor does the fire of death, disease, and old age, even when blazing up, consume it. (Mokṣopāya 1.63)
(MAU 1.64) By implication, this *gotra* does not turn toward karma, afflictions, and so forth; furthermore, its essential nature cannot be altered by adventitious causes.
From the very beginning, it has a luminous nature like space, and it is neither subject to arising nor to destruction.
The abiding of the qualities of the Tathāgata is in this very [reality];
it dwells within embodied beings like pure water within the earth.
Nāgārjuna says: Just as water remains pure even when hidden within the earth.
Thus, wisdom remains stainless, though it has been obscured by the afflictions.

The purification of the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*) consists precisely in the manifestation of its luminosity, and not in its arising from causes consisting of effects and conditions. As it is said: "Just as fire [is pure] and a cloth soiled by various impurities..."
Just as cloth thrown into the midst of fire is burnt and no longer possesses the nature of cloth.
(Se. Ṭī. pṛ. 66) Just as the practitioner abandons adventitious afflictions through the practice of the means of knowledge, so too does the quality of luminosity blossom therein.
Ultimately, the means and the practitioner become one, just as the moon of the bright fortnight attains fullness through the purification of its dark aspect.
This is precisely the sequence for the lineage that is nourished by traversing the path.

The Lord Maitreya, clarifying through metaphors the qualities of those who possess the lineage (gotra) residing within their bodies, has declared its essential nature as follows: "The establishment of the Jina-embryo (jinagarbha) is thus taught in ten ways;
furthermore, its state of being an embryo enveloped by afflictions (kleśakośagarbhatva) should be understood through illustrative examples."
The Buddha is present within the withered lotus, as honey among bees, as kernels within husks, and as gold in filth;
he is a treasure buried in the earth, as sprouts in small fruit, and the body of a Jina within soiled garments.
Just as kingship may exist within the womb of a lowly woman, or as the image of a jewel within clods of earth,
so too does this element abide within sentient beings who are shrouded by the adventitious stains of afflictions.

(Mahāyānottaratantra 1.15–97) Just as honey exists within a scentless flower, grain within a husk, gold in filth, a treasure in the earth, a crop produced by plowing and so forth, a jewel wrapped in a damp cloth, a divine image, or a universal monarch within a woman’s womb—
so too do the qualities of the Tathāgatas abide in the form of the element (*dhātu*) within the beginningless luminous mind of sentient beings.
The very manifestation of that [nature] through the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is designated as the "fully nourished lineage" (*paripuṣṭagotra*).
This is also the Form Body (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddha.
As stated in the *Mahāyānottaratantra*: "The attainment of the three bodies of the Buddha is held to result from these two lineages."
From the first [verse], the first body [is obtained]; from the second, however, the two final ones.
The attainment of the Dharma-body arises from the first *gotra*, and from the second, the Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya arise.
For this very reason, it is said that even the Nirmāṇakāya manifests from the Dharmakāya;
because all qualities reside solely within the first *gotra*.

Because the first lineage (*gotra*) is equal to space, all living beings are also equal. Just as it is impossible for the space-element (*dharmadhātu*) to have multiplicity, likewise there is no disparity in the natural lineage (*prakṛtigotra*). And in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* it is said: "Since the dharma-element is undifferentiated, a distinction of lineages is not tenable."
However, its differentiation is proclaimed due to the differentiation of the attributes to be contained within it.

(1/40) A distinction among sentient beings can be established based on the differences in their dependent qualities. Just as there may be a difference between vases made of gold, silver, iron, and so forth—such that their value and location can also be distinct—yet no distinction whatsoever can exist within the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) residing therein; in the same way, due to the differences in the intrinsic natures and inclinations of sentient beings, they are designated as followers of the Śrāvaka-vehicle, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas according to their respective capacities.
The supreme state is attained.

Because it is distinct from that which abides in primordial nature (*prakṛti*), this distinction does not exist; however, for one whose spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is fully developed, it arises through the distinction between fullness and non-fullness.
The Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and Vijñānavādins accept the state of a Śrāvaka Arhat, the state of a Pratyekabuddha,
and the state of a Samyaksambuddha as three distinct and independent categories; however, this is not appropriate.

However, the Mahāyānists determine that what is called the state of an Arhat or Pratyekabuddha is merely a station for rest; as long as perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) has not been attained, it cannot be called *nirvāṇa*.
This is because the first lineage (*gotra*) and the second lineage exist like the moon and its moonlight.
As it has been said: "Wisdom is so called because of the brilliance, pervasiveness, and purity of knowledge and liberation."
And there is similarity by way of non-difference with light, rays, and the solar orb.

The purification of the lineage (*gotra*) itself is the means of accomplishment; it is divided across the five paths known as the equipment (*saṃbhāra*), application (*prayoga*), seeing (*darśana*), cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that which is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
As it is said: "The realm of beings (*sattvadhātu*) is declared to be, respectively, impure, impure-and-pure, and then perfectly pure. (MAU Ta 1.13)
The Bodhisattva is the Tathāgata.

(MAUT 1.47) This impure state is indeed the *sattvadhātu*; the state that is both impure and pure belongs to the Bodhisattva from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the end of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); however, the perfectly pure state is Tathāgatashood. We can say that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), being possessed of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), is impure; yet they are pure with respect to the afflictions through the correct grasping and retention [of the teachings], while remaining impure with respect to the obscurations of the knowable.

Thus, the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are pure and impure; when completely purified of the two obscurations, one becomes such [a Buddha]. However, to speak of the essential point: the practitioner, having performed the practice in accordance with their own particular yoga, attains the supreme state.
The power of the practice consists of the *kula* and the *gotra*.
*Kula* is that wherein the fruit ripens; it is precisely there, in the practice of the path or even as the cause of the path, that it exists.
Just as in the world, one born into a noble lineage becomes the foremost authority.

In reality, however, the *kula* is exactly like a human being; furthermore, many divisions can be established according to the variations of the intellect. Just as in the world many divisions of a human being are observed through differences in complexion, physical form, and so forth, in the same way, various *kula*-practices are discussed in the Tantric texts according to their specific applications.

For instance: (ka) because practitioners possess varying degrees of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) for the afflictions (*kleśa*), the methods for transforming those respective afflictions into the path were described in the tantric scriptures.

In the *Vajrapañjara*, the Buddha stated: "In order to favor those people seized by hatred, delusion, egoism, passion, envy, and so forth, I have established that path by assuming the forms of the Akṣobhya family for practitioners dominated by hatred, and the Vairocana family for those dominated by delusion."

(kha) In the *Hevajra Tantra*, the family deity (*kuladeva*) for practitioners has been described according to their respective complexions as follows: "The yogi who is black has Akṣobhya as his deity;
the yogi who is very fair has Vairocana as his family deity."
For whichever yogi is Mahāśyāma,
his deity is Amoghasiddhi;
for whichever yogi is Mahāpiṅga, Ratneśa is his family deity.
For the yogi who is red and white,
Amitābha is the family deity;
for the yogi who is white and pale, Vajrasattva’s family shall belong to him.

(2-11-5-7) (ga) Furthermore, according to the characteristics residing in the body, it is observed by what family the practitioner is connected and what kind of store of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) they possess.
As it is said in the *Hevajra*: "In whose [hand] at the base of the ring finger..."
Whether of a woman or a man,
the nine-pronged vajra is the supreme family of Akṣobhya.
Vairocana’s [symbol] shall be a wheel, Amitābha’s a lotus,
Ratnasambhava’s a great jewel, and that of the Karma family a sword.
(2/11/3-4) According to the Buddhist tradition as well, the practitioner is considered to belong to various families: "Because of having minds of manifold forms, five types of persons are recognized:
the Ratna, the Candana, the Padma, the Puṇḍarīka, and likewise the Utpala."
(Pradīpodyotana-paṭala, p.

4) (gha) Thus, even according to the varying intentions and capacities of practitioners, there are innumerable divisions of the *kula*—and also in the *Guhyasamāja*: "The reality is said to be the five *kulas*."
The triad of families (trikula) is called the secret;
it is the presiding deity, the mystery, and the supreme hundredfold family.
(18/36) Furthermore, from the five families, innumerable divisions of families arise in detail. As it is said in the *Hevajratantra*: "The single Great Mind is established in five forms;
its manifestation within the five families occurs there in many thousands."
Therefore, this great bliss, which is of a single nature and eternally supreme,
attains a fivefold state through the differentiation of the five mental states beginning with passion.
As many as the sands of ten Ganges rivers are the assemblies of Tathāgatas within single families;
for within those assemblies of families there are indeed many families,
and within those families there are hundreds of families.
And those hundreds of thousands of families become many millions of families;
within those families, there are countless families born from the family of supreme bliss.
(2/2/58–61) In reality, although there is infinity in detail,
in brief, within body, speech, and mind— ultimately because the body itself is the mind and the mind itself is the body— it enters into the luminous innate mind and the great mind.
This very thing is also the lineage (*gotra*) and the family (*kula*).

Having accepted the *kula* as an auxiliary to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) within the context of innate perfection (*sahajasiddhi*), it is described thus: "In this world, one should resort to the *kulas*, which have their abode in the fivefold [elements].
Through service to the *kula*, there arises auspicious success that grants all desires."
Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasambhava, Vairocana,
and Amoghasiddhi are likewise proclaimed as the causes for the accomplishment of sentient beings.
(2/6) Accomplishment is attained through the practice of the families (*kula*) beginning with Akṣobhya.
Furthermore, it is stated in that very same [text]: “Success arises from the service of the family; this was spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One” (2/8).
For the sake of attaining the fruit, the cultivation of one’s own respective path is called the "service of the family" (*kulasevā*), which is to say, the practice of the family (*kulācaraṇa*).
For this reason, in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, immediately after receiving the initiation of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), the practitioner considers himself born into the family of the Buddhas;
and thus, regarding himself as a future successor to the Buddha, he deems his own rare human life to be blessed.
As it is said: "Today my birth has become fruitful; a human existence has been well-attained."
Today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; I am now a son of the Buddha.

(3/25) In the *Sampuṭodbhavatantra*, the practitioner, having received the empowerment, joyfully expresses his own outpourings, saying: "A person who has obtained the empowerment, having accomplished his purpose and being filled with great joy, should speak very sweet words that bring bliss to the world."
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
today I am born into the family of the Buddhas and have now become a son of the Buddha.

(2/1–2) Having thus deliberated upon the general means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) within the Tantras, one should determine the *kula* (spiritual family) appropriate to the nature of the individual and then perform the practice.
Hereafter, the methods for accomplishing the *Kriyā*, *Caryā*, and other Tantras will be explained according to the distinctions among those qualified to practice them.

The Second Chapter: The *Kriyātantra*. Regarding the manifestation of the *Kriyātantra*, it was stated by the Blessed Tathāgata in the context of teaching the *Kriyātantra*: "In Śrāvastī, for three months, [the Blessed One] dwelt in the world of the Trāyastriṃśa gods..."
He went to favor his own mother with instructions on the Dharma;
from there, he proceeded at the appropriate time to places such as Mount Sumeru and taught numerous tantric scriptures.
Then, returning to Jambudvīpa, he taught the tantras to disciples of various inclinations in diverse locations such as Magadha and Śrāvastī.

Among these, the Kriyātantra was divided into six sections known as the Mañjuśrī-tantra, the Avalokiteśvara-tantra, the Vajrapāṇi-tantra, the Acala-tantra, the Vidyādevī-tantra, and the Uṣṇīṣa-tantra.
Within this very sequence, the flourishing and the manifestation of the Kriyātantra are examined.

The teaching of the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, the tantra associated with Mañjuśrī, was delivered by the Tathāgata in the Śuddhāvāsa world: “At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa... ”
"He dwelt within the mandala circle of the inconceivable, marvelous, and wondrous assembly of bodhisattvas," as can be seen in the detailed exposition in this section [of the *Gaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*].
Regarding the *Avalokiteśvara-tantra*, there are many tantric texts associated with Avalokiteśvara.
Among them, the *Āryāmoghapāśa-tantra* was taught by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, on Mount Potalaka.
And where the field of Avalokiteśvara arises, there indeed this instruction was obtained by incalculable bodhisattvas and beings of the realm of form. 2.

The Blessed One [taught] the *Āryāvalokiteśvarapadmajālamūlatantrarāja* in the great forest of the Himalayas to the venerable Mahākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, Ānanda-kumāra, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Subhūti, and others.
3. He instructed many monks, novices, nāgas, devas, asuras, kinnaras, gandharvas, and others;
on the banks of the Ganges, the Buddha taught the *Āryāparimitāyurjñānahṛdayanāmadhāraṇī* to the community of monks and the bodhisattvas.
4. On the Ṛṣi Mountain, the Blessed One revealed the *Āryāvalokiteśvaraguhyakośāsaṅgacintāmaṇicakrahṛdayanāmadhāraṇī* to the bodhisattvas.

5.
