The *Āryamukhadeśaka-vidyāmantrahṛdayanāmadhāraṇī* was taught by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, while residing at Śrāvastī in the Bamboo Grove together with the community of monks and bodhisattvas such as Maitreya, following a request from the sages beginning with Avalokiteśvara and the holders of spells (*vidyādharas*). 6. The *Āryasamantabhadranāmadhāraṇī* was taught by the Blessed One on Mount Rājagiri in an assembly filled with a community of eight thousand monks, incalculable bodhisattvas, and the deities of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsakula*).

While composing the *Pravacana*, he instructed Avalokiteśvaras who were bowed down to teach that *dhāraṇī*. 7. The *Āryāmoghapāśakalpa* was taught by the Blessed One on Mount Potalaka at the request of Avalokiteśvara.

8. The *Āryāvalokiteśvaranāmadhāraṇī* was personally taught to the bodhisattvas by Avalokiteśvara himself, who out of compassion manifested with one face and four arms upon a seat of lotus, moon, and sun.

9. The Blessed One himself, having manifested in the form of Padmāvalokiteśvara, taught the *Siṃhanāda-tantra* to Vajrapāṇi while seated upon the vajra-throne. 10. The *Āryāvalokiteśvarāṣṭaśataka* was taught by the Blessed One while dwelling together with his disciples—the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, asuras, and kinnaras—in the presence of Brahmā and other bodhisattvas; therein, Avalokiteśvara is praised through various discourses.
The *Acalatantra* 1. Numerous sub-divisions of this [tantra] are also found.

Among these, the *Āryācalanāmadhāraṇī* was composed by the Blessed One while dwelling together with bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra, Ākāśagarbha, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Mañjuśrīpāṇi, Avalokiteśvara, and Maitreya—bodhisattvas residing on the tenth stage—in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, at the request of Maitreya.
2. The Blessed One taught the *Ārya-vighna-vināyaka-dhāraṇī* at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove upon the request of the Venerable Ratinivedana.
3. The illustrious Vajrabhairava himself taught the *Śrī-vajrabhairava*.

Vajrapāṇi Tantra 1: The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, [taught] the tantra named *Ārya-vajrapāṇi-nīlāmbaradhara-vajrapāla* in the world of Pātāla to the Bodhisattvas Nāgarāja Ānanda and Upananda, Vajrapāṇi, and others.
While dwelling together, he taught:

2. The Noble Tantra entitled *Vajrapāṇi-nīlāmbara-trilokavijaya* was fully taught by the Blessed Tathāgata to the Bodhisattvas, along with Vajrapāṇi and infinite gods and asuras, in Alakāvatī on the southern side of Mount Sumeru.
3. The teaching of the *Trilokavijaya-pratyakṣatantra* of the Blue-Robed Vajra was composed by Vajrapāṇi.
4. The *Vajracaṇḍacittaguhyatantra* was taught by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, through an instruction to Indradeva.
5. The *Śrīvajracaṇḍacittaguhyatantrōttaratantra* was taught by the Blessed One through an instruction to the Blessed Vajrapāṇi.

6. The Blessed One taught the *Vajrahṛdayavajrajihvānalā-nāma-dhāraṇī* in the great charnel ground of Śītavajra to the assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, gods, asuras, humans, and others.

7. When Vīreśvara questioned the Blessed Tathāgata in the palace of Alakāvatī in the Akaniṣṭha realm, the *Śrīguhyavajrapāṇy-abhideśa-tantra* was taught by the Blessed One in the form of answers to those questions.
8. The *Āryalohatuṇḍanāmadhāraṇī* was taught by the Blessed One while residing in the Videha Cave in the Mango Grove at Magadha, following a request from Indra.
9. The *Āryamekhalānāmadhāraṇī* was taught at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Garden, following a request from Prince Rāhula.
10. The *Āryavajrapāṇihṛdaya* was taught by the Blessed Buddha at Śrāvastī in the Jaitravana, in response to questions such as "What is the family of Vajrapāṇi? posed by Ānanda and others.
The *Vidyādevī-tantra*: 1. The *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī* was taught by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, while residing in the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.

After receiving initiation, a certain period had passed since the monk named Śāri entered the community of monks when he was suddenly bitten by a snake. Seeing him unconscious, Ānanda informed the Blessed One, who then taught the *Vidyārājñī* for the liberation of all living beings from various diseases.
2. The Blessed Buddha taught the *Mahāmantrānudhāraṇī-sūtra* at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove when Indra, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the world-protectors, yakṣas, and others had made their request.
3. The Blessed Tathāgata taught the *Āryamahāpratisarā-vidyārājñī* on Vajraparvata.

4. The Blessed One, while residing on Mount Videha at Rājagiri, [taught] the *Āryajayavatī-mahāvidyārājñī* for the sake of the instruction of the community of monks, the community of nuns, the community of novices, and the lay followers.

Having perceived the obstacle, he himself manifested in the fierce form of Vajradhara and, facing eastward, extended a thousand vajra-flames while threatening the host of spirits; thus he instructed [the *Āryatārāsragdharāstotra*].
5. The *Āryatārābhaṭṭārikānāmāṣṭaśataka* was taught by Ārya Avalokiteśvara.
6. The *Sarvatathāgatamātṛtārāviśvakarmabhāva-tantra* was taught by the Tathāgata Buddha in the Tuṣita heaven at the request of Mañjuśrī and other bodhisattvas.
7. The Noble Sūtra of Tārā, the Savior from Eightfold Fears, was taught by the Blessed One on Mount Sumeru at the abode of the gods.
Regarding the Uṣṇīṣa Tantra: many texts of this [cycle] are also available.
Among these, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, taught the Noble Dhāraṇī named Mahādaṇḍa at Vulture Peak in Rājagiri at the request of the venerable Rāhulabhadra.

2. At that time, the Blessed One taught the *Āryasarvāntarāyika-viśodhanī-nāma-dhāraṇī* while he was dwelling in the cave named Indra, located to the east of Rājagiri, to the south of the Āmra grove inhabited by brahmins, and to the north of Mount Videha. Indra, together with his attendants, approached there to receive the instruction; at his request, the Blessed One taught this dhāraṇī to him.
3. Furthermore, the *Āryasarvābhayapradāna-nāma-dhāraṇī* was also taught by the Blessed One in Magadha at the request of Indra.

4. The *Āryabāhuputra-pratisāraṇa-nāma-dhāraṇī* was taught by the Blessed One in Śrāvastī when King Prasenajit, the son of Anāthapiṇḍada, launched an attack; having been asked how his protection could be ensured, this dhāraṇī was bestowed upon him.

5. When the Blessed One was dwelling in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada at Śrāvastī, together with two thousand five hundred (2,500) monks, Ānanda—having completed the three-month *upoṣadha* fast during the summer season—came from Ayodhyā to Śrāvastī in order to behold the Buddha.
Then the Blessed One addressed Ānanda: "This Noble Great Dhāraṇī was previously taught even by seventy-seven crores of Perfectly Awakened Ones prior to this day."
Furthermore, I shall teach you the Noble Great Dhāraṇī.
6. The *Āryabhadrarātrī-nāma-sūtra* was taught by the Blessed One to the monks in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha.
7. The *Āryaojaḥ-pratyaṅgirā-sūtra* was fully taught in Śrāvastī to Ānanda and the other monks.
8. The *Āryajvarapraśamanī-nāmadhāraṇī* was taught by the Blessed One to the community of monks at the cemetery called Śīla in Rājagiri.

9. The instruction on the *Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣavijaya-nāmadhāraṇīkalpa* was completed through the presentation of Amitāyus, the Blessed One, to Avalokiteśvara in the world of Sukhāvatī. 10. While residing in the courtyard of the Veṇu-constructed pavilion in Śrāvastī, the Buddha taught the *Āryadraviṇavidyārājatantra* to Ānanda and others.

The nature of Kriyātantra was thus explained by the Tathāgata in the *Jñānasamuccaya*: "A practitioner of Kriyātantra, fearing conduct that might cause contempt in the world, emphasizes external purification.

In this [system], there is an absence of the Jñānasattva, an absence of the meditation on the deity’s body within one's own body, and an absence of the fitness for entry upon the most distinguished path."
Therefore, he resorts to conceptual construction for the sake of exhausting those defects.
Thus, the practitioner established in the Kriyātantra is so designated.
Explaining this, Koṅṭula Rin po che says: "The person of dull intellect—the practitioner..."
One fears the profound meaning [because it has not been experienced when passion arose].
Due to one's own lack of capacity for the meditation on the Samaya-deity, there is an absence of meditation upon the deity-body within one's own body.
In the absence of this, one is unable even to effect the dissolution of the Jñāna-deity into oneself after having summoned it.
Even when imitating the most distinguished paths sealed in *sandhyābhāṣā*, there is an incapacity [to realize them].

For the sake of abandoning faults, those who perform rituals such as bathing while relying on conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*)—having cultivated the visualization of themselves as the servant and their chosen deity as the Lord—desire to be presided over;
thus, such practitioners are said to possess the *Kriyātantra*.

With the desire to independently practice the eight mundane accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*) such as mantra and collyrium (*añjana*), one performs the practice of the means (*sādhana*) after carrying out the repetition of the mantra (*mantrāvṛtti*) for the sake of attaining them. Furthermore, the Master has described the nature of the *Kriyātantra* as follows: "The practitioners of both the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* tantras perform meditation by encompassing the entire path within ten principles (*tattva*): the place of practice, independence, the knowledge (*vidyā*), the repetition of the mantra, fire-abiding, sound-abiding, that which abides within sound, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the procedure for entering the mantra-practice, and those known as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*)."
These ten principles are considered to be the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Providing an illustration from the *Jñānasamuccaya-vacanavyākhyā* composed by the Buddha, the venerable Ācārya Coṅkhāpā states: "Those disciples of the Action Tantra (*kriyātantra*) who are fearful of one-pointed concentration (*ekāgratā*) within the yoga of the deities..."

Because such highly specialized conduct is subject to worldly censure, those [practitioners] are indeed incapable of accomplishing this goal. Furthermore, by means of [addressing] defects such as birth, aging, and destruction, the truth of all phenomena has been established for sentient beings;

likewise, the absence of both the visualization of oneself as a deity (*devabhāvanā*) and the penetration of gnosis (*jñānāveśa*) has been demonstrated for practitioners who are oriented toward conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

However, this does not apply to complete practitioners of Action Tantra (*kriyātantra*). As for those distinguished practitioners who are capable of practicing through the path of visualizing one's own body as a deity, the penetration of gnosis, passion, laughter, gazing, and so forth—[for them...]
In the Kṛta age, permission [to perform rites] is fully granted.
Thus, in this system, the nature of ritual action has been accepted according to the levels of those who accomplish it through both general and specific means.

The conclusion is that the very nature of Kriyā-tantra is that in which external purity—such as bathing and other outward observances—and internal purification—such as the repetition of mantras—are strongly established, [and which addresses] the four levels of passion (*rāga*).
The method for bringing the state of the first vision onto the path has been set forth.
Regarding the intermediate divisions of Kriyātantra, two types of *kula* (families) are prescribed for both Kriyātantra and Caryātantra, as follows: 1. Lokottarakula (the supramundane family).

2. The worldly family (lokakula) and 1. the supramundane family (lokottarakula), which is the Tathāgata family. Within the supramundane family, three families—known as the Lotus family (padmakula), the Vajra family (vajrakula), and [the Tathāgata family] itself—are subsumed.
These are respectively called the superior, the middling, and the inferior.

Buddhaguhya, clarifying the intention regarding the three families, proclaims: In the Tathāgata family, having correctly understood all phenomena as they were in the past, when infinite Buddhas and Bodhisattvas existed, one who proceeds likewise upon that very path and brings about the attainment of enlightenment is said to belong to the Tathāgata family, just like the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
And in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha* it is also said: "The awakening of a Buddha arises from the penetration of one's own mind according to the prescribed method."
That very Blessed One would become the entire family of all Tathāgatas.
That very [family] is the Tathāgata family; that very one is known as the Vajra family;
that very one is the pure Padma family; and that very one is said to be the excellent Maṇi family.
The practitioner’s own mind also exists as being similar to the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgatas. For example: "Speech, movement, and rest are themselves the Tathāgata family.
In numerous tantric texts such as the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, it says: "Oṃ, I am of vajra nature."
It is described as "I effect the penetration of the mind.
That which consists of the three syllables 'A', 'U', and 'Ma' and is like the three vajras—
the very method of penetrating that is designated as the Tathāgata family.
By this also, it is established that the very reality of the mind (*cittatattva*) is the *kula*;

for by the power of the path, the practitioner realizes that very [reality], and thus he is considered a practitioner of the *kula*. One who belongs to the Lotus Family (*padmakulika*) is free from afflictions; having observed helpless living beings throughout the six watches of the day and night, his heart becomes moistened with compassion, and he exerts himself for the sake of liberating those beings—such a practitioner belongs to the Lotus Family.
It is explained as follows: here, Avalokiteśvara, Tārā and others who preside over it, and the gods and goddesses of this family exist.
The Vajra family, which protects the Buddhist teaching and subdues enemies, is called the Vajrakula.
For just as there exists the Vajra-family, consisting of Bodhicitta-Samantabhadra arising from the six perfections, empowered through the sequence of gnosis, and including Caṇḍa, Caṇḍī, and so forth;
furthermore, there are many internal subdivisions of the three families.

And just as there are eight divisions of the Tathāgata family: the Primary Family, the Lord’s Family, the Mother’s Family, the Uṣṇīṣa Family, the Wrathful Family, the Messenger and Messengeress Family, the Bodhisattva Family, and the Śuddhāvāsika Family.
An explanation of the texts for each family: 1. In the *Pradhānakula* (Principal Family), there are many texts, such as the *Trisamayavyūharāja-tantra*.

2. For the *Tathāgatādhipatikula* (Family of the Lord Tathāgatas), the principal text is the *Āryamañjuśrīkalpa*. 3. In the *Mātṛkula* (Mother Family), there are texts such as the *Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī*.
4. In the Uṣṇīṣa family, there are texts such as the noble *Sarvatathāgata-sitātapatrā-nāma-aparājitā-pratyaṅgirā-mahāvidyārājñī*.
5. In the Tathāgata-krodha family, there are numerous texts such as the *Viṣayakalpa-guhyatantra*.
6. In the Dūta-dūtī family, the noble *Bhadrarātri-nāma-sūtra* is counted.

7. In the Tathāgata-Bodhisattva family, there are texts such as the *Āryamaitreya-nāmāṣṭottaraśataka-dhāraṇī-saṃhitā*. 8. In the Tathāgata-Śuddhāvāsika-deva family, there are texts such as the great sūtra named the *Āṭānāṭīya-sūtra*.
Among these, whichever text a practitioner follows by means of its dhāraṇī and practices as their own sādhana, they are said to belong to that very family.

Within the Padma family, five subdivisions are established: the Pradhānakula (Principal Family), the Adhipatikula (Lord’s Family), the Mātṛkula (Mother’s Family), the Krodhakula (Wrathful Family), and the Ājñākārikula (Command-Observing Family).
1. In the Pradhānakula, works such as the *Āryāparimitāyurjñānanāma-mahāyānasūtra* are counted.
2. In the Adhipatikula, there are texts beginning with the *Āryāvalokiteśvarapadmajālamūlatantrarāja*.

3. In the Mātṛ family, there exist the *Viśvakarmabhavatantra*, the *Nāmādidhāraṇī* of Tārā—the mother of all Tathāgatas—and numerous other sūtras and texts. 4. In the Krodha family, texts such as the *Āryāvalokiteśvarahṛdaya-grīvā-dhāraṇī* have been collected.
5. In the Ājñākārin family, there are many mantras, streams [of teachings], and dhāraṇīs, beginning with the *Āryamahālakṣmīsūtra*.

Furthermore, for the Vajra family, there are these five sub-divisions: the Primary Family, the Family of the Overlord, the Family of the Mothers, the Family of the Wrathful and Wrath-inducing Deities, and the Families of the Messengers and Female Messengers who carry out commands.

1. In the Primary Family, there occur texts such as the *Ārya-sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanī-nāma-dhāraṇī* and others. 2. In the Family of the Overlord, there are texts such as the *Ārya-vajrapātāla-nāma-tantrarāja* and others.
3. In the Mātṛkula, there arrive such works as the *Āryavajrājitānalapramohanī-nāma-dhāraṇī* and others. 4. In the Krodha-krodhinīkula, there is the *Āryajayavatī-nāma-mahāvidyārāja*.
5. In the Dūta-dūtīkula, or alternatively in the Ājñākārikula, there arrive many works such as the *Mahābala-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, as well as various sūtras, dhāraṇīs, mantras, stotras, and tantras.
These are the divisions: Buston’s [work] is the fourteenth (94).
Thus, these have been set forth based upon the *Sāmānyatantra*, the ninth among the *Khasaḍubaja* [texts].
A detailed introduction was provided by Śrī Banārasīlāla Mohodaya in the fifth issue of the journal *Dhīḥ*.

The Lokakula consists of three internal divisions: the Maṇikula, the Pañcakakula (also known as the Puṣṭikula), and the Lokakula itself. 1. In the Maṇikula, there are included such texts as the *Āryamaṇibhadranāmadhāraṇī* and likewise the *Āryajambhalajalendrathālabdhakalpanāmaprabhṛti*.
2. In the Pañcakakula, there are the *Āryamekhalānāmadhāraṇī* and others.
3. Works such as the *Āryamantrarājamahāśvāsa* come under the *Lokakula*. If their inclusion within these families is desired, it can be accomplished by dividing them into three parts.
The Maṇikula is included within the Padmakula for the sake of nourishment, or within the Vajrakula for the sake of the five families; all other worldly deities are merged into the Lokakula.

This is established in the *Piṇḍārthavidhi* commentary on the *Subāhuparipṛcchā*: "Those who are not subsumed within these three families do not believe that they have been empowered or manifested by the Tathāgata.
Regarding this, it is also said: "Even though these worldly deities wander in the world while maintaining their own worldly forms,"
Furthermore, having been tamed by the Tathāgata, they abide in the discipline and maintain it;
therefore, they consider themselves to have taken refuge in the Tathāgata.
Many gods from the world-families, such as Brahmā, Garuḍa, Sūrya, and Candra, come together [there].
Generally, one’s family affiliation can also be determined by means of its mantras;
for example, the mantras of the Tathāgata family are: "Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels;
homage to the Buddha..."

"Homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha"— beginning with these words, [the recitation] commences. For the Lotus Family, the mantras begin with "Homage to the Noble Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, the Greatly Compassionate One," and so forth.
The mantras of the Vajra family begin with “Namo caṇḍapāṇaye mahāsenāpataye” and so forth.
The mantras of the Maṇi family begin with “Oṃ namo maṇibhadrāya mahāyakṣasenāpataye” and so forth. And the mantras of the Pañcaka and Puṣṭi families are “Namaḥ pañcakāya.”

The mantras of the Lokakula begin with "Namo Mekhalāyai" and so forth; since they commence together with the salutation to one's own Lord (svādhipati), no certain determination [of their specific application] is possible. The purpose of the division of the Kulas is as follows: for Vidyā, it is Sarasvatī; [and so on].

Dhanamangala and others consider the two deities Kubera and Gaṇeśa to be preeminent here for the accomplishment of rites of pacification (*śāntika*). Likewise, the Tathāgata family is favored for the accomplishment of rites of enrichment (*puṣṭika*), the Lotus family for fierce rites (*raudrakarma*), and the Vajra family for swift accomplishment.
Furthermore, internal subdivisions are prescribed for those vessels belonging to the Tathāgata family who desire enrichment and fierce rites.

Just as the Tathāgata family is considered appropriate for the accomplishment of pacifying rites (*śāntika-karma*), the Tathāgata-lord family for enriching rites (*puṣṭi*), and the Wrathful family for the practice of fierce rites (*raudra-karma*), so too should the Lotus family, the Vajra family, and the others be understood.
The ritual manual for the practice of Action Tantra (*kriyā-tantra*) consists of four limbs of the practice of Action Tantra.
They are also referred to by the term *caryā*.
These names are: *praveśacaryā*, *yogacaryā*, *sādhanacaryā*, and *siddhicaryā*.
Regarding *praveśacaryā*, in the *Kriyātantra*, the necessity of the two consecrations known as *jala* (water) and *paṭa* (cloth) is required for entry.
Through the attainment of the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), the practitioner becomes a partaker in the attainment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Through the cloth (*paṭa*) consecration, one becomes a partaker in the attainment of the Enjoyment-body (*sambhogakāya*).

In the water consecration, for the purpose of entering the outer maṇḍalas; through the vase consecration, for entry into the second maṇḍala; through the consecration with the vases of all the deities, for the third; and with the vase of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—
In the fourth [initiation], the water-consecration is performed with the Bodhisattva vase; in the fifth, with the Buddha vase; and likewise with the Jinavijaya vase.
Upon the head of the practitioner, the cloth-consecration (paṭābhiṣeka) is performed by means of hand-gestures (mudrā) and so forth.
Thus, having obtained the two principal consecrations of Kriyātantra, one should maintain one's respective commitments and vows (samaya-saṃvara).

Along with that very [initiation], for the sake of attaining the status of a Vajrācārya according to the various traditions of Kriyātantra, the water and cloth initiations (*jalapaṭābhiṣeka*) are bestowed; and for the sake of accomplishing the *vidyā-mantra*, the "pronouncement of the mantra" (*mantravyākaraṇa*) is necessary, wherein the practitioner must recite the mantra of whichever deity upon whom his flower falls. Furthermore, during the practitioner's period of practice, the "ablution initiation" (*snānābhiṣeka*) is given for protection against obstacles encountered, and the "initiation of the eight auspicious substances" (*aṣṭamāṅgalikadravyābhiṣeka*) is given for the purpose of increasing sovereignty.
Although this [consecration] is already included within the consecrations of water and crown,
nevertheless, considering the capacity of those to be trained (*vineyajana*), even such an arrangement is required for the sake of expansion. Furthermore,

by obtaining the consecration of the Tathāgata family even within the [other] families, it can be understood as if the family consecration of all the principal lords of the families has also been obtained.
In the same way, the Lotus family and the Vajra family should also be understood [in this manner].
In the Kriyātantra, there is only the established rule for a mandala made of clay for the purpose of initiation;
therein, no established rule exists for the mind-mandala, the body-mandala, and so forth.
The practice of yoga (*yogacaryā*) consists of these two divisions: 1. secondary preparatory practice (*gauṇaprayogacaryā*), and 2. primary preparatory practice (*mukhyaprayogacaryā*).

Regarding the first: for whichever deity is to be accomplished by a practitioner of Action Tantra (*kriyātantrin*), one should—with a mind of total dedication toward the painted cloth, the image, and the ritual substances—practice in suitable locations such as mountains, caves, and other such sites.
The practice should be commenced after being perfected through ten factors, beginning with the spring season and the time of dawn;
this is the secondary practice of application (*gauṇā prayogacaryā*).

2. Regarding the primary practice of application (*pramukhā prayogacaryā*), there are four factors: the cultivation of one's own reality (*svatattvabhāvanā*) and the cultivation of the deity-reality (*devatattvabhāvanā*).
These consist of the cultivation of recitation (*japa-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of the reality of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-tattva-bhāvanā*).

1. Cultivation of one's own reality (*sva-tattva-bhāvanā*): Immediately after receiving initiation (*abhiṣeka*) for entry into the tantra, the practitioner becomes authorized for the practice of the tantra.
Otherwise, the tantric practice becomes fruitless.
In Kriyātantra, immediately after receiving the vase empowerment (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), the practitioner becomes a partaker in the attainment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Through the accumulations of wisdom and merit that serve as the causes for the Dharma-body, he meditates on emptiness, his own true nature (*svatattva*) endowed with the six dharmas.
At the time of meditating on emptiness endowed with the six dharmas, the practitioner must first perform rituals such as bathing and remain pure.
Then, for the sake of self-protection, one should visualize a protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*).
Following that, having summoned one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) and established him upon a consecrated cloth painting, statue, or image placed before oneself, one should perform his worship.

Thereafter, having prepared a seat resembling that of the chosen deity, one should abide in the luminosity free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), which is endowed with the six dharmas and the four limits on the path to attaining the *dharmakāya*.
And the six dharmas are:
(1) the non-existence of conceptual constructions such as the grasped and the grasper; (2) the non-appearance of the non-conceptual; (3) ...
(3) the absence of forms such as subtle atoms and so forth;
(4) the absence of all signs;
and (5) emptiness devoid of all conceptual construction.
That which is non-implicative yet luminous, and the meditative concentration that is self-realized through its own intrinsic nature—
these six qualities are precisely the paths for attaining the Dharma-body.
2. Cultivation of the Reality of the Deity (*devatattvabhāvanā*). The reality of the deity is said to be the path for attaining the form body (*rūpakāya*).
It has six divisions, namely: the empty deity (*śūnyadeva*), the syllable deity (*akṣaradeva*), and so forth.
Dhvanideva, Rūpadeva, and Mudrādeva.
And the deity of signs (*nimittadeva*).

(a) The deity of emptiness (*śūnyadeva*, i.e., the deity of reality): having established that the bodhicitta—which is non-different from the ultimate reality desired within one's own mind—is empty by nature, the very abiding in that state is called the meditation on the reality of the deity (*devatattvabhāvanā*).

(kha) The Letter Deity (*akṣaradeva*): Prior to meditating upon whichever chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) is to be realized by the practitioner, one should contemplate one's own body as being transformed into the void of space and then further transformed into the moon-maṇḍala of one's own mind.
Having placed the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of that mantra within that moon-maṇḍala of one's own mind, remaining in a state of oneness with it is declared to be the meditation on the Letter Deity.
(ga) The Sound Deity (*dhvanideva*): Suddenly, from the seed-syllable of the mantra in the center of the moon-maṇḍala of one's own mind, a sound resonates like a humming bee.
Thinking thus, meditative absorption (*samādhi*) itself is designated here as the "cultivation of the sound-deity" (*dhvanideva-bhāvanā*).

(Gha) Rūpadeva: Having visualized one’s own mind within the expanse of the sky as resembling the lunar disc, and having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*) of whichever chosen deity therein, one attains one-pointedness of mind through the procedure for cultivating the syllable-deity (*akṣaradeva*) and the sound-deity (*dhvanideva*). From that seed-mantra, a mass of five-colored rays radiates forth; by means of this, one performs worship and veneration of the deities to be propitiated, as well as of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who illuminate the ten directions.
One should reflect in this way: "Subsequently,

the mass of light radiates out to the limit of the six realms of existence— hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and so forth— and having cast away the sins of all living beings, brings them to fullness through the accumulation of merit."
In this way, one should investigate [the practice] repeatedly with profundity.
Then, having visualized the seed-mantra as transformed into one’s own chosen deity, one should maintain one-pointed concentration.
(Ṅa) Regarding the *mudrā*-deity: when the hand-mudrās touch one’s own *uṣṇīṣa*, forehead, throat, and so forth, one becomes personally empowered by the *samaya*-mudrā.
Thus, the very method of cultivation is called the cultivation of the *mudrā* deity.

(c) The sign deity (*nimittadeva*): the practitioner, having meditated with one-pointed concentration while regarding his chosen deity as non-different from the maṇḍala of his own mind, perceives thereafter, upon the background level, the entire receptacle world and the world of sentient beings as pure radiance;
that is to say, the locus and the physical assembly of his chosen deity exist [therein]. Cultivation in this manner is designated as the cultivation of the sign deity.

In order to attain proficiency in meditation, the practitioner practices *prāṇāyāma*. Although the term *prāṇāyāma* is found in both the Anuttara and Kriyā Tantras, there is nevertheless a difference in their ritual procedures (*vidhi*). For instance, in the *Guhyasamāja*, there is the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*).
And that which is the *apāna* bestows longevity upon the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Therefore, it is bound by both *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and its restraint constitutes *prāṇāyāma*.
In the *Kālacakra*, *prāṇāyāma* is said to be the very effort to restrain the moving wind within the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels and cause it to enter into the central channel (*madhyamā*).
In this regard, having established control over the prāṇa and apāna— the inhalation and exhalation— one must effect the cessation of the arising of conceptual constructions therein.
Then, their external movement alone is restrained,
and the internal portion becomes purified.
The manifestation of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) becomes apparent.
Furthermore, in the system of the Tantras, the time for the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is distinct [from other stages].

In the *Anuttara Tantra*, the cultivation of breath control is performed precisely at the time of meditating on the perfected stage (*niṣpannakrama*), and not during any other state; herein, breath control is prescribed within the meditation on the causal deity (*nimittadeva*).
The purposes of *prāṇāyāma* are also distinct.
In the Anuttara Tantra, *prāṇāyāma* is prescribed for the purpose of causing the wind (*vāyu*) to enter the central channel (*madhyamā*).
Here, however, in the Kriyā Tantra, this is accomplished solely for the purpose of obstructing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Through the bondage of conceptual construction, the appearance of the deity becomes clearly manifest.
There is also a distinction regarding the method of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*):

in the *Anuttara Tantra*, it is through the experience of the great bliss produced by the upward and downward movements of the semen obtained from the father, which resides in the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra, and the blood obtained from the mother, which resides in the navel-cakra (*nābhicakra*).
Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is realized.

Here, having restrained conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), one grasps the meditation on the deity with a one-pointed mind; remaining focused on the object of observation (*ālambana*), the unification of the mental continuum is established for the arising of the manifestation of the deity.
3. Regarding the meditation on recitation (*japabhāvanā*), there are two methods of recitation: (ka)
The preliminary rite (*pūrvakarman*) is the primary cultivation.

According to the commentary on the *Dhyānottaratantra*, having become purified through bathing and other rites, one invokes one’s chosen deity before oneself; this includes the performance of worship, offerings, the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and so forth—this is termed the "preliminary rite."

(kha) Regarding the primary cultivation (*pradhānabhāvanā*), relying on the statement in the *Dhyānottaratantra*, the practitioner, endowed with the four limbs, should perform recitation (*japa*) together with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). These four limbs are: the deity who is the support (*āśrayadeva*), the bodhicitta which is the supported, and the sound suddenly arisen from the seed-mantra.
And there is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
For this is an indispensable principle of mantra recitation.

Regarding the visualization of the presiding deity and so forth: the "presiding deity" (*āśrayadeva*) is the practice of visualizing the desired deity (*iṣṭadeva*) in one's own presence, in a form that is both clearly manifest and complete.

In the heart of Āhrīdeva, the very cultivation of the maṇḍala of one’s own mind is called the "reliant bodhicitta" (*āśritabodhicitta*). [Page 73] Regarding the manual for the practice of Kriyātantra, there are four limbs of Kriyātantra practice which are also designated by the name "conduct" (*caryā*).
These names are: the conduct of entry (*praveśacaryā*), the conduct of yoga (*yogacaryā*), the conduct of accomplishment (*sādhanacaryā*), and the conduct of success (*siddhicaryā*).
In the *praveśacaryā* of Kriyātantra, the necessity of the two initiations known as the water (*jala*) and the cloth (*paṭa*) for entry is required.
Through the attainment of the vase initiation (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), the practitioner becomes a partaker in the attainment of the *dharmakāya*;
and through the cloth initiation (*paṭābhiṣeka*), one becomes a partaker in the attainment of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

The water consecration is performed for the purpose of entering the outer maṇḍalas; the vase consecration for entry into the second maṇḍala; the consecration with the vases of all the deities for the third; with the vase of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas for the fourth; with the vase of the Bodhisattvas for the fifth; and with the vases of the Buddhas and the victorious Jina-vijaya vases, the water consecration is carried out.
Furthermore, the cloth consecration is performed upon the head of the practitioner by means of hand-gestures (*mudrā*) and so forth.

In this way, together with the attainment of the two principal empowerments of Kriyātantra, one should maintain the respective commitments and vows (*samaya-saṃvara*). Along with that very [attainment], together with the attainment of the two principal empowerments of Kriyātantra, one should maintain the respective commitments and vows.

Together with that, according to the various traditions (*āmnāya*) of Kriyātantra, for the sake of attaining the status of a Vajrācārya, for the water and cloth empowerments, and for the accomplishment of the mantra of the deity in which the practitioner [is engaged]—

If a flower falls upon that deity, the exposition of the mantra (*mantravyākaraṇa*) is necessary for the recitation of the mantra. At the time of the practitioner’s spiritual practice (*sādhana*), the ritual bath (*snānābhiṣeka*) is bestowed for protection against obstacles that may arise; furthermore, the consecration with the eight auspicious substances (*aṣṭamāṅgalika-dravya*) is given for the sake of increasing sovereignty. Although this is included within the water-bath and the cloth-bath, it is specifically provided here.
Nevertheless, observing the capacity of those to be trained (*vineyajana*), even such an extensive arrangement is required.

Furthermore, by obtaining the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) into the Tathāgata family, one may be considered to have effectively obtained the family consecration of all the principal lords of families; likewise, the Padminī family and the Vajra family should also be understood in this way.
In Kriyātantra, there is only the formal arrangement of an earthen maṇḍala for the purpose of initiation;
therein, there is no arrangement of the mind-maṇḍala, the body-maṇḍala, and so forth.
Yogacaryā consists of these two divisions: the secondary practice of conduct (gauṇaprayogacaryā) and...

2. The primary practice of application (*mukhyaprayogacaryā*). 1. For a practitioner of Action Tantra (*kriyātantrin*), the sādhana should be commenced by first perfecting ten factors—such as the spring season and the time of dawn—with respect to the deity to be accomplished, his painted image on cloth (*paṭacitra*), his physical form (*mūrti*), and the auxiliary materials, while maintaining a state of total dedication toward them in suitable locations for practice, such as mountain caves and valleys.
This is the secondary practice of application (*gauṇeyam prayogacaryā*).

2. Regarding the primary practice of application (*pramukhaprayogacaryā*), there are four limbs: the cultivation of the reality of oneself (*svatattvabhāvanā*), the cultivation of the reality of the deity (*devatattvabhāvanā*), the cultivation of recitation (*japabhāvanā*), and the cultivation of the reality of meditative concentration (*dhyānatattvabhāvanā*); these are they.
1. Cultivation of one's own true nature (*svatattvabhāvanā*): Immediately after receiving initiation for entry into the tantra, the practitioner becomes authorized to practice the tantra.
Otherwise, the tantric practice becomes fruitless.
In the *Kriyātantra*, immediately after obtaining the vase initiation (*kalaśābhiṣeka*), the practitioner becomes a partaker in the attainment of the *dharmakāya*.
Through the two accumulations of wisdom and merit, which serve as the causes for the *dharmakāya*, he meditates on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), his own true nature endowed with six qualities.
At the time of meditating on emptiness endowed with these six qualities, the practitioner must first perform the ritual of bathing and so forth and remain pure.
Then, for the sake of self-protection, he should visualize the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*).
Thereafter, having summoned one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) and established them in a painting on a cloth or in a physical image placed before oneself, one should perform their worship.

Following that, having prepared a seat resembling that of the chosen deity, one should abide in the non-conceptual luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) endowed with the fourfold sixfold yoga (*ṣaḍdharma-yukta-catuṣoṭi*), which is the path for attaining the *dharmakāya*.
And the six dharmas are: (1) ...
(1) The non-existence of conceptual constructions such as the grasped and the grasper;
(2) the absence of appearance in that which is free from conceptual construction;
(3) the non-existence of subtle atoms and the like; (4) [and so forth].
(5) the absence of all signs,
and emptiness free from all conceptual constructions, which, while not being a mere negation, is luminous; (6)
And there is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) experienced as the delight in one's own intrinsic nature (*svasvabhāva-rati*).
These six factors alone constitute the paths for attaining the *dharmakāya*.
2. The cultivation of the deity-reality (*devatattva-bhāvanā*) is said to be the path for attaining the *rūpakāya*, the reality of the deity.
This has six divisions, namely: the deity of emptiness (śūnyadeva), the deity of the syllable (akṣaradeva),
and the deity of sound (dhvanideva).
The deity of form,
the deity of the seal, and the deity of the sign.

(ka) Śūnyadeva (Tattvadeva): Having established that the bodhicitta—which is non-different from the ultimate reality desired by one’s own mind—is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), the very abiding in that state is called the meditation on the deity-reality (*devatattva-bhāvanā*). (kha) Akṣaradeva: The practitioner should first transform his own body into the void of space within the sphere of emptiness, and then contemplate it as transformed into the moon-maṇḍala of his own mind, wherein the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) is to be meditated upon.

Having placed that seed-syllable of the mantra upon the moon-maṇḍala of one's own mind and remaining in a state of oneness with it, this very state is declared to be the meditation on the Letter Deity (*akṣaradeva*).

(ga) As for the Sound Deity (*dhvanideva*): having realized that a humming sound resonates suddenly from the mantra-seed within the center of the moon-maṇṍala of one's own mind, the meditative absorption (*samādhiti*) therein is designated as the meditation on the Sound Deity.

(gha) Rūpadeva: Having visualized one’s own mind in the expanse of the sky as resembling a lunar disc, and having established therein the seed-syllable (*mantrabīja*) of whichever chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) one desires, through the method of meditating upon the syllable-deity (*akṣaradeva*) and the sound-deity (*dhvanideva*), the mind becomes one-pointed. From that seed-mantra, a mass of five-colored rays radiates forth; by means of these, the worshipers perform offerings and veneration to the deities to be propitiated, to the Buddhas, and to the Bodhisattvas who shine throughout the ten directions.
Thus one should reflect. Thereafter,

one should contemplate with profound depth and repeated application how this mass of light, having extended as far as the six realms of existence— beginning with hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and humans, and including all others— dispels the sins of all living beings and brings them to complete fulfillment through the accumulation of merit.
Having visualized that seed-syllable mantra as transformed into one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), one should practice one-pointed concentration.

(Ṅa) Murādeva states: when one’s own crown, forehead, throat, and so forth are touched by the hand-gesture (*mudrā*), one becomes empowered by the pledge-gesture (*samayamudrā*); such a method of meditative cultivation is precisely what is called the meditation on the deity of the gesture.

(ca) The deity of signs (*nimittadeva*): The practitioner, having meditated with one-pointed concentration while regarding his chosen deity as non-different from the circle of his own mind, then perceives the entire environment (*bhājanaloka*) and the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) upon that foundation as pure radiance;

that is to say, the abode and the physical assembly of his chosen deity exist in this manner. Such meditation is designated as the meditation on the deity of signs. To attain proficiency in meditation, the practitioner practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Although the term *prāṇāyāma* is found in both the Anuttara-tantra and the Kriyā-tantra, there is indeed a difference in the ritual injunctions.
For instance, in the *Guhyasamāja*, there is the *prāṇa*-wind, and the *apāna* is that which bestows length upon the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

Therefore, *prāṇāyāma* consists of the binding of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, as well as their restraint. In the *Kālacakra*, *prāṇāyāma* is defined as the very effort to restrain the moving wind within the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels and cause it to enter the central channel (*madhyamā*).
Here, having established control over *prāṇa* and *apāna*, that is, inhalation and exhalation, one must effect the restraint of the arising of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) therein.
Then, only the movement toward that external [object] is established;
at that time, the internal portion becomes purified,
and the manifestation of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) becomes evident.
In the system of the Tantras, the timing for the practice of *prāṇāyāma* is also distinct.

In the *Anuttara-tantra*, the cultivation of *prāṇāyāma* is performed specifically at the time of meditating on the *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion), and not during any other state; here, *prāṇāyāma* is prescribed within the meditation on the causal deity (*nimittadeva*).
Furthermore, the purposes of *prāṇāyāma* are also distinct.
In the Anuttara Tantra, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed for the purpose of causing the wind to enter the avadhūtī;
however, in this Kriyā Tantra, it is performed solely to restrain conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Through the binding of conceptual construction, the manifestation of the deity becomes clearly manifest.
There is also a distinction regarding the procedure for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*):

in the *Anuttara-tantra*, great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) is directly realized through the experience of the great bliss produced by the upward and downward movements of the paternal semen received at the crown wheel (*uṣṇīṣacakra*) and the maternal blood received at the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*).

In this regard, without allowing conceptual constructions to enter, one should grasp the visualization of the deity with a one-pointed mind; remaining fixed upon the object of focus, the unification of the mental fluctuations is prescribed for the purpose of generating the appearance of the deity.
3. Regarding the practice of recitation (*japa-bhāvanā*), there are two methods of recitation: (ka) preliminary action (*pūrvakarma*) and (kha) [the subsequent practice].
The Primary Cultivation (*pradhānabhāvanā*).

(a) According to the commentary on the *Dhyānottara-tantra*, having become purified through bathing and other rites, one performs the preliminary action (*pūrvakarman*), which consists of invoking the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) before oneself, performing worship and veneration, generating the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and so forth.

(b) Regarding the primary cultivation, relying on the teaching of the *Dhyānottara-tantra*, the practitioner, together with the four limbs, should perform recitation (*japa*) along with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
These are the four factors: the deity who is the support, the bodhicitta which is supported,
the sound suddenly arisen from the seed-mantra,
and breath control (prāṇāyāma).
This is indeed the indispensable reality of mantra recitation (*mantra-japa*).

Regarding the meditation on the deity as the support and so forth: the "deity as support" (*āśrayadeva*) refers to the practice of meditating on one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) in a form that is perfectly clear and complete, directly before oneself.
The very meditation on the maṇḍala of one’s own mind within the heart of that deity as the support is called the "bodhicitta as supported" (*āśritabodhicitta*).

Above that, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), which is uttered through its innate nature; this is called the "sound-seed mantra" (*dhvanibījamantra*).
Having performed the meditation on these three constituent parts with perfect clarity, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

That is to say, having restrained the vital air and become steady upon the focal point endowed with its three limbs before oneself, the repetition of the mantra should be performed within the mind alone.

During the period of mantra recitation, one should contemplate that the mantra is being uttered by the heart of the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) visualized before oneself as if it were one's own self; and one should restrain the breath according to the requirements of the practice. At the time of releasing the breath, considering oneself non-different from the chosen deity, one should assume the ego-identification (ahaṅkāra) of the chosen deity.
During the state of mantra recitation (*japa*), there should be a very clear pronunciation of the short and long vowels, such as *i* and *u*.
When one becomes fatigued from repeated recitation, one should rest by becoming absorbed in the non-conceptual nature of one's own reality (*svatattva*).

Apart from the time for rest, one should remain with a one-pointed mind focused on the object of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) before oneself, until the experience of the non-duality of the deity and one's own self arises.

In this Kriyātantra, for those who regard their own body as having the nature of the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), there is this procedure for the recitation of mantras according to the ritual manual (*paddhati*).

Those scholars who accept the method of meditating on the form of the deity within one’s own body should, having themselves become endowed with the three limbs described above, meditate upon themselves as the chosen deity;

then, at the time of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), during the duration of the breath, they should contemplate that everything—the seed-mantra and so forth residing in the support of one’s own heart—has become composed of light. Thus, having closed the nine gates [of the body], they should fix the mind upon the seed-mantra.
Having set [the breath] in motion, the recitation (*japa*) is performed.

At the limit of the release of the inhalation (*śvāsa*), the exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is visualized as having entered the mandala of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) situated externally before one's eyes.
4. Regarding the cultivation of the reality of meditation (*dhyāna-tattva-bhāvanā*), there are three divisions: (ka)
Meditation on that which abides in fire; meditation on that which abides in sound.
(ka) Meditation (dhyāna), situated within the resonance (dhvani).

Meditation on the Fire-Abiding (Agnistha-dhyāna): Having contemplated the seed-syllable as being extremely peaceful and uninterrupted, like the flame of a lamp, in the center of the moon-mandala in the heart of one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) visualized before oneself, and having restrained the prāṇa and apāna breaths by holding the breath as far as possible, the one-pointed concentration of the mind upon that focal object is called Agnistha-dhyāna.
By means of this, assistance is obtained for the accomplishment of rites of pacification (śāntika) and other such purposes.

(kha) Meditation on Sound (*dhvani-dhyāna*): One should visualize the chosen deity within the lunar disc at the heart-lotus, adorned with the seed-mantra surrounded by a mass of fire in the four directions; having thus directed the mind for a brief moment, one should behold [the deity].
Then, gradually, the seed-syllables are dissolved, and from that, the resonance of the mantra (*mantra-dhvani*) arises.
Having meditated in this way, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) as before and achieve one-pointedness.

Herein is the intended meaning of breath control: the wind that has entered all the apertures is called *prāṇa*, and the wind that has exited from there is called *apāna*; these two winds are known as inhalation and exhalation.

By restraining them, the abiding of the sound of the mantra—equal to the sound of a bell arising suddenly from the lunar orb—is precisely what is called "meditation abiding in sound" (*dhvanistha-dhyāna*).

(ga) Meditative concentration on the internal resonance (*dhvanyantaḥstha-dhyāna*): When one reflects upon the sound of mantra within this state of meditative concentration, and when one is poised in a non-conceptual self-nature that is devoid of arising, abiding, destruction, and cessation, the wisdom known as *adhiprajñā* arises; this serves as the material cause for both liberation and omniscience.
This method of practice has been described primarily by relying upon the commentary on the *Dhyānottaratantra* composed by Buddhaguhya.

The practice of accomplishment (*sādhanācaryā*) is described in the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*: if, after the recitation of mantras according to the prescribed ritual, one wishes to achieve mantra-siddhi, then one must perform the conduct for the accomplishment of the sādhana. In this regard, it should be understood that if a practitioner of mantra fulfills the required number of recitations without having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he will obtain only the fruits of those belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.
Furthermore, one will not attain the state of Vajradhara by that [means alone].
Therefore, for a practitioner of Mantrayāna, the generation of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is indispensable.
A practitioner of Kriyātantra attains three kinds of accomplishment according to their spiritual lineage (kula).

From the Tathāgata family, the rite of pacification (*śāntika*) is obtained; from the Lotus family, the rite of excellence (*śreṣṭhakarma*); and from the Vajra family, the rite of ferocity (*raudrakarma*).

Furthermore, according to the internal distinctions among the families, pacification is accomplished through the Principal Family (*pradhānakula*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*) through the Sovereign Family (*adhipatikula*), and the rite of ferocity through the families of the Wrathful and the Wrathful Consorts.

One who follows the path of ritual action (*kriyātantrī*) attains three kinds of accomplishments (*siddhi*) according to their essential nature: the superior *kriyātantrī* attains the station of a *vidyādhara*; the middling one attains the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and so forth; and the inferior *kriyātantrī* attains subtle knowledge of all scriptures, as well as minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*) such as levitation (*laghimā*), alchemy (*rasāyana*), swift movement, subjugation, and killing. According to the specific accomplishment they rely upon, the practitioners of ritual action gradually become partakers of the accomplishment of the body (*kāyasiddhi*), the accomplishment of substances (*dravyasiddhi*), and the accomplishment of enjoyment (*saṃbhogasiddhi*).

For the attainment of this accomplishment (*siddhi*), once the required number of mantra recitations has been completed, the practice of the means of achievement (*sādhanācaryā*) must indeed be performed, and not otherwise.

There are two rules for the practice of the means of achievement: in the general practice, one must perform at the three times of day the worship and adoration of one’s chosen deity according to the ritual, including the confession of sins, supplication, and dedication of merit;
furthermore, the *Sūtrānta* should be recited.
Thus, during the practice (*sādhana*), the manifestation of light through an image established before one's eyes or a stūpa and so forth;
the absence of hunger, thirst, and the like during the practice; the vigor of the body; and the vision of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) in dreams—these are the signs of success in the practice.
When these signs have arisen, one should consult one’s own guru and undertake the conduct for attainment (*siddhicaryā*).

In order to achieve the specific accomplishments (*viśeṣasādhana*), one should take up the sword and other implements, perform the recitation of mantras (*japa*), fire offerings (*homa*), and so forth.
Having gone to a pure field such as Khecarī and having employed the ointments (*añjana*) and other means, the practices (*caryā*) should be undertaken;
by that, one must strive to attain the state of a Vidyādhara.

Having rendered one's own body subtle, the eight qualities of the Lord are to be attained. Following the conduct of accomplishment (*siddhicaryā*) according to the method of practice of the Action Tantra (*kriyātantra*), the practitioner is able to obtain accomplishments (*siddhi*) at will.

As stated above, in the absence of the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), through this very practice one is able to attain the state of a Śrāvaka and all types of mundane and supramundane accomplishments—whether inferior, middling, or superior.
Therefore, the supreme state (*paramapada*) must be the objective;
the objective of the practice of *Kriyātantra* is not the attainment of minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*),
but rather the very attainment of Buddhahood.

According to the practice of Kriyātantra, a period of eight kalpas or three kalpas elapses for the attainment of Buddhahood. However, in Kriyātantra texts such as the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, it is taught that through intense exertion, a practitioner may attain the supreme state even in a single lifetime.

In Kriyātantra, there are five paths and ten stages; the systematic explanation of these five paths and ten stages according to Kriyātantra is as follows: 1. Immediately after receiving the initiation (*abhiṣeka*) of Kriyātantra...

Starting from the arising of an uncontrived aspiration, "I, as a practitioner, shall attain perfect enlightenment through the practice of Kriyātantra," the path that precedes the direct realization of the insight (*vipaśyanā*) which awakens one to emptiness—by means of the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) based on the internal recitation of mantras—is called the *saṃbhāramārga* (path of accumulation) of Kriyātantra. 2. Starting from the generation of insight (*vipaśyanā*), the stage prior to the direct realization of emptiness through the cultivation of the union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight is designated as the *prayogamārga* (path of application).

3. Having realized emptiness through the gateway of the meditative concentration of insight (*vipaśyanā-samādhi*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—which is the path for generating the antidote to the coarse portions of the great afflictive obscurations (*mahākleśāvaraṇa*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—arises; this is the stage of the Joyous (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). 4. Beginning from the generation of the antidote to the coarse portions of the great afflictive obscurations to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, up until the exhaustion of the subtlest of subtle obscurations, there is the meditative concentration known as the "Vajra Seat" (*vajrāsana*), which brings about the attainment of Buddhahood.
The state of the preceding moment is the path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
There are nine stages, beginning with Vimalā and Prabhākarī.
The afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are what are to be abandoned through the path of meditation.

The afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are divided into coarse, medium, and subtle; likewise, there are three divisions each for the medium obscuration and the subtle obscuration. Thus, there are nine divisions, which are also described as the factors to be abandoned on the various stages (*bhūmi*). When these nine afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) pertaining to their respective stages have been eliminated, the practitioner gradually attains the higher stages.
5. In Kriyātantra, the state of perfect enlightenment itself constitutes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) and the supreme state (*paramapada*).
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Jñānasamuccaya* for the practitioner of Kriyātantra: "In that regard, there is an absence of the cultivation of the deity’s body within one’s own body.
Based on this statement, a difference of opinion exists among the learned.
Jonang Je Tsunpa and others accept the absence of the meditation on the deity’s body within one’s own body here.
However, scholars such as Ācārya Chökyi Zangpo (Chongkhapa) and others have accepted the method of meditating on the deity’s body within one’s own body in the Kriyātantra,
providing numerous scriptural citations and logical arguments in its support.

Ācārya Karmāṭhinala and others maintain that for a practitioner of the *kriyātantra*, there are two levels: the primary and the secondary. It is also stated that the primary practitioner visualizes the deity within his own body, whereas the other, having visualized the deity facing him, recites the mantra.

This final position alone appears most consistent, since in numerous authoritative texts of Kriyātantra, the existence, non-existence, or both of the contemplation of the deity within one's own body are frequently encountered. Therefore,
it is difficult to determine how appropriate it would be to provide an explanation based on a single specific meaning.
Even through a general investigation, it is understood from this statement of the *pāramitānaya*: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess unimpeded vision everywhere;
everything is indeed before them, and I stand before them.
[It is said: "Whatever practitioner intensely desires, the Teacher always remains in his presence. One who maintains this intention with absolute conviction—

In the ritual procedure of Kriyātantra, for the purpose of engaging in that practice, it is not improper to invoke one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) before oneself and establish the rules for worship, veneration, and meditative cultivation.

Furthermore, the absolute absence of the conception of the deity within one’s own body must not be accepted; for if this were the case, there would be no distinction whatsoever between the Mantranaya and the Pāramitānaya based on such a conviction.
Moreover, there would be an absence of the material cause for the Form Body (rūpakāya), and consequently, the transformation of the result into the path would also be impossible here.

It has been stated in the *Maitreya-sādhana* composed by Ārya Asaṅga, in the *Ekādaśānana-sādhana* composed by the Bhikṣuṇī Śrīdevī, and in the *Tārā-sādhana* composed by Candragomin, that one should meditate on the divinity within one's own body;
all of this would likewise be invalid.

Therefore, by examining the aforementioned method, it is understood that in Kriyātantra, two distinct procedures are obtained—one for the cultivation of the divine nature within one's own body and one for its non-cultivation; it does not even seem appropriate to establish the logical justification for either one side alone.
This distinction arises in accordance with the capacity of those to be trained (*vineyajana*).
From the perspective of the dissemination of the Tantric scriptures in the land of Tibet, during the earlier period of the teachings, the Kriyā and Caryā Tantras were predominant;
furthermore, the methods of exposition and practice primarily followed the system of Ācārya Buddhaguhya.
During the later period of the teachings, the Ubhaya and Yoga Tantras became predominant in both external and internal practice.

Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna also established in his own commentary on the *Bodhipathapradīpa* that all dhāraṇīs are subsumed within Kriyātantra. Therefore, this question arises here: since the method for the practice (*sādhana*) is generally not present in the collections of dhāraṇīs, by what procedure should that practice be performed?

Regarding this, it is stated by Buddhaguhya in his *Commentary on the Subāhuparipṛcchā Sūtra* that the practice of the sādhana of all Action Tantras (*kriyātantra*) should be performed by condensing it into its four branches: the conduct of entry (*praveśacaryā*), the conduct of application (*prayogacaryā*), the conduct of accomplishment (*sādhanasiddhicaryā*), and the conduct of success (*siddhicaryā*). In those texts where the complete procedure is not set forth, one should practice by taking as one's basis the *Dhyānottaratantra*, the *Susiddhitantra*, and the *Subāhuparipṛcchā Sūtra*.

The practice of entry (*praveśacaryā*) is primarily taught in the *Guhyasāmānyatantra*, the practice of application (*prayogacaryā*) in the *Dhyānottaratantra*, and the practice of accomplishment (*sādhanācaryā*) in the *Susiddhitantra*; furthermore,
the characteristics and classifications of these practices were delineated in the *Subāhuparipṛcchāsūtra*.

Among the *Guhyasāmānyatantra*, the *Susiddhitantra*, the *Subāhuparipṛcchāsūtra*, and the *Dhyānottaratantra*, the preceding *Guhyasāmānyatantra* is of extensive scope, while the *Dhyānottaratantra* is a jewel of a concise work.
In the *Guhyasāmānyatantra*, the procedure for initiation (*abhiṣeka*) was taught for the sake of bringing those who are not yet mature vessels to full maturity.
In this [text], one thousand five hundred mandalas of the Tathāgata and other families are described.
Herein, indications regarding the mandalas of all families within Kriyātantra are also found.

Beyond this, the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) mandalas to be performed on the first day of the mandala consecration for Caryātantra, Yoga[tantra], and Anuttarayoga[tantra] is also obtained.
In this [work], there is only one section (pariccheda).
In the Susiddhitantro, thirty-eight sequential procedures are summarized, as follows:
(1) the sequence of the characteristics of secret mantras; (2) ...
(3) The sequence of the characteristics of the teacher; (4) The sequence of the characteristics of the means of accomplishment; (5) The sequence of the practitioner of mantra.
(6) The sequence of the characteristics of the locations;
(7) the sequence of the disciples for the vidyās and mantras;
(8) the sequence of the characteristics of the flowers.
(9) The sequence of the characteristics of fragrance;
(10) the sequence of the characteristics of incense;
(11) the sequence of the characteristics of light.
(12) The sequence of the ritual for the bali offering;
(13) The sequence of the ritual for the practices of pacification, enrichment, and subjugation;
(14) The sequence of the characteristics of the different types of accomplishments.
(15) The sequence of the ritual for invocation; (16) The sequence of the ritual for worship; (17) The sequence of the ritual for protection.
(18) The sequence of the ritual for recitation (*japa*), (19) the sequence of the ritual for the propitiation of the deity,
and (20) the sequence of the ritual for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the deity.
(21) The sequence of the ritual for acceptance;
(22) the sequence of the ritual for receiving the knowledge-mantras; (23) the sequence of the ritual for perfecting the knowledge-mantras.
The sequence of ritual procedure beloved by the gods (aojas), (24) the sequence of ritual procedure for the collection of the components of the means of accomplishment, (25)
(26) the sequence of the procedure for the characteristics of substances;
(27) the sequence of the procedure for the acquisition of substances;
(28) the sequence of the procedure for the purification of substances.
(29) the sequence of rules for the measurement of substances,
(30) the sequence of rules for the substratum of substances,
and (31) the sequence of rules for the time of the performance of the means.

(33) the sequence of the ritual for the consecration of substances;

In the *Subāhuparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the procedure for initiation as taught in the *Guhyasāmānya-tantra* is clarified, along with the procedures for mantra practice and the fulfillment of rites according to the *Susiddhi-tantra*; furthermore, the methods for attaining both common and uncommon accomplishments (*siddhi*) based upon the activities of pacifying, enriching, and subjugating are clearly elucidated.
This work is divided into eleven chapters,
and it is stated that Subāhu is Vajrapāṇi,
who is a bodhisattva destined to attain the state of enlightenment in his very next life.
His very name was Subāhu.
For the *Dhyānottaratantra* is indeed one part of the *Mahākriyātantra-uṣṇīṣatantra*; for this reason, it is called the *Uttaratantra*.
Herein, the ten principles (*tattva*) of the *Kriyātantra* are set forth.
In this work, *prāṇāyāma* is also investigated, and this text is composed in fifty-three verses.
Buddhaguhya and Bodhisattvaśrī are considered the two great masters of the Kriyātantra.
Buddhaguhya composed a commentary rich in essence for the *Dhyānottaratantra* and the *Subāhuparipṛcchāsūtra*, and he also sketched the general outline of the words and meanings of the sutra.
The work titled *Upāyopasaṃgraha* was composed by Bodhiśreṣṭha within the *Susiddhitantra*.

This text is of great utility for the detailed understanding of the methods of practice (*sādhanavidhi*) described in the *Kriyātantra*. Chapter Three: *Caryātantra*, the *Caryātantrābhyudaya*. In his own commentary on the *Bodhipathapradīpa*, Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna mentions the *Vairocanābhisambodhitantra*, the *Vajrāvalyabhiṣekatantra*, and others as belonging to the *Caryātantra*.
Eight thousand tantras were established.

Buston also [identified] the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* as the Root Tantra (*mūla-tantra*) and the *Guhyasamāja-tantra* (referred to here as *Guhyaśreṣṭha-tantra*) as the Explanatory Tantra (*uttara-tantra*).
He also considered the three tantric texts beginning with the *Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka* to be included within the Carya-tantra.
Among other scholars, such as Ḍod-gon Chos-rgyal and Fags-pa-prabhu of the Śākya tradition, they maintain that there is no cultivation of the deity’s body within one's own body in the Kriya-tantra;
for this very reason, they also consider the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa* to be included within the Carya-tantra.
According to this master’s view, the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, the *Acalamahākalpa-tantra*,
and the *Yamāntakakrodhavijaya-tantra* are also Caryātantras.
Among other groups of scholars, such as the great paṇḍita Puṇyakīrti and others, seven texts were counted, including the *Acalamahākrodharāja-tantra* and the *Nīlāmbaradhara-vajrapāla*.

In brief, the preliminary background for this [work] is presented here: (1) According to the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana generally teaches the Dharma in the Akaniṣṭha realm throughout the four periods of time.
Furthermore, according to the occasion, he manifests as a nirmāṇakāya on Mount Sumeru, in Jambudvīpa, and other locations to teach the Dharma.

In particular, the teaching of the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Tantra*, which is unique among the Carya Tantras, was delivered by the Blessed One Vairocana at the place of attaining the reality of Buddhahood known as the *Kusumatalagarbhālaṅkāravyūha*.
In connection with this, it is stated in the introductory chapter (*nidānaparivarta*) of the *Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka Tantra* that this field indicates the infinite realms of saṃsāra.
Within a single *saṃsāradhātu*, infinite world-systems (*lokadhātu*) are subsumed.

A hundred billion sets of four continents, a hundred billion Mount Sumeru mountains, a hundred billion great oceans, the sun, the moon, and so forth—all these together are called a *trisāhasramahāsāhasraloka* (trichiliocosm).
Thus, [a collection of] a hundred billion such is termed a *kusumatalagarbhālaṅkāra*.
Thus, it is called the "Ornament of the Flower-Bottom Womb" (*kusumatalagarbhālaṅkāra*),

which refers to the field that was purified through the conduct of Bodhisattvas prior to their attainment of Buddhahood by the Blessed Vairocana; it is precisely this field of the array of the Flower-Bottom Womb Ornament that has arisen through the perfection of inconceivable maturation.

Just as when the light of the sun has spread through space, space and that light become non-different, in the very same way, the Buddha Mahāvairocana, abiding in the state of non-duality, teaches to sentient beings the Dharma-discourse named "Abiding in the Equality of Body," the Dharma-discourse named "Abiding in the Equality of Speech," and the Dharma-discourse named "Abiding in the Equality of Mind.
Because body, speech, and mind are unfathomable, the body, speech, and mind of the Blessed One Vairocana are worthy of entering all the stages (*bhūmis*).

Thus, in this very field, the Blessed One Vairocana was questioned by Vajrapāṇi; at that time, having made a detailed analysis of this tantric treatise into seven sections (*skandha*) and twenty-four chapters (*parivarta*), it is taught.
Its exposition is as follows: (1)
(2) The sequence of the analysis of the mind (*cittavibhaṅgakrama*) which establishes the method for generating the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*);

(3) The sequence of the analysis of entering the maṇḍala impelled by great compassion, including the procedure for initiation (*abhiṣeka*), the characteristics of mantras, and the pacification of obstacles;
(4) The sequence of the analysis of the general treasury of mantras (*sāmānyamantrakośa*).
(5) The sequence of the analysis of worldly accomplishment;
(6) The sequence of the analysis of the reality of the means for achieving accomplishment;
(7) The sequence of the analysis of the instruction on the meditation on the deity.
(8) The sequence of the analysis of the signless;
(9) The sequence of the analysis of the recitation of supramundane mantras;
(10) The sequence of the analysis of the wheel of syllables.
(11) The sequence of the analysis of the sequence of mudrās;
(12) The sequence of the analysis of the entry into the mantra-maṇḍala;
(13) The sequence of the analysis of the eight mudrās of mantra.
(14) The sequence of the analysis of knowledge, mantras, and vows;
(15) The sequence of the analysis of the means for the training of a bodhisattva;
(16) The sequence of the analysis of the master’s knowledge of reality.
(17) The sequence of the analysis of the arrangement of syllables;
(18) The sequence of the analysis arising from the hundred-syllable [mantra];
(19) The sequence of the analysis as specified by the application of fruits.
(20) The sequence of the analysis of the means for accomplishing one’s own true nature;
(21) The sequence of the analysis of the ritual of the hundred syllables;
(22) The sequence of the analysis of the instruction on the intrinsic nature of perfect enlightenment.
(23) The sequence of the analysis of the practice of the three samayas;
(24) the sequence of the analysis as taught by the Tathāgata; and the ritual for the conduct of a Bodhisattva according to the mantras, together with the sequential analysis.
The great scholar Buston also counted the twenty-sixth chapter. When,

during the time of the Buddha’s previous birth as a Bodhisattva, he was questioned by Brahmins regarding the different types of sacrificial fires, he explained that because he had attained Buddhahood through the practice of the forty-four types of fires prescribed in the Vedas—
having previously mastered twelve of those fires— the ritual procedure for the fire offering (*homa*) was also included in the count.
This final chapter is not currently found in the edition of the *Derge Tanjur*.
There exists the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, which is the root tantra;
herein, there are three mandalas.
The *Guhyasreṣṭhatantra*, found in the Tibetan language together with this *Mūlatantra*, is designated as the *Uttaratantra*.
It contains seven chapters (*parivarta*), namely: (1) the fire sacrifice for pacification (*śāntihoma*) for the purpose of the four rites beginning with pacification; (2) ... [and so forth].
(3) The ritual procedure for the nourishment-homa; (4) the ritual procedure for the subjugation-homa; (5) the fire-offering for the sake of accomplishing the fierce conduct.
(6) The procedure for meditative cultivation preceded by the presentation of the vowels, consonants, and initial syllables;
(7) the rite of expiation for past actions prior to the cultivation of the deity;
and the procedure for entering the secret maṇḍala together with the arising of great compassion, empowered by the Tathāgatas.

Regarding the subject matter of this tantra, according to the account of Buston, this [text] is incomplete, because many statements extracted under its name are presented in the treatise that are not found in the currently available *Guhyatantra*. (2) As for the *Acalamahākrodharājatantra*, it is stated in this very work regarding the scope of its teaching that the Blessed One [taught it] within a celestial palace adorned with various jewels upon a wind-mandala, amidst infinite arrays.

Seated upon a lion throne arisen from infinite merits, surrounded by a full assembly of Bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi, Avalokiteśvara, Maitreya, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana, as well as Śrāvakas and deities beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the Blessed One dwelt there. Impelled by great compassion, he taught this tantra with a mind directed toward sentient beings.

(3) This teaching of the *Nīlāmbaravajrapātāla-tantra* was proclaimed by the Blessed One while dwelling together with Vajrapāṇi in the world of the Nāgas situated in the seven successive subterranean realms, manifesting a mass of light from his two feet.
Having converted King Nāgānanda, Upānanda, and others, as well as the *nāgas*, and having performed their subjugation and consecration, this tantra was taught.
There are seven chapters herein, namely: (1) the Introduction Chapter (*nidāna-parivarta*); (2) ...
Chapter 3: The Removal of Obstacles to Wealth and Means; Chapter 4: The Removal of Irremediable Diseases; Chapter [5]: The Maṇḍala.
(5) The Chapter on the Accomplishment of Yakṣas; (6) The Chapter on the Accomplishment of Nāgas; and (7) The Chapter on Narratives.

(4) This *Nīlāmbaratrilokavinaya-tantra* was taught by the Blessed One while residing in the palace known as Laṅkāvatī on the southern side of Mount Sumeru to the gods among the infinite asuras, beginning with Vajrapāṇi. And in this [tantra], there are four chapters. (1)
Chapter 2: The Introduction; Chapter 3: The Subduing of Pātāla;
Chapter 4: The Subduing of the World of Men.
And there is the section on the Taming of the World of Space.

From the observation of the introductory section, it is understood that the practitioner, by the power of the means of faith and devotion, may realize reality directly and establish a straightforward relationship with the Tathāgata; having posed questions and taken them as a basis, he is able to compose a treatise.
The teaching of the *Caryātantra* was imparted by Mahāvairocana at all times.
From the observation of the *Kusumatalagarbhālaṅkāravyūha* and other realms, the entire world is perceived as the field for the Tathāgata’s teaching.
By this it becomes perfectly clear that whenever meditation and cultivation are performed by any practitioner in any corner of the world, the Tathāgata manifests and instructs them.

The nature of Caryātantra is as follows: a practitioner who, having purified themselves through external bathing and other rites, meditates upon their chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), and who also prescribes the practice of internal meditation, is said to be a follower of Caryātantra.

In the *Jñānasamuccaya*, the Blessed One, clarifying the nature of Caryātantra, stated: "In Kriyātantra, there is the cultivation of various ritual practices for the sake of purifying body, speech, and mind through the method of meditating on the six deity-tattvas;
and there is meditation preceded by the experience of bliss through acts such as laughter with the Action Seal (karmamudrā) goddess described therein."
The essential nature of the path of Caryātantra is as follows:
in the Caryātantra, by primarily perceiving one’s own body as the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya*), the practitioner swiftly attains the blessing of the body;

by meditating on one’s own speech as the form of mantra, one attains the blessing of speech; and by meditating on the nature of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) within one’s own mind, one attains the blessing of the mind.
