By meditating on oneself as having a divine form, attachment and delusion toward one's own body are extinguished, and divine qualities are easily attained.
That is to say, by meditating on the result as being the path itself, the fulfillment of the two accumulations of merit occurs.

Having visualized one's chosen deity in a painted cloth or similar medium, and having transformed one’s own body into the form of the deity for the sake of propitiation and so forth, the two accumulations are swiftly gathered through the practice of such meditation.
This very procedure was taught in the *Caryā-tantras*.
Therefore, this method is considered superior to that of the ordinary *Kriyā-tantras*.
Regarding the internal divisions of the *caryātantra*, just as with the *kriyātantra*, there are three divisions of the *caryātantra*:
(1) the Tathāgata family, (2) the Lotus family, and (3) [the Vajra family].
And the Vajra family.
According to the opinion of Koṅṭul Rin-po-che Mahodaya, this can also be divided into the three families known as body, speech, and mind;
for just as the Tathāgata family exists as the body family.
The Lotus family, the Speech family,
the Vajra family, and indeed the Mind family exist;
this very [set] is also called the gateway of the Caryātantra.

In general, all Tathāgatas and their families (*kula*) are in reality entirely non-different; they merely manifest in diverse forms according to the skillful means (*upāya*) employed to follow the inclinations of those to be trained (*vineyajana*).
Just as a practitioner, having taken the form and appearance of the Blessed Śākyamuni as an object of focus in the mind, meditates and thereby directly realizes that very form.
In this very way, the people of Siṃhala fashion the image of the deity as their own self; likewise, those from China, Japan, and Tibet do so in the form of their own physical appearance.
Thus, body, speech, and mind are in reality entirely non-different.

As it is said in the *Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka Tantra*: "O noble son, for one who enters the maṇḍala and practices the mantra-conduct, there is no mind apart from speech, nor is there speech apart from the mind."
Speech does not exist apart from the body, nor does the body exist apart from speech; therefore,
it should be understood that speech itself is the mind.
The mind alone is the form of the deity, and speech indeed possesses that very form of the deity.
Having thus realized the non-difference of these three, through the practice of meditation, one's body becomes the mantra-speech in the form of the chosen deity.
It will be established in the mind and the consciousness.
By this it is made perfectly clear that body, speech, and mind are also one and the same.
Even in the Caryātantras, as in the Kriyātantras, the family (*kula*) was divided into three parts for the sake of accomplishing the rites of pacification, enrichment, and subjugation.
In this context, the nature of the deity differs from that of the Kriyātantra;

for instance, in the Tathāgata family, Vairocana and Acala or Akṣobhya are accepted, while in the Vajra family, Vajrapāṇi and Nīlāmbara are accepted. Padyakarapa states: "The Caryātantra is also for the most part similar to the Kriyātantra."
Therefore, apart from Kriyātantra, there are no separate divisions of *kula* within this [system].

Although it is possible to establish five *kula* divisions for both Kriyātantra and Caryātantra, since the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the practitioners (*sādhaka*) of these two tantras are subsumed within the three *kulas*, only a threefold division of *kula* is appropriate.
The master known as Ḍoṅ-ñag Chos-’byuṅ-bzaṅ-po considers the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, a text of the Tathāgata family within the *Sāmānyacaryā-tantra*,
to be the *Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka-tantra* belonging to the Vajra family. By this it is stated that the *Padyakula-tantra* has not been translated into the Tibetan language.
According to the opinion of Paṇḍita Puṇyakīrti, the *Hayagrīva-tantra* is a work belonging to the *Padyakula*, which was indeed translated into the Tibetan language.
Buston considers the *Caryā-tantra* to be equivalent to the *Kriyā-tantra*; therefore, he explains the *Caryā-tantra* separately.
The *Caryā-tantra-sādhanapaddhati* and the *Caryā-tantra-sādhanavidhi* are divided into four sections by Śrī Buddhaguhya: (1) ...
(2) The practice of entering, (3) the practice of yoga, and (4) the accomplishment of the means of attainment.

And the conduct for attaining accomplishment (*siddhicaryā*). 1. Regarding the conduct of entry (*praveśacaryā*), there are further two divisions: external entry, which is the ritual of initiation (*abhiṣeka*), or internal entry, which is the observance of the pledges and vows (*samaya-saṃvara*).
The matter of consecration will be explained in detail later. Now, regarding the practice of Caryātantra, we shall provide an enumeration of those consecrations whose attainment is indispensable.

It is also stated in the *Jñānatilaka*: "A practitioner of the Carya-tantra must receive all the empowerments of the Kriya-tantra; that is to say, the water, cloth, vajra, bell, and name empowerments must be received. Through the vase empowerment, one's rebirth in the lower realms is destroyed."

This consecration washes away the seed of the wheel of existence; having dispatched the practitioner from the first stage, the Joyous (*pramuditā*), up to the tenth stage called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), it causes them to attain Buddhahood.

From the cloth-consecration (*paṭābhiṣeka*), the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics are obtained; from the bell-consecration (*ghaṇṭābhiṣeka*), the attainment of the sixty qualities of Brahma’s voice occurs; and from the vajra-consecration (*vajrābhiṣeka*), there is the path to the attainment of gnosis (*jñāna*) as it truly is.
The staircase is now opened.

For the attainment of initiation (*abhiṣeka*) in the Carya Tantras, there exists a systematic arrangement of both the elaborate (*prapañca*) and the non-elaborate (*niṣprapañca*) mandalas. In the elaborate mandala, a mandala made of clay is accepted, while in the non-elaborate, the mental mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*) is accepted. Prior to obtaining initiation at the time of entering the mandala, and after obtaining initiation—during these three stages— [The text continues with the description of the three states.]
The observance of the three types of pledges (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*) is essential.
Regarding the pledges and vows, they will be explained in detail later;
here, however, only a brief indication of the pledges and vows that must generally and invariably be observed by a practitioner of the *Caryātantra* is provided.
To obtain the consecration, the practitioner offers his body, speech, and mind to the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva).
Thereupon, the practitioner also becomes a member of the family (kulika) of the chosen deity;
at that time, he should perform his activities according to the training of that family.

Immediately after obtaining the empowerment, the practitioner must constantly perform the meditation on the deity yoga—both with and without characteristics—for the sake of practicing the Caryātantra according to its true meaning;
that is to say, the practitioner must meditate on the profound and vast deity yoga with and without characteristics, while reflecting at the three times: "I am Vajrasattva."
Furthermore, so that there may be no simultaneous destruction of the pledges (*samaya*) and the vows (*saṃvara*), one must remain armored for this purpose as well.
2. Regarding the practice of yoga (*yogacaryā*), it also has two divisions: yoga with characteristics (*salakṣaṇayoga*) and yoga without characteristics (*nirlakṣaṇayoga*).
Even for the application of the characteristics (*salakṣaṇayoga*), two methods were established, joined with four external and four internal factors.
Furthermore, there are two divisions of the method of the fourfold means (*caturaṅgasādhana*):
(1) the general method of means (*sāmānyasādhanavidhi*) and (2) [the specific method].
And the procedure for the specific means of accomplishment (*viśeṣa-sādhanāvidhi*).

(ka) The procedure for accomplishing the external universal (*bāhyasāmānyasādhanāvidhi*) is exactly like that of the *Kriyātantra*: there are four limbs for the principles of the deities, such as the deity of emptiness (*śūnyadeva*), the syllable-deity (*akṣaradeva*), and the form-deity (*rūpadeva*): (1) the supported (*āśrita*), (2) ... [and so forth].
Meditation is performed by means of this fourfold set: (3) the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), (4) the seed-syllable of sound-mantra, and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having become pure through external and internal bathing and so forth, and having visualized the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*), one should invoke one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).
After the worship, ritual service, and petitioning of the chosen deity, the meditation on emptiness itself is called the "deity of emptiness" (*śūnyadeva*).
The meditation on the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra of the chosen deity is the "syllabic deity" (*akṣaradeva*).

Indeed, the deity of sound (*dhvanideva*) is the meditation on the emanation and reabsorption [of the universe] together with the resonance of the mantra; the deity of form (*rūpadeva*) is the form of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*);
and the deity of gesture (*mudrādeva*) is the meditation on the weapons and so forth within the heart-lotus of the chosen deity.
Having empowered one's own body with the mantra and meditating upon it as having the form of a deity, that is called the "deity according to its characteristics" (*lakṣaṇadeva*).
This method of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the six deities and their principles exists exactly as in the *Kriyātantra*.
This is called the general rule.
(kha) The Procedure for Accomplishing External Distinctive Qualities: In the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, Vajrapāṇi asks the Tathāgata Vairocana: "O Blessed One!
If a practitioner, being endowed with the form of a deity or assuming the form of a deity, performs the conduct (*caryā*), he will swiftly be transformed into that very form of a deity."
"Therefore, let the form of the deity be described to me.
[The Buddha replied: "Excellent, excellent! This question is very well-posed. O Vajrapāṇi!"
Listen: the Lord has three natures—the syllable (*akṣara*), the seal (*mudrā*), and form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the syllable has two divisions: sound and the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*).
The seal also has two divisions: the material and the immaterial.
Furthermore, regarding form (*rūpa*), there are two types: completely pure and impure.
Thus, there are six divisions of the deity consisting of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
Within the lotus of one’s own heart, the bodhicitta resides as the mandala of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).

Above that, the very contemplation of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) constitutes the contemplation of the Sound-Deity (*śabdadeva*) and the Awakening Mind (*bodhicitta*).
For the wheel, vajra, and so forth are the Form-Seal (*rūpimudrā*), while the Source of Phenomena (*dharmodayā*), which brings about the realization of emptiness, is the Formless-Seal (*arūpimudrā*).
That which is non-conceptual and devoid of all characteristics is perfectly pure;
whereas that which is endowed with characteristics, color, and shape is impure.
The purpose of these two final forms of the Deity is to represent the fruit as both having characteristics and being devoid of characteristics.

(2) Regarding the procedure for the means of internal commonality: when Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi asked the Blessed One in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, "How should the practice of the secret mantra be performed?",
the Blessed One, in explaining these very four limbs, prescribed the recitation of ten hundred thousand mantras for the sake of accomplishment.
Therefore, having completed the general procedure for the preceding ritual actions, one should meditate upon a lunar disc as a conventional appearance, in the form of the ultimate bodhicitta.
Upon that, one should place the seed-syllable,
which should suddenly manifest in the form of sound.

One should reflect that the seed-syllable and the moon-maṇḍala, having undergone transformation, manifest within one's own body in the form of the deity. This should be meditated upon as being directly before oneself, just like the reflection of a form in a mirror.
Having fixed the mind on the seed-syllable placed in the heart-lotus of the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Having clarified the intended meaning of *prāṇāyāma*, it is described in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* that there are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the downward-voiding breath (*apāna*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Indeed, *prāṇāyāma* joined with mindfulness consists of concentrating the mind on the mantra by restraining the path through which the wind enters the body.
One should recite the mantra while performing *prāṇāyāma* until the manifestation of the deity occurs.
Regarding the procedure for accomplishing the internal distinction: within one’s own lunar disc of bodhicitta, one should meditate upon any one of the four syllables—*a*, *ā*, *aṃ*, or *ā*.
Thereafter, the accomplishment of one’s own welfare and the welfare of others is to be contemplated through the radiance of that light and the process of its reabsorption.

Immediately thereafter, one should abide with the sense of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) in the following way: "My own form is that of the Buddha-deity himself, transformed into the nature of a seed-syllable—yellow in color, with one face and two arms, resting in the *dhyāna-mudrā*, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, bearing the *uṣṇīṣa* and the *pāda*, and clad in saffron robes; he shines resplendently upon a white lotus and a moon disc. Thus should one remain.
Thereafter, one should again perform the meditation on the seed-syllable of Vairocana within the heart-lotus and the moon-maṇḍala.
Then, having placed the seed-mantra upon that moon-maṇḍala in the heart-lotus, one should recite the mantra by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
This very procedure for mantra-recitation, endowed with the four internal limbs, is what is taught.
The procedure for the practice of the signless (*nirlakṣaṇasādhanā*): there are two divisions of the signless practice—(ka) the general and (kha) the specific.
(ka) The general: [one should] within the lotus of one's own heart, having made one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) the object of meditation...
Having meditated on the sequence beginning with the weapon, the wheel, the vajra, and the seed-syllables, one performs breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then,

having visualized the mutual gazing and laughing nature of the deity and consort, the very abiding within the object (*viṣaya*, i.e., emptiness) along with the procedure for transforming passion into the path is called the general method of practice characterized by the absence of marks (*sāmānyanirlakṣaṇasādhanāvidhi*).

(kha) The distinction [is as follows]: having realized, through the Madhyamaka reasoning concerning the fourfold alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) applied to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, the non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) of the fourfold alternatives accompanied by qualities such as being unarisen and unceasing, one must abide in reality.

Furthermore, seeing those sentient beings who are unacquainted with this truth and consequently experience various sufferings for that very reason, one should—becoming melted with compassion—desire to favor them;
that is to say, one should proceed by establishing the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of things through logical arguments.
Following that, there is abiding in reality as far as possible, and finally, arising from meditative absorption; subsequently, the application of means for the benefit of sentient beings—
this practice of cultivation endowed with these three limbs is indeed called "cultivation without characteristics."
In the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*, the meditation on the signless is urged as being more powerful than the meditation on that which possesses signs;
for from the yoga with signs, the accomplishment of that which possesses signs is obtained,
whereas from the yoga with the signless, the accomplishment of both the sign-possessing and the signless is attained.
The essential point regarding the Action and Performance Tantras is that there are four major components of yoga:
the union of the deity and emptiness, and the union of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and mantra recitation.
Ultimately, it is the cultivation of emptiness, and conventionally, the cultivation of the deity's form, that constitute the primary causal basis for attaining the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya.
In the recitation of mantras, whatever chosen deity is meditated upon, that constitutes the invocation; and the self becomes established in that very form.
The practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the means for attaining firmness in both types of yoga.
Therefore, this is a common and indispensable limb for both the yoga with signs (*salakṣaṇa*) and the yoga without signs (*nirlakṣaṇa*).

3. The practice for the accomplishment of the means (*sādhanāsiddhicaryā*): When the recitation of the mantra (*mantrajapa*) is complete, the practitioner becomes authorized to attain the common and uncommon accomplishments (*siddhis*).
To attain the common accomplishments, the practitioner should take up an object such as a sword and recite the mantra.
And by that, the accomplishments (siddhis) such as those of a Vidyadhara are attained.

In the state of uncommon accomplishment, within the support of the internal mandalas of earth, water, fire, and so forth, the nourishment of power attains fullness in rites such as the fierce (raudra) and the subjugating (vaśya).
Through miraculous powers, superknowledges, and so on, one effects the welfare of oneself, others, and both.
This is the measure for success.
Thus, the practice should be performed preceded by stability and arrival.

During the time of ordinary practice, a vision of the chosen deity in a dream, the worship and veneration of the mandala of the chosen deity, and even the observation of dreams and so forth, are considered auspicious signs of the practice.

By gradually refining [the practice] until there is a direct vision of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), all kinds of common and uncommon accomplishments (*siddhi*) are attained. Beyond these common and uncommon accomplishments, once the recitation of the mantra is perfected, the practitioner’s attainment of *siddhi* proceeds according to their wish. 4. Regarding the conduct of accomplishment (*siddhicaryā*): through this conduct of accomplishment, a person of dull faculties will certainly attain perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) within eight aeons (*kalpa*).
One of sharp faculties attains the supreme state within three eons;

however, a practitioner who possesses the aspiration for attainment may attain the supreme state even in a single lifetime. Conclusion: The great master Buston stated that the method of practice in the Kriyā and Caryā tantras is identical.
Therefore, the ritual manual for the practice of Caryātantra was not clearly analyzed by him.
Even the great scholar Puṇyakīrti understood Caryātantra only as far as the *Samayasamvara-tantra* and merely its classification into families (*kulabheda*).
According to his view as well, the ritual manual for practice is exactly like that of Kriyātantra.
The great scholar Ācārya Coṅkhāpā has briefly elucidated the ritual manual for the practice of Caryātantra.
Here, based upon the *Jñeyakośa*, a few notes are written.
Just like Kriyātantra, Caryātantra is also divided into three sections according to the families (*kula*): the Tathāgata family, the Padma family, and the Vajra family.

Regarding the method of meditation endowed with the four limbs in the *Sādhanāpaddhati*: although the procedure for meditation is essentially the same as in the Kriyātantra, and the meditation procedure of the Caryātantra is not significantly different from the Kriyātantra— such that there would be no necessity for its distinction from the Kriyātantra— nevertheless, while in the Kriyātantra there is a difference of opinion as to whether or not one must meditate on the body of the deity within one's own body, here the necessity of the procedure for meditating on the body of the deity within one's own body is beyond dispute.
He established [this practice].
Furthermore, having summoned the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) as the object of meditation (dhyeya) before one's own eyes, the method for even dissolution was revealed.

This very means of accomplishment is known by the names "Yoga with Characteristics" (salakṣaṇadevayoga) and "Yoga without Characteristics" (nirlakṣaṇadevayoga), and it is subtler than the Kriyātantra.

The essential meaning of the practice of the deity endowed with characteristics (*salakṣaṇadevayoga*) is as follows: having personally meditated upon one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), one performs the procedure for the recitation of the mantra (*mantrajapa*) according to the previously mentioned fourfold method.
In this regard, it should be understood how the practitioner (*sādhaka*) himself becomes transformed into the form of the chosen deity.
For example, our own body (*skandha*), which is composed of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*), is not merely a collection of various principles (*tattva*).
Arising from the fruits of prior karma,

when that [self] is deconstructed by us through reasonings that establish the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it then attains emptiness (*śūnyatva*). Furthermore, even while causes and conditions are perceived, it manifests as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), like a reality reflected in a mirror.
In the same way, all phenomena are to be understood.

Just as things manifest in the nature of emptiness, so too does the practitioner manifest as the chosen deity through the manifestation of the self as the deity, through the empowerment bestowed by the guru, and through the empowerment of the power of the chosen deity and other such methods arising from dependent origination. Thus, one becomes manifest as the chosen deity.
Therefore, prior to this state of stability, one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) should be meditated upon in this way: "I am indeed the chosen deity; I am within the chosen deity.
Thus, the performance of mantra recitation through such meditation on the chosen deity is here described as yoga characterized by signs (salakṣaṇayoga).
The yoga of signlessness (*nirlakṣaṇayoga*) is, in general, the causal agent for the attainment of the activity of phenomena (*dharmakārya*).
At the limit of the yoga with signs (*salakṣaṇayoga*), even the meditated upon tutelary deity (*iṣṭadeva*) must be dissolved.

Through this dissolution, just as no existence whatsoever remains for phenomena such as form and so forth, likewise the existence of the body of the tutelary deity does not remain; and thus one's own mind is devoid of the three times regarding all characteristics.
One attains the state of non-conceptuality;
this very method for the cultivation of non-conceptuality is what is being taught.
Kamalaśīla also described this very truth in his *Bhāvanākrama*.

Some scholars consider that after the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the cultivation of the deity is the "cultivation without characteristics" (*nirlakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*); they regard its absence and its further absence as the "cultivation with characteristics" (*salakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*).

For example, immediately after the direct realization of emptiness, the perfection of generosity and circumambulation occur simultaneously with the arising of powerful wisdom in the mind that realizes that very emptiness.
Acts such as prostration and so forth do not themselves indicate emptiness;
however, because the mind is filled with the realization of emptiness, even those actions are said to be impelled by emptiness.

Just as when one has generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) and immediately becomes absorbed in emptiness, the continuity of the flow of bodhicitta is maintained within that state of absorption, so too here, [the continuity] of the knowledge of emptiness—
In the flow [of practice], there is the cultivation of the deity,
which is called the cultivation of the signless deity.
Such an arrangement is possible in the Pāramitā system, but it is not possible in the Tantras.

The excellent preceptor Gurūvara Ācārya-Chulaṭhima also, clarifying the nature of the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-yuganaddha*), said: "Just as a mother with an only son experiences extreme suffering upon his death, yet she nevertheless carries out her entire daily routine along with that experience of pain and feeling—likewise, the accomplishment of generosity and the other perfections impelled by emptiness is called the state of non-dual wisdom and means in the Pāramitā-naya.
Therefore, while such an explanation is certainly respected according to the Pāramitā-naya, it is not respected at all according to the Vajrayāna."
For in the tantras, the union (*yuganaddha*) of the nature of the deity and emptiness is required;
the nature of the deity is the appearance of the conventional mind,
while its emptiness is the ultimate, which is non-dual and of a single form.
Being of a single flavor and indivisible, it is also the object of a single cognition.
In the state of fruition, the physical basis of the body— adorned with the primary and secondary marks (the divine body)—
and the non-referential compassion supported by that basis, both abide in a state of non-duality just like a lamp and its light.

The body of the Tathāgata and its lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) are, in fact, nothing other than the cultivation of the non-duality of wisdom and means; this is indeed the cultivation of the deity who is devoid of characteristics.
Here, the non-dual and the deity of the unified pair (yuganaddha) have been explained as being "mind-made" (manomaya); having fashioned it with the mind, this is what is cultivated.

Furthermore, in the Yoga Tantras and the Unsurpassed Tantras (*anuttarayogatantra*), this [deity] is generated and cultivated by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*) and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), through the subtle method of vital energy and mind (*prāṇacitta*). There is a great difference between these two modes of cultivation, which will be explained further on.
The Fourth Chapter: The Success of the Yoga Tantra. 1. *Tattvasaṃgraha*: In the commentary titled *Tattvasaṃgrahatantrārthāvatāra* by the verse-Vajra Tathāgata...

Clarifying the procedure for teaching the Yoga Tantra, it is stated as follows: In general, the Blessed One, by means of generating the bodhicitta which is the cause for the welfare of both self and others, through the exhaustion of obscurations and the complete fulfillment of the accumulations of merit and wisdom, attains the vajra-body; he then pervades all phenomena like space and abides in a nature that is non-referential and free from conceptual construction.

Even in such a state, being under the influence of the vow made for the benefit of sentient beings— that is, for the sake of fulfilling the conduct of awakening— he manifests as the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*,
and thereby effects the welfare of beings. Consequently, in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, the Dharma is taught either gradually or simultaneously in both forms.
The Teacher has three bodies, known as the dharma-kāya, the saṃbhoga-kāya, and the nirmāṇa-kāya.
The Dharma is also threefold: the causal vehicle (hetuyāna) and the outer vehicle (bāhyayāna).
And there is the inner vehicle.
The retinue is also threefold: that which is dependently originated, that which is produced by aspiration, and that which is produced by gnosis.
The locations for the teaching of the Dharma are also three: those known as cities, celestial palaces, and circular pavilions.
The world is also threefold: the subterranean world (*pātālaloka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), and the celestial world (*devaloka*).
The Tathāgata taught the *Mahāyogatantra-tattvasaṃgraha* through the gateway of the *saṃbhogakāya* in the celestial world, and from there, he gradually disseminated it in Jambudvīpa.
And this [teaching] became blossomed and fully developed through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the compiler of this tantra.
Regarding this subject matter of the teaching at the commencement of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the following explanation is found:
relying on the first part of the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (the Vajradhātu), Buddhaguhya composed an excellent work entitled the *Vṛhattantrārthāvatāra*.
At the beginning of this work, while clarifying the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*), he enumerated those thirty-seven limbs of reality (*tattvāṅga*) of the *Tattvasaṃgraha* as follows:
1. the heart (*hṛdaya*), 2. the mudrā, and so forth.
3. Mantra, 4. Vidyā, 5. Adhiṣṭhāna.
6. Consecration, 7. Meditation, 8. Worship,
9. the reality of one's own nature (svatattva), 10. the reality of the deity (devatattva), 11. the mandala.
12. Wisdom (prajñā), 13. Skillful means (upāya), 14. Cause (hetu).
15. *phala* (result), 16. *yoga* (proper application), 17. *atiyoga* (excessive application).
18. Mahāyoga, 19. Guhyayoga, 20. Sarvayoga.
21. Recitation (japa), 22. Fire-oblation (homa), 23. Vow (vrata).
24. Accomplishment (siddhi), 25. the means of accomplishment (siddhisādhana), 26. meditative absorption (samādhi).
27. the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), 28. the knowledge of emptiness (śūnyatājñāna), 29. the mirror-like knowledge (ādarśajñāna).
30. the knowledge of equality (samatājñāna), 31. the knowledge of discernment (pratyavekṣaṇajñāna), 32. the knowledge of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna).
33. the pure gnosis of the dharmadhātu, 34. attracting, 35. establishing;
36. Binding (bandhana) and 37. subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa).
These thirty-seven methods of accomplishment (sādhanāvidhi) are well-compendiated.
Therefore, the title *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Compendium of Reality) of this tantra is meaningful.

Regarding the discourse on the secrets of the Buddha: these thirty-seven realities (*tattva*) can, in turn, be subsumed within the heart-seals (*hṛdaya-mudrā*), the mantras, and the reality-knowledges (*vidyā-tattva*). This treatise consists of four sections: 1. The Vajradhātu section; [and so forth].
2. the section on the Conqueror of the Three Worlds, 3. the section on the Discipline of the Entire World, and 4. the section on the Accomplishment of All Aims.
In each section, there are six mandala-chapters, as follows: 1. The Vajradhātu section—(a) the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala;
(b) [the Vajradhātvīśvarī-maṇḍala].
(ga) the Vajra-secret Vajra-maṇḍala; (gha) the Vajra-knowledge Dharma-maṇḍala; (ṅa) the Vajra-body action maṇḍala.
The fourth is the mandala of four mudrās, and [the fifth is] the mandala of one mudrā.
2. In the Trilokavijaya mandala—(ka)
(kha) The Great Maṇḍala of the Conqueror of the Three Worlds; (ga) The Maṇḍala of the Secret Mudrās of the Wrathful Deities; (gha) The Maṇḍala of the Samaya of the Dharma-Jñāna of the Vajra Family.
The mandala of the sequence of Trilokavijaya (Ṅa),
the fourth mandala of Trilokavijaya (Ca), and the mandala of the single mudrā.
3. The portion concerning the discipline of the entire world:
(ka) the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) maṇḍala of the discipline of the entire world; (kha) the secret lotus (*padmaguhya*) seal maṇḍala; (ga) [the remainder].
The maṇḍala of gnosis (gha),
the maṇḍala of action (ṅa), and the fourth, the maṇḍala of the mudrā (ca).
The mandala that is the sole seal of the entire world;
4. The portion for the accomplishment of all aims—(a) the great mandala of the accomplishment of all aims (b).
(ga) the Jewel Secret Maṇḍala; (gha) the Wisdom Maṇḍala; (ṅa) the Action Maṇḍala.
The fourth is the Maṇḍala of the Single Mudrā for the Accomplishment of All Aims (*Sarvārthasiddhi-ekamudrāmaṇḍala*).
The arrangement of these six aforementioned maṇḍalas is provided here according to the *Tattvasaṃgrahaṭīkā* composed by Ānandagarbha.
This commentary on the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, known as the *Atibṛhatī* and *Sundarī*,

maintains that in the very first chapter of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the section concerning the "Introduction" (*nidānavastu*), the term *Vairocana* is discussed as being endowed with the three purposes: for oneself, for others, and for both.
By means of this, the practitioner should cultivate an intense longing for the attainment of that state.
Subsequently, together with the specific means for attaining that state, the path for obtaining both mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) was also fully described.
Although the term "Tathāgata" is employed in all five families of Tathāgatas,

When only the Tathāgata family is employed, then it pertains only to the bodhisattvas belonging to the Vairocana family, and not to the bodhisattvas of the four families. In the first limb of this tantra, the path connected with the Tathāgata families was set forth; likewise, in the second limb, the Vajra family—that is, the Akṣobhya family—was established; in the third, the Lotus family; and in the fourth, the Jewel family, which bestows the accomplishment of the cause for all living beings, was established.
In this context, only four families are described:
the Jewel Family (*ratnakula*), which brings about the attainment of wealth for sentient beings; and the Action Family (*karmakula*), which accomplishes activities—that is, Amoghasiddhi.
These are subsumed under a single form.
Therefore, the five families are gathered within these very four sections.
Along with the *Mūlatantra* known as the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, both the *Uttaratantra* and the *Uttarottaratantra* are also found,
in which the means for attaining the supreme state taught in the four limbs are explained in detail.
This has been clarified in detail in the subsequent tantras (*uttarottara-tantra*).

For those practitioners of Yoga Tantra who understand that they lack the capacity for the practice of internal yoga (*abhyantara-yoga*), the external practices such as recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*) have been prescribed.

Furthermore, regarding the four branches of the Root Tantra (*mūla-tantra*), whatever was unclear or incomplete in the arrangement of the path for attaining worldly accomplishments (*laukika-siddhi*) has also been clarified and completed here.

In this context, regarding the sub-classification of Yoga Tantra within its relation to the *Uttaratantra*, the following question arises: Is it to be said that Kriyā Tantra is one wing of Yoga Tantra, since [the practitioner of Yoga Tantra] contemplates external purity and also performs recitation (*japa*) and so forth? To this there is also an answer: while there exists a gross distinction between the four general classes of Tantra, it is impossible for there to be any appearance of mutual contradiction between them.

As the great master Candrakīrti states, clarifying the disciples of the *Guhyasamāja*: "The practitioner who, immediately after attaining perfection in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), does not strive for common accomplishments (*sādhāraṇasiddhi*) but exerts himself solely for the attainment of the supreme state while meditating on the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*)—such a practitioner is called a worthy vessel, resembling a jewel.

That practitioner who, having gained proficiency in the generation stage, strives for the attainment of common accomplishments is designated as a 'white lotus of the lowest kind' (*adhamapuṇḍarīka*)."
Just as both the primary and secondary practitioners (sādhaka) are found here, such is also the case in the Yoga Tantra.
Furthermore, a question arises here:

among the four parts of the tantra, is the path for attaining the supreme state described for only a single practitioner, such as Vairocana, or is the path to be accomplished described for four distinct types of practitioners?

The very clear answer to this is described thus in the Paramādya-tantra: among those who perform the sādhana of the five Tathāgatas, that in which the threefold [passions—namely desire, delusion, and anger] exist in equal form, from those "Great Passionates" (mahārāgin), the first portion—that is, the Dharmadhātu-maṇḍala;
and from the "Great Haters" (mahādveṣin), the second portion—that is, the Trailokyavijaya-maṇḍala.
To those who were greatly deluded, he taught the mandala called Sakalajagadvinayamaṇḍala as the third portion, and to those who were extremely miserly, he taught the Sarvārthasiddhimaṇḍala;
this very same approach is also adopted by the master Buddhaguhya.

The master Kun dga’ ñi ma’i sñiṅ po, Mahodaya, also related a similar account in the *Sāmānyalaghutantra*: "When a practitioner is unable to reach a definitive conclusion by himself, he seeks out various gurus and follows their instructions; sometimes he practices a path associated with passion, sometimes one associated with hatred, and even considering external purification and the like to be the Dharma, he carries out these conducts. It was for the sake of leading such individuals onto the authentic path that the Buddha taught the Yoga Tantras."

And just as (1) in the first part of the *Yogatantra*, for the sake of favoring those possessed of passion (*rāgin*), the deities’ colors, ornaments, and garments were shown in red, and thus the method of accomplishment (*sādhanavidhi*) was primarily taught for those with passion; (2) in the second part, in order to favor practitioners for whom hatred (*dveṣa*) is predominant, [the deities] are depicted in terrifying, fierce, and black colors.
In the section on the Devas, he described the *sādhanā* manual.

(3) In the section concerning those to be trained in the entire world, for the sake of favoring practitioners dominated by delusion (*moha*), the whiteness of the gods’ complexions, peaceful natures, garments, ornaments, and so forth was demonstrated.

(4) In the fourth section, for the practitioner endowed with all three faults in equal measure, the colors of the gods were shown to be diverse and manifold, and their ornaments and garments were displayed in many different varieties.
Buston also explained it in exactly this way:

Ānandagarbha stated that these four sections of the Yoga Tantra correspond respectively to the nature body (*svabhāvakāya*), the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), as well as to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*), and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Furthermore, within these four sections, the perfections of bodhicitta, generosity, wisdom, and diligence are predominant, respectively.
This has been explained by combining [the following points] together:
according to their families, 1. the deities of the first portion are born from the heart of the Tathāgata’s moon-maṇḍala; 2. the deities of the second portion belong to the Vajra family;
3. the deities of the third portion belong to the Lotus family.
All the deities of this fourth part are emanated by the mind-vajra of Avalokiteśvara; furthermore, the weapons of all these deities consist of lotus-vajra garlands, lotus-vajra cloths, and so forth.
Regarding the fourth part, all the deities explain the mind-vajra of Ākāśagarbha; for this very reason, they are called the Ratnakula (Jewel Family).

Although the deities themselves do not possess forms of anger or diverse appearances—since the state of the supreme realm belongs only to the supremely peaceful—they nevertheless manifest in various forms for the sake of those to be trained (*vineya*) according to specific purposes.
As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Aha! What a great skillful means of the Buddhas, whose very nature is compassion!"
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, those who are peaceful even manifest ferocity.

This is not the intended meaning: that a single practitioner would attain the state of purity solely through the performance of the fourfold sādhana, or that each individual could reach the supreme state by practicing even a single method of sādhana within a particular section.

The practice of Yoga Tantra is performed through three meditations: the meditation of higher yoga (*adhiyoga-dhyāna*), the meditation on the king of the maṇḍala (*maṇḍalarājāgra-dhyāna*), and the meditation on the king of rites (*karmarāja-dhyāna*).

In each section of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, an extensive, intermediate, and concise method of practice (*sādhanāpaddhati*) has been taught for practitioners of superior, middling, and inferior dispositions. In the *Tattvāloka*, Ānandagarbha described this as follows: "For that practitioner who desires to perform the practice of the *Padyakula* in detail, [there is taught] the great maṇḍala of the nature of the *Padyakula*."
The maṇḍala of dhāraṇīs,
the maṇḍala of dharma, and the maṇḍala of karma exist.
For one who follows the middle path, the arrangement of the four mudrās is prescribed;
and for one who desires meditation in extreme brevity, a single-mudrā maṇḍala is taught.
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the four types of mudrās, beginning with the *karmamudrā*, are explained in conjunction with the four families:
the *kāyamahāmudrā* belongs to the Vairocana family,
and the *cittasamayamudrā* belongs to the Akṣobhya family.
Speech is the Dharma-mudrā and belongs to the family of Amitābha; action (karma) is the Jñāna-mudrā, which arises from the Ratna family.
This basis for differentiation exists by relying upon predominance.
Otherwise, the Buddha states in the *Guhyatantrārthāvatāra*: "Without the body, mind cannot arise;
and without mind, speech also cannot arise.
Therefore, in all families, the four mudrās are present."

In terms of essential meaning, it is appropriate to speak of the *Tattvasaṃgraha* as a single work; however, enlightenment can be attained by practicing the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for even one part of it, or for four parts of one of its limbs.
For this very reason, scholars separated the four parts of the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and composed commentaries on them independently.

Among these, for the *Vajradhātu* section there is Buddhaguhya’s *Tantrārthāvatāra*; for the *Trailokyavijaya*, Ānandagarbha’s commentary; and for the four parts [of the other sections], there are works for those desiring a concise, detailed, or extensive treatment.
When the complete text was produced, it was divided into three sections and two editions, for which commentaries titled *Tattvāloka* were composed.

The *Tattvāloka* commentary is considered the most extensive and clear sub-commentary on the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. 2. Regarding the *Vajraśekhara Tantra*: according to the opinion of scholars such as Buston, the *Vajraśekhara Tantra* is an explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*) of the Yoga Tantras, and it consists fundamentally of four principal chapters.
Namely: (1) the chapter titled "The Lord" from the *Sarvatathāgataguhyasūtra*;
(2) the chapter on the Tathāgata Family from the *Sarvatathāgataguhyasūtra*;
(3) the chapter on the explanation of the *Trilokavijaya*; and (4).
And there is the chapter on the explanation of the reality of the Tathāgata-vajra family;
there are sixteen realities, twenty explained realities,
and numerous intermediate sections such as the explanation of the secret fire-offering (homa) and so forth.

Indeed, the *Vajraśekhara Tantra* is not recognized as an explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*), because this first chapter, titled "The Lord of the Sūtras of Secrets of All Tathāgatas," is found in the form of questions and answers according to the explanatory style of the *Uttaratantra*.
[Question: What is the non-conceptual meaning of phenomena (*dharmārtha*)?
Furthermore, what is the intention here in demonstrating conceptual construction? What is the purpose of the proof?
And how is this the *Uttaratantra* (the Sublime Continuum)?
What is the reply?
What is called the *tantra*?
And who is the Wrathful One, the Vajra-holder?
"How is Vajracaṇḍa?
And how many kinds is he?"— such questions were asked both briefly at once and again in detail.
Furthermore, in the form of a question and answer, it is asked: "In how many ways is Vajradhara?
In response to this, it is stated that because the *dharmadhātu* pervades all directions and is infinite, Vajradhara is likewise infinite.
How is this answer established within this very text?
What is the *tantra*?

It is understood as follows: from the examination of the statement, the first chapter is recognized as the *Uttaratantra*, or as an explanatory *tantra* (*vyākhyātantra*) taught within the teaching style of the *Uttaratantra*.
Furthermore, the introductory chapter (*nidānaparivarta*) of the *Uttaratantra* does not exist as a separate entity.
Here too, the text begins from the passage: "Then King Vajradhara...
By this, the following is also established: immediately after the teaching of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, this [text] was also taught within that same maṇḍala;
the *Uttaratantra* is then imparted by the Blessed One in response to the questions of the assembly.

And just as with the *Guhyasamāja-uttaratantra*, it is understood that the first chapter of the *Vajraśekhara* is presented in the form of an *uttaratantra*, while the remaining portion is taught as an explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*). 3.

The *Trilokavijaya-mahākalpa*: Vajrapāṇi, having descended from the path of space, pays homage to the Blessed One with the eight limbs [of prostration], in order to teach the procedure for establishing the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*) for those of cruel and wicked nature who abide in the world.

When he made this request, the Blessed One, while dwelling together with infinite gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, bhūtas, piśācas, and others, in the palace named Maṇiratnāgra on Mount Sumeru at the time of teaching the *Trilokavijaya-mahākalpa*, spoke as follows:

"In this *Trilokavijaya-mahākalpa*, there are the *Vajrahuṃkāra-nāma-kalpa*, the *Tathāgata-kalpa*, the extensive ritual procedure for the *Vajramahācakra*, the ritual procedure for the *Karmamaṇḍala*, the *Vajrapāṇi-kalpa*, the *Avalokiteśvara-kalpa*, the *Gaganagarbha-kalpa*, the *Gaganakośa-kalpa*, and the *Karmaprasara-kalpa*."

There are the following divisions: the *Vidyāmantramahākalpa*, the *Karmasamūhakalpa*, the *Karmadūtīkalpa*, the *Sevakakalpa*, the *Karmavajrasamūhamātṛkalpa*, the *Karmavajrīdūtīkalpa*, and the *Karmasevakakalpa*.
This much constitutes the root tantra (*mūlatantra*).
Subsequently, in this treatise, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, was questioned by Vajrapāṇi: "How does he arise?
From what does the Vajra arise?
In response to that, whatever was spoken by the Blessed One is called the *Uttaratantra*.

4. The Ritual Manual for Purifying All Evil Destinies (*Sarvadurgatipariśodhanakalpa*): The teaching of this tantra was delivered by the Tathāgata in the celestial realm, in the grove named Nandana. 5. The *Paramādya-tantra*: The *Paramādya-tantra* was taught to the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjuśrī, Ākāśagarbha, and others, in the palace of the King of Gods within the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) in the Desire Realm (*Kāmadhātu*).

In this *Tathāgataguhyaka*, there are nine chapters known as the *Tathāgatakalpa*, *Trilokavijayakalpa*, *Muṣṭikalpa*, *Vajracakrakalpa*, *Ākāśagarbhakalpa*, *Vajrayakṣakalpa*, *Kulasaṃgrahakalpa*, *Vajrakulamaṇḍalakalpa*, and *Mahāsukhavajrāmoghasamayakalpa*. 6. Regarding the *Vajragarbhālaṅkāra Tantra*: the teaching of this tantra was empowered by all the Tathāgatas at the place where infinite Buddhas appear, in the Vairocana-heart-luminous celestial palace (*vimāna*), the abode of the Tathāgatas.

This was composed in the assembly of infinite bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the *Vajragarbhālaṅkāra*. Its subjects belonging to the first part include the *Mahāmaṇḍalavidhi*, the *Jaladevamaṇḍalavidhi*, the *Agnidevamaṇḍalavidhi*, the *Vāyudevamaṇḍalavidhi*, the *Jātattvavidhi*, the *Srotovidhi*, and the *Tathāgatakāyasiddhopāyikā*, among others.

The means for accomplishing substances; the means for accomplishing speech; the means for accomplishing mantras; the means for accomplishing all appearances and the *uṣṇīṣas*; the means for accomplishing the *vajra* of the afflictions; the means for accomplishing the fist of all Tathāgatas; the means for accomplishing the *uṣṇīṣa* of all Tathāgatas; the means for accomplishing the white parasol; the means for accomplishing all *uṣṇīṣas*; the means for accomplishing Mañjuśrī; the means for accomplishing Jagadīśvara; the means for accomplishing Vajradhara; the means for accomplishing Maitreya; the means for accomplishing Ākāśagarbha; the means for accomplishing Samantabhadra; the means for accomplishing Sāgaramati; the means for accomplishing Ratnasaṃbhava, and so forth.
These are the means for the accomplishment of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Through the means for the accomplishment of Yamāntaka, the means for the accomplishment of Krodhakaṇa, and the means for the accomplishment of Hayagrīva, the mandala of the Wrathful Ones (krodha) is perfected.

Together with these, through the means for the accomplishment of the Buddha-eye mudrā, the means for the accomplishment of Pāṇḍarā, the means for the accomplishment of Bhṛkuṭī, the means for the accomplishment of Māmakī, the means for the accomplishment consisting of the Vajra-garland, the means for the accomplishment of Cundā, and so forth—by means of these principles of mantra (mantratattva)—[the mandala is perfected].

The Guhyamaṇḍala is accomplished. Following this, numerous other maṇḍala procedures have also been set forth, such as the Vajraratnamaṇḍala, the Nābhicakra-dharmacakramaṇḍala, the Gaganakośamaṇḍala, the Vajrajinamaṇḍala, and the Suvajramaṇḍala.
At the end of this [section], a list of the names of the thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), along with their commentary, was also composed.
7. Regarding the *Kāyavākcittaguhyabhūtālaṅkāra-tantra*, Buston did not include this tantra in his *Sūcī* (Catalogue) of the Yoga Tantras.
Its maṇḍala is the *Jñānaśreṣṭha*.
There exists the Great Mandala of the Secret Ornament,
which consists of three parts known as the secrets of body, speech, and mind.

This *Ārya-Guhyamaṇitilaka-tantra* was taught by the Blessed One while residing in the palace of the King of Gods in the Akaniṣṭha realm, for the sake of Bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi, Avalokiteśvara, Ākāśagarbha, Vajramuṣṭi, and others.
When ninety-nine (99) bodhisattvas made their request for the instruction on the *Guhyatilaka*, it was taught.
In this [work], there exist four sections known as the *Vajratilaka-pratyavekṣaṇā-devī-tantra-vidhi*, the *Sarvatattva-rahasya-vidhi-vistara*, and the *Paramatattva-rahasya-tilaka*.

9. The Blessed One, while dwelling on Mount Sumeru together with the sons of the gods, asuras, vāyus, devas, garuḍas, nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras, rākṣasas, vidyādharas, bhūtas, vināyakas, piśācas, and so forth, as well as an infinite multitude of Mothers, taught this exposition of the twenty-five gateways of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitāmukha).
Vajrapāṇi descended from the sky, circumambulated the Blessed One, and sat down.
At that time, addressing Vajrapāṇi by the name Guhyādhipati, he began with the syllable *oṃ*, reciting: "Oṃ, the entrance to the perfection of wisdom of the vajra-bodhicitta, hūṃ;

oṃ, the entrance to the perfection of wisdom of the conduct of Samantabhadra, hūṃ. Having thus adorned the Perfection of Wisdom with twenty-five specific epithets, he taught it as the entrance—that is, the gateway to liberation.
In this way, there are numerous texts of Yoga Tantra,
which are known by the names *mūlatantra* (root tantra), *vyākhyātantra* (explanatory tantra), *uttaratantra* (subsequent tantra), and *sabhāgīyatantra* (concordant tantra). Furthermore,
the scholar Dvags po Chos ’byuṅ bzaṅ po considers both the *Khasamatantra* and the *Supratiṣṭhitatantra* to be included within Yoga Tantra.

The essential nature of Yoga Tantra is defined by its establishment in the non-dual emptiness that appears as both the profound and the vast— namely, the ultimate truth of profound meaning and the conventional truth of vast meaning.
In Yoga Tantra, the body is [purified] by the action seal (*kāyamudrā*),
speech by the dharma seal (*dharmamudrā*), and mind by the commitment seal (*samayamudrā*).
Having sealed the activities of the chosen deity with the action seal (*karmamudrā*), the practitioner attains suchness (*tathatā*) and the supreme state through meditative cultivation.

According to Butön, in the Yoga Tantra, the method for attaining enlightenment is brought onto the path because the cultivation of the deity is performed by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*).

Furthermore, unlike the Unexcelled Tantra (*anuttara-tantra*), there is no practice of the generation stage (*samutpatti-krama*) and the completion stage (*niṣpanna-krama*) regarding birth and death here.
In the *Jñānasamuccaya*, while clarifying the nature of Yoga Tantra, the Blessed One stated:

"One who resides within the mandala together with the knowledge goddesses (*vidyā-devī*) and studies the ten principles beginning with the principle of the mandala is called either a practitioner of the Dual Tantra (*ubhaya-tantrī*) or a practitioner of Yoga Tantra (*yoga-tantrī*)."
It is also stated in the *Trinayapradīpa* that the cultivation of the non-dual reality (*advayatattva-bhāvanā*) is extremely pleasing to others [i.e., those of other *yogatantras*];
they consider external, divergent practices to be causes for the distraction of the mind.
And they impel [the mind] toward internal objects;
for that very reason, they are called practitioners of the *caryātantra*. Here, the intended meaning of the term *caryātantrin* is to be understood by the term *yogatantrin*.

The internal divisions of Yoga Tantra: Yoga Tantra is divided into five sections according to the *kulas* (families), as follows: (1) the Tathāgata family, (2) the Vajra family, (3) [the Ratna family], (4) [the Padma family], and (5) [the Karma family].
the Ratnakula, (4) the Dharmakula, and (5) the Karmakula.
In detail, however, there are one hundred divisions;
for each family, there is the Tathāgata family and the Tathāgata-vajra family.
Thus, there are five [families]: the Tathāgata Jewel family, the Tathāgata Dharma family, and the Tathāgata Action family.
When each of these five families is further divided according to the distinctions of heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā), mantra, and vidyā-mantra families, one hundred families arise.
Clarifying the heart-seal (hṛdayamudrā), mantra, and so forth, it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Through the performance of what is desired, that which is desired is accomplished;
since he is the means for accomplishing meditative absorption (samādhi) and resides in the heart, he is therefore called the 'Heart'."
Just as the royal seal and supreme edict are difficult to transgress and indestructible, and are trusted as the mark of a great soul, so too is it celebrated as the "Seal" (mudrā). || 2 ||
For it is indeed not to be transgressed, difficult to pierce, and secret;
because it is deliberated upon as the state of secret accomplishment, it is therefore defined as "mantra. (31)

Because it exists for the destruction of ignorance and for the attainment of the supreme perfection of speech, and because the perfection of knowledge is found therein, it is proclaimed as "Vidyā" (Knowledge). || 141 ||
It is also stated in the *Vajraśekhara Tantra*: "Because it protects against poisonous creatures and sinful beings, this is called a *mudrā*.
Through the recitation of the mantra, the expulsion of malevolent creatures and the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) occur.
By the power of the mantra, the practitioner becomes empowered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
Therefore, this mantra brings about the direct realization of reality after one has abandoned defects such as ignorance and passion;
for this very reason, it is called "knowledge" (vidyā).

The dhāraṇī destroys all unwholesome states that rely upon phenomena and grasps those that are wholesome; therefore, it is called "dhāraṇī. Padyakarapa said: "The heart is indeed the body-seal; the heart exists as the center of the body."
In Mahāmudrā, one-pointedness is meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Abiding in the heart, one attains accomplishment;
therefore, this is the "Heart."
The seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), which is the very form of the heart of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), is called the "heart" (*hṛdaya*).
The practitioner must act in imitation of the conduct of the Tathāgatas; its transgression is impossible.
Therefore, this is the seal (mudrā).
A mantra wards off the defects of the mind; for this very reason, it is called a mantra.
Through knowledge (vidyā), the destruction of ignorance (avidyā) occurs.
The arising of gnosis is for this very reason called "vidyā" (knowledge).

The "heart" is said to be the body-maṇḍala when the mahāmudrā is predominant; the dhāraṇī-maṇḍala when the mudrā-samayamudrā is predominant; the dharma-maṇḍala when the guhya-mantra-dharmamudrā is predominant;
and the karma-maṇḍala when the vidyā-karmamudrā is predominant.

The intended meaning of the *dhāraṇī-maṇḍala* is indeed the arrangement of the *maṇḍala* in the form of the names of the goddesses as *dhāraṇīs* and weapons, as well as the arrangement of the attendant goddesses who exceed the number of the *karma-maṇḍala* Tathāgatas.
These distinctions are, in brief, subsumed within wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*).

As the great master Butön stated: "The intention of the mantra family consists primarily of the Father, who is the means (*upāya*), and the Knowledge-mantra (*vidyā-mantra*), which is wisdom (*prajñā*)."
There is also the family in which the mother is preeminent.

These two, that is to say, wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), dissolve into the reality of the immutable (*akṣara-tattva*); thus, by means of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), the mind can be protected from corruption.
Therefore, within a single mantra-family, all families are merged.
Through the arising of the counteractive knowledge (*pratipakṣijñāna*) that opposes ignorance, there occurs the exhaustion of all defects and the attainment of qualities.
Therefore, it is also called the "family of *vidyā*.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Dvyantanivāraṇa* composed by Jñānaśrī: "The *puruṣadeva* is the secret mantra (*guhyamantra*), and the *strīdeva* is the *vidyā* mantra."

A mantra that is employed for both the father and the mother is called a *dhāraṇī* mantra. While clarifying the Tathāgata family, the great master Buston stated: "The wisdom of realizing the vajra-realm of the nature of all Tathāgatas, as well as the wisdom of the dharmadhātu which is the naturally pure essence of the nature of bodhicitta—this alone constitutes the Vairocana family, that is, the Tathāgata family."

The Vajra family, whose nature is the Akṣobhya-svabhāva, exists as the embodiment of the skillful means that accord with the authorization of all Tathāgatas, manifested according to the desires of living beings; it is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

The Ratnasambhava jewel family exists as the embodiment of the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) of the Tathāgatas, fulfilling the mental aspirations of sentient beings; it is the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
The Lotus family exists as the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*), which is the embodiment of the wisdom of the Tathāgatas.

The family of activity (*karmakula*), which has the nature of the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), is the accomplishment of all the essential natures of the vigor of the Tathāgatas.
In the Yoga Tantra as well, there is the Mother Tantra of Wisdom (*prajñā*) and the Father Tantra of Skillful Means (*upāya*).
This is discussed in the *Guhyālaṅkāravyūha Tantra* regarding body, speech, and mind.
Buston also states in the *Laghusāmānyatantra*: "The *Tattvasaṃgraha* is indeed an *upāyatantra*.
Since this [tantra] primarily elucidates the ten principles (*tattva*), it is therefore a *pitṛtantra*. [It is also] the *Paramādya-tantra*..."
The twenty-five texts beginning with the *Prajñāpāramitā-mukha* are included within the Mother Tantras (*mātṛtantra*), which are characterized by a predominance of wisdom (*prajñā*).
In this way, even within Yoga Tantra, it is possible to divide it into two sections known as the Father and Mother Tantras.
The nature of these two types of tantras is distinct from that of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*).
In this context, "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) refers merely to emptiness (*śūnyamātra*), whereas in the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*), it is the emptiness of great bliss (*mahāsukhaśūnyatva*).
Furthermore, even the emptiness of appearance here consists merely of what is mentally constructed;

however, in the Unsurpassed Tantra, following the entry of the vital winds (*vāyu*) into the *avadhūtī*, there is the very manifestation of the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*) through the method of arising, which constitutes the emptiness of appearance.

The essential point is that, in comparison with the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* tantras, the *Yoga* tantra teaches the methods for the independent accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the Tathāgata family, the Wrathful families, the Vajra family, the Lotus family, and so forth, in a detailed and very clear manner through the meditation on the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*).

Regarding the practice manual of the *Yoga* tantra: for the sake of accomplishing a *Yoga* tantra practice, one must first enter the maṇḍala of whichever one of the five families is appropriate and receive initiation (*abhiṣeka*).
At the time of the consecration, whichever deity the flower falls upon, that alone should be determined as one’s own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).

At the time of the consecration, first of all, one should bathe with the water from the action-vase (*karmakalaśa*); thereafter, the consecration by means of the chosen deity’s vase should be received.

Then, having bestowed the cloth-consecration (*paṭābhiṣeka*) for the five Tathāgata families in the second stage, the vajra-consecration in the third stage, and the bell-consecration (*ghaṇṭābhiṣeka*) in the fourth stage, the practitioner [should cast] the flower...
Whatever [flower] falls upon [the deity] above, according to that chosen deity, the Name-Initiation (*nāmābhiṣeka*) is bestowed;
these are those known by the name "Initiation of the Disciple" (*śiṣyābhiṣeka*).

Thereafter, in the Vajrācārya Initiation, six initiations are bestowed: the Non-returner Initiation (*anāgāmibhiṣeka*), the Secret Initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*), the Authorization (*anujñā*), the Prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), the Encouragement (*āśvāsa*), and the Praise (*praśaṃsā*).
Thus, in the Yogatantra, eleven consecrations are to be received by the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
This is elaborated in detail in the *Jñānatilakatantra*:
"The practitioner who is unable to undertake the vow (*saṃvara*) of the Tathāgata family..."
To one who is able to undertake merely the bodhisattva vow, the *pañcaśiṣyābhiṣeka* alone is granted.
To those practitioners capable of undertaking both the bodhisattva vow and the inclusion of the Tathāgata family (*tathāgatakula*), the *vajrācāryābhiṣeka* should also be bestowed.
Immediately upon receiving this consecration, the practitioner should study the lower methods of practice (*sādhanāvidhi*) of Yoga Tantra.
The practice of the three meditations (*tridhyāna*) and the four yogas (*caturyoga*) of Yoga Tantra is sealed by the four seals (*caturmudrā*).
Therefore, here first, a general introduction to the nature of the three meditations and the four seals is presented.
Regarding the three meditations: generally, an advanced practitioner of Yoga Tantra cultivates the system of practice taught in Yoga Tantra through the three meditations.

In the work titled *Vajradhātumaṇḍalārthabhāvanāpiṇḍārtha*, while clarifying the procedure for the three meditations (*tridhyāna*), the Indian preceptor Kumārakalaśa has analyzed the reality and essential nature of the cultivation of the three meditations in extreme brevity.
Herein, (1) the *Ādiyoga*...
2. The supreme king of the mandala, and (3) that called the supreme king of activities—thus the manifestation of the threefold meditation is performed.
Here, we shall describe them briefly in sequence.

1. The Initial Yoga (*ādiyoga*): First, having meditated upon selflessness (*nairātmya*), one proceeds sequentially through the purification of the neck (*kṛkāṭikā*), the removal of obstacles, the protection of the site, the construction of the maṇḍala, the offering of flowers and so forth, prostration, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, entreaty, supplication, the twentyfold worship, self-dedication, dedication of merit, the making of vows, the generation of the bodhicitta, the taking of the twenty vows, the generation of the supreme form of the bodhicitta, the construction of the maṇḍala of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvamaṇḍala*), the meditation on the reflection of the maṇḍala within the visualized maṇḍala, and finally, the binding of the mudrās.
The ritual action is completed in brief.
Then, there is the characteristic of the vajra-mudrā, the consecration mantra for that, the arising of the vajra-entrance,
and the firming of the vajra.
The extraction from all miserable rebirths,
the warding off of evil, the release of the mudrās, the unsurpassed nature of reality,
and the placement of the heart-mantra upon the vajra of one's own heart.
The meditation on the two moons and the meditation on the vajra are prescribed.
When the practitioner performs the sādhana for the benefit of others, he then performs the meditation on another mudrā and the placement upon the heart (hṛdayanyāsa).
The pride of the mudrā, entry into the previously described maṇḍala,
and the meditation on Vajrasattva.
The pride of Samayavajrasattva is the pride sealed by the Jñānamudrā; by that [pride], there is the consecration of the other four,
as well as the heart of Mahāmudrā and the recitation of mantra.
The visualization of the mandala within one's own heart, the performance of recitation while holding a rosary,
and the entry into the mandala.
Having taken up the garland, there is the binding of the turban, the removal of the face-cloth,
and the showing of the mandala.
In the mandala attained through vision, there is the attainment of firmness;

the five empowerments are the consecration for the purification of each individual mandala, and the self-consecration is by means of each individual mandala. Thus, one must perform the practice of the five hundred and ninety-two yogas, which is the unification within the heart mandala.
Following the placement of moon-discs upon one’s own body, there is the placement of moon-discs in space, the placement at the heart,

and the placement of the vajra-weapon and so forth; through these, as well as by the invocation, visualization, and other rites of the reality of gnosis arising from the maṇḍala of that ego-sense, [the deity] becomes dissolved into oneself.
The stabilization by means of the heart-mantra of color, form, and so forth;

the entry of the Tathāgatas; the visualization of the Vajradhātu and the consecration by the five Tathāgatas; the placement of the vajras in the four directions; and the sealing with the fourfold mudrās.
The binding of all mudrās through a general invocation, the stabilization of that by means of the Śatākṣarī Dhāraṇī,
and the subsequent attainment of consecration.

With joy, through dance, *lāsya*, and so forth, one takes up the vajra, bell, and other implements for worship; there is the recitation of the essential mantra (*tattvamantra*), the singing of songs in three tones,
and the meditation on selflessness (*nairātmya*) together with the recitation of mantras whose nature is devoid of intrinsic existence.
The entrance into immovability (*acalapraveśa*) consists in the purification of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*);

it is the meditation on the general seat (*sāmānyapīṭha*), the special seat (*viśeṣapīṭha*), and the accomplishment of all aims (*sarvārthasiddhi*), as well as the formless cultivation (*dhyānamarūpiṇī bhāvanā*).
The entrance into immovability is the being raised up by the Tathāgatas.

Beholding that, venerating that, receiving instruction from that, and the fivefold perfect enlightenment: (1) the nature of Akṣobhya through discernment; (2) the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), whereby Ratnasambhava arises from the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*); (3) Amitābha, pierced by the vajra; (4) the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), abiding as atoms within the bodies and so forth of all the Tathāgatas.

5. The Perfection of Vigor is, by implication, the Amoghapāśa; 5. the perfection of form (*rūpa*) is the Tathāgata-nature Vairocana, the vajra-jewel initiation, the granting of permission, and the meditation on the celestial palace mandala upon Mount Sumeru.
There is also the yoga-meditation consisting of remaining pervading all directions by means of the four Tathāgatas, and so forth.
(It is stated therein that these aforementioned principles are connected with the internal practice:
the internal ritual bathing of the self.
The application of mindfulness to the body has the tongue as its basis;
the application of mindfulness to feelings has the hands as its basis.
There is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of the dharma that dispels obstacles;
there is the basis of psychic power of the mind that destroys obstacles.
The supernormal power of investigating the fetters of obstacles; the relinquishing of unwholesome states arising from prostration;
and prostration toward the east and other directions.
The non-arising of what has not yet arisen; the prostration at the doors of the five mandalas through the emanation of the mandala;

the production of unarisen wholesome dharmas; the twentyfold worship beginning with the confession of misdeeds; the ritual for the limit of attaining the vows; and the protection of arisen wholesome dharmas—all these constitute the path of accumulation (*saṃbhāramārga*).

The path beginning from the yoga of meditating on the reflected image up to the point of the great yoga constitutes the path of application (*prayogamārga*). Within this path, there exist the vajra-joined palms, the vajra-salutation,
the vajra-penetration, the vajra-firmness, the purification of the miserable realms, and the faculty of faith.
The cultivation of selflessness is the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*);
the cultivation of the two moons is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*);
and the entry into the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*) is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
The placement of the mandalas within the heart-mandala is the power of faith;
entry into the mandala is the power of vigor;
and the garland empowerment is the power of mindfulness.
The song of the three samayas is the power of meditative concentration (*samādhibala*),
and the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatābhāvanā*) is the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*);
this constitutes the path of application (*prayogamārga*).
In the realm of Akaniṣṭha, there is the subtle mental state consisting of the factors of meditation and enlightenment; the visualization of Sumeru is the factor of vigor for enlightenment;
and the visualization of the sacred seats (pīṭha) is the factor of joy for enlightenment.

The going of all Tathāgatas is the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*); seeing them is the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
and instruction regarding them is the factor of enlightenment that is right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The relinquishing of one's own speech and immovable meditation is the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
This is the path of seeing, which is called the first stage, the Joyful (*pramuditā*). Furthermore, analytical inspection is right view, which is called the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*).
The generation of the mind of awakening is right intention, which is the stage of the Radiant; the meditation on the nature of the diamond is indeed right purified speech, the stage of the Flaming;
and the entry into all Tathāgatas is right conduct, the stage of the Unconquerable.
The accomplishment of form is the stage of Right Effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*) which has become manifest;
the basis is Right Action (*samyak-karmānta*) which is the Far-reaching stage (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*);
and in the salutation to the sound of consecration is Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), which is the Immovable stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Through the *Śatākṣarī-dhāraṇī*, firmness is attained; the stage of *sādhumatī* is characterized by right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*); and the attainment of the five permissions is called the *dharmameghā*.
These stages are included within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

2. The meditation on the supreme king of the mandala (*maṇḍalarājāgradhyāna*): In order to fulfill the preliminary limb of the diamond-like meditation (*vajropamasamādhi*), there occurs the stage of the meditation on the supreme king of the mandala through the designation of cause and fruit; that is to say, this is the stage of the transformation of the cause into the fruit.

3. Regarding the *Karmarājāgradhyāna*, here the predominance of the karma of sentient beings is present; that is to say, the *Karmarājāgradhyāna* consists precisely of the Buddha-activity on the eleventh stage, the *Samantaprabhā*, or the Buddha-stage itself.
It appears that Upādhyāya Kumārakalaśa has provided a summary of the subject matter of Ānandagarbha’s commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on the *Tattvasaṃgraha*.

And since, in the first part of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, while commenting on the three meditations (*tridhyāna*) in his *Vajradhātumaṇḍalaṭīkā*, he explained— in detail within the eight-petaled base— the analysis of the syllable *hrīḥ* flowing into the middle of the nape (*kṛkāṭikā*) for the sake of purifying the nape; [this includes] from the first up to the sixteenth [chapter], which is contained within the yoga-meditation (*yogadhyāna*), and from the sixteenth up to the nineteenth (16–19),
which is the explanation of the *maṇḍalarājāgra* and the procedure for emanation and reabsorption (*sphuraṇa-saṃharaṇavidhi*).
From the nineteenth to the twenty-second [chapter], the procedure for the Supreme King of Rites (*karmarājāgravidhi*) has been analyzed.
By examining this commentary, it is understood that the process for attaining Buddhahood consists of the meditation of the Initial Yoga (*ādiyoga*).

This is because the construction of the external maṇḍala, the ritual of worship, consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicittotpāda*), and so forth, are described herein.

In that very same internal form, having cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the attainment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is described as the "initial yoga" (*ādiyoga*); the attainment of Buddhahood is the state of the meditative absorption called the "Vajra Seat" (*vajrāsana*), which is the "supreme king of the mandala" (*maṇḍalarājāgra*);
and the subsequent activities for the attainment of Buddhahood are described as the "supreme king of actions" (*karmarājāgra*).

According to the text known as the *Vajraśekhara*, in the initial yoga of the three meditations, the practitioner himself shall attain enlightenment in the realm of Akaniṣṭha by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*); one should meditate in this manner.
Thereafter, having granted the prophecy to the members of the Bodhisattva assembly, one should place them within the mandala.

Having realized that the second dhyāna of the retinue and one’s own self are non-different, the practice for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings is called the King of Rituals, the Supreme Dhyāna.

It is also stated in the *Jñeyakośa*: "By a supreme practitioner of Yoga Tantra, in order to attain Buddhahood in the realm of Akaniṣṭha, having approached Mount Sumeru and the like in the center, [one should bestow it] upon the attendants..."
The instruction on Yoga-tantra consists of first introducing those disciples into their respective families according to their suitability as vessels, and then performing the rite of grace;
this is also celebrated as the procedure for the three meditations (*tridhyāna*).
In the *Tattvāloka* as well, the three meditations have been briefly analyzed in one place.
Just as the practitioner should meditate on the lotus family,

the meditation on the celestial mansion, the seat, and so forth— consisting of the deity-visualization and the mahāmudrā— is known as the initial yoga (*ādiyoga*). Immediately thereafter, having identified another deity as being identical [to oneself], the performance of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is the second meditation.
The stages beginning with withdrawal (saṃhāra) and empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) are included within the third meditation (dhyāna).

Regarding the four yogas: those practitioners who are unable to perform such meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) accomplish the Yoga Tantra by means of the four yogas. Their names are known as Yoga, Anuyoga, Sarvayoga, and Atiyoga.

The yoga of the deity of that family is the meditation upon the deity of the family from which the practitioner receives initiation; the subsequent yoga (*anuyoga*) is said to be the invocation of the Gnosis-Deity (*jñānadeva*) and its subsequent dissolution [into that deity].

The practice of meditating on the nature of one’s chosen deity, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), and the entire world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) is called the universal yoga (*sarvayoga*).
And the attainment of one-pointedness through these three yogas is called the supreme yoga (*atiyoga*).

One should accomplish the Yoga Tantra by means of the four seals (*caturmudrā*), through the three meditations (*tridhyāna*) or the four yogas (*caturyoga*), or by some other method; one should meditate upon it while sealing it with those four seals. Regarding the realization of the intention of being sealed by the seals, it is stated in the *Paramādya-tantra*: "Whoever is to be sealed by whichever seal, that person shall become of that very nature. When the Samaya-deity is sealed by the Samaya-seal, the deity who is invoked and dissolved by the Jñāna-seal is called the Jñāna-deity.
Through the practice of the sādhana sealed by the four mudrās, various types of gnosis are attained.
Just as it was established in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* that the attainment of supreme majesty results from the transformation of passion and the five sense faculties,
so too should it be understood here.

(1) Through the yoga of the body-seal (*kāyamudrā*), the adventitious delusion (the stain) within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is destroyed, and thus the gnosis of seeing (*darśanajñāna*) manifests.
