(2) Through the yoga of the mind-samaya-seal (*cittasamayamudrā*), the delusion of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is eliminated, and thus the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) arises.
(3) Through the yoga of the Dharma-mudrā of speech, the adventitious impurities of mental consciousness are exhausted, and the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*) manifests.

(4) Through the yoga of the Karma-mudrā by means of body, speech, and mind, the adventitious impurities of the five sense faculties are destroyed, and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) arises.
(5) The wisdom of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātujñāna*) abides in equality across all natures.
The practitioner of Yoga Tantra, having been sealed by the four mudrās, accomplishes the chosen deity. Here,

by explaining a general introduction to the four mudrās, their purification, that which is to be purified, and the method for attaining the fruit, the nature of the four mudrās as described in Yoga Tantra will be defined.

The intention of *mudrā* is simply non-transgression; it is indeed *mudrā*. As the Tathāgata has said: "Just as a king's edict is sealed with his own seals, so too are people sealed by the Great-Souled One with his own seals."
Through the application of the reflection of the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
one who understands that this is the Mahāmudrā of the Great Beings attains accomplishment.

The divisions of mudrā consist of four divisions pertaining to the essential nature of mudrā: namely, mahāmudrā, dharmamudrā, samayamudrā, and karmamudrā. There are likewise four phenomena to be purified by mudrā: namely, the body of ordinary beings, speech and mind, action, and delusion and anger; as well as envy, and the elements of earth, fire, water, and air.
The body is purified by the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), speech by the Dharma Seal (dharmamudrā), the mind by the Commitment Seal (samayamudrā), and action by the Action Seal (karmamudrā).
Furthermore, according to the path, there is the Seal of the Objective Meaning (lakṣyārthamudrā) among these four seals.
Three types of entities arise, consisting of three categories: those characterized by external mudrās, those characterized by internal mudrās, and so forth.

Mahāmudrā is the very body of deities such as Vairocana; it possesses a physical form and is thus a mudrā with defining characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*). Hand gestures that resemble that body are called the externally characterized mudrā (*bāhyalakṣitamudrā*).
At that time, the state of meditating on the forms of the deities such as Vairocana is the internal *dharmamudrā*.
The sixty Brahma-voices of Vairocana’s speech are designated as the *lakṣaṇika-dharmamudrā*.

Having meditated upon oneself as Vairocana, the external *dharmamudrā* is characterized by the placement of the syllable *hrīḥ* on the tongue, the nape of the neck, and so forth; it is the arising of the words being manifested in the form of syllables.
The inner *dharmamudrā* is now explained.
The *samayamudrā* is, in reality, the non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*) of the mind of Vairocana;
for ritual actions and so forth that resemble it are merely the external *samayamudrā*.
The arising of one’s own mind as the form of gnosis (*jñāna*) together with Vairocana himself is designated as the *samayamudrā*.
The *karmamudrā* is the activity of Vairocana; in reality, it is called the *karmamudrā*.
Following the meditation on one’s chosen deity Vairocana, the practice of the procedures for radiating [light] and reabsorbing [it], and so forth, is the external *karmamudrā*.
The effortless wandering in the form of what is to be done is called the internal *karmamudrā*.
That which is to be purified, the *mahāmudrā*, is also fourfold, known as the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, *nirmāṇakāya*, and *svabhāvakāya*. The method of sealing is the cause of the *mudrā*.
The four methods of sealing are: the procedure for sealing, the cause of accomplishment, and the attainment of sovereignty.
The cause of Mahāmudrā is the vajra-fist;
the vajra-fist is precisely the form that gathers the vajras of body, speech, and mind.
The procedure is sealed by Mahāmudrā, which abides in its own nature.

Indeed, the meditation on the five-limbed vajra within the lotus of the deity’s heart is the cause of accomplishment; it is said that the meditation on the profound, vast, and non-dual yoga is the cause of sovereign power.
The utterance of sound is the dharma-mudrā.

Having visualized a five-pronged vajra at the throat (*devakṛkāṭikā*) by means of the syllable *hrīḥ* at the two lotus-tongues, the procedure for sealing with the Dharma-mudrā through the recitation of the mantra is proclaimed.
Visualizing the Dharma-syllable-vajra thus situated around the navel is the cause of accomplishment.

Having become established in the profound, vast, and non-dual reality, one should move the tongue against the palate, visualize a subtle vajra at the tip of the nose, and the procedure for attaining mastery over the Dharma-mudrā through one-pointedness of mind is described.
Vajra-recitation is the cause of the *samayamudrā*.

Having transformed oneself into the form of Vairocana, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*) within the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) along with inhalation and exhalation— accompanied by the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*) with one’s chosen deity— is precisely what is called the "sealing reality" (*mudritattva*) of the *samayamudrā*.

Immediately after meditative absorption (*samādhi*), having established the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which has become the object of the five supreme cultivations (*pañcāgrabhāvanā*), the triple recitation of the mantra is declared to be the cause for the accomplishment of the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*).

Following that, the analytical separation [of the body] by means of logical arguments in order to demonstrate the emptiness of one's own aggregates and so forth is said to be the cause for attaining sovereignty.
In the *Tattvārthāvatāra*, according to the method of exposition, there is no speech without the body.
Without speech, body and mind cannot exist; and without body, speech and mind are not possible either.
Therefore, just as the rites for each of the four mudrās are marked by their respective seals, so too each individual mudrā must be sealed by the four mudrās.
According to the family system, the Tathāgata family is Mahāmudrā.
The Vajra family is the pledge-seal (samayamudrā), the Lotus family is the dharma-seal (dharmamudrā), and the Jewel family— and by implication the Action family— is the action-seal (karmamudrā).
The manifestation of an inexhaustible body arises from the Tathāgata family.
Through the Mind-Vajra family, knowledge is practiced both in its full extent and according to its specific nature.
By means of speech, such as the proclamation of the Dharma and so forth, one abides in the Lotus family.
Diverse activities possess the nature of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and belong to the Jewel family (*maṇikula*),

because through them great benefit for sentient beings arises. Regarding the specific procedure for the practice of Yoga Tantra, concerning the subject matter of Yoga Tantra practice, the master Ānandagarbha [states that] the determination of the practitioner’s necessary qualifications, the causal factors for the objective to be accomplished, the means of accomplishment, and so forth, must necessarily be established in the presence of the practitioner.
What is required?

By describing this, the method of practice (*sādhanāpaddhati*) is clarified: 1. The qualification of the practitioner (*sādhakayogyatā*): he alone is a practitioner in whom both types of bodhicitta—known as the *praṇidhāna* (aspiration) and *prasthāna* (engagement)—have arisen.

The clarification of these two types of mind is set forth in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* as follows: the aspiration for the attainment of enlightenment in all living beings is the *praṇidhāna-citta* (the mind of aspiration), and the practice of the perfections (*pāramitās*) for that purpose is called the *prasthāna-citta* (the mind of application).

For a practitioner endowed with both these types of mind, there is an uninterrupted faith toward the *tantra* scriptures and a longing to practice the trainings as they have been taught in order to attain the state of a Tathāgata.
A firm and deep-seated trust is required toward the teacher who reveals the path and the Instructor.

Vajreśvara also stated that even a householder must observe all those ethical precepts (*śīla*) which are not to be abandoned even by those who have gone forth into homelessness. 2. Determining the Goal: The goal of Yoga Tantra is Vairocana himself, who is free from all obscurations, endowed with all qualities, and perfected in the four bodies (*kāya*).

In the *Koṣālaṅkāra*, a commentary on the *Tattvasaṃgraha* by Ānandagarbha, it was stated: "Vairocana, whose nature is the Tathāgata-Vajraskandha, is the 'Minor Vairocana' (*laghuvairocana*). There exists the 'Great Vairocana' (*mahāvairocana*), who consists of the *dharmadhātu*, is devoid of beginning and end, and is the reality (*tattva*) free from obscurations.

3. The material cause (*upādāna*), the reality of the purity of the support for the deity and mantra—which is characterized by the discernment of the naturally luminous Samantabhadra-bodhicitta that is devoid of beginning and end—are the causal factors for the attainment of Vairocana."
4. There are two divisions of *sādhana*: *sevā* (service) and *sādhana* (accomplishment).

Furthermore, for *sevā*, two divisions are made: those called "with characteristics" (*salakṣaṇa*) and "without characteristics" (*nirlakṣaṇa*), or alternatively, method (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

5. Method, or yoga with characteristics, consists of the three meditations (*tridhyāna*), the fourfold yoga, or being sealed by the four mudrās; the cultivation of the family maṇḍala is called the cultivation of yoga with coarse characteristics (*sthūla-salakṣaṇa-yoga*).
After attaining firmness in the gross yoga (*sthūlayoga*), the practitioner cultivates the subtle yoga with its characteristics (*sūkṣmasalakṣaṇayoga*).
In the cultivation of the subtle yoga with its characteristics, the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) is meditated upon by means of any one of the three meditations (*tridhyāna*) or the four yogas.
Having directed the tongue toward the palate, the form of the chosen deity—resembling a sesame seed and possessing a subtle nature—is meditated upon in the center of the navel.

Together with the exhalation, the subtle vajra is slowly raised from the navel-center; at the time of its exit through the nostrils, practitioners—endowed with mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*)—restrain the upper breath and, having established the mind in the nature of that vajra, meditate as much as possible. As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Having placed the tongue against the palate..."
One should contemplate the tip of the nose;
through the touch of the bliss of the subtle vajra, the mind becomes concentrated.
Because the mind is situated at the tip of the nose, as the wind and the mind subside,
bliss is experienced throughout the entire body;
this very state is called bodily pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*).

Through the flow of the movement of the winds within the body and by attaining a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*), stability suddenly arises even in the mind that is dependent upon the winds— this is what is called "pliancy of mind" (*cittaprasrabdhi*). Following that, for the sake of becoming fit for mental conformity according to his wish, the practitioner, through daily practice, generates a distinguished meditative absorption (*viśiṣṭadhyāna*) by emanating infinite subtle vajras at the tip of the nose during the time of exhalation,
thereby pervading the three worlds.
Furthermore, when the limit of the breath has been reached, one is able to withdraw [the mind] into the field of the navel and establish stability there.
Regarding this meditation on the object, it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "When the sign of the touch of the subtle vajra-bliss arises, one should expand that very sign."
That mind should radiate everywhere.
By radiating the mind as desired, it may radiate even throughout the three realms;
then, one should withdraw it again until it reaches the tip of the nose.
From that time forward, whatever one may visualize with a well-composed mind,
one should make all of it firm, as it is fashioned by the knowledge of meditative concentration.

In the *Tattvaloka*, a practitioner (*sādhaka*) who possesses the application of the characteristics [of reality] should be endowed with the ten principles (*daśatattva*), distinguished by the means of practice at the beginning, middle, and end.
For example: 1. the mandala of the formed and the formless; 2. the mantra that is both external and internal; 3. the state of being sealed by the four seals (*caturmudrā*).
4. Guarding the yoga of the place;
5. The withdrawal and invocation of the gnosis-beings;
6. The recitation of mantras with the mind by means of the sound of the *vajra*.
7. Cultivation of the three dhyānas and so forth;
8. Outer and inner homa, such as the mandala worship and so forth; 9. Release of the mudrās and the conclusion.
10. Following worship is the dismissal (*visarjana*);
these are the ten principles (*tattva*) of yoga with characteristics (*salakṣaṇayoga*).
Wisdom (*prajñā*) [is] yoga without characteristics (*nirlakṣaṇayoga*).

The cultivation of general wisdom (*sāmānyaprajñā*)—that is, the state of self-cognizing knowledge for the direct realization of the reality of the mind (*cittatattva*)—is indeed designated as "signless yoga" (*nirlakṣaṇayoga*). Furthermore, according to the system of the *Viśeṣayogatantra* and also in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "By means of entering the syllable A..."
Through the knowledge of all syllables,
one shall attain accomplishment by meditating upon one's own face and the faces of others.

Even with full proficiency in the yoga with signs (*salakṣaṇayoga*), the realization of knowledge as it is and in its full extent (*yathāvadyāvajjñāna*) is not possible without the yoga without signs (*nirlakṣaṇayoga*), which constitutes higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).

In the yoga without signs, one establishes the state beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) by means of wisdom, having separated [the mind] from the heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*), secret mantras, dhāraṇīs, and so forth.
This matter is also clarified in the following passage from the *Nāmasaṃgīti*:
The meaning of "A" is that which is unarisen.
For this very reason, the seed-syllable (bījākṣara) produced from vowels such as "A" and from consonants is devoid of a locus of support, selfless, and empty.
The arising of the letter "A"—the first among all letters and the most excellent—occurs without the conjunction of any [other] limbs.
For example: "The Great Vital Breath is indeed non-arising, devoid of verbal expression;
the letter A is the foremost of all letters, of great significance, the supreme syllable."
The letter *a* emerges from the great vital breath (*mahāprāṇa*), and it is that which brings about the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus, all seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) are likewise.
Here, the intention regarding the "face" or "mouth" is the gateway of entry.

Therefore, the practitioner himself is said to have entered into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) via the gateways of the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*). He should likewise personally meditate upon entering the mandala of his chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), who has been visualized before him.
Furthermore, in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-uttaratantra*, it is stated: "The wisdom known as 'penetrating' (*nairvedhikī*) is proclaimed as the samādhi;
by means of it, the mudrās are accomplished."
By meditating [upon this], one attains accomplishment in an instant.
That is to say, there is wisdom that penetrates reality;
this is the vision of selflessness which is unarisen.

The very state of abiding in emptiness, which is the appearance of the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), is declared to be the yoga without characteristics (*nirlakṣaṇa-yoga*).
Through the cultivation of this yoga without characteristics alone, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is swiftly attained.
As it is said in that very same [text]: "In the case of knowledge-mantras (*vidyā-mantra*), no distinction among distinctions exists."
Cultivating in this way with wisdom, accomplishment will swiftly and certainly be attained.

The essence of the entire exposition is as follows: through the practice of both yogas, one-pointedness and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are accomplished by means of the yoga with signs (*sanimitta-yoga*), while the fruit of union (*yuganaddha*) is attained through signless and causeless meditation (*nirlakṣaṇānimitta-dhyāna*), through wisdom that is free from conceptual elaboration (*nairvedhika-prajñā*), through meditation consisting of analytical inspection (*pratyavekṣaṇātmaka-dhyāna*), and through the meditation of the union of both (*ubhaya-yuganaddha-dhyāna*). Regarding the general procedure for recitation (*japa*) and the sequence for achieving specific accomplishments (*viśeṣa-siddhi*): within the three types of meditation or the four yogas, following the visualization of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) according to any single method, the recitation is performed for the sake of accomplishment.
Generally, there are two types of *japa*: *vajrajapa* and *śabdajapa*.
In his work *Siddhabārāvā-Mahodaya*, the author proposed six varieties of *japa*:
1. *Nirodhajapa* is the concentration of the mind on the syllable *A* without focusing the meditation on inhalation and exhalation.

2. When the syllable *oṃ* is associated with inhalation (*praśvāsa*), *hūṃ* with exhalation (*śvāsa*), and *āḥ* with the retention of breath, the practice of filling, emptying, and retaining the wind (*pūraka-rechaka-kumbhaka*) is called "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajapa*). 3. Having visualized the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) of one's chosen mantra within the heart-lotus, and having performed the emanation and reabsorption of its mass of light rays while performing worship to the Tathāgatas and the welfare of sentient beings—the practitioner’s method of meditation is termed "recitation through emanation and reabsorption" (*sphuraṇa-saṃharaṇajapa*).
4. Performing the recitation mentally alone;
5. performing the practice of recitation by means of the palate, tongue, and lips without sound;
6. the procedure for recitation while contemplating the mere sounds together with ordinary vocalization.

These are the six aspects of recitation (*japa*). In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the varieties of recitation are described as follows: "One who has not excessively moved the tip of the tongue and whose two lips and teeth are joined together, and who is devoid of the sound of 'vajra-speech,' shall accomplish all ritual manuals."
With a voice as deep as the wrathful *hūṃ* syllable clouded by thunder, steady,
and bursting with fury, this is the practice of the speech of the Vajra-Wrathful One, the Great Vajra.
Without exhaling, with subtle breath and subtle speech, very clearly,
all recitations are accomplished through that which has meditative concentration and primordial wisdom as its essence.

Regarding vajra-recitation: immediately after meditating on one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), one should visualize that very chosen deity, who is identical to oneself, as being present before one. One should then perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and fix the mind upon the exhaled breath and the chosen deity facing oneself.
During exhalation, one should meditate on the non-differentiation between one's own physical body and the body of the deity.
At the time of arresting the internal wind, the recitation of the mantra is performed mentally;
this alone is called "vajra-recitation" (vajrajapa), which is endowed with the characteristics of the conventional truth.
The practitioner himself, as well as the deity, mantra, and all other phenomena, are utterly pure like the empty sky;
realizing this, one should remain having restrained the breath within emptiness according to the specific practice.
At the moment of releasing the breath, one should simply recollect the characteristics of the chosen deity.
Furthermore, having become established in the ultimate reality at the limit of the breath, the performance of the vajra-recitation is called the "ultimate vajra-recitation.
This method of recitation is for the practitioner with sharp faculties;
by means of this, supramundane accomplishment is attained.
The practitioner of soft faculties performs the recitation of sound (*śabdajapa*).

Just as the practitioner prepares the seat of his chosen deity, holds the weapon of his chosen deity in his left hand, and grasps the rosary with his right hand according to his lineage, he recites clearly, following the procedure for the recitation of the lineage mantra (*kulamantra*).
And that is proclaimed as the recitation of sound (*śabdajapa*).

Having meditated upon the fullness of the short, long, and other measures (*mātrā*) within this, the recitation is to be performed. By means of this, the accomplishments of substances, the sky-farers (*khecarī*), the sciences (*vidyā*), and so forth, are attained.

The practice for the attainment of special accomplishments (*viśeṣasiddhicaryā*) is carried out through the threefold method consisting of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the procedure for recitation (*japa*), and the procedure for fire-offerings (*homa*).

Immediately after attaining firmness in the service (*sevā*) and in the subtle vajra-meditation, this practice is prescribed for the sake of obtaining mundane and supramundane accomplishments. Relying on the method for accomplishing mundane accomplishments, it is also stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "The vajra-image situated within a treasure..."
One should contemplate it within the heart.
By contemplating it, one sees treasures situated in the earth.
Having drawn the vajra-image,
one should contemplate it in the sky;
wherever one sees it fall, there one should indicate that a treasure-trove lies hidden.

Having visualized a treasure jar within the lotus of one’s own heart, a moon mandala above that, and a five-pronged vajra above that, one should recite the Vajranidhi mantra until signs such as its touch or appearance become manifest.

Alternatively, having visualized a universal vajra within oneself and a vajra in the sky, through the performance of the recitation, wherever the appearance of a vajra falling occurs, there indeed the treasure will be found.
It should be understood in this way:

likewise, for the sake of achieving the power of moving upon water, one should fill a large vessel with water in a stream or in some somewhat still place; while gazing at it, the recitation of the *vajra-jala* mantra should be performed, and one should contemplate that the water has been transformed into the nature of the *vajra*.
Gradually, the water will appear like a diamond (*vajra*).
Thereafter, as soon as the yogi desires to go into the water, he should concentrate in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and thereby attain the capacity for movement.
As it is said in the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha*: "When the diamond-entrance (*vajrāveśa*) has arisen, there is water consisting of diamond-forms."
The lord of yogis who meditates thus may walk upon the surface of the water.

For the sake of supramundane accomplishment, one should personally meditate upon any one of the five Tathāgatas while reciting "Vajradhātu Hūṃ," contemplating that space is pervaded by the bodies of the Tathāgatas.

Having reflected thus, at the time of inhaling, just as water dries up in the sand, all the Tathāgatas dissolve into the lotus of one's own heart; and at the time of exhaling, they expand once again throughout the mandala of space.
One should meditate in this way.
By meditating thus, the practitioner will become a Bodhisattva bearing the form of a Buddha and a holder of the Vidyā-mantras.

Whether of dull faculties or middling faculties, the practitioner will gradually attain the Mahāmudrā-siddhi within three lifetimes or sixteen lifetimes, and through the five awakenings (pañcābhisambodhi), will attain the five gnoses (pañcajñāna) in the Akaniṣṭha realm.
Having realized [this], one attains awakening.
A person of sharp faculties may attain the supreme state through the practice of Yoga Tantra even in a single lifetime or three lifetimes.
In conclusion, the term "Amudrā" is found generally in both the Sūtra and Tantra systems.

In the Buddhist tradition, however, one such seal (mudrā) is accepted, whose essential nature is as follows: 1. Conditioned phenomena are impermanent and momentary; 2. Phenomena associated with outflows are suffering; 3. All phenomena are empty of self and lack a self-nature (nairātmya);
4. Nirvāṇa is supreme peace.
These four are not to be transgressed;
therefore, these are adorned with the name of "seals" (mudrā). Whoever, having understood these four seals, acts [otherwise], [is a transgressor].
Those are Buddhists, and others are non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, in the sūtras, emptiness and so forth are designated as "seals" (*mudrā*).
As it is said in the *Sāgaramatiparipṛcchā-sūtra*: "O Sāgaramati! All phenomena are sealed with the seal of liberation; all phenomena are non-dual and utterly pure, indivisible like space."
Therefore, all phenomena are sealed by equality; prior to that, there is the stainless seal due to the complete purity of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Thus, twenty seals are enumerated.

In the *Maitreyaparipṛcchāsūtra* it is also said: "O son of noble family! The nature of all phenomena is the seal of emptiness. And in the *Ratnadārikāparipṛcchā*, it is stated: "The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like space."
This very characteristic belongs to the *mudrā*.
Sometimes the *prajñāpāramitā* is also designated as a *mudrā*.
In the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*: "The middle fingers joined together shall certainly form a single crest (*ekashikhā*)."
This mudrā is the Mahāmudrā,
revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.

Hand gestures (*hasta-mudrā*) have also been taught in the form of *mudrās*. In the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra*, the term *mudrā* is even applied to divine weapons. In Yoga Tantra, the four *mudrās* beginning with the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) are defined as the very visualization of oneself as resembling the body of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), as described above.

In the Anuttarayoga Tantra as well, the four mudrās, beginning with Mahāmudrā, are discussed in the same manner as in the Yoga Tantra; however, there is a fundamental difference in their essential nature.
As it is stated in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "Vajra is indivisible gnosis (*jñāna*); by means of this, one is sealed (*mudryate*).
'Mud' means joy (*harṣa*), and because great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is produced by that cause, it is called 'mudrā'."
The meaning of *mudrā* is that reality (*tattva*) by which joy (*mud*) or, alternatively, great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is produced.
It has four divisions.

Thus, Nāgārjuna states in the *Caturmudropadeśa*: "The action seal (*karmamudrā*), the wisdom seal (*jñānamudrā*), the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), and that which is called the commitment seal (*samayamudrā*), which is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*)."
The cause, that which is to be cultivated, that which is to be attained, and likewise the indestructible—these are the fourfold [aspects].
Regarding this, there are many types of explanations in the Unexcelled Tantra (*anuttaratantra*).
Among them, the action-born consort (*karmamudrā*) and the mentally constructed conceptual consort (*jñānamudrā*) are generally [distinguished].

Indeed, emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects is called the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), while the reality of luminosity (*prabhāsvaratattva*), characterized by perfect awakening through its nature of immutable bliss, is the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*).
The cause is the action seal (karmamudrā), the means of accomplishment is the wisdom seal (jñānamudrā), and that which is to be accomplished is the great seal (mahāmudrā).
Furthermore, the state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) is also called a "pledge-seal" (*samayamudrā*).
Thus, even though the word *mudrā* refers to a single [conceptual] entity, it is seen to possess different essential natures.
The term *tridhyāna* (the three meditations) is observed to be used extensively in both the Yoga and Anuttara Tantras.
In both cases, the initial yoga is cultivated for one's own benefit as the *maṇḍalarājāgra* and the *karmarājāgra* for the benefit of others.
Likewise, the application of the four yogas is also observed in the *pitṛtantra* texts.
Even though there is a similarity in terminology, the *Anuttara-tantra* is superior from the perspective of its underlying intent (*bhāva*).

For in the Unexcelled Yoga Tantra (*anuttarayogatantra*), the meditation on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) or the meditation on one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) is brought forth in the form of the union of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya-yuganaddha*).
However, the moon, seed-syllables, and hand-emblems are meditated upon by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*).
Furthermore, in the Yoga Tantra, the transformation of passion (*rāga*) is limited to embracing.
Furthermore, in the *Anuttarayogatantra*, the method for bringing the two types of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) onto the path has been clearly demonstrated.
The procedure for the practice of the *Anuttarayogatantra* will be explained below.
Because the description of the limbs of practice (*sādhanāṅga*) is common to both these tantras, many scholars consider them to be one and the same.
The term "threefold meditation" (tridhyāna) is also employed in the Anuttara Tantras;
for they are indeed distinct from the Yoga Tantras.
Due to this similarity in nomenclature, two traditions developed within the Bhārata [tradition].
One [tradition] was at Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in the region of Vaṅga, while the other was indeed in Madhyadeśa.

Regarding the Śākya tradition known as the *Jamgon Amas Jabsa*, King Jagaddala— also called Prakāśacandra, who is said to be an emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Vajrasattva— had a disciple named Ānandagarbha, who had been prophesied by Tārā.

Following the *Nṛpaprakāśacandra*, the *Guhyasamāja-mūlatantra* and the *Vairocanamāyājāla* are explained by being sealed with the ten principles (*tattva*) beginning with the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) and the four seals (*mudrā*), according to the system of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. According to the opinion of Ānandagarbha, after attaining enlightenment, the Tathāgata taught the *Tattvasaṃgraha* seven days later.
Subsequently, commentaries on the *Buddhakapāla*—an *mātṛtantra*, or "mother tantra"—the *Guhyasamāja*, the *Māyājāla*, and others were established as tantras.
Indian scholars of the past considered the divisions of tantra to be known as Kriyā, Caryā, and Yoga;
thus, the tantras that followed the Caryātantras are subsumed within the Yogatantra itself.
The Yoga and Anuttarayoga Tantras are one.

Commentaries on the *Nāmasaṃgīti* and other texts have been composed by Mañjuśrī and others precisely along these lines. In that very context, Jamgon Amgasab, according to his own conviction, maintains that among the tantras—such as the *Hevajra*, *Cakrasaṃvara*, and *Guhyasamāja*—the scholars and kings of Northern India acknowledge the *Kālacakra Tantra* to be the most excellent.
And they explain it according to the *Kālacakrapaddhati*.
This is the fifth chapter. Regarding the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*), there are three divisions of the Unsurpassed Tantra consisting of Father Tantra, Mother Tantra, and Non-dual Tantra.
Here, we shall sequentially examine the emergence of the Father Tantra.

The prosperity of the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*): therein, for the sake of favoring those to be trained (*vineyajana*), the Father Tantra is divided into three classes according to the predominance of passion, hatred, and delusion.
For those possessed of passion, the *Guhyasamāja* was taught; for those dominated by hatred, the *Yamāri-tantra*; and for those dominated by delusion, the *Nāmasaṃgīti*.

This *Guhyasamāja* is the principal text of the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*). It is accepted that the root tantra (*mūlatantra*) consists of 25,000 verses, while the condensed root tantra (*saṃgrahamūlatantra*) consists of 1,800 verses,
which has been applied across eighteen chapters.

The *Saṃgrahatantra* has at various times been designated as the *Mūlatantra*, because in the eighteenth chapter of the *Uttaratantra*, questions regarding the *Saṃgrahatantra* are raised and its explanation is provided;
this is also generally done.
The master Seratogapa stated that the *Guhyasamāja* is, in general, the root of all tantras.

For in these three tantras marked as Kriyātantra and so forth, the path to the attainable *siddhi* is also found by means of the presence or absence of signs (*sanimita*) and the application of what is auspicious or inauspicious (*sadasadyoga*).
Therefore, this [Guhyasamāja] is designated as the *Samāja*.
To clarify the intention that the *Uttaratantra* constitutes the eighteenth chapter, it is stated in that very same work: "This Guhyasamāja also exists."

For the teaching of this tantra was indeed given within that very celestial palace (*vimāna-maṇḍala*) in the midst of the attendant deities, and it exists as having been composed in that specific sequence. A true understanding of the *Guhyasamāja* can only occur when there is a thorough study of its explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*).
There is a hexad of such explanatory tantras, namely: the eighteen chapters of the *Guhyasamāja*;...

The *Caturdevīparipṛcchā*, the *Sandhivyākaraṇanirdeśa*, the *Vajramālā*, and likewise the *Jñānavajrasamuccaya*— the latter being unavailable in the Tibetan language— as well as the *Devendrapariccheda*: in its eighteenth chapter, the *Uttaratantra* explains the *Guhyasamāja* by providing a commentary in the form of questions and answers for each individual chapter.
The *Caturdevīparipṛcchātantra* elucidates the methods of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and reveals the secret clearly.

The *Sandhivyākaraṇanirdeśatantra* clarifies the intended meaning of the *vajrajāpa* and *tattvakrama* as they appear in the *Guhyasamāja*. The *Vajramālātantra* [explains] the twenty sections on the rites of death, birth, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the channels (*nāḍī*), winds (*vāyu*), and the tilaka-consecration; the generation stage (*utpattikrama*); the three meditations (*tridhyāna*); the four yogas; and the forty-nine principles (*tattva*).

Through the medium of an explanation of the forty syllables beginning with ‘A’—which represent the definitive meaning of the thirty-two deities—and through the medium of the introductory chapter (*nidāna-parivarta*), he provides a clear commentary while gathering all the complete constituent parts of the tantra.
The *Jñānasamuccaya-tantra* offers a lucid exposition on the ornaments of the subject matter of the *Guhyasamāja*, as well as the procedures for the practice of the illusory body (*māyā-kāya*).
Dagpo Trashi Namgyal states that within the *Guhyasamāja* there exists an unclear explanation regarding these thirty-two deities.
The *Vajramālā* clarifies that commentary;
it also fulfills those twenty methods in the *Mūlatantra* related to the *utpannakrama* (generation stage) which were incomplete.
The *Jñānasamuccaya* provides a commentary on the *Guhyasamāja Mūlatantra* by adorning its words with the seven ornaments.
The *Sandhivyākaraṇa* explains the secret intention (*rahasyābhiprāya*) of the root text by clarifying it.
A brief introduction to these works is presented here: regarding the teaching of this tantra, the *Guhyasamāja*, it has been mentioned previously;
it consists of seventeen chapters (*paṭala*).
The eighteenth chapter is accepted as the *Uttaratantra*.

Buston Rinpoche, correlating these chapters with their subject matter, enumerated them as follows: 1. An exposition of the generation and completion stages preceded by the presentation of the diagnosis (*nidāna*);
2. An exposition of the bodhicitta of the completion stage.
3. The yoga of the pure deity;
4. The instruction on the ritual of consecration within the maṇḍala of the mind;
5. The practice of yoga.
6. The empowerment of body, speech, and mind; 7. The expansion of yogic conduct; 8. The secret empowerment.
9. The exposition of the prophecy of wonders;
10. The exhortation of the heart-essence of the external and internal deities facing accomplishment;
11. The origin of the mantra-deity and the gnosis-deity.
12. The cultivation of Mahāmudrā; 13. The collection of activities proceeding internally;
15. Meditation resembling an illusion; 16. The procedure for the extensive clay maṇḍala that transcends the body-vajra maṇḍala.
17. And [this is] the principal exposition of the commitments (*samaya*) and the vows (*saṃvara*).
18. The eighteenth chapter, the *Uttaratantra*, exists.
Having been questioned by Maitreya and other bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata, saying "Excellent, excellent," taught it in the form of a reply.

Here, according to the tradition of Siddha Thagana Pāda, there are answers to fifty-four questions; according to the tradition of Bhavyakīrti, there are answers to seventy-two questions; and according to the tradition of the *Śrīguhyasamājatantra-upadeśasāgara-kaṇa* composed by Viśvamitra, there are answers to fifty-six questions, through which the doubts of the Bodhisattvas were dispelled.
Viśvamitra and Ānandagarbha accept that, following the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, all the tantric scriptures (*tantraśāstra*) were taught as the *Uttaratantra*.

The teachings of the explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*) such as the *Vajramālā* occurred at various locations according to the tradition of Ācārya Alaṃkalaśa. On the northern mountain of Oḍḍiyāna, Vajrasattva manifested in the form of the ten wrathful deities (*daśakrodha*) and, in order to discipline the ten guardians of the directions, gave the instruction on the *Bṛhadvajramālā* consisting of twelve thousand verses, as well as the *Laghuvajramālā*.
Upon the request of the goddesses in the Himalayas, the *Sandhivyākaraṇatantra* was taught; the *Caturdevīparipṛcchātantra* on Mount Vaipulya; and the *Jñānavajrasamuccaya* on the banks of the Gaṅgā.

Herein, a brief introduction to the explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*) is presented: the *Vajramālā*, known as the *Vajramālā*, is a very extensive and highly important work that elucidates the branch of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
It is accepted.
At the request of Cakrapāṇi, the Blessed One taught this treatise, which is divided into sixty-eight chapters, as a response.
1. The Chapter on Etiology (Nidānaparivarta).
2. The procedure for consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by means of the examination of the teacher and the disciple;

3. The meaning of the name *Vajramālā*, the names of the one hundred and eight winds, their location, the method of their movement, and the classification of the term *vajramālā*; 4. The explanation of the word *samāja*.

5. The meaning of the word *śūnyatā* (emptiness); 6. The classification of the *vāyutilaka*; 7. The yoga of *vajrajāpa* as well as the method for attaining the supreme state (*paramapada*) by means thereof.
7. An explanation of the word *nāda*;
8. An explanation of the word *bhaga* as the *dharmadhātu* (the realm of phenomena) in its secret sense;
9. *Saṃvara* (vow) and *samaya* (pledge).
10. An explanation of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the commitments (*samaya*) regarding foods, drinks, and so forth;
11. An explanation of the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*); 12. The reality of wind (*vāyutattva*).

The procedure for recitation by means of counting the breaths, the functions of the winds, and the exposition of the wind-elements; 13. the meaning of the four empowerments as well as the explanation of the term *mahāmudrā*.
14. The emptiness of the channels (*nāḍīśūnyatā*), the yoga of the lotus-wind-heart-vajra-lotus;
15. The reality of the secret mantra (*guhyamantratattva*).
16. The means for attaining the immeasurable vital airs (*vāyu*) through the observation of the moment-by-moment dissolution and emergence of the *prāṇas* by relying on the vital air (*vāyu*).
17. The number of channels (*nāḍī*) and their names within the assembly of the four channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*).
18–32. The inclusion of all channels within the principal channels.
19. An exposition of the four factors beginning with maturation (*vipāka*);

20. The characteristics and divisions of the four joys (*ānanda*); 21. The specific distinctions regarding the methods of cultivation for the *mantra-tilaka*, *vāyu-tilaka*, and *dravya-tilaka*; 22. The method of cultivation for the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, which by implication explains the channels (*nāḍī*), winds (*vāyu*), and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as the essence of body, speech, and mind (*kāya-vāk-citta*).

23. A description of the secret nose-tip, the navel-nose-tip, the mouth-nose-tip, and so forth, as well as the five winds (*pañcavāyu*), the method for their circulation, and the procedure for the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of substances, mantras, and *tilakas*;

24. An exposition on the term "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*); 25. The instruction on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) as deities, along with their characteristics; 26. The names and sequence of the goddesses residing within the four channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*).

27. The presentation of the channels (*nāḍī*) as having the nature of goddesses, and the yogic procedure for their rising and setting; 28. The conceptualized procedure for great bliss (*mahāsukha*) by means of the collection of the six channel-wheels (*ṣaḍnāḍīcakra*), as well as the characteristics of the various joys (*ānanda*);
29. The procedure for the entry of semen, blood, and wind into the channels, and their characteristics.
30. The function of the three principal channels; 31. The method of the body’s formation according to the ten winds, resembling the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu;
32. Following the process of origination by means of the wind, the gradual exhaustion of the vital breaths along with the cessation of the winds.

33. Through the fire of the Cāṇḍālī, there is the gathering of all ḍākinīs. 34. The method for the cessation of conceptual construction by means of the generation and completion stages; that is to say, the characteristic of the severing of the wind of conceptualization. 35. The instruction on the non-conceptual wind within the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the characteristic of non-conceptuality. 36. Through the cultivation of the wind, the dissolution of the network of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) is described.
37. The meditation on the six cakras together with the four nāḍī-cakras, the fire-cakra, and the wind-cakra;
38. The clarification of the meaning of the fourth consecration and the explanation of the secret term;
39. The exposition of the dharmadhātu.
40. The meaning of *vajra*;

41. The arising of one hundred families from a single family, as well as their dissolution into that one family; 42. The four seals (*caturmudrā*), the six divisions of the action seal (*karmamudrā*), their dissolution into a single family, and the divisions of the great seal (*mahāmudrā*).

43. The characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas) and the sense bases (āyatanas); 44. The divisions of Mahāmudrā; 45. The clarification of the eight experiences that arise because the winds depend upon the channels (nāḍīs).
46. The explanation of the word "I" (ahaṃśabda); 47. The definition of the eighteen emptinesses (aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā);
48. The arising of the vajra-garland through the cultivation of the emptiness of the wind-element (vāyutattva).

49. An extensive commentary on day and night; 50. A specification of the types and times of Ālokāloka and Bhāsā, as well as an extensive commentary thereon; 51. An explanatory commentary on the characteristics of the arising at the boundary.
52. The twentyfold method; 53. The exposition of the performance of the twentyfold ritual action;
54. The exposition of the procedure for internal worship after having abandoned external worship.
55. The instruction on the channel (nāḍī) goddess and likewise the characteristics of the goddesses;
56. the explanation of the word "thus" (evam);
57. [the section] on those assembled in the Chapter on the Origin (nidānaparivarta).
40. An explanation of each of the forty syllables;
58. The procedure for the internal fire sacrifice (adhyātmahoma);
59. The procedure for the preparation of the nectar-pill (amṛtaguṭikā) as well as the procedure for consuming the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
60. The ritual procedure for the *gaṇacakra* and the procedure for responding to the secret signs; 61. The secret signs of speech and the explanation of esoteric terminology.
62. The exposition of the mandala of body, speech, and mind, complete with the body of the Master;
63. The characteristics of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; 64. The exposition of the conduct of disciples and the results of activities such as pacification and so forth.
65. The procedure for accomplishing ritual actions through the service of the deities of the Four Wrathful Ones;

66. The procedure for accomplishing the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*); 67. The procedure for the purification of the deities of the body-maṇḍala through the practice of the union of luminosity (*prabhāsvara-yuganaddha*);
68. Finally, the praise of the Bodhisattva, the Supreme Lord.
The conclusion of the *Vajramālā-tantra* occurs at this very point.
At the beginning of the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-tantra*, the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is absent;

By means of the compendium of luminaries (*jyotiṣasaṃgraha*), [there is] the astronomy of the constellations (*nakṣatra-jyautiṣa*) and the method for the movement of planets and constellations in the sky. 4. By means of the *Svarodaya* and the compendium of instruments (*yantrasaṃgraha*), there is the examination of the skill or lack of skill in predictive astrology (*phalitajyotiṣa*) and the method for the destruction of enemies. —By these [means], the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) effects the eradication of the barbarian religion (*mlecchadharma*). Together with the instruction on the arrival of the Universal Monarch in the twelve divisions of the five continents (*pañcakadvīpa*), the conclusion of the first chapter occurs.
The Chapter on the Inner Science (*adhyātmapaṭala*): First verse: Because of the statement accepting the request and the commentary, it exists.
1. In this chapter, there are 180 verses comprising seven groups of summaries.

Through the summaries of the exposition on the origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and path (*mārga*) of the suffering arising from body, speech, and mind, [it describes] the method for the perfection of the body, beginning from the union of semen and blood during the embryonic state up until the attainment of intelligence. 2. Through the summary of the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*), [it describes] the method for the actual arrangement of the channels (*nāḍī*), winds (*vāyu*), and vital points (*tilaka*) within the perfected body.
3. The universal monarchs, barbarians, the Kālacakra, the lineage of the family, and so forth;

through the summary of their emergence, there is a complete exposition of the non-differentiation of external and internal phenomena within the body. 4. Through the summary of the signs of death—the cutting off (or exhaustion) of the channels—there is an exposition indicating the death of the perfected body. 5. The characteristic of a single moment, which is the cause of the arising and cessation of the world. 6. Through the summary of the exposition of the Kālacakra.
The exposition on death includes elixirs and the like;
by means of a systematic collection concerning children, the signs of death and the causes of death are identified, followed by the procedure for rising above death.
Seventh, the method for entering the correct path through the investigation of one's own and others' philosophical systems—these were delineated in the second chapter on the inner science.

The first verse of the Chapter on Empowerment (*Abhiṣeka-paṭala*) exists in accordance with the preceding chapter and because the explanation of the request has been stated. Herein there are seven summaries (*saṃgraha*):

1. The characteristics of the master and the disciple, by way of a summary of the characteristics of the means for accomplishing the expansion of all activities beginning with those of the Master (*ācārya*).

2. The teacher’s comprehension of the characteristics of the entire range of ritual activities for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, as well as the procedure for gathering disciples and the method for taking possession of the site;
3. The procedure for drawing the mandala after having taken possession of the site by means of a summary of the rules for mandala-drawing;
4. The entry of the novice disciple into the drawn mandala and the procedure for the seven empowerments by means of a summary of the mandala-consecration.
5. Through the procedure for the gaṇacakra at Pratiṣṭhāna,
the establishment of the disciple— who has been consecrated by means of the compendium of yogic conduct— in the state of an ācārya,
and the establishment [of him] in the three supports known as body, speech, and mind.
6. The higher consecration consists of the gaṇacakra,
the mudrā, the gaze, and the dismissal.

7. By means of the summary of the Hero’s Festival (*vīrotsava*), this chapter reaches completion together with the sections on the essential mudrās, gazes, empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), and so forth, as well as the dismissal of the maṇḍala and the detailed exposition of the Hero’s Festival.
The first verse of the *Sādhanāpaṭala* expresses the acceptance of the request and the purpose of the commentary.
In the second verse, having described the Blessed One’s body of purity (*viśuddhikāya*) and having established its practice through the five summaries, its illumination is effected.

1. The site for practice (*sādhanāsthala*), including the protection of the location, the atonement for misdeeds, and so forth; as well as the protection against obstacles and the ritual for the accumulation of merit.

2. The generation stage (*utpattikrama*) through the summary of conventional reality; the procedure for conception from emptiness; the generation stage; and the supreme king of mandalas (*maṇḍalarājāgra*).
3. Through the generation and completion stages of the *prāṇadeva*, there is the emergence from the womb;
this serves to demonstrate the factors (*aṅga*) for the perfection of the generation stage.

4. Following the generation stage, through the completion stage, there is the *tilaka* and the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*), intended for the perfection of the mind and gnosis (*cittijñāna*) by way of experiencing happiness during the sixteen-year lifespan immediately after birth.

5. Following the stage of sixteen years, just as one produces sons and daughters through the gathering of diverse activities (*vibhinnakarmasaṃgraha*), the presentation of the means for accomplishing diverse activities (*vibhinnakarman*) by means of producing a reflection of the vital breath (*prāṇapratibimba*) has been made. Herein, in the chapter on knowledge (*jñānapaṭala*), there exists a fourfold compendium (*saṃgrahacatuṣṭaya*).
In the first verse, there is a statement regarding the acceptance of both the request and the exposition.

Following that, it is described in sequence: 1. In the summary of the composition of the *Yoginītantra* and other texts, having set aside the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and all elements (*dhātu*), the procedure for the maṇḍala of deities—the basis and the based—is described.

2. Through the systematic summary of the purification of the four bodies and so forth, the presentation of the four bodies of the unobscured state, as well as the fourth empowerment and the gnosis of the syllable, is established.

4. By means of a compendium of diverse disciplinary methods (*vinayopāya*), there arises the presentation of numerous general and specific means for practice, in order to characterize the procedure for benefiting sentient beings after the attainment of enlightenment.

At the conclusion, in the form of a summary, there is a decade of verses in which the qualities of the Teacher Kālacakra and the method of gathering [disciples] through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are described.

That which was not compiled from the *Mūlatantra* was divided by the Tibetan master named Koṅtula into thirty-two summaries (*saṃgraha*) for the purpose of purifying the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the *Kālacakra*, and into eighty locations (*sthāna*) for the purpose of thoroughly purifying the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).
(ka) The thirty-two summaries are as follows: 1. In the *Jagaddhātu*, there are ten summaries.

These have been offered for the purpose of purifying the seed-syllable of the ten modes of subjugation (*ha kṣa ma la va ra yaṃ*); there are ten means of attraction (*saṅgraha*) for the purpose of completely purifying the inconceivable world-realm.

Among these, there are six compendia for the purpose of purifying the general tantra, the inconceivable world-realm (*acintyalokadhātu*), making ten compendia in total. Among these, the explanation of the pervasion of the general tantra through the six compendia, as well as the explanation of the outer wheel (*bāhyacakra*) through the remaining four compendia, has been provided for the sake of the tantra that is to be pervaded.

2. In the chapter on the internal (*adhyātmapaṭala*), the presentation of the initiation chapter (*abhiṣekapaṭala*) is made by means of the six compendia for the purpose of purifying the four great elements, the sun, the moon, Rāhu, and the [five] constituents (*dhātu*).
3. In the *Sādhanāpaṭala*, an explanation is provided for the five compendia of means (*sādhanasaṃgraha*) in order to purify the five Buddha-families.
4. In the *Jñānapaṭala*, the fourfold compendium is assembled for the complete purification of the four vajra-phenomena;
therein, within the first three compendia, an explanation is given of the supreme Kālacakra, that is, the ritual of the deity Kālacakra.

In the final compendium, the fifth chapter reaches its conclusion through these detailed analyses: the purification of the Buddha-stage, the accomplishment of the reality-meaning, and the dedication of aspirations.
Thus, the *Kālacakra* is divided into thirty-two compendia (*saṃgraha*).
(b) There are eighty cognitions: in the first chapter, twenty-four points for the purification of the forward and reverse order of the twelvefold dependent origination;
in the second chapter, eighteen points for the purification of the eighteen realities—namely, the six sense faculties, the six objects, and the six intrinsic natures.
In the third chapter, there are twelve locations for the purification of the preliminary initiations;
in the fourth chapter, seven locations for the purification of the seven places of origin;

and in the fifth chapter, twenty locations for the presentation of the twenty types of perfect awakening—thus, eighty locations in total—and furthermore, the presentation of Kālacakra across all eighty-two locations above those.
It has been produced.
This intention of the compendium is that other minor subjects as well have been included herein.
Mañjuśrī is the compiler of this work titled *Śrī-Kālacakra-Uttarottara-Tantra*.
There are 157 verses here.
Following the exposition of the *nidāna*, there is here an exposition of the wholesome and unwholesome, as well as a presentation of the [four] truths.
Subsequently, while explaining the actual status of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth in succession, the demonstration of the reality of the self (*ātman*) has been performed.
The stability of the twelve-linked dependent origination is the characteristic of the four bodies;
it is the introduction to the tantra and the explanation of the chapter.

An exposition of the division of families, the division of meditations, the six-limbed yoga, the five superknowledges, the six families, the purification of the body, and the five stages of the Guhyasamāja;
a refutation of Māra, malevolent rites, and the like; and the accomplishment of the Vidyādharas.
The refutation of inferior views and conduct; the view and conduct regarding persons; and [the distinction between] the local dharma and the false dharma (or the dharma of the barbarians).
The revelation [of the teachings],

the revelation of the various dharma traditions, the destruction of the barbarians by the Kulikas, and their expulsion from the sacred seats through harsh conduct for the sake of pacifying the wicked.

In this work, there has been a clear exposition of the following subjects: the virtue of wholesome conduct; the Buddha’s intention regarding the attainment of the Great Parinirvāṇa; the teachings on the Dharma delivered through the medium of the Buddha; and the compilation of those [teachings] by Mañjuśrīmahodaya. Regarding the lineage of the *Guhyasamāja*, there were seven principal lineages of the *Guhyasamāja* in the Noble Land (India).
Their names are as follows:
1. the Ārya tradition, 2. the Jñānapāda tradition, 3. the lineage of Śāntipāda, and 4. the lineage of Lalitavajra.
5. the lineage of the wise ones’ mindfulness and knowledge; 6. the lineage of the six gatekeepers; and 7. the lineage of Ānandagarbha.

1. The Noble Tradition (*āryāmnāya*): Through the medium of Jñānaḍākinī, Saraha received instructions that were subsequently propagated and disseminated by masters such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti;
this is known as the Noble Tradition.
Master Nāgārjuna, taking all the facts related to the generation stage found within the *Guhyasamāja-mūlatantra*, composed the *Piṇḍīkṛta-sādhanopāyikā*.

Herein is the meditation on the thirty-two deity mandalas of the Guhyasamāja; that is to say, the three meditations: the meditation of the initial yoga and the meditation of the sovereign king of the mandala.

The *Karmarājāgradhyāna* is performed according to the prescribed ritual. However, for one who has dissolved the deity—the means of the condensed practice (*piṇḍīkṛtasādhanopāyikā*)—into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) and is undergoing the process of re-emergence, the procedure remains incomplete.
To fulfill that, the Master composed the *Sūtramelāpaka*, which is a commentary on the *Sādhana* of the generation stage from the *Guhyasamāja-mahāyogatantra*.

In connection with the *niṣpannakrama*, the composition of twenty types [of works] was made, including the *Pañcakrama*, the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*, and those related to the initiation (*abhiṣeka*) and the mandala for the sake of the practitioner’s maturation. It is the opinion of some scholars that the twenty types were composed by Nāgabodhi.

Āryadeva, the principal disciple of Nāgārjuna, composed the work titled *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa*, consisting of eleven chapters, which is connected to the Guhyasamāja through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). Beyond that, he also composed the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa*, which issues from the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*); the *Svādhiṣṭhānakrama*, which issues from the illusory body (*māyākāya*); and the work titled *Abhisambodhikramopadeśa*, which is superior to the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

Siddhanāgabodhi composed the *Karmāntavibhaṅga* for the purpose of establishing the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), while clarifying the distinct limbs of the *Maṇḍalarājāgra*— the body mandala— as the procedure for entering the clear light through divine empowerment by merging the condensed sadhana with birth, death, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). He also elucidated the sequence of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) according to the system of the *Guhyasamāja*.
The master Rāhuladharaśrīmitra composed a manual titled *Yugalānandaprakāśa*,
which exists as an authoritative and complete work on the mandala rituals of the Noble Tradition (*ārya-āmnāya*).
When the twentyfold consecration of the *Guhyasamāja* has been conferred, the two subsequent consecrations are to be obtained with the assistance of this very text.

Regarding the master Śākyamitra, although no independent works by him are found under his name within the *Guhyasamāja* tradition, his name appears in the second stage (*dvitīyakrama*) of Nāgārjuna’s *Pañcakrama*.
On this matter, there is a divergence of opinion among Tibetan scholars;
for instance, [the view of] the *Nīlagrantha* (Blue Annals).

In the *Vairocananāmapañcakramavṛtti* composed by Lakṣmīṅkara, it is accepted that the portion ending with "Having known him thus, the wise are said to be [freed] from the cage of existence" is the composition of Nāgārjuna, while the remainder is the composition of Śākyamitra. This Śākyamitra was one of the sharpest intellects among the disciples of Nāgārjuna;

therefore, out of affection, he inscribed the name of his own disciple in the second sequence of his work. Furthermore, Vajrāsanapāda also places him in the 64th position within the sequence of the 84 *siddhas*.
Thus, this wood-gatherer was established as being of such a caste; likewise, he was accepted as a disciple of Nāgārjuna of the Mahāyāna.
According to the opinion of certain scholars, Śākyamitra is actually another name for Nāgārjuna himself.

Candrakīrti, having adorned the views of these five masters as well as the stages of generation (*utpattikrama*) and completion (*niṣpannakrama*) with the method of the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) and the four systems (*caturnaya*), [composed] the work titled *Pradīpoddyotana* on the *Guhyasamāja*.
The composition of the *Ṭīkā* treatise was undertaken.
In this very sequence (*āmnāya*),
Abhayākaragupta [composed] the *Pañcakramamatīṭīkā Candraprabhā*.
The *Pañcakrama-pañjikā* titled *Pramāṇārtha* by Vīryabhadra; the *Pañcakrama-pañjikā* by Bhavyakīrti; the *Pañcakrama-vivaraṇa* by Līlāvajra;
and the *Pañcakrama-pañjikā* by Samayavajra.
The *Pañcakramavṛtti-vairocananāma* was composed by the illustrious Kashmiri Lakṣmīṅkara,
and the *Pañcakramārthayoginī-manohara-ṭippaṇī* was composed by Muniśrīmahodaya.

Beyond these, many other works concerning the family [of practices] (*pārivārika*)— such as fire offerings (*homa*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth— have been composed within this tradition by numerous accomplished masters (*siddhācārya*).

In brief, the tradition concerning the practitioner of the meditation on both the generation stage (*utpattikrama*, consisting of three meditations) and the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*, consisting of five stages) is designated as the "Noble Tradition" (*ārya-āmnāya*).
In the lineage of the Noble Tradition (Āryāmnāya), Buston made the following enumeration: Vajradhara, the Bodhisattva Matiratna,
Nāgārjuna, Mataṅga, and Tilopāda.
Nāḍapāda and Dharmamati;
through this lineage of the tradition of Ācārya Jñānapāda, the seventeen chapters of the Guhyasamāja [were transmitted].
Scholars maintain that the eighteenth chapter is the *Mūlatantra* and that the *Vajragarbhālaṅkāra* is the explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*).

Having heard the prophetic words of Mañjuśrī, the master Jñānapāda relied upon these three aforementioned texts; he composed fourteen independent works on the *Guhyasamāja* and wrote extensive commentaries upon them.
He composed [this]. This very tradition is called the Jñānapāda-āmnāya. Its principal texts are: 1. Dvikramatattvabhāvanā;
2. The Sadhana titled Samantabhadra;
3. The Sadhana of the Four Limbs titled Samantabhadra; 4. The [Sadhana] titled Muktitilaka.
5. And regarding his own spiritual realization (*ātmasādhanāvatāra*):
among his disciples, Dīpaṃkara, Bhadra-praśāntamitra, Rāhuladharabhadra, Vajramukha, and others are well known. (From the *Nīlagrantha*)
The following enumeration of this lineage has been made: Dīpaṅkarabhadra; Ānandagarbha; Gaganapāda; Śāntipāda; Śraddhākara; Padyakara; and Ratnabhadra, the great Tibetan translator-ācārya.
According to the system of Bu ston, the sequence of the masters is as follows: Mañjubodha; Avadhūtapāda; Buddhaśrījñāna; Dīpaṅkara; Ānandagarbha; Jayavajra; Śāntipāda; and Śraddhākara.
— Padyākara and Ratnabhadra.
In this tradition, there is the cultivation of the generation stage (utpattikrama).
The practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is accomplished through the four limbs of service;
furthermore, in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the meditation on the four tilakas within the four wheels and the arising of the four joys (*caturānanda*) are performed.

Although this tradition primarily belongs to the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), its method of practice and its ritual of initiation (*abhiṣeka-vidhi*) exist just like those of the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*).

3. The Lineage of Śāntipāda: Śāntipāda, having composed the work titled *Kusumamañjarī*, a commentary on the *Guhyasamāja* that synthesizes the *Mūlatantra* and the *Uttaratantra*, provided an exposition of the *Guhyasamāja* according to its own independent system (*svatantrapaddhati*).
Through this, he studied the *Guhyasamāja* from Ācārya Jinaputra of the Noble Tradition (*ārya-āmnāya*) and from Ācārya Bhaiṣajya of the lineage of Jñānapāda.

However, by means of these two traditions, an independent lineage of the maṇḍalas of the Akṣobhya-pradhāna family, distinct from others, was established; furthermore, even in terms of philosophical view, they followed the Vijñānavādins rather than the Mādhyamikas. Thus, this constitutes one independent lineage.

4. The lineage of Ācārya Lalitavajra: This lineage provides an explanation of the *Guhyasamāja* according to the *Mātṛtantra* (Mother Tantra) of the *Nidānaparivarta*. Thus, this too is accepted as an independent lineage. 5. The lineage of Paṇḍita Smṛtijñāna: Paṇḍita Smṛtijñāna studied the *Guhyasamāja* under Guru Bhadrapāda; likewise, his independent explanation is distinct from other lineages.
He also established the ritual manual for the sādhana.
He traveled to Tibet as well;
he himself translated works such as the commentary on the Six-Branch Yoga (Ṣaḍaṅgayoga) into the Tibetan language.

6. According to the *Kālacakravyākhyā*, following the lineage of the *Guhyasamāja* from Nālandā, after the arrival of Naḍapāda and the other six gatekeepers, the *Kālacakra* spread from Śambhala to the Noble Land (Āryadeśa).
Generally, the explanation of the Unsurpassed Tantra began according to the *Kālacakra* system.
Among these, the *Guhyasamāja* contains the procedures for establishing the deity maṇḍalas of 9, 13, 19, 25, 32, and 34 deities.
7. From King Jahora Prakāśacandra, who was the very embodiment of the Vajra-reality, the lineage of Ānandagarbha descended; by Ānandagarbha, the study of the eighteen tantras was performed.
These [masters] were empowered by Tārā.

By him [were composed]: the *Guhyasamāja-mūlatantra*, the *Vairocanamāyājāla-mūlatantra* along with its explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*), the section on the first element from the *Tattvasaṃgraha* of the Yoga Tantras, and the ritual for the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra-vidhi*).
Having sealed [this work] with Mahāmudrā, the author composed this commentary on the *Guhyasamāja* according to the system of the Yoga Tantra, following the method of meditative cultivation.
In accordance with this, the teaching of the *Guhyasamāja* was delivered by the Teacher seven days after his parinirvāṇa.
Subsequently, all the instructions that arose regarding the tantric treatises were accepted as explanatory tantras (*vyākhyātantra*).
Thus, through the immersion in the Guhyasamāja Yoga Tantra within the Āryāvarta, there were seven principal lineages of the Guhyasamāja associated with its exegetical tradition.
Furthermore, in the *Jñeyakośa*, Mr. Coṅṭula acknowledged the existence of twenty-four lineages of the Guhyasamāja in the Noble Land (Āryadeśa).
Among these were Mahāpadmavajra, Anaṅgavajra, Nāgārjuna, Līlāvajra, Vajrahāsa, Trikaṇṭheśvara, Sughoṣarakṣita, Buddhajñānapāda, Ratnākaraśāntipāda, Ānandagarbha, and others.
There were several principal lineages.

From these lineages in Tibet, the traditions of Āryanāgārjuna, Jñānapāda, Śaktipāda, Vajrahāsa, Padmavajra, Ānandagarbha, and others were transmitted. Among those, the lineages of Ārya [Nāgārjuna] and Jñānapāda were preeminent.
The lineage, dissemination, and spread of this *Kṛṣṇayamāritantra* have been clearly elucidated in the *Jñeyakośa*, divided across five periods of time: 1.
Namely, that shortly after the Third Council, the *Kṛṣṇayamāritantra* began to circulate, and it remained so for approximately two hundred years.
This very period is called the "time of accomplishment" (*siddhikāla*). 2. The time of attaining the various modes of conduct (*caryā*) lasted for three hundred years.
3. During this time (within the teaching),...
Many obstacles arose, and at that very time, many perfected beings (siddhapuruṣas) also appeared,
who attracted people through the power of their own tantras.
It was precisely during this period that figures such as the Brahmin Cāṇakya emerged.
This period lasted for five hundred years.
4. Within this, the period from Lalitavajra up to Kamalarakṣita arrives, which is called the time of the accomplishment of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) [and] conduct (*caryā*).

5. This period of partial practice (*āṃśikacaryākāla*) is accepted as beginning from Kamalarakṣita and continuing until the present time. Generally, during the aforementioned periods, the propagation and spread of the *Kṛṣṇayamāritantra* occurred. Among these, the first to achieve excellence in conferring empowerments (*abhiṣeka*) and providing explanations among the general public was Ācārya Lalitavajra; in the middle, Jñānapāda; and finally, the Brahmin teacher Śrīdhara.
He attains [this].

In this regard, the synthesis of the three realities (*tattva*) and the lineage of the instructions is found particularly in the works of Ācārya Śrīdhara— namely, in the *Kṛṣṇayamāri* and *Raktayamāri* traditions—
and it is from that very source that the introduction of this lineage occurs in the land of Tibet.
It is likely that in Tibet as well, the great Emperor Srong-btsan sgam-po composed this *Sādhanopāyikā*,
which is accepted as the very first work of the Tantra.
It is stated in the *Nīla-grantha* that the sādhana of the *Yamāri-tantra* composed by Srong-btsan is still extant today.
Tārānātha accepted that the *Kṛṣṇayamāritantra* was brought to the common people by Lalitavajra.
Regarding Hevajra, two lineages are generally found as the primary lineages of the tantric scriptures:
the long lineage (*dīrghaparamparā*) and the short lineage (*upaparamparā*).
The lineage of rebirth (*upaparamparā*) can be described as a lineage of oral transmission (*karṇatantraparamparā*),
because in this case, even without any prior lineage, the practitioner directly realizes the chosen deity— that is, the Teacher— and thereby receives the complete tantric scripture.
Such a twofold lineage is found in the *Hevajratantra*.
1. Regarding the long lineage: according to the first chapter, the teaching of the *Hevajratantra* was given at that time when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment on the Vajrāsana (at Buddhagayā).
At that moment, the Teacher arose in the form of Heruka, the eight-faced and sixteen-armed Hevajra, within the family of Heruka.
In response to the request made by the Bodhisattvas Vajragarbha and Nairātmyā, he taught this [tantra] in the form of a *saṃgrahatantra*, having condensed the essence of the extensive *mūlatantra*.
Some scholars believe that his teaching originated in the Tuṣita heaven;
others believe it was in Dhānyakaṭaka. Regarding the question of who first introduced and propagated his teachings in Jambūdvīpa, there is no single consensus of opinion.
The view of the great scholar Dagpo Trashi Namgyal is that King Visukalpa of Oḍiviśa in South India was a preeminent scholar of the Hetulakṣaṇayāna (the Pāramitāyāna).

When he saw certain scriptural passages in the Sūtras concerning the classification of desire— that is, the abandonment of desire— without [explicitly] mentioning passion, he developed an intense desire to understand them.

At that time, he made a formal aspiration, and the ḍākinīs uttered a prophecy stating that this *Āoḍiyāna-jñāna* could be obtained from the ḍākinīs. In accordance with that, he went to Oḍḍiyāna; having performed the tantric practices there, he attained accomplishment (*siddhi*).
He was the very first to bring the *Hevajra-tantra* from that place.
This very [lineage] is called the "Long Succession" (*dīrghaparamparā*).

Within this succession, Buston established the sequence of the masters beginning with Vajradhara, Vajraḍākinī, Virūpāda, Ḍombīpāda, Lalitavajra, Vīṇāpāda, Garbhapāda, Peṇḍapāda, Durjayacandra, Vīravajra, Akṣobhyavajra, and Dveṣavajra.

2. Regarding the lineage of transmission (*upaparamparā*) or the oral lineage (*karṇatantraparamparā*), according to the view of the Tibetan *Ṅog ston pa* (Dharmakāyavajra), it is held that Nāgārjuna himself was the very first to bring the *Hevajra*, *Vajrapañjara*, *Catuṣpīṭha*, and other tantras from Oḍḍiyāna after having written them upon palm leaves.
According to the view of Smaluṅ pāda and the Nepalese master Phalamthīṅ pāda, it was Saroruhapāda (Kukkurīpāda) [who brought them].

Having attained accomplishment from the *Guhyacandratilaka*, he invited the *Hevajratantra* from Oḍḍiyāna. There, he composed numerous means for practice (*sādhana-upāyikā*). Following Mi-ston, Puṇyadhvaja, and Rampā, Virūpapāda received the *Hevajratantra* along with its explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*) from the Jñānaḍākinīs; regarding this matter, he [composed] the *Svasaṃvedyanāma-niṣpannakramanirdeśa*.
The composition was made.
By this, Indrabhūti Mādhyama was also favored.

According to the opinion of some scholars, the disciple of Virūpapāda, Caryāpāda, having subdued Senara—the former king of Oḍiviśa, who had attained siddhi through the grace of Ḍombīpāda—then went to Oḍiyāna.
Through the instruction of the Jñānaḍākinīs, the *Kulakullā*, the *Aśalisadvaya*, and the *Hevajragarbha-tantras* were brought forth.
Subsequently, he composed two treatises: the *Nairātmyāsādhana* and the *Sahajasiddhi*.
Tārānātha accepted that the *Hevajra-tantra* was requested by Kambalapāda from the lotus feet [of the Buddha].
Following the treasury of what is to be known (*jñeyakośa*), there were many lineages of Hevajra in the land of Bhārata.
Among them, the lineages of Saroruhavajra, Kṛṣṇasamayavajra, Durjayacandra, Ratnākara, Nāḍapāda, Maitrīpāda, and others were the most prominent.
Among the commentaries on the Hevajra, there is the *Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā* composed by the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
The *Padyinī*, a commentary on the *Sarorūhavajra-pañjikā*; the *Hevajravyākhyāvivaraṇa* by Bhavabhadra;
and the *Pañjikā-yogaratnamālā* by Kṛṣṇapaṇḍita.
Daṇḍaśas’s *Suviśuddhasampuṭa*, Durjayacandra’s *Pañjikā Kaumudī*,
and Sukīrtibhadra’s (Nāḍapāda’s) [work].

The *Vajrasārasaṃgraha*, Kṛṣṇapāda’s *Pañjikāsmṛtinipāta*, Padyāṅkuravajra’s commentary on the *Hevajratantrarāja*, Śrī Ratnākaraśāntipāda’s *Pañjikāmuktāvalī*, and the *Kāmadhenu*— including its *Pañjikā* and excerpts from verses— are well known.

In this way, there were many lineages of Hevajra in the land of Bhārata; however, within the framework of the *sādhana* manuals, the *Cakrasaṃvara* and *Guhyasamāja* possessed their own distinct and independent lineages.
In the land of Bhārata, the lineage of Cakrasaṃvara developed numerous traditions of practice for the purpose of maturing and liberating the practitioner in accordance with the *Cakrasaṃvara Tantra*.

This is the manual for the practice of the *Akrama* (non-successive) individuals, consisting of sixty-two principal deities, according to the lineage held by the *Ḍākārṇava* and following the tradition of the accomplished master Luipa, as propagated by Dharmarājaprakāśacandra.
The procedure for the manifestation of the sixty-two deities of Cakrasaṃvara according to the tradition of Ācārya Kṛṣṇapāda;
the manual for the simultaneous (zhaṭiti) meditation upon the sixty-two deities of the Siddha Vajrapāda’s Cakrasaṃvara together with the extremely profound body-maṇḍala.
In accordance with the tradition of the *Siddhalāvāpādīya*, there is the lineage of the *Cakrasaṃvara-vajraḍākārṇava*;
the lineage of the sādhana for sixty-two deities by Ācārya Nāgārjuna; and the lineage of the sādhana for sixty-two deities by Indrabhūti as well.

There is the ritual procedure for the sādhana of Cakrasaṃvara associated with the thirteen *evakula* [deities] by Maitrīpāda; and the manual of practice (*sādhanāpaddhati*) composed by Ācārya Trinetra following the *Sahajasaptama-tantra*.

The first translation of the *Cakrasaṃvara-mūlatantra*—consisting of 700 ślokas and comprising 51 chapters—was made in Tibet by Ratnabhadra and Marado Dharmendra. Following that, there are three lineages of the *Cakrasaṃvara* as follows:
1. Vajradhara, Vajrapāṇi, Brahman, Saraha-pāda, Nāgārjuna, Śabarī-pāda, Luipa, Dārika-pāda, Gandha-pāda, Maṇḍūka (Medaka).
Pāda Jālandharapāda, Guhyapāda, Vijayapāda, Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, and others belong to the first lineage. This lineage reached Tibet from Cī-therapāda of Nepal down to Marapā.
2. Vajradhara, Vajravārāhī, Luīpāda, Ḍeṅgīpāda, Vajraghaṇṭāpāda, Jālandharapāda, Kṛṣṇapāda, Kuśalanātha, Maṇḍūka (Medaka).
Pādaguptapāda, Vijayapāda, Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, and others are counted among the second lineage.
This lineage arrived in Tibet by way of Ṅog.
3. From Vajradhara, Vajravārāhī, Kṛṣṇavārāhī, Kṛṣṇapāda, Guhyapāda, Vijayapāda, Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, and others, this lineage arrived in Tibet.

The author of the *Nīlagrantha*, Gos Lo tsā ba Mahodaya, accepts the *Cakrasaṃvara* lineage as follows: Vajradhara, Vajrapāṇi, Saraha, Śabarīpāda, Luīpāda, Dārikapāda, Ḍombīpāda, Vajraghaṇṭāpāda, Medakapāda, Jālandharapāda, Kṛṣṇācārya, Vijayapāda, Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, Śāntipāda, Maitrīpāda, and likewise Dīpaṅkara;
and from Tibet, the great translator Ratnabhadra.

Following that, in the lineage of Tibet’s second Marpa, there were Buddhajñānaḍākinī, Luipāda, Ḍeṅgīpāda, Lāvāpāda, Indrabhūti, Kacapāda, Ghaṇṭāpāda, Jālandharapāda, Kṛṣṇapāda, Kuśalana, Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, and Manakaśrījñāna.
There were also the Bhadanta of Nepal as well as Marpa and others of Tibet.
It is stated in the *Jñānakosa* that twenty-seven oral traditions (*āmnāya*) of the Cakrasaṃvara exist.
Almost all lineages converged in Tibet;
all the Indian Siddhas attained accomplishment in accordance with this tantra.
Therefore, there is no doubt that there would be many lineages of practice.

Among them, Luipāda, Ghaṇṭāpāda, Kṛṣṇāpāda, and others are the most prominent. In addition to these, Dārikapāda, Ḍombīpāda, Kaniṣṭha Indrabhūti, Laṅkājinabhadra, Durjayacandra, and Pūrvadigvatilāvāpāda (that is, Śūnyatādhyāna), as well as Balabhadra, Brāhmaṇa Ratnavajra, and others of the Northern Tradition of Vajrapāṇi, have established the excellent path of the commentaries, sādhana-s, and vital instructions (*prāṇālī*) upon the Root Tantra in an independent form.
