Beyond this, there is the ritual for Nāgabodhi,
the ritual for Kalahaṃsakumāra,

the ritual of Dharmapāda for performing meditation upon the assembly of all deities within the Black Vajra, and likewise [the ritual] for the purpose of visualizing the other attendant deities— who possess colors identical to those of their fathers, mothers, and gods— in various distinct forms.
The *ghuṇḍarīpādavidhi* is thus described;
there are also other procedures for the *caḍīpāda*, *nāḍīpāda*, and *dhanyapāda*.
Beyond these, there are fifteen further procedures, such as the *vīṇāpāda*, *anantapāda*, *bhadrapāda*, *laḍakapāda*, *kaṅkalapāda*, *jayānanda*, and so forth.

These were propounded by the Siddhas in an independent form. Beyond this, the manual of Bodhivajra was expounded in the Kālacakra; however, it did not exist in Central India, but rather its full circulation and dissemination occurred in the Draviḍa region, where it is still available today.

Butön accepted the following lineage for the *Cakrasaṃvara*: Vajradhara, Vajrapāṇi, Sahaja, Nāgārjuna, Śabarīpāda, Luīpāda, Dārikapāda, Vajraghaṇṭāpāda, Kukkurīpāda, Jālandharapāda, Kṛṣṇācārya, Guhyapāda, Vijayapāda, Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, Abhayakīrti, Vāgīśvara, Prajñākuṭa, the Tibetan Matikīrti, Akṣobhyavajra, and others.
Consequently, there are numerous commentaries and ritual manuals (*sādhanāpaddhati*) on the *Cakrasaṃvara*.

In that regard, having composed a single treatise consisting of an explanation of the latter half of the *Mūlatantra* by the Bodhisattva Cakrapāṇi, [the author] provided a commentary by integrating the hidden meanings and essential principles of the *Anuttarayogatantra* into the *Kālacakra-sādhanāpaddhati*. By King Indrabhūti, the intention of the *Mūlatantra* was [explained] according to the general manual of the *Mātṛtantra* (such as the *Sampuṭatantra*).
The commentary has been composed.

Having heard the direct oral instruction from the Yoginī, the master Nakṣatracandra, while composing an exposition on the intent of the Root Tantra in his work titled *Abhidhānottara-tantra* according to the generation stage (*utpattikrama*),
produced the treatise named *Amṛtatṛṣita*, which is a practical manual (*upāyikā*) for the *Cakrasaṃvarodaya-sādhana*.
A commentary on that was composed by Bhavyakīrti;
then, having combined the *pañjikā* (verse-by-verse commentary) and the prose commentary, Tathāgatarakṣita likewise composed this commentary.
All these works explain the *Cakrasaṃvara* according to the method of a *mātṛtantra-paddhati*.

In this lineage, commentaries on the *Cakrasaṃvara* were also composed by Lāvāpāda, Devagupta, Sumati, Kīrti, and others. Beyond these, among the works translated into the Tibetan language that elucidate the words and meaning of the *Cakrasaṃvara*, the principal ones include Alābhacandra’s *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayapañjikā* and Śāśvatavajra’s *Saṃvaravṛtti*, among others.
In this way, numerous lineages and ritual manuals (*sādhanāpaddhati*) of the *Cakrasaṃvara* were prevalent.
Generally, even eighty-four *siddhas* attained accomplishment through the practice of *Cakrasaṃvara* alone.

Regarding the *Mahāmāyā*, besides the lineage of the *Mahāmāyā-tantra* transmitted from masters such as Ācārya Vinayadatta, Ratnākara, and Śāntipāda, there were many other lineages of the *Mahāmāyā-tantra* in the land of India.

It was in Tibet that the Mahāmāyā Tantra first appeared and spread; however, although Nīlagranthakāra Gosalomahodaya and Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna translated it into the Tibetan language, their lineage is no longer extant there today.
The lineage of Śāntibhadra and others also existed in India, which was propagated and disseminated by the great Tibetan translator Marpa Lotsāwa (Dharmapāla) through oral tradition.
According to Buston, the lineage of Mahāmāyā is as follows: Vajradhara, Ḍākinī, Kukkurīpāda, Saroruhavajra, and Heruka.
Also Tilopāda, Nāḍapāda, Jñānabhadra, the great Tibetan translator Dharmamati, and others.

Among the commentaries on the *Mahāmāyā Tantra*, there are Durjayacandra’s *Pañjikā Māyāvatī*; Ratnākaraśāntipāda’s commentary *Guṇavatī*; Kṛṣṇasamayavajra’s *Mahāmāyātantrasmṛtivṛtti*; Alaṅkārapāda’s *Pañjikā*; and Dharmamati’s [works] on the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) of the *Mahāmāyā* and so forth. Furthermore, there are many principal texts such as the *Sādhanopāyikā* and others by Anaṅgavajra, Ratnavajra, and others.
The Lineages of the *Catuṣpīṭha*: There were many lineages of the *Catuṣpīṭha* in the land of Bhārata.

Among these, the lineage established by Āryadeva, which relied upon the commentaries on the root-tantra of the *Catuṣpīṭha*, and the lineage of Bhavabhadra, which was based on the *Catuṣpīṭhasaṃgraha*, were the primary ones. These were translated into the Tibetan language by Gayādhara and Ḍogbhīma Mahodaya.
There, having received the empowerment and oral instructions from the Ḍākinī Narāsthidhāriṇī, Marapa Dharmamati propagated and spread that lineage.
Butön accepted the lineage of the *Catuṣpīṭha* as follows: Vajradhara, Vajraḍākinī, Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Prajñābhadra, Nāḍapāda, the Tibetan translator, Dharmamati, and so forth.

Among the commentaries on the *Catuṣpīṭha*, the principal works are considered to be: Bhavabhadra’s *Śrīcatuṣpīṭhatantrarāja-smṛtinibandha*; Kuśalavarman’s *Catuṣpīṭhaṭīkā*; Āryadeva’s *Gambhīrārthanirdeśa*; the *Ekadrumapañjikā*; the *Catuṣpīṭhayogatantrasādhanā*; and the *Śrīvajracatuṣpīṭhasādhanā* composed by Jagadānanda and Jīvabhadra.
Regarding the lineage of the *Buddhakapāla*, two lineages of the *Buddhakapālatantra*— those of Saraha-pāda and Abhayākaragupta— converged in Tibet.

In addition to Saraha-pāda’s *Jñānavatī* commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Buddhakapālatantra* and Abhayākaragupta’s work titled the *Abhayapaddhati* manual for the means of accomplishment (*sādhanopāyikā*), Padyavajra’s commentary entitled the *Tattvacandrikā* is also available, accompanied by a Tibetan translation.
Regarding the lineage of Śambhala for the Kālacakra: the Blessed Buddha gave the instruction of the Kālacakra to Sucandra, the king of Śambhala.
Having compiled the Kālacakra Root Tantra and composed the treatise titled *Anuśaṃsā* in six thousand verses of meter, he established its practice and dissemination in the land of Śambhala.
Just three years after the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa, King Sucandra attained parinirvāṇa after having constructed the great maṇḍala of Kālacakra.
Subsequently, in his lineage, six Dharma Kings named Devendra-tejasvin, Candradatta, Devendra, Virūpa, and Devendravan appeared.
All of them composed commentaries on the Root Tantra. Thereafter, among the kings of the Kulika dynasty, some had already appeared and others were yet to appear.

Among them, Mañjughoṣakīrti was the very first to propagate the *Kālacakra-mūlatantra*. Just as the great compendium of the *Mūlakālacakra-tantra* was composed in the *sragdharā* meter in three thousand verses by the ṛṣis and munis such as Sūryaratha and others upon their request, so too was the twelve-thousand-verse commentary, the *Vimalaprabhā*, composed by Kulika Puṇḍarīka, a member of his own lineage.
Following Puṇḍarīka, there were successively the kings Bhadra, Vijaya, Miśrabhadra, Raktapāṇi, Viṣṇugupta, Sūryakīrti, and others.
It is stated that during the time of the eighth king, named Sudivya, the appearance of the Mleccha religion occurred.
A detailed commentary on this is found in the *Vimalaprabhā* commentary on the *Kālacakra*.
Following Sudivya, there exists a succession of Kulika kings as follows: Sāgaravijaya,
Sūrya,
and Virūpa.
Candraprabha, Ananta Bhūmipāla, Śrīpāla Siṃha, and...
Vikrānta, Mahābala, Aniruddha, Narasiṃha, Maheśvara, Ananta, Vijaya, and finally Krodhacakrī— these shall appear in the future.
All will carry out the teaching for a period of one hundred years each.
According to the system of Kālacakra, it is the opinion of the learned scholars of Tibet that the religion of the Mlecchas will gradually emerge during the time of King Sudivya.
The final Wrathful Wheel-turner (Krodhacakrin) will utterly destroy the Mlecchas along with their very roots, propagate the True Dharma (Saddharma), and once again usher in the Kṛtayuga.

According to the opinion of the Āryas who follow the science of astrology (*jyotiṣa*), the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha occurred 2,867 years before today. Sucandra made a compendium of the Root Tantra (*mūlatantra*) 2,866 years before [today], and his Parinirvāṇa occurred 2,864 years before [today]. Kulika Mañjukīrti further condensed the Compendium Tantra (*saṃgrahatantra*) 2,264 years before [today], and likewise, the era of the Mlecchas began 1,363 years before [today].

Based on the year 1988, the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha occurred 788 years prior to that; likewise, the time of the appearance of the Mlecchas occurs near the year 625 CE. The final Kulika King will arrive near the year 2221. Regarding the Indian lineage of the Kālacakra according to Buston: the propagation of the Kālacakra in Āryāvarta was [initiated] by the Paṇḍita Cilupa, who was invited from the land of Śambhala during the reign of the three kings.

It has been stated by Mahodaya in the *Nīlagrantha* that, in general, the dissemination and spread of the Vajrayāna among the common people occurred during the time of King Prakāśacandra, an inhabitant of the eastern region.
By him [Anandagarbha], the commentaries on the *Tathāgatavyūhanirdeśa*, the *Lokasaṃgraha*, and other *Yogatantras* were composed.
Immediately thereafter, the master Nāgārjuna and his disciples composed the commentaries on the *Guhyasamāja-pitṛtantra* and others in South India.
Following that, Lāvāpāda brought the *Yoginītantra* (the *Mātṛtantra*) from Oḍḍiyāna and other regions in the north.
Having invited [the teachings], their dissemination and expansion were carried out in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa).
Then, having brought the Kālacakra from Śambhala, its propagation was undertaken by Cilupa and others.
This master Cilupa was born at that time in Aodiviśa within the five frontiers of the present and past.

This scholar, the Tripiṭakācārya Cilupaṇḍita, having studied all the treatises found in Ratnagiri Monastery, Vikramaśilā, Nālandā, and other centers, formed the desire to propagate and spread the practice of the *Kālacakra*— the special bodhisattva conduct that grants the attainment of awakening within a single lifetime. Having received a prophetic word from his tutelary deity, he returned to the Middle Country (*Āryāvarta*) together with merchants carrying precious gems.
He established its practice.
According to the opinion of some other scholars, the scholar Cilupa was the son of a certain yogin;
he went to the land of Śambhala together with his father, and there he had a vision of a handsome monk who was an emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Avalokiteśvara.
By his grace, he became a memorizer of these one hundred verses.

Immediately thereafter, having committed the complete commentary on the *Kālacakra*, the *Vimalaprabhā*, to memory, he returned from there and, while residing in the royal court of Kaṭaka, committed the *Vimalaprabhā* to writing.

He had three principal disciples: among them was Jinākaragupta, who attained spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*); the second was the eminent scholar Piṇḍācārya; and the third was a master of the *Kālacakra*.
The learned Piṇḍācārya took Mahākālapāda, born in the region of Varendra, as his disciple.
This [master] was a contemporary of Nāḍapāda.
According to the opinion of some scholars, Ācārya Mahākālapāda was empowered by Tārā;
Avalokiteśvara provided him with instruction on the path and consecrated him in Śambhala, and thus the complete teaching was bestowed upon him.
By this very [line], Kālacakra was invited from Śambhala. Furthermore,
it was stated by the master Koṅkaṭula Rinpoche Mahodaya that these three— the master Mahākālapāda (Mañjuvajra), the master Cilupaṇḍita, and the master Piṇḍa— went to Śambhala.
Therefore, these [masters] each separately commented upon the *Kālacakra*.
Consequently, there arises a difference between one or two verses in those [commentaries].
The venerable teacher Mahākāla had several eminent disciples, such as Kaniṣṭhakālapāda, Siṃhadhvaja, Ananta, and others.
This Kaniṣṭhakālapāda was an Indian of the East; Bodhināleṃdrapāda and others were among his namesakes.
The Tibetan tradition of the Kālacakra accepts that Ratnākaraśāntipāda was his disciple.
He was also the administrator of the Odantapurī Monastery in Magadha.

At that very time, he went to Nālandā, where he declared: "Any person who does not know the *Kālacakra* *kūṭākṣara* (the syllables consisting of the symbols of the *Acintya-lokadhātu*) and the *Ādibuddha*, will not be capable of correctly understanding the *Nāmasaṃgīti*."
When this was said, a discussion on the meaning of the scriptures took place between him and the local masters.

Many scholars who were defeated in that scriptural debate became his disciples, including Mañjukīrti, Abhayamahāpuṇya, the Kashmirian Gaṃbhīravajra, Śāntigupta, Guṇarakṣita, and others. Among them, the Kashmirian master Somanātha was the very first to propagate the *Kālacakra* in Tibet.
Buddhikīrti, who was born near Kham in Tibet—
these were all his principal disciples.

While enumerating the various lineages of the Kālacakra in Tibet, the venerable Ācārya Koṅ-sprul Blo-gros-mtha’-yas stated that the very first propagation of the Kālacakra was by the scholar Śrī Bharabodhi.
The translation of both the root text and the commentary was made by Gyijo Lo-tsā-ba Ba-mo-dha;

this translation is known as one independent tradition according to the lineage of Tho-gu Lo-tsā-ba and others. Furthermore, Buddhi-kīrti, having heard the *Kālacakra* from the Indian master Kālapāda, made a translation of the great commentary, the *Vimalaprabhā*.
The Gyalo (Gyalos) preserve this tradition from the very beginning without abandoning the lineage, and they explain this tradition as follows:

Having studied under the Nepalese Paṇḍita Samantashrī [the text] "Rachosa Rabe" (meaning *paradharmeṇa*), and having produced a translation of both the root text and the great commentary (*mūla-mahāvṛtti*), its dissemination was carried out; that is called the "Ra" tradition.
The great commentary was translated by Ḍo Locāvā Śerap Ḍagā Sa Mahodaya (Prajñākīrti) together with Somanātha.
This lineage, transmitted from Ḍoto Ākāśakuṭa onwards, is called the Ḍo-āmnāya.

The great Kashmiri Paṇḍita Śākyaśrībhadra gave the instruction on the Kālacakra to the Arhat Chag, Caladharma, Bhadra, and Śākyapaṇḍita; these three established the transmission of their respective independent lineages. Furthermore, the Paṇḍita Vibhūticandra also gave the instruction on the Kālacakra to many people in Tibet.
In this way, numerous lineages of the Kālacakra also flourished in Tibet.
Many translations of the Kālacakra as well as their various successions became widespread in Tibet;
among these, the *Vimalaprabhā* translated by the Kashmiri Paṇḍita Somanātha and Ḍo-pa Śākya-ye-shes (Śākya-ye-shes) attained the greatest circulation and dissemination throughout Tibet.
From this very [source], the dawn of the year 1027 occurred.
In these lineages, there were many accomplished masters (*siddhācāryas*); among them was Buston (*Mahāratnasiddha*).
Dolavo Pā (Prajñādhvaja and others) were the foremost [disciples].

In the *Nīla-grantha*, the lineage of the *Ḍo* tradition is enumerated as follows: beginning from Kulikarāja, [it proceeds through] Mahākālapāda, Kaniṣṭhakālapāda, Somanātha, and Ratnarakṣita of Tibet.
In the *Ra* tradition, there were Kulirāja, Cilupaṇḍita, Piṇḍopāda, Mahākālapāda, Kaniṣṭhakālapāda, Samantaśrī of Nepal, Ra Chotara, Jñāna, and others.
Buston made the following enumeration of the *Ra* and *Do* traditions: "In the *Ra* tradition: Śākyamuni, Sucandra, Sūryeśvara, Tejasvī, Somadatta, Sūryeśvara, Viśvamūrti, Yaśas..."

Puṇḍarīkabhadra, Vijaya, Sumitra, Raktapāṇi, Viṣṇugupta, Arkakīrti, Subhadra, Vijaya, Ajaya, Sūrya, Viśvarūpa, Śaśiprabha, Ananta, Mahīpāla, Śrīpāla, Vikrama, Mahābala, Aniruddha, Narasiṃha, Maheśvara, Anantavijaya, Mahācakrikrodha,
Cilu, Paṇḍita, Piṇḍa, Ācārya Mahākāla, Catuṣpāda, Alpakālacakrapāda, Ratnākara, Mañjuśrī, Samantaśrī (Nepāla), Paradharma (Tibbatīya).
Jñānasiṃha, Lakṣasiṃha, Amoghavajra, Prajñāsiṃha, Mānasiṃha, Vajradhvaja, Bhadra, Hitasukha, Buston, and others;

in the Ḍo tradition: Mahākāla, Alpakālacakrapāda, Somanātha, Taibbat Ratnarakṣita, Khakūṭa, Akṣobhya, Dharmeśvara, Gaganāṃśa, Gaganadhvaja, Prajñābhāva, Amoghavajra, Prajñāsiṃha, Vajradhvaja, Śrībhadra, Buston, and others (as well as Ratnasiddhi and so forth).

Regarding the nature and divisions of the Unexcelled Tantra (*anuttaratantra*), while the Tibetan masters have provided clear explanations by making distinct classifications of the Father Tantras (*pitṛtantra*), Mother Tantras (*mātṛtantra*), and Non-dual Tantras (*advayatantra*) as independent categories,
Indian masters did not establish them in such a clearly defined manner; nevertheless, the use of terminology equivalent to those [Tibetan terms] is found among them.

As stated in the *Vajrapañjara*, that tantra in which the yoga of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and the methods of its accomplishment are taught is the *Yoginītantra* (also known as the *Mātṛtantra*).

In the *Buddhakapāla*, it is declared that the number of Yoga Tantras is sixty million, while the number of Yoginī Tantras is sixteen million; furthermore, the status of the *Buddhakapāla* as the sovereign king of the Unsurpassed Yoginī Tantras is affirmed.
In the *Vajragarbhālaṅkāra*, it is stated that the *Ḍākinīpitṛtantra* and the *Ḍākinīmātṛtantra* constitute the final tradition (*āmnāya*).

In the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*, two divisions are stated: because of the predominance of the meditation on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), there is the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*) which is the origin of the Unsurpassed Tantras and emphasizes the generation stage, and the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*) which emphasizes the completion stage. In the *Vajrapañjara*, there exists the *Ḍākinīmātṛtantra*, a tantra compiled by the Venerable Ladies (*Bhaṭṭārikā*).
Where great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which serves as the means, is predominant,

it is stated that for the sake of those disciples who are men, the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*) was taught, and likewise for the sake of those disciples who are women, the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*) was taught. These six— the *Hevajra*, *Guhyakośa*, *Vajrāmṛtodbhava*, *Cakrasaṃvara*, *Vajrapañjara*, and *Saṃvarodaya*— are proclaimed among the Mother Tantras.

In the *Yogāvatāra*, Śraddhākaravarman made a twofold division of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*): the Method Yoga Tantra (*upāyayogatantra*) and the Wisdom Yoga Tantra (*prajñāyogatantra*).
They state that whichever [tantra] contains instruction on vast and profound realities primarily in their principal form is a Wisdom Tantra;
whereas that for which the disciples are proponents of self-interest and are predominantly male is the Father Tantra, the primary Method Tantra (*pitṛdevapradhānopāyatantra*).
Furthermore, for those disciples whose inclination is toward the supreme state of womanhood, there exists the Wisdom Tantra (*prajñātantra*), which is primarily focused on the Mother-deity.

That in which the process of deity cultivation through the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth is taught is the Means Tantra (*upāyatantra*); and that in which the purified *bodhicitta* is seen manifested in the form of a deity is the Wisdom Tantra.

In the same way, wherever an exposition occurs that conforms to the world of the gods, that is an *upāya-tantra*; whereas wherever an exposition occurs that is the opposite of that, it is a *prajñā-tantra*. Bu ston has thus conceived of the slight difference between the Father and Mother Tantras as follows: 1. According to the *Anuttarayogāvatāra*, that in which *upāya* is explained in detail is the Father Tantra (*pitṛ-tantra*), and that in which there is an extensive explanation of the profound meaning is the Mother Tantra (*mātṛ-tantra*).
2. According to the *Guhyatattvaprakāśa*, a *pitṛtantra* (father-tantra) exists as that which primarily teaches the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

A *mātṛtantra* (mother-tantra) is said to be that which primarily teaches the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*). 3. According to the *Vimalaprabhā*, a *pitṛtantra* is that in which the method of meditation and the means (*upāya*) are set forth for the ritual of the vajra-ground, the maṇḍala, and so forth, after having gradually dissolved the elements.

The tantra that teaches the method for the practitioner’s visualization of the maṇḍala of the celestial palace as he ascends from the element of earth up to the mountain Sumeru is called the *prajñā-tantra*.

4. The deity of the Father Tantra (*pitṛ-tantra*) is the Means (*upāya*), possessing equal faces and arms, whose body is in the form of *yuganaddha* (union). That deity of the Mother Tantra (*mātṛ-tantra*) is said to be one in whom the faces, arms, and so forth of the male and female deities become distinct, yet whose form is that of the *yuganaddha* body.

In those cases where the principal male and female deities in union (*yuganaddhakāya*) have identical numbers of arms, faces, and so forth, but the attendant deities in their forms of union differ in their faces, arms, and so on, that is a deity of the *Advaya-tantra*. According to the *Vajrapañjara*, where the Tathāgata appears in the form of Vajraḍākinī and the mother goddesses hold predominance among the attendants, that is called a *Mātṛ-tantra* (Mother Tantra), with the deity belonging to the families of the five Tathāgatas.
When he becomes manifest among the attendants of the ancestral deities (*pitṛdeva*), and the preeminence therein belongs to them, then that is the Pitṛtantra.

6. Where there are a seat and a lion-throne made of jewels, and upon them the deity himself is manifest in the *krodha* and *pratyālīḍha* gestures, adorned with jewel ornaments, wheels, and so forth—that is the deity who exists in the Upāyatantra.

Wherein the corpse-seat is adorned with skulls and bones as ornaments, and the deity—holding a knife, skull-cup, sword, hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), and so forth in his hands, clad in tiger and elephant skins, naked and unclothed—is declared in both the *Deva* and *Devaprajñā Mātṛtantras*. 7. That maṇḍala which is surrounded by cremation grounds is a *Mātṛtantra*, and in the absence of such [surroundings], it is a *Pitṛtantra*.

8. That in which the yogin is described together with the sublime and great means (*mahopāya*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) is the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*); and that in which there is a primary exposition of the stages of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) and manifest enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) is the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*). 9. That in which the channels (*nāḍī*) and winds (*vāyu*) are primarily expounded is the Mother Tantra; and that in which the winds are primarily expounded is the Father Tantra.

10. According to the *Guhyasamāja*, that in which the procedure for the practitioner—who has been transformed into the five Tathāgatas through the purification of the five aggregates—is taught is the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*); and that in which the procedure for describing the five elements as the five goddesses after having purified them is described is the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*).
11. That in which there is the practice of transforming [the winds] into the form of the five Tathāgatas through the complete purification of the subtle winds...

That is the Mother Tantra (mātṛtantra). 12. A collection of Tantras taught by Vajrasattva and Cakradhara to the Bhaṭṭārikās is the Father Tantra (pitṛtantra); and that Tantra taught by Heruka and Vajraḍākinī is designated as the Mother Tantra.

13. Among the Teacher, Vajradhara, his attendants, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, when a request is made by those to be trained (vineyajana), the instruction given is the Father Tantra; likewise, when a request is made by the Mother Goddesses (mātṛdevī), [it is the Mother Tantra].

The taught Tantra is called Mātṛtantra. 14. Depending on the disciples to be trained, that in which the male group predominates is Pitṛtantra, and that in which the female group predominates is designated as Mātṛtantra.
These distinctions cannot be accepted as being of the nature of pervasion (vyāpti).
The distinctions [among the tantras] have been made solely on the basis of the predominance of certain primary limbs and their principal forms, due to variations in degree.
The Tibetan scholar Padma dkar po established three divisions of the Unexcelled Tantra based on the foundation of the practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).

According to the *Pañcakrama*, that in which the meditation of the completion stage is performed primarily through the five stages is the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*); that in which the meditation of the completion stage is performed by means of the four seals (*caturmudrā*) is the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*).

And where the practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) occurs through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) consisting of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth, that is the non-dual tantra (*advayatantra*).
This very point was also stated by Siddhagodachanpāda in his commentary on the *Cakrasaṃvara*:
"The primordial teachers divided the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*) into two categories based on the distinction between Father and Mother tantras."

Thus, it is accepted that the *Guhyasamāja*, *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, *Vairocanamāyājāla*, *Anuttaramāyājāla*, *Vajrasattvamāyājāla*, and so forth, are included within the Father Tantras (*pitṛtantra*); likewise, the *Cakrasaṃvara*, *Hevajra*, *Kālacakra*, *Mahāmudrātilaka*, *Mahāmāyā*, *Buddhakapāla*, and so forth, are included within the Mother Tantras (*mātṛtantra*).

The Śākya tradition masters, the venerable Chos rgyal lha sga pa, have enumerated [the following]: the *Hevajra* (the uncommon explanatory tantra), the *Vajrapañjara* (the common explanatory tantra), the *Saṃpuṭa*, the *Jñānatilaka*, the *Uttara-tantra*, the *Jñānagarbha-yoginī-tantra*, the *Tattvapradīpa*, the *Guhyapradīpa*, the *Mahāmudrātilaka*, the *Uttarottara-tantra*, the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the *Kālacakra*, and so forth.

In the *Prajñātantras*, there is an inclusion (*samāveśa*) of the *Cakrasaṃvara*, *Mahāmāyā*, *Buddhakapāla*, and others; and in the *Upāyatantras*, there is an inclusion of the *Guhyasamāja*, *Vajramālā*, *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, and others. Jamagön Masajab Samahodaya established three divisions of the *Mahāyogatantra*.
According to his view, all [tantras] such as the *Guhyasamāja*—which belongs to the Father Tantras—and the Mother Tantras, are indeed included within the *Cakrasaṃvara*.

Furthermore, regarding the Non-dual Tantra (*advayatanttra*), after dividing it into two categories based on the names *Ābhyantara* (Internal) and *Udāragambhīrārthavistāra* (Extensive and Profound Meaning), the first is assigned to *Hevajra* and the second to *Kālacakra*.

According to the *Mahodaya*, which treats them as merely of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), a threefold division is made into Father, Mother, and Non-dual Tantras. However, in terms of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), all Anuttara Tantras are accepted as being exclusively Non-dual Tantras.
Their view is that in the Father Tantras (*pitṛtantra*), there is a predominance of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) of the Father Deity and the ritual procedures of the mantra.

In the Mother Tantras (*mātṛtantra*), however, there is a profound depth of numerous significant methods combined with the generation stage and mantra rituals of the Mother Deity. Therefore, the Mother Tantra is more profound than the Father Tantra.
According to the view of the venerable Ācārya Serdog Pema Özer, the non-duality (*advaya*) of the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*) and Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*) itself constitutes the *Advayatantra*.
That is to say, this *Advayatantra* is not some independent tantra;
rather, terms such as *Pitṛtantra*, *Upāyatantra*, *Ḍākinīmātṛtantra*, and *Yoginītantra* are merely synonyms for it.
First, this *Pitṛtantra* is explained, for it is the substantial cause and the seed-like source of the Buddha’s *rūpakāya*.
This *tantra* is the method (*upāya*) of both wisdom (*prajñā*) and method; that is to say, it belongs to the side of appearance (*ābhāsa*).

The second tantra is called Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), because this Wisdom Tantra (*prajñātantra*), which resembles a mother, is primarily the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Dharmakāya— the fruit of the non-dual knowledge of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) according to ultimate truth—
and it belongs to the side of wisdom (*prajñā*) within the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*).
As it is said in the Pāramitā system regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

When the various means (*upāya*) of the *Prajñāpāramitā* converge, the various types of fruits and the host of deities (*devakāya*)—that is, the means—are found to possess the state of union (*yuganaddhatva*), given that they are non-different from the great bliss and emptiness (*mahāsukha-śūnyatā*), which is like a mother. Even in the world, a lineage of sons is determined by means of the father.
The essential point of this entire section is this: the Tibetan masters have accepted this *Anuttaratantra* as a "Father-Mother Non-dual Tantra" (*pitṛ-mātṛ-advayatantra*).
According to the opinion of Indian masters, there is nowhere to be found a clear explanation of this tantra as being divided into three parts in such a manner.
In the *Vajragarbhālaṅkāra*, only the two tantras of the *Ḍākinīmātṛ* and the *Ḍākinīpitṛ* are accepted as the final ones.
Therefore, it appears that the Tibetan masters, taking these two tantras as their basis, made the divisions in the form of Father, Mother, and Non-dual tantras.
Otherwise, let there be only a single nondual tantra in its independent form.
It is impossible to accept even the two tantras of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) as they appear in the *Kālacakra* as being independent tantras;
for if only wisdom were taught, the attainment of the body of unified union (*yuganaddhakāya*) would be impossible due to the absence of means.
The same applies even by means of the method alone.

Furthermore, according to the views of those who maintain that the *Guhyasamāja* and other such texts belong to the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), there too an explanation and a manual of practice (*sādhanāpaddhati*) emerge in which the two—wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*)—appear in an inseparable form, as follows: "The union of wisdom and method is designated as 'yoga'."
That which is wisdom through the absence of intrinsic nature is the characteristic of existence as skillful means.
The text of the Mātṛtantra is called Hevajra;
therein also, it is taught for the purpose of the non-dual cultivation of both the Mother and Father Tantras.
Just as by the syllable *he*, the great eons (*mahākalpa*), the vajra, and wisdom (*prajñā*) are counted—
listen as I declare to you that tantra which consists of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).

In this way, the entire Anuttara Tantra provides an exposition solely of the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-yuganaddha*); it does not exist as separate and independent entities. Different names have been assigned to it based on specific purposes.
At the time of practice, practitioners of the Mother Tantras primarily accomplish great bliss (*mahāsukha*) or emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As stated in the thirteenth chapter of the *Vajrapañjara*, "The Yoginī Tantra is the method (*upāya*) for the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
By means of the application of Mahāmudrā, yogins enter into this [state].
Therefore, this *Yoginītantra* has been taught.

That is to say, in the *Mātṛtantra*, having made the meditation on Caṇḍālī and so forth the primary practice, when the seminal essence (*śukra*) descends from the lotus of the *uṣṇīṣa* and subsequently ascends again, one effects the direct realization of the four joys and the four emptinesses;

having attained firmness within the emptiness of great bliss (*mahāsukhaśūnyatā*), [the practitioner] is raised up within the conventional illusory body (*saṃvṛtimāyākāya*) by means of the wind endowed with five rays, which serves as the support for the gnosis of great bliss.
The practice (*prakriyā*) is taught as the primary form in the *Mātṛtantra* or the *Hevajra*.

Yoga occurs in the form of non-duality with the Great Bliss-Emptiness (*mahāsukha-śūnyatā*), which brings about the attainment of the Dharmakāya and is the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) of the Innate (*sahaja*).
This is the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*) within the category of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, this wisdom (*prajñā*) is called "the mother.

In the *Guhyasamāja*, which follows the *Pitṛtantra* tradition, and according to the *Ḍākārṇava Tantra*, the method for yogins to attain the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*) through the accomplishments of the luminous body (*prabhāsvara-kāya*), the illusory body (*māyā-deha*), and so forth, has been taught.

That is to say, at the heart lotus—the site of the arising of luminosity—the wind gradually undergoes dissolution; having realized the four emptinesses through both the forward (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) sequences, and immediately after the perception of light (*āloka*) and the manifestation of light (*ālokābhāsa*), [the process continues].
One realizes the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), and through the wind that serves as its support and is endowed with five rays, the arising of the conventional illusory body (*saṃvṛtimāyākāya*) occurs.
This Father Tantra is the *Guhyasamāja*;
a detailed commentary on it in connection with the generation stage (*utpannakrama*) was composed by Nāgārjuna in the *Pañcakrama*.

This procedure is called the "Father Tantra" (Pitṛtantra) procedure. Although these three tantras all establish the very reality of non-duality—and thus non-duality is uniform throughout in the realization of the ultimate state—nevertheless, regarding the method of practice (*sādhanāvidhi*), there is a subtle distinction observed among these three texts: namely, that in the Father Tantras, the subtle vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*) and the yoga of the *tilaka* (mark) are emphasized; whereas in the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), the illusory body (*māyākāya*), and the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the emphasis lies on the practice of the illusory body (*māyākāya*). Thus, a subtle difference is seen within this triad of works.

In the Unsurpassed Tantra, there are two stages; in the Pāramitāyāna, the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) and the relative truth (saṃvṛtisatya) are mutually non-contradictory. The relative truth, according to its own nature, nourishes the ultimate truth, because the relative truth effects the negation of nihilism (uccheda).
Ultimate truth is also eternal.

Alternatively, ultimate truth, having negated existence by way of intrinsic nature, implies relative truth through its dependence; likewise, the understanding of the ultimate occurs only by relying upon relative truth. Therefore, the two truths exist in the form of property and substratum, like fire and its heat.
Whatever is the locus of these two truths in the Pāramitā-naya, that very same locus belongs to the two stages in the Vajrayāna.
As it is said in the *Hevajra-tantra*: "The teaching of the Dharma by the Vajradharas relies upon the two stages;
the stage of generation has been explained, now I shall explain the stage of completion."
It is also stated in the *Samājottara Tantra*: "The teaching for the Vajra-holders therein relies upon two stages:
the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) and likewise the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*)."

Clarifying the purpose of the two stages within the *Vajrapañjara*, the Blessed One said: "Just as the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is practiced for the sake of abandoning ordinary conceptualization (*sāmānyavikalpa*), so too is the completion stage (*utpannakrama*) practiced for the sake of abandoning conceptualization regarding purity—or rather, for the sake of abandoning attachment to the form of a sublime deity. It is also stated in the *Hevajra*: "By means of the yoga of the generation stage, the practitioner of vows (*vratī*) should cultivate the manifold elaborations (*prapañca*)."
Having rendered conceptual proliferation like a dream, one should become free from conceptual proliferation by means of conceptual proliferations.

The generation stage (*utpattikrama*) consists of the practice of meditating upon the maṇḍala of deities and goddesses—who are by nature devoid of intrinsic existence—as a general conceptualization of the supported and the support, like a reflection appearing in a mirror.

This same meaning is established in the *Yogaratnamālā*, a commentary on the *Hevajra*, as well. Dagpo Trashi Namgyal also stated that the generation stage is the practice of meditating upon the deity maṇḍalas by forming a conceptual construction of the faces, arms, and so forth, within the form of the deity through the seat, weapons, seed-syllables, and other attributes, just as in the generation of reality (*tattva*).

Likewise, at the time of death, just as there is a process of dissolution for beings, one performs the *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion) by transforming the colors, forms, and other attributes of the deities of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) into the *bindu* (the drop), and then gradually dissolving even the *bindu* into the *nāda* (the sound), and finally dissolving the *nāda* as well, thereby abiding in the non-dual state like the unmanifested sky.
This is also stated in the *Yogaratnāvalī*, a commentary on the *Hevajratantra*: "The arisen [form] is indeed the very nature of reality."
That very [reality] which is resolved upon and cultivated in its true nature within a yoga is the *utpannakrama* (the stage of completion).
Regarding this, the following statement is also cited: "The innate (*sahaja*) is said to be heard; it is divided into two distinct types.
From the perspective of the *utpattikrama* (the stage of generation), the conventional form of the deity is [one of them]."
But from the perspective of the stage of completion, it has the nature of the bliss of manifestation;
the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon these two truths.

In the *Pradīpoddyotana* commentary on the *Guhyasamāja*, having explained the interpretable (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meanings of the generation and completion stages, the first is designated as "conceptual" (*kalpita*). This conceptual stage is stated to be the means for achieving the second, the completion stage. While clarifying these two—the conceptual means and the completion stage—His Holiness Ācārya Tsongkhapa stated that although both types of means are accomplished within the body of a deity by relying upon their respective methods of approach (*upāyakrama*), nevertheless, regarding the conceptual means (the generation stage):

The practitioner, having been transformed through the vowels and consonants into the weapons of the sun, moon, and so forth, personally brings about the visualization of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) through conceptual construction.
In the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), the intended meaning of the vowels, consonants, and other syllables is the *bodhicitta*.

Having caused the white and red winds to enter the *avadhūtī* channel, when the [three] luminosities—the light (*āloka*), the increase of light (*ālokābhāsa*), and the attained knowledge (*labdhajñāna*)—have become manifest, one arises in the illusory body (*māyākāya*) by means of the subtle vital wind and mind.
Therefore, due to the distinction between the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized, the body of the deity residing therein also possesses two forms.

Regarding the systematic presentation of the stages and paths of the Vajrayāna, the master Serdog Panchen Mahodaya states briefly as follows: "Indeed, for a practitioner who is unable to cause the winds to enter the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) through the power of meditative cultivation, and likewise, for the sake of bringing to maturity the continuity of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) of one's own practice, [one employs] conceptualizations such as the intellect resembling birth, death, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)."
Having formulated a novel conceptualization (*prajñapti*), one performs meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Its synonyms include artificial yoga (*kṛtrimayoga*), yoga of conceptualization (*prajñaptiyoga*), initial yoga (*prathamayoga*), ripening yoga (*paripācakayoga*), and so forth.

Following the entry of the vital wind (*vāyu*) into the central channel (*madhyamā*) by the power of cultivation, the yoga of the trained continuum (*śaikṣasamtatiyoga*)—which arises through the stabilization and dissolution [of that wind] within that very [channel]—is the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
*Akṛtrima-yoga*, *aprajñapti-yoga*, *dvitīya-krama-yoga*, and *mukti-yoga* are synonyms for this very [practice].
In the cultivation of the two stages (*krama*), practitioners transform the entire universe into the form of the Goddess and the deities and meditate upon it.
As it is stated in the *Vasantatilaka-ṭīkā-rahasya-dīpikā*:

"This [mandala] consists of all three families and has the nature of the five Buddhas. In that very same source it says: "Men are the forms of Vajradhara, and women are Vajrayoṣits. Because of the activities of body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings, the secret of the three families has come forth as the beginning. It is also stated in the *Guhyasamāja*: "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed to be the five Buddhas."
The vajra-spheres themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the essence of awakening.
Thus it is said.
In that very context, the conceptualization of all beings as having the nature of goddesses is established: "The earth element is called Locanā; the water element is remembered as Māmakī;
fire shall be known as Pāṇḍarā; and wind is proclaimed as Tārā."
The commitment of the space-vajra-realm is itself known as Vajradhara.

In this way, by means of the meditative practice (*bhāvanā*) through which the entire world— consisting of both the stationary and the moving— becomes the transformation of the God and Goddess, the abandonment of the grasping at a self (*ātmadhāraṇa*) or the abandonment of ordinary conceptualization (*sāmānyavikalpa*) with respect to common objects arises;
and this is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

Furthermore, if there should be an attachment to the forms of gods and goddesses, that too, as before, leads to bondage. In this state, whether the bondage is by an iron chain or a golden chain, both are equal in their capacity to bind.
Therefore, for the sake of abandoning that clinging, the cultivation of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) becomes necessary.

Clarifying the method of cultivating the completion stage, it is stated in the *Pañcakrama*: "By means of the process of grasping the whole (*piṇḍagraha*), and likewise by means of sequential analysis (*anubheda*), [the visualization] proceeds from the head or from the feet until it reaches the heart."

The yogin should enter the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); this is known as the "grasping of the mass" (piṇḍagrāha). Having first rendered both the stationary and the moving world into clear light (prabhāsvara), he should subsequently make himself likewise so; for this is the sequence of non-differentiation.

This means that the very abiding in reality through the dissolution of the entire world—comprising all that is stationary and moving—into the luminous state (*prabhāsvara*) is called the general *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage) procedure.
For example, without relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), the direct realization of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is not possible;
or rather, conventional truth itself is the means for awakening to ultimate truth.

In the same way, for the sake of realizing the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), the prior progression through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is indispensable. As it is stated in the *Pañcakrama*: "For those established in the generation stage and desiring the completion stage, the Fully Awakened Ones have fashioned a means like a staircase."

Āryadeva also stated in the *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa*: "For the sake of beginners who have not yet realized reality, in order to lead them into that [reality]—namely, the completion stage—the Blessed Buddha, through his skill in means, taught the generation stage as if it were a staircase.

Having meditated upon the yoga endowed with prior conceptual elaborations, the purification of ordinary conceptualization is performed; furthermore, having carried out the deconstruction of the conceptually constructed form, one abandons attachment through non-conceptual meditation."
Enlightenment is attained by performing the practice of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).

Regarding the cultivation of the two stages, Dagpo Trashi Namgyal Mahodaya stated in his work titled *The General Tantra* that the followers of Nāgārjuna’s tradition perform the cultivation of the completion stage immediately after attaining Buddhahood through the generation stage.

In that very context, Padyavajra, Ajitacandra, and others state that one should perform the meditation on the generation stage during the first watch of the night, and likewise, the meditation on the completion stage during the second watch.
According to the opinion of the scholars of Tibet, just as two wings are necessary for birds to fly, so too the meditations on the generation and completion stages are practiced simultaneously.
The status of the two stages is equal regarding flowers and perfumes;
therefore, according to their view, the cultivation of the two stages should be performed simultaneously.
This very statement is also expressed in the *Hevajra*: "This yoga of the completion stage is considered to be bliss, the great bliss."
If one who has already produced [the realization] lacks cultivation, what is the purpose of its production?
In the absence of a body, from where could there be happiness? It cannot even be said [to exist]. The entire world is pervaded by happiness in the form of the pervaded and the pervader.
Just as fragrance supported by a flower is not perceived when the flower is absent,
so too bliss is not experienced in the absence of meditative concentration.
Furthermore, only that practitioner who is fully matured and endowed with sharp faculties is capable of following this manual;
this path is not suitable for all disciples.

As the Buddha stated in the *Vajragarbha-vyākhyā-tantra*: "For the sake of liberating beings bound by the webs of infinite conceptual constructions from the suffering of the three worlds, [the teaching] follows their respective inclinations and capacities."
In the scriptures, instruction has been given on numerous methods (rites) contained within the two stages.

For those who are excessively consumed by the latent tendencies of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-vāsanā*), the teaching of the *utpannakrama* (the stage of completion) was provided through rites such as the worship of the nature of conceptual construction and the construction of mandalas.

Just as a field is made fertile through plowing, digging, and so forth, likewise, when the practitioner has become fully ripened, he is impelled toward the cultivation of the perfected stage (*niṣpannakrama*). When the practitioner has ascended to the actual yoga of the perfected stage, he should then abandon the cultivation of the emanation stage (*utpattikrama*), which is a conceptual construction and a mere designation.
It is also stated in the *Ḍākārṇava Tantra*: "For the sake of attaining actual yoga, one should perform the cultivation of artificial meditation."
By means of the practice of artificial mantras and so forth, the practitioner becomes established in the non-artificial yoga.
When the practitioner is able to abide in the non-artificial yoga, then he must abandon the cultivation of artificial meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Just as when a bridge has been built across a river, there is no further need for a boat, and people leave the boat right there; likewise, when one is established in the non-artificial state through the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), the cultivation of the yoga of artificial deities [is abandoned].

It is abandoned. It is also stated in the *Guhyasiddhi* and other works: "Having abandoned the extensive generation [stage], which is the meditation of the beginner, far away through all effort by means of the yoga of the completion stage."
Relying upon the *Tantrasadbhāva*, [I shall explain] the characteristics of the attainment of siddhis,
setting aside all extensive elaborations that are obstacles to meditative cultivation.
In the *Vasantatilaka* as well, it is stated thus: "Having abandoned the artificial mandala, the artificial fire-offering ritual (*homakarma*),
the artificial meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and even the artificial recitation (*japa*)—
all such things are artificial because they consist of the yoga of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
Artificial grammatical analysis is for the purpose of understanding the external form;
however, once the true nature [of the word] is understood, such analysis is no longer a cause [for that understanding].
Just as a raft is well-employed by certain people seeking the further shore,
and then abandoned upon reaching that shore, so too is that very process [of meditation].

In the *Ḍākārṇava Tantra*, whatever ritual activity such as the mandala and so forth is constructed with an artificial mind is designated as "external conduct" (*bāhyacaryā*). This is taught for beginners; through it, worldly accomplishment (*laukikasiddhi*) is obtained, but the attainment of supramundane, extraordinary accomplishment (*alaukikyā asādhāraṇasiddhi*) does not occur.

In the *Guhyasamājottaratantra* as well, it is stated that the attainment of common accomplishments (*sāmānyasiddhi*) occurs through the four vajra-yogas of service (*sevā*), further service (*upasevā*), and so forth, while the attainment of uncommon accomplishments (*asāmānyasiddhi*) occurs through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) consisting of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and the rest:
"By means of these four vajras, the common practice of service is accomplished;
and in the supreme nectar of gnosis, the practice should be performed by way of the six-limbed yoga."
Having performed the supreme practice through service by means of the six-limbed yoga, one should then accomplish [the goal];
otherwise, the highest siddhi will not arise.

In the explanatory tantra of Hevajra, the *Vajragarbha-tantra*, the Blessed One says: "Just as the production of rice fruit does not occur from the seed of *kodrava* grain, likewise, the fruit produced from the seed of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would itself be conceptual. The Blessed One says in the *Sampuṭa-tantra*: "Conceptual construction is indeed great delusion; it causes one to fall into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Abiding in non-conceptual meditative absorption, one shines like the stainless sky."
While providing a commentary on this, the great Buston states that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must indeed be abandoned.
This is twofold: 1. general conceptualization, which is called "false conceptualization" (*durvikalpa*); and 2.
the conceptualization of deities and so forth, which pertains to the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
It is called "auspicious conceptualization.

The second is the negation of the first, and this auspicious conceptualization is abandoned by the non-conceptual gnosis of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*). What, then, is to be abandoned? It is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Because it is created through mere designation and conceptual construction, one might ask:
"If it is to be abandoned, then how can there be the attainment of the holder of the wheel of union (*yuganaddha*)?
For it is by practicing the cultivation of the non-duality of wisdom and means that the attainment of union occurs at the stage of the fruit.
Not only this,
but in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pradīpa*, it is stated that wisdom without skillful means,
and skillful means without wisdom, are both called bondage.
This very statement is spoken in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra*.

Also, in the *Hevajra*, when Vajragarbha poses the question: "If the attainment of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) could occur through the meditation on the completion stage (*niṣpattikrama*) alone, then what is the necessity of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*)?"—in response to this question, the Blessed One says: "In the absence of a body, whence can there be bliss?"
This fragrance, residing in the flower, is inseparable from its form.
Therefore, without the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), there is no possibility of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
Furthermore, a question arises here: why, then, was it stated that "birth should be abandoned like a bond"?

Having stated that "this conceptual construction (vikalpa) is artificial," was it intended as a dismissal of it? Rather, the sequence of the arising of the universal (sāmānyotpattikrama) is said to be the antidote for abandoning attachment to objective entities.

By practitioners of the Tantra (*tantrasādhakaiḥ*), just as in the perception of a new cycle of existence, the nature of the world consisting of the mobile and the immobile is transformed; and through the light of the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the gods and goddesses, even the states of the mandala-nature are [transformed].
It must be practiced so that one's common perception functions toward the discernment of the object.

This alone is the one significant distinction of the Tantric scripture: herein, the abandonment of conceptual construction is achieved by means of conceptual construction itself, and the destruction of passion is brought about by passion itself.
It is said in the Hevajra Tantra: "By that very same portion of poison by which all living beings die, one who knows the reality of poison should expel the poison with that very poison."
Just as bean-based food is given to one seized by wind,
whereby the wind is destroyed by the wind through the application of contrary medicine.
Pure existence is conceptualized as existence itself;
it is like water that has entered the ear and is drawn out by more water.
In the same way, conceptualization regarding existence is indeed purified by means of its own forms;
just as things burnt by fire are moistened again by fire,
so too those scorched by the fire of passion are moistened by the very agitation of passion.
While explaining this, Koṅṭul Rinpoche states that the yoga of the deity brings about supreme greatness for the purpose of ceasing conceptualization of the universal (*sāmānya-vikalpa*).
For example, by repeatedly reflecting upon someone as "this person is our friend" with respect to an enemy, that enmity is diminished.
As it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "Therefore, whether real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon..."
Upon the completion of cultivation, that is the fruit: a cognition that is vivid and free from conceptual construction.
Those overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, madness, thieves, dreams, and the like,
perceive even non-existent things as if they were standing right before them.

In the Mantra system, meditation is performed by transforming suffering itself— the Noble Truth of Suffering— which comprises both the stable and the moving worlds. In the Pāramitā system, effort is directed toward the cessation of its causes, such as the Truth of Origination and so forth.
Just as a cause is itself subsumed within its effect, one should understand passion (rāga) in the same way.

In the manner of the Pāramitā-naya, when passion is not present to direct perception, by establishing the emptiness of passion through ultimate reasonings, one must again exert great effort toward the arising and cessation of passion.
In the Mantra system, the opposite of this occurs: passion (*rāga*) is generated as the antidote.
When this passion has arisen, ordinary mental factors of passion dissolve back into themselves.

In this state, if one enters into non-conceptual emptiness (*niṣprapañca-śūnyatā*) with full awareness (*sasamprajanya*), then passion, having ceased to be passion, becomes the Great Passion (*mahārāga*), which is the nature of emptiness and Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*).

This is precisely the reason why the Blessed Buddha, having classified practitioners of tantra according to their degrees of passion (*rāga*) into four levels, taught in the *Saṃpuṭatantra* the transformation of passion into the path through the stages of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Anuttarayoga. "Laughter, gazing, and holding hands— these are established in the tantra."
Having chewed up both passion and dispassion, the wood-worm remains.
Furthermore, it would likewise be inappropriate for us to adhere to that very same "excellent conceptualization" (*bhadravikalpa*).

Therefore, it is understood that just as Nāgārjuna, in establishing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), analyzed the Tathāgata’s Four Noble Truths and established emptiness (*śūnyatā*), so too, while elucidating his own system within the common completion stage (*sāmānyaniṣpannakrama*), he has revealed his own preferred position regarding the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Otherwise, the very existence of the sequence of generation (*utpattikrama*)—which has the appropriated body as its cause—would not be possible;

and in this state, may the existence of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) also arise not merely as a negation, but as the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), in the form of an affirmative exclusion (*paryudāsavidhi*).

When the life-force wind born of karma is made to enter the *avadhūtī*, that which is the arousal within the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) by means of the subtle wind is designated as the very form of the sublime generation stage.
Even when that which is beyond the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) has arisen, there remains the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

To state it briefly and clearly: that which was established in the *Kriyā*, *Caryā*, and other tantras as the form of the deity consisting of the coarse mind-body (*sthūla-manomaya-deva-rūpa*) must be abandoned in its corresponding form;
however, the complete generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is not to be abandoned.

Dagpo Trashi Namgyal Mahodaya has also stated this very point: that once the generation of the distinguished completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) has occurred, the negation of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) that follows is a negation of conceptual meditation (*vikalpa-bhāvanā*), and certainly not of the divine wheel (*devacakra*) whose nature is mere appearance. In the *Pañcakrama* as well, Nāgārjuna spoke regarding the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*): "The practitioner by whom the stage of self-consecration is not attained..."
His labor in the sūtras, tantras, and kalpas is in vain.
The samādhi of self-consecration and likewise the state of luminosity are known as the two truths, distinguished by their respective natures as cause and fruit.

By implication, in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), one must necessarily abandon the meditation on the deity after having established it through either ritual procedure or conceptual construction; however, the meditation on the deity within this self-consecration stage (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) is not to be abandoned, because without such realization, the attainment of perfect awakening (*sambodhi*) is impossible.
Without the meditation on the form of the deity, there will be a decline of relative truth (*saṃvṛti*).
Only the ultimate reality remains, for one must abide in the supreme state through the union of the two;
as Nāgārjuna has said: "This is the stage of generation, and this is also the stage of completion."
But where there is a unity of these two, that is called "yoked together" (yuganaddha).

In this context, the *rūpakāya* is precisely the body that has arisen upward through the entry, abiding, and emergence [of the winds] within the *avadhūtī* channel; it is the fruit of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
Therefore, it is understood here that the effect itself is designated by the name of the cause.

Through the entry of the wind into the *avadhūtī* and the conceptualization of the form as having been raised up, there exists the *prabhāsvararūpakāya*, which is a conventional form and not an ultimate reality.
This fire is its heat, and likewise the flower is like its fragrance;
and that which exists as both distinct and non-distinct—
this form abides with the luminosity just as a tree abides with its shadow.
Therefore, this is the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*);
for this form-body (*rūpakāya*) is indeed the enjoyment-body (*sambhogakāya*).
[Thus it is stated] in the *Pañcakrama*.
It has been said: "This very [nature] is to be attained, characterized by the teaching of illusion;
like an illusion, it is conventional truth, and that is indeed the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya)."

Therefore, considering the form-deity (rūpadevatā), which is the cause of the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya), to be like an illusion, practitioners must always perform the practice of mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, and so forth, as being like an illusion.
Regarding this, it is said: "The application of mantras and mudrās, and the delineation of the maṇḍala and so forth..."
One should always perform the entire ritual of the bali-offering as being like an illusion.

The meaning is this: as long as the subtle vital wind and mind have not been raised up into the body of the deity immediately following the entry and stabilization of the vital winds within the *avadhūtī*, one must perform the meditation on the generation stage by creating through conceptual thought. Once this state has been attained, it is entirely pointless to subsequently perform the extensive meditation on the generation stage, such as the mandala and the celestial palace.
From another perspective, the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) consists precisely in the arising of the deity’s body from the subtle vital wind within the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*).

Therefore, we can say that once this state has been attained, the subsequent cultivation of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), such as the creation of the mandala and celestial palace in their expanded form, is purposeless;
furthermore, the completion stage is simply the arising of the deity’s body from the subtle vital wind within the body of union.
Therefore,

we can say that once this state has been attained, the meditation on the generation stage (utpattikrama) should likewise be abandoned, just as a traveler who has reached the far shore of a river leaves the boat behind.
This alone is appropriate.

The intention behind this full discussion is this: that which consists of the artificial cultivation of the state of being a deity, performed by means of the method (*upāya*), is indeed to be abandoned; however, the cultivation of the form of the deity arisen through the method is not to be abandoned.
As it is stated in the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilaka*: "When the goal (*upeya*) has been attained, they declare those methods to be things to be abandoned."
By the very name "generation stage" (*utpattikrama*), it is understood that this is a meditation newly constructed through conceptual and designated cognition,
which is to be abandoned;
it is not otherwise.
Even the cultivation of non-conceptualization must be abandoned;
that is to say, the attainment of the supreme state is impossible through the mere knowledge of conceptual and non-conceptual cognition alone.

For even abiding in absolute emptiness is one extreme, and furthermore, if one were to become attached to the cultivation of a deity within that very state through conceptualization, that too would become a cause of suffering.
Just as it occurs through adherence to generalities,
for this [suchness] remains untouched by reality and is indeed painful, just like emptiness (suchness) during the stage of the path.
Having understood conventional reality, that which is real is called true life.
Likewise, even at the stage of fruition, if one were to remain in mere non-conceptuality alone, how could the welfare of sentient beings be possible?
Therefore, there must be a union [of the two truths] and it must be uncontrived; for this, right knowledge is indispensable.

This would only be possible when there is non-differentiation between gnosis and the body—that is to say, when the practitioner has been raised within the body by virtue of the reality of non-duality.
In this state, no existence whatsoever of conceptual construction remains. Conceptual construction can only arise where there is the activity of subject and object.

Therefore, this is the very distinction of the Mantra system: that where the body itself is the mind, and the mind itself is the body; where the body itself is speech, and there is no separate existence for subject and object.
As long as the practitioner does not attain a correct awakening to this state, he will not understand the reality of this vision.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Vasantatilaka*: "Buddhahood does not arise from the absence of conceptualization, nor likewise from that with conceptualization;
it occurs for the wise only through perfectly pure thorough knowledge."

In the practice of the Mantra system (*mantranaya*), due to its clarity, there exists a utility characterized by an equal primacy between the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).

In the Father Tantras (*pitṛtantra*), there is a general generation stage; in the Unsurpassed Tantras (*anuttaratantra*), there is a general procedure for the generation stage. Within the Unsurpassed Tantras—specifically the Father Tantras, Mother Tantras (*mātṛtantra*), and Non-dual Tantras (*advayatantra*)—differences have arisen in the names of certain elements during the meditation on the generation stage according to their respective divisions.
It is inclined toward that [Father Tantra]:
(ka) *Pitṛtantra*. This *Guhyasamāja* is considered the principal text of the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*).

Herein, the method of cultivation for the Stage of Completion (*utpannakrama*) is taught through the fourfold division of service (*sevā*) and so forth within the Stage of Generation (*utpattikrama*).
It is stated in the *Guhyasamājottaratantra*: "The fourfold means has been described in the *Bodhivajra*;
it is always praised by the yogi in all the Yoga Tantras."
The names of these four yogas (or means) are given in that very same source: "The first is the procedure of service (sevā), the second is the near-accomplishment (upasādhana),
the third is indeed the accomplishment (sādhana), and the fourth is the great accomplishment (mahāsādhana)."

The generation stage (*utpattikrama*) consists of four types of practice (*sādhana*), distinguished as service (*sevā*), near-attainment (*upasādhana*), attainment (*sādhana*), and great attainment (*mahāsādhana*).
Furthermore, because of the distinction between the generation and completion stages (*niṣpannakrama*), service is also twofold.
As it is stated in the *Samājottaratantra*: "Service is of two kinds, through the division of common and supreme."
The common and supreme [attainments] are achieved through the fourfold vajra and the nectar of gnosis.
While providing an explanation of the four means of accomplishment (*catussādhana*), Candrakīrti stated: "Service (*sevā*) is that which is attended to and practiced by those seeking liberation.

What is it? It is the perfectly pure form of the deity; it must be performed and accomplished through the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) alone, by means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) alone. Having said this, he clarified the method of cultivation for service as the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).

Regarding the intention of service within the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), it was declared to be meditative absorption (*samāhitir*) upon suchness (*tathatā*) and the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
It is stated in the Root Tantra: "One should cultivate supreme enlightenment through the union of service and meditative absorption."

While providing a commentary on this, Candrakīrti stated: "That which is served—that is, taken as an object—is *sevā* (service); that very thing is *samaya* (the commitment). The joining together (*saṃyojana*) and the accomplishment (*niṣpādana*) of the site and so forth is the union of service and commitment (*sevā-samaya-saṃyoga*), which is the first limb. Elucidating the meaning of this, Bhavyakīrti stated in his *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*: "The cultivation of emptiness is the cultivation of the stage of gnosis (*jñāna-bhūmi*) and likewise of the ultimate maṇḍala;
this alone constitutes *sevā* (service)."

The venerable Ācārya Coṅkhāpā Mahodaya has also stated: "In the emptiness of *bodhicitta*, the very act of taking it as an object of focus is 'service' (*sevā*); the one-pointed stability therein is 'meditative absorption' (*samādhi*).

Quoting the words of Ācārya Bodhiśreṣṭha, he further states: "Reality itself is awakening (*bodhi*); the practice of its cultivation is 'service. The visualization of celestial palaces and so forth are the auxiliary limbs of service."

The great master Ācārya Daṅ-po-sde-zhiṅ-ma-rgyal-ma-ho-day also clearly explained *sevā* as follows: from the practice of meditation by transforming into that [state of] universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*), up to the visualization of the celestial palace (*vimāna*), the seat (*āsana*), and so forth, is designated as *sevā*.
Regarding *upasādhana*, it is stated in the *Guhyasamāja*: "At the culmination of the accomplishment of *upasādhana*, there is the investigation of the vajra-abodes (*vajrāyatana*)."
In the *Pradīpodyotana*, a commentary on this [text], it is stated: "The support of emptiness and the support of the sun and so forth constitute the *upasādhana*.
Since that very process culminates in the arrangement of mantras (*mantravinyāsa*), the second stage is the occurrence of the *upasādhana*.

For the practitioner performing the meditation on emptiness, the *upasādhana* consists of the accomplishment of the body of the Mahāmudrā through the sequential placement of the solar disc, lunar disc, seed-syllables, and so forth, followed by their transformation.

In the high stage of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), that which is generated by the subtle vital wind and mind and arises in the form of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is called the pure, perfected gnosis body (*śuddhaniṣpannajñānakāya*).
In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), this is called the impure body, because it is a perfected body generated by means of mantra.

Among the four yogas found in the *Guhyasamājapañjikā*, the *Kṛṣṇayamāritantra*, and other such works, it is included within the practice of "accomplishment" (*sādhana*) and "near-accomplishment" (*upasādhana*), up to the third yoga, "excessive yoga" (*atiyoga*).

In the *Pradīpodyotana*, while providing the literal meaning of the *Mūlatantra*—namely, "the investigation of the vajra-abodes at the summit of the accomplishment of the near-attainment" (*upasādhanasiddhyagra*)—it is stated:
"Because that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is produced in proximity (*upa*), it is called 'near-attainment' (*upāsādhana*);

'accomplishment' (*siddhi*) refers to the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. That which has the *praṇava* and other mantras as its beginning or summit is the 'summit of the accomplishment of the near-attainment. This is the form of Mahāmudrā, in which all the syllables of the mantras are arrayed."

In this [tantra], beginning with Vajravairocana and ending with the seventh, their sense bases (*āyatana*)—namely the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth—are established by transcending the third arrangement; thus, the investigation into the thorough knowledge of cause and effect is accomplished.
For the sake of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is propitiated; therefore, the instruction for its accomplishment is given.
In other texts, the practice starting from the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*) up to the empowerment of the sense bases is called "accompanied practice" (*sopasādhana*).

In this context, there is an underlying intention regarding the basis of the *āyatana*s (sense bases), namely the placement (*nyāsa*) of seed-syllables or deities and so forth upon the body-mandala. The practice (*sādhana*) is stated in the *Guhyasamāja Mūlatantra*: "In the practice, the exhortation is proclaimed, as well as the meditation on the Lord of Mantras. Regarding this, Candrakīrti, while providing the commentary, stated: "The purpose for the presence of the practice is the request; the purpose of the practice is the *samaya*. [It is called] *samaya* because one comes together (*sameti*) and proceeds (*gacchati*)."

The Samādhisattva and the Jñānasattva, as well as the purpose of the sādhana and the samaya—this is the third [point]. Having exhorted the three vajras—the meaning of the empowerment of body, speech, and mind—by means of the Lord of Mantras, beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, one abides in the conduct-samaya which is non-different from oneself and of a single flavor; this is the practice (*sādhana*) of this [body, speech, and mind].

Because they are indivisible from the three vajras, this accomplishment through the success of the Samayasattva, Jñānasattva, and Mantrādhipatisattva is called the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*). At the times of the Great Accomplishment, one should meditate on the form of the Mantravajrin; having visualized the Lord upon the crown, one attains the state of the Jñānavajrin.

The Mantravajrī—that is, the practitioner himself—according to the sequence arrived at during the practice, brings about the meditative union (*abhisamāpatti*) with the Vajra-lotus of the presiding deity by means of [the mantra] "Vajradhr̥k" and so forth. He generates the thirty-two deities within his own body in the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). Likewise, while visualizing the presiding deity upon his own head, as well as Vairocana and the others upon the heads of the deities placed within his own body, he receives empowerment from them and cultivates the realization that the accomplishment of the body of the Great Seal has been attained.
Such a meditation alone is called the "great accomplishment" (*mahāsādhana*).
As it is stated in the *Pradīpodyotana*:

"In brief, by clarifying these four yogas of service and so forth, the venerable master Dga’-ba-rdo-rje (Dagapokuśīna) stated that, having performed the transformation within the emptiness of all phenomena—"
The procedure of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) up to the throne of the celestial palace (*vimāna-āsana*) is the yoga of service (*sevā-yoga*).
The sequence beginning with the visualization of the principal deity (*pradhānadevatā*) up to the consecration of the abode (*āyatanādhiṣṭhāna*) is the yoga of close service (*upasevā-yoga*).
[This pertains to] body, speech, and mind—the three vajras.
The practice of performing the rites with undivided focus throughout the triad [of yogas] constitutes the *sādhanayoga*;
the yoga of consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), praises (*stuti*), and so forth, constitutes the *mahāsādhanayoga*.

Among these four yogas beginning with *sevā*, the first three are said to be the yogas for achieving one’s own welfare (*svārthasiddhi*), while the last is the yoga for achieving the welfare of others (*parārthasiddhi*).
In this very way, within the three meditations (*tridhyāna*), the first triad of yogas is called the "meditation of the initial yoga" (*ādiyogadhyāna*);
the final one, the yoga of the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhanayoga*), becomes integrated with the King of the Mandala (*maṇḍalarājāgra*, or *karmarājāgra*).

The venerable Ācārya Koṅṭula stated that because one performs the meditation prior to the completion of the other two meditations of the primary creator of the maṇḍala, who is the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*), this is called "the beginning" (*ādi*); likewise, when the non-dual union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) has arisen, it is called "yoga.

Thus, from the three meditations, the procedure is consolidated up to the meditation on the primary body of union from within the celestial palace maṇḍala during the meditation of the initial yoga (*ādiyoga*).

Having placed the mantra-deity with the *bodhicitta* within the body of union (*yuganaddha*), the yoga that continues until the complete perfection of the mandala is called the second, the "Supreme King of Mandalas" meditation (*maṇḍalarājāgradhyāna*).

Immediately following that, the purification of the divine field and so forth, as well as the performance of activities equal to those of a deity, is called the final, the "Supreme King of Actions" meditation (*karmarājāgradhyāna*).

According to the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, the cultivation of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is performed by means of the fourfold yoga method: first, one should cultivate the yoga; the second is the subsequent yoga (*anuyoga*).
Atiyoga is the third, and Mahāyoga is the fourth.
While defining the state of the four yogas, it is said in that very same [text]: "The accomplishment of Vajrasattva is designated as Yoga;
the arising of its natural outflow, O Lord, is proclaimed as Anuyoga."
The accomplishment of the entire wheel is manifested as the *atiyoga*,
which is the consecration of the divine eye and so forth, as well as of body, speech, and mind.
The entry into the wheel of gnosis, the tasting of nectar,
the great worship, and the praise— this is known as the Great Yoga.

In the *Ratnamālā-ṭīkā*, a commentary on the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, Vanaratna clarifies the stages of *yoga*, *anuyoga*, *atiyoga*, and *mahāyoga*, providing a detailed analysis of them as follows: *Yoga* is defined as the very procedure beginning with the sevenfold supreme worship and culminating in the accomplishment of the *vajra-tattva* through the fivefold designation.
*Anuyoga* consists of the manifestation of the form of Kṛṣṇayamāri as white in color by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*).
Among his three faces, the central one is white,
the right is black, and the left is red;
he is seated upon a moon disc.

Immediately following the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the Vajra Tantra, this subsequent practice (*anuyoga*) consists of remaining in meditative equipoise together with Vārāhī of red complexion.
Following such a meditation, one causes the syllable "A-Haṃ" to flash forth within the lotus of one’s own heart,
and having drawn in the maṇḍala of Kṛṣṇayamāri, causes it to enter through the mouth.
