The procedure beginning with the entry [of the seminal essence] into the lotus of the Goddess via the vajra-path— which has become liquefied (or flowed out) through passion and attachment— and the generation of the mandala by means of the bodhicitta, as well as the placement of the seed-syllables within that mandala, is called the *anuyoga-vidhi* (the subsequent ritual procedure).
Atiyoga: Following Anuyoga, by means of the internal sequence (*ābhyantarakrama*), the deity is raised from the seed-syllables that have been deposited;
for example, the raising of Moha and Kṛṣṇayamāri by the syllable *kṣe*, and the raising of Kṛṣṇayamāri and others by the syllable *ma*—this is Atiyoga.

Mahāyoga: the accomplishment of Vajrasattva, the deposition of seed-syllables, the manifestation of the chosen deity through those seeds, the appearance of the complete principal deity together with the attendant deities and so forth, and the fullness of the maṇḍala.
The presiding over the sense organs, such as the eyes, nose, and tongue, of the perfected deities;
the causing of the vibration of the syllable *HŪṂ*, consisting of five rays of light, within the heart-lotus of the chosen deity;
and, having performed worship to the Tathāgatas, the invitation of them for the purpose of their consecration.
The bestowing of empowerment upon them and the summoning of the wheel of gnosis: "You are the Lord whose nature is Passion-Vajra, the source of the phenomena of passion.
O supreme among all excellent sounds, O Vajra of Speech, homage be to you!"
The performance of praise through the initial words and the tasting of the nectar are called the "Great Yoga of the Beginning.
An extensive explanation of these four yogas is provided in the seventeenth chapter of the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*.

In brief, the great master Dagpo Trashi Namgyal stated that for one who cultivates the fourfold yoga, the yoga consists of the meditation beginning from the visualization of the celestial palace as the support up until the causal Vajradhara (Vajrasattva);
immediately following that is the [meditation on] the effect.
The practice consisting of the meditation from the generation of the Vajra-holder Falavajradhara up to that point is *anuyoga*.
The meditation from the generation of the complete mandala onwards is *atiyoga*.
And the procedure for the empowerments of body, speech, and mind, as well as the offerings, praises, and so forth, is *mahāyoga*.

In this regard, it is extremely necessary to understand that, according to the Tantra, the principal deity of the mandala, the attendant deities, the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*), and so forth—all these belong to a single nature, that is, to the continuum (*santati*);
there is no other characteristic.
Therefore, in clear terms, we can say that the entire goddess-deity [is one].

The seed-syllables and so forth are the expanded form of one’s own mind—that is, the mind of Vajrasattva itself. Regarding the four branches of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), there is no procedure for meditating on the generation stage according to the four branches in the primary *Hevajra Tantra* of the Mother Tantras; [the first is] the awakening to emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*).
The second is the gathering of the seed-syllables;
the third is the perfection of the seed-syllables; and the fourth is the placement of the syllables.

That is to say, just as in the Father Tantras, all dharmas— such as the services and so forth— are to be transformed here also into the bodhicitta that is emptiness and luminosity; this is the basis for the meditation of the generation stage,
wherein one should effect the arousal of one’s chosen deity within the midst of that luminous mind (the intrinsic nature).

Having performed the meditation on the seed-syllable *hūṃ* according to the meaning of Heruka, and having carried out the imitation of the process of radiating, expanding, and withdrawing light, one then performs the second limb, which is the imitation of the arising of the chosen deity through the rite of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*). Alternatively, when the radiation and withdrawal of the seed-syllable— or the five awakenings— are complete, the third limb is the "accomplishment of the image" (*bimbaniṣpatti*), which is the complete meditation upon the reflection of the chosen deity.

When the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) has been generated solely by means of the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*), this is designated as "birth from a womb" (*upapādaka-bahūtpannatva*). Once the abode of the chosen deity has been presided over through the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) during the three meditations (*tridhyāna*), the attainment [of that state] following the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth is called the fourth limb.
This same sequence is also found in the *Sampuṭatantra*: "Again, the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*), and in the second [stage], the gathering of the seed-syllable (*bījasaṃgraha*)."
In the third [stage] is the perfection of the image; in the fourth is the placement of the syllable.

Beyond this, following the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), there is described the procedure for meditating upon Vajrasattva by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*).
[This is done] by means of the form of the moon situated within the *āli* [vowels], and the form of the sun within the *kāli* [consonants].
The union of the moon and the sun is proclaimed as Gaurī and the others.
The moon possesses mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), while the sun possesses the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*);
the discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*) is said to be the sign within the seed-syllable situated in one's own body.
All should perform this single practice for the sake of the purity of the manifestation of the image;
the wise one should thus meditate upon the form according to the prescribed rites.
Through the union of the vowels and consonants, there is the seat of Vajrasattva.
This subject is described in detail in the *Devatāpaṭala* (Chapter on Deities) of the first *kalpa* of the *Hevajratantra*.
In the *Vajrapañjara*, the method of cultivation for the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is taught.
The arising of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) through the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) purified by the emptiness of clear light (*prabhāsvaraśūnyatā*) is a limb of the Vairocana family.
The cultivation of the deity of the Samayacakra, which relies upon the five types of perfect awakening, constitutes the limb of the Vajrasattva family.
The water consecration in the form of Akṣobhya from the eight goddesses of the vidyās constitutes the limb of the [Akṣobhya] family.
For the sake of satisfying Vāgvajra, there is the limb belonging to the Lotus family, which consists of the tasting of nectar.
And for the purpose of offering praise to all the deities of the mandala, there is the limb belonging to the Jewel family.
It is also stated in the Guhyasamāja: "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas."

While providing this commentary, Candrakīrti stated that for the sake of abandoning the attachment of that practitioner who—without realizing the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*)—accepts and clings to the notion that there exists a Tathāgata or Bodhisattva distinct from himself, and who desires to attain that [state], it is said: "All exists by itself;
he himself is the self-deity; his own five aggregates alone exist in the form of the five Tathāgatas."
Apart from that, there is no external object of perception, nor any probandum or reason, nor anything such as the Bodhisattvas Kṣitigarbha and others, existing outside the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, whatever ritual arrangements exist for the Tathāgata family and so forth, all of them are contained within these five Buddhas, Vairocana and the rest.
The very nature of the five Tathāgatas consists of their own form and so on, which are nothing other than the five aggregates; there is no other external reality whatsoever.
We perceive that duality, as well as the earth, water, fire, and so forth external to the three realms— all of these exist as the expansion of one whose mind is equal to Vairocana.
And those who are designated as goddesses, such as Locanā and the others,
are likewise the five aggregates (the five Tathāgatas) beginning with Vairocana.
The luminosity that takes as its object the very nature of the means—
this abides in the state of non-duality;
this alone is the reality of the self.
Vajrasattva and Vairocana and the others are present.
It is stated likewise in the *Sampuṭodbhava Tantra*: "Buddhahood is considered to exist elsewhere than in the body, obscured by ignorance;
yet the great wisdom of one's own body is entirely free from conceptual construction."
According to the process of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), only the names are distinct, whereas the reality (*tattva*) is one and the same.
In this context, Vairocana alone is said to be the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Here, the essential meaning of "form" (*rūpa*) exists as luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
And whatever other support there is for the aggregates,
this is the support for both body and mind.
It is also stated in the *Vasantatilaka* that [the support] is complete [as the elements, bases, aggregates, and so forth].
That is to say, the entire world of the moving and the non-moving is the form of the deity Ātman.
Just as Vairocana exists as Rūpa-Buddha, so too does Vedanā exist as Vajrasūrya.

The *saṃskāra* is Padyanarteśvara. This very point is also stated in the *Vajraḍākārṇava-tantra*: "In the *Māyājāla*, the procedure for the three yogas is taught: 'Yoga is to be known as threefold—*adhiṣṭhāna*, *parikalpita*, and *niṣpanna*.
This yoga of the mental image (*cittabimba*) has been described by the Buddhas.'"
The conjunction with the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) consisting merely of the substratum is called the "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*);
however, the purification of the *bodhicitta* is the great arising of the seed-mantra (*mantrabīja*).
But the form perfected through the sequence, which is fashioned by the assembly of mudrās, is called "imagined" (kalpita);
thus the yoga is said to be "imagined."
Endowed with the excellence of all aspects, he radiates and performs the act of withdrawal;
the yoga that is instantly perfected through gnosis is called "perfected."
Thus,

regarding the triad of yogas described here— namely, *adhiṣṭhānayoga*, *parikalpitayoga*, and *niṣpannakrama* and so forth— the master Koṅṭula Mahodaya established the sequence as *adhiṣṭhāna*, *pariniṣpanna*, and so on.

By this, while clarifying the two procedures—the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*)—within these three yogas, it is stated: 1. The generation stage (*utpattikrama*), which is the arising of the deity possessing faces and arms produced from the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) and the weapons etc. through the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*), is called "deity yoga" (*devayoga*).

The completion stage with signs (*sanimittaniṣpannakrama*) consists of the withdrawal (*saṃharaṇa*) and so forth of the seed-syllable situated in the heart-lotus by means of the radiance and shimmering of the *tilaka*.

2. Having established the mantra within the great bliss of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mahāsukha*), the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) consists of the meditation upon the deity’s maṇḍala in that form instantaneously.

The completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) consists of abandoning the instantaneous meditation on the form of the deity—once the wind and mantra have become non-dual in nature—and remaining in a state where no examination of mental isolation (*cittaviveka*) and so forth is performed.

3. The yoga of the perfected stage (*pariniṣpannakrama*) exists as abiding in the luminosity of great bliss (*prabhāsvara-mahāsukha*) by either [visualizing] the great bodies of the yoked union (*yuganaddha*) with faces and arms, or by abandoning the faces, arms, and so forth.
In this context, the five stages (*pañcakrama*) of the method of cultivation belonging to the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) are also integrated within these three yogas.
In the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*, a triad of yogas known as *saṃsthāna*, *mantra*, and *dharma* is described.
The procedure that follows the accomplishment of Vajrasattva and continues up until the *maṇḍalarājāgrya* is called *saṃsthānayoga*.

The Karmarājāgramandala, the Mantrayoga, and the Dharmayoga are called the Niṣpannakramayoga. That is to say, the Sūkṣmatilakayoga is the Dharmayoga; this is also to be conjoined with the fully perfected Niṣpannakrama.
Namely: 1. The yoga of form (*saṃsthānayoga*), which is the instantaneous cultivation of the deity; that is to say, it is the isolation of body (*kāyaviveka*). 2.
The yoga of mantra (*mantrayoga*), which is the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*); that is to say, it is the isolation of speech (*vāgviveka*). 3.
The yoga of phenomena (*dharmayoga*), which is the method of cultivating the union of the illusory body and clear light through entering, abiding in, and arising from the clear light.

In certain tantras such as the *Vajramālā*, the method for cultivating the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is explained through the three meditations: the meditation of the initial yoga (*ādiyoga-dhyāna*), the meditation of the supreme king of the mandala (*maṇḍalarājāgradhyāna*), and the meditation of the supreme king of activities (*karmarājāgradhyāna*).

Clarifying this, the master Seratogapa Mahodaya stated that the meditation beginning from the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) up until one’s own manifestation as the form body of the unified state (*yuganaddha-rūpakāya*) within the mandala circle constitutes the meditation of the initial yoga.

Having emanated the mandala through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the *bodhicitta*, and having performed the placement of the mantra-deities therein, the visualization that brings about the arising of the deities is called the "supreme meditation of the King of Mandalas" (*maṇḍalarājāgradhyāna*).
The performance of activities corresponding to the deeds of one’s chosen deity (the Tathāgatas) is called the "supreme meditation of the King of Activities" (*karmarājāgradhyāna*).
In the Abhidhānottara Tantra, the fourfold yoga is described:
the sequence of the methods of Yoga, Mahāyoga, Jñānayoga, and Vidhiyoga;
and the subtle yoga is seen as the one who knows the application of the method of Binduyoga.
In the *Kālacakra* as well, the method for meditating on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is described by means of four yogas.

As it is said: the "supreme king of the mandala" is the yoga of service (*sevāyoga*); the "supreme king of activities" is the yoga of near-service (*upasevāyoga*); the perfection of the "tilaka" is the tilaka-yoga; and likewise, the perfection of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is the subtle yoga (*sūkṣmayoga*).

Thus, although many different varieties of sequential procedures and names for the stages are seen within the Mother Tantras, Father Tantras, and Non-dual Tantras, there is no appearance of mutual contradiction among them; the generation stage of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttara-tantra*) can be meditated upon by means of any procedure whatsoever. Buston states that a practitioner who wishes to meditate on the generation stage of the Unsurpassed Tantra in brief should do so by means of the four yogas taught in the *Hevajra*, and whoever...

If a practitioner wishes to perform the meditation extensively according to the method of intermediate extent, he can do so either by means of the four services (*sevā*) and so forth, which consist of the *prakṛti* (nature) as presented in the *Guhyasamāja*, or else by means of the fourfold yoga beginning with the *maṇḍalarājāgra* as presented in the *Kālacakra*. In that very context, it is also stated there that in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) there are two modes: one is the performance of the meditation on the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), while the other is the meditation on the generation stage together with the celestial palace (*vimāna*), the mandala, the mantras, the goddesses, the deities, the attendants, and so forth.

Furthermore, because the capacity for the gradual stages of meditation (*utpannakrama*) is indispensable, and given the environment of practitioners, it is essential to have properly practiced the two common paths beforehand. Specifically,

one who has received the initiation (*abhiṣeka*) for whichever chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) is to be practiced, and who correctly observes its respective commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*), alone possesses the qualification for performing the meditation of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

In the absence of entry into the maṇḍala, if one has fallen from the commitments (samaya) and does not know the secret procedures of the practice, whatever the practice may be, its accomplishment is simply impossible. Regarding the location: a beginner should first go to an auspicious place and perform the practice where no kind of worldly distraction would either corrupt or hinder the practice.
Practice performed in places presided over by great gurus and at sacred sites (*tīrtha*) becomes particularly fruitful.
It is also stated in the *Guhyasamāja-mūlatantra*: "In great wilderness regions, in vast solitary places, and in mountain caves and groves, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is always attained."

It is also stated in the *Abhidhānottaratantra*: "By performing the practice (*sādhana*) in mountain caves, on mountain peaks, on the banks of great rivers, on the shores of the ocean, at a solitary tree, in a pure place, in a cremation ground, in a temple of Śiva, in a temple of the gods, at a stūpa, or at a crossroads, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is swiftly obtained.
It is also stated in the *Hevajra*: "The location for the time of initial practice should indeed be chosen as auspicious."
Established in that place, with a one-pointed and concentrated mind, the mantra is accomplished.
In his own home at night, he thought to himself, "I have attained perfection."

If beginners do not find any pleasing location anywhere, then they should perform the practice even in a secluded corner of the house while all their attendants are asleep. 2. Regarding the method of meditating on the special generation stage (*utpattikrama*) in the Father Tantra, this can be divided into three parts: (ka) the preliminary practices for the generation stage, and (kha) [the main practice].
The method of practice for the fundamental generation stage (ga),
and the intermediate yoga;
furthermore, there are three divisions of the first.
1. The offering of bali for the purpose of pacifying obstacles; 2. The accumulation of the two merits for the purpose of accomplishing the task;
and 3. The method of meditating on the protection wheel for the purpose of guarding against anticipated obstacles.

1. To ensure that no obstacle (*vighna*) shall arise during the practice (*sādhanā*), the ritual of the offering (*bali*) must be performed. It is stated in the *Hevajra*: when Nairātmyā asked for the purpose of protecting sentient beings from obstacles and for the sake of the ritual procedure, the Blessed One said: "In that regard, Nairātmyā asks for the great offering (*mahābali*) for the benefit of sentient beings."
Seated thus within the syllable E-Vaṃ, Vajrasattva should offer the bali.
For the protection of the life-force of sentient beings, even from obstacles and hindering spirits.

In that very same [text], it says further: "If yogins perform worship with this offering for the sake of auspiciousness toward all beings—for the sake of proficiency in subjugation (*vaśya*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), killing (*māraṇa*), and so forth—the worship of offerings is described as existing. 2. For the accomplishment of any task whatsoever, a person must be meritorious.
Only for the fortunate do all undertakings succeed;
in the absence of fortune, the accomplishment of any task is impossible.
This too is true: that the cause of fortune lies within one’s own hand.
That is emanated.

Among Buddhists, the accomplishment of what has been undertaken arises from the accumulation of the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) and the accumulation of the equipment of knowledge (*jñānasaṃbhāra*).
Revealing the equipment of merit, the Blessed One stated in the *Hevajra*: "One should first cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and likewise compassion (*karuṇā*) in the second."
In the third [stage], one should cultivate joy and, finally, equanimity toward all.
The four Brahma-vihāras, the seven-limbed unsurpassed worship beginning with prostration, and so forth, constitute the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*).

To clarify the accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*), Dagpo Trashi Namgyal Mahodaya stated that by reciting "Oṃ! All phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature," one should cultivate the realization of the non-duality of subject and object.
Oṃ, he is the essence of the three bodies (trikāya).
The intended meaning of "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) is the primordial purity and emptiness of all phenomena, including the grasped and the grasper; or rather, emptiness exists.

The knowledge of object and subject is non-dual and indivisible, being of the nature of the primordial essence, which from beginningless time has been free from all conceptual elaborations and is unarisen.
While maintaining such mindfulness, one should cultivate the meditation on non-duality.
Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna also stated: "By reciting the mantra beginning with *oṃ svabhāva* three times and realizing its meaning, one attains the capacity to awaken to emptiness;

the repeated mindfulness of emptiness therein leads to its stabilization, as well as the accumulation of the equipment of wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*), including the mandala of the deities—the support and the supported—all of which are the manifested forms of emptiness."
Such a firm meditation should be performed.

3. Regarding the meditation on the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*): in the general meditation on the protection wheel, the practitioner performs this kind of visualization such that the place where he performs the practice becomes a ground fashioned by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*).
He meditates in this manner.
It is stated in the *Hevajra*: "Having visualized the sun with the syllable REPHA, upon that sun one should visualize a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from HŪṂ.
With that very vajra, one should visualize the letter PA and the fivefold binding."

One should perform the meditation on the wheel endowed with ten spokes within the special protection wheel (*viśeṣarakṣācakra*). Likewise, having performed the meditation on Hayagrīva, Yamāntaka, and the ten wrathful deities beginning with Canda in each spoke and in the center, the command for the destruction of obstacles must be given. Because of this particular quality, people call this extraordinary protection wheel the "Command Wheel" (*ājñācakra*).

The fundamental generation stage (*maulotpattikrama*) is divided into three parts: the procedure for the generation stage, its purification, and the distinction between recitation (*japa*) and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

In the first part, the following are enumerated: the procedure for generating the celestial palace (*vimāna*) as the support, the procedure for generating the deity who resides therein, and the perfected procedure (*sampannavidhi*) of the generation stage.
Regarding the procedure for generating the celestial palace as the support, the intention behind the palace is that it is a place where infinite and incalculable bodhisattvas may dwell.

There are three purposes for the cultivation of the stages of generating the celestial palace (*vimāna*) as the support: in the stage of the basis (*ādhārāvasthā*), the capacity to enjoy all worldly things;

in the stage of the path (*mārgāvasthā*), the attainment of the power of the ripening of merit by creating a celestial palace as the illusory support for the body; and in the stage of the fruit (*phalāvasthā*), the establishment of a staircase for the accomplishment of the mandala of the light of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).
Immediately after attaining enlightenment oneself, one should perform the consecration of the place of enjoyment.

Having first uttered "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness," one should effect the transformation of the entire world into emptiness within the state of the celestial palace (vimāna) as the basis.
The meaning of this mantra is stated in the treatises as follows:
That which is produced by these syllables—A, Oṃ, Āḥ, and Ma—is the awakener of body, speech, and mind.
It exists as emptiness (śūnyatā), devoid of the intrinsic nature, causes, conditions, and so forth of all phenomena;
that is to say, it is devoid of the intrinsic nature, cause, and condition of all phenomena.
The cause is empty; it exists as unproduced by conditions.
Within the emptiness characterized by the emptiness of knowledge, signlessness, and wishlessness, there is the awakening of the entire mind.
The Vajra is the undifferentiated form of both the object, which is empty, and the subject-knowledge.

That which exists as the destruction of objects, devoid of beginning and end, has a nature free from adventitious impurities and is of a perfectly pure essence; it exists as the "I," pure by its very nature.
This realization does not consist in a mental form or in mere conceptualization, but rather one abides in the nature of internal bliss and consciousness.
And there exists that one supreme state of ultimate peace;

as it is said in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind, then, due to the absence of any other alternative, the mind, being without support, becomes tranquil."

By this, the following also becomes clear: having been fallen into the wheel of existence since beginningless time, we have practiced through the dogmatic attachment of "I" and "mine" without knowing the true state of things;

therefore, the knowledge of emptiness—the luminosity whose nature is vajra-wisdom—will not arise for us. Thus, if one becomes a practitioner while remaining attached to the grasping of a self, [the Master] previously stated in the *Mādhyamakakārikā*:

Through various logical arguments that have been assembled, one must certainly practice the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and selflessness (*nairātmya*), which means "I am not" and "mine does not exist.
For this meditation on "I am not" and "mine does not exist" is the direct antidote to the notions of "I" and "mine.
Therefore, practitioners must first make the meditation that "nothing exists" an absolute necessity.
When this awakening has arisen, even that external momentum of conceptual thought or of the mind must be abandoned.
For instance, through the practice of "nothing exists," even that [notion] is later relinquished.

When we effect the dissolution of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then its own nature will not be perceived; it will become devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and without objective support (*nirālambana*). In that case, even the awakening of that which is without objective support—

In the absence of an object, negation perishes. As it is said in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "When no entity is found which could be conceptualized as 'non-existent,' then how can a non-entity, being without a basis, remain before the mind?"
At that time, there will arise a knowledge that is supremely peaceful, free from dualities, and liberated from the four extremes.

When this state has been correctly understood, the practitioner, through the meditation on the deities who have gathered as the support within this tantra, shall become an authority for the attainment of the union (*yuganaddha*); otherwise, the entire process of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) will be merely conceptual.
This is precisely the reason why the practitioner seals the nature within the tantra and becomes endowed with luminosity and clear awareness (*samprajanya*).
When the body is sealed by the mind, the body arises as the form of the mind.
As it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "To him whose single embodiment is both knowledge and the object of knowledge."
The mind is also sealed by means of the body;
having sealed the cause with the fruit, the practitioner is raised up in the saṃbhogakāya.
The fruit, moreover, is sealed by the cause.

As it is stated in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordial Buddha, without lineage. Likewise, in the Tantric scriptures, where the attainment of initiation by Akṣobhya and others is described as being raised up by Hevajra and other deities themselves, that is called the sealing (*mudraṇa*) of nature by nature.
The entire threefold world-realm is the expansion of the mind of clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
Therefore, whatever forms of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and so forth exist, all of that is nothing other than the mind; there is nothing else whatsoever.
For this very reason, it is said that "form is Vairocana," and the earth element and so forth are the forms of the goddesses Locanā and the others.

Having designated envy, avarice, and so forth as being of the nature of the Vajra of Envy (*īrṣyāvajrin*), it is stated that [this is] for the purpose of sealing the intrinsic nature by means of the intrinsic nature itself.

The protection-wheel, the celestial palace, the maṇḍala, and so forth, which take the form of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*); the universal wheel (*viśvacakra*) and the vajra, which take the form of the surrounding perimeter—all these arise within the mind.
By this it is established that all of this exists for the sake of the knowledge of the mind.

In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no such thing as the agent, the object, or the means of accomplishment, nor the collection of factors such as the worshiper, the worshiped, or the act of worship;

rather, it is the demonstration of oneness throughout all of these. Likewise, regarding the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), this is what is said: "As many parts of a tree as exist outside the earth, so many parts are internal;

within the inert nature of the tree situated in the womb of the earth, there is no external existence whatsoever. In the same way, whatever colors, forms, shapes, and so forth exist externally, all of that belongs only to a mind that is like an insentient object.
There is an extensive treatment [of this].

Generally, in all the texts of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*Anuttara-tantra*), the meditation on the celestial mansion (*vimāna-bhāvanā*) of the generation stage (*utpatti-krama*) is performed by means of two methods: through the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) and through the dissolution of the elements (*bhūta-ucchedana*).

Either the meditation on the celestial mansion is performed within the *dharmodaya* upon a universal lotus and a universal vajra after the elements have been dissolved, or else, the elements are sequentially placed upon Mount Sumeru, and above that, upon a universal lotus and vajra.
In the midst of that, the visualization of the celestial mansion (*vimāna*) is performed. There is no rule for producing the identity of the celestial mansion and the deity.

The production of the celestial mansion is performed by means of seed-syllables such as *bhrūṃ* and through the visualization of the vajra, according to the procedure for the emanation of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].

In the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantrīya-ratnāvalī-ṭīkā*, the procedure for the meditation on the celestial palace (*vimānamaṇḍala*) is as follows: Having recited the mantra, "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the diamond of the wisdom of emptiness," and having made the mind equal to space, one should visualize the sun in front by means of the syllable *raṃ*. Upon that sun, one should visualize a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) arising from the syllable *hūṃ*.
With that very vajra, one should visualize the enclosure of the fivefold rampart.

Upon that ground-base, in the space situated above the universal vajra (viśvavajra), there arises from the black syllable *yaṃ* a black wind-maṇḍala in the shape of a bow, with two fluttering banners at its two ends. Above that, from the red syllable *raṃ*, there arises a red triangular fire-maṇḍala marked with the syllable *raṃ* at its corners. Above that, from the white syllable *vaṃ*, there arises a white water-maṇḍala marked with a bell, facing downwards. Above that, from the yellow syllable *laṃ*, there arises a yellow square earth-maṇḍala marked with three-pronged vajras at its corners.

Having visualized [the seed-syllables], through the instantaneous transformation of the wind-maṇḍala and all else, one meditates upon a two-storied peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) atop a multi-petalled lotus, with moon and sun seats situated as appropriate; it is square, adorned with eight pillars, decorated with four gate-arches (*toraṇa*), and complete with all characteristics, including necklaces, half-necklaces, bells, banners, and so forth. This very same [description] is found in the *Ādibuddha* and the *Abhidhānottara Tantra*.

It is also stated in the *Guhyasamājottaratantra*: "One who is skilled in constant meditative concentration should visualize a wheel-mandala with an extent of one hundred yojanas, and should establish the [deities of the] families therein."
The wise one should visualize a lotus, a vajra, a sword, and an utpala flower,
each extending for ten million yojanas, square in shape, and most beautiful.

In the *Hevajratantra*, it is stated regarding the purpose of drawing the cremation grounds (śmaśāna) all around the celestial mansion (*vimāna*): "By means of the eight cremation grounds, and likewise by means of the charcoal from the cremation grounds..."

In the *Saṃvarodayatantra* as well, the meditation on the eight cremation grounds outside the celestial mansion maṇḍala is taught: "Within the diamond cage (vajrapañjara), it is adorned with the eight cremation grounds: Caṇḍogra, Gahvara, and likewise Vajrajvālākara... [and so forth].
Aṭṭāṭṭahāsa is in the northeast, Lakṣmīvana-hutāśana in the southwest,
Ghorāndhakāra in the northwest, and Kilikilārava in the southeast.

In the *Hevajrasādhanavajrapradīpa-ṭippaṇī* by Saroruha-vajra, the locations of the eight cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*) are marked as follows: 1. In the east is the great cremation ground named Caṇḍogra. There, upon a śirīṣa tree, is Gajamukha, who possesses great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) and is white in color.
Indra is the guardian of that direction; he is tawny, has a thousand eyes, and sits upon the white elephant Airāvata.

The nāga king Vāsuki is yellow; the thundering cloud is multicolored; Mount Sumeru consists of precious gems; and the white caitya is named White Thunderbolt (Sita-vajra). 2. To the south is the great cremation ground named Karankabhīṣaṇa. At the aśvattha tree is the buffalo-faced [deity] of great supernatural power, who is black.
Yama, the guardian of the direction, is mounted upon a buffalo and is black. The nāga Padya is white.
The cloud Avittaka is multicolored;
Mount Malaya is white;
and the shrine named Piśunavajra is black.
3. In the west is the great cremation ground named Jvālākula.
At the Aśoka tree is the white, highly powerful Makarānana.
Varuṇa, the lord of the quarter, is white; Karkoṭaka, the nāga, is red.
The cloud is formidable and multicolored;
Mount Kailāsa is white;
and the shrine named Saṃjñāvajra is white.
4. To the north is the great cremation ground named Gahvara.
At the Aśvattha tree dwells a being with a human face, possessing great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), who is fair-complexioned.
Kubera is the guardian of that direction.
Gaura is one who rides on a man;
Takṣaka is a black serpent;
a cloud is whirling.
Mandara Mountain is multicolored;
the shrine named Cittavajra is dark blue and fair-complexioned.
In the northeast is the great cremation ground named Lakṣmīvana; there, at a banyan tree, is Gomukha, who possesses great supernatural power and is white.
Maheśvara is the guardian of the direction, white in color, and has a bull as his vehicle;
Śaṅkhapāla is the nāga, yellow in color;
Caṇḍa is the cloud, possessing all colors.
Mount Māhendra is black;
the shrine named Cittavajra is white;
and in the southeast is the great cremation ground named Aṭṭāṭṭahāsa.
On the Karañja tree is Chāgānana, possessed of great supernatural power;
he is the guardian of the direction of the red fire (southeast),
red in color, and seated upon a goat.
The nāga Mahāpadma is dark green;
the cloud Ghana is of all colors;
Mount Gandhamādana is yellow; and the red caitya named Kāyavajra is [yellow].
In the southwest is the great cremation ground named Ghorāndhakāra.
At the *latāparkaṭī* tree dwells the black, highly powerful Śavamukha;
the Rakṣasa is the guardian of the direction, seated upon a corpse, and is black in color.
The nāga is Ananta, white in color. The cloud is Pūraṇa, possessing all colors. The mountain is Hemaparvata, white. The sacred tree is named Ratnavajra.
In the northwest is the great cremation ground named Kili-kila-rava;
there dwells the one of great supernatural power named Gajānana, who is dark-complexioned and resides in a Pārthiva tree.
The guardian of the northwest quarter is Mārūta, who is dark-complexioned and mounted upon a deer.
The Kulika nāga is Kurbura;
Varṣaṇamegha is Viśvavarṇa;
Śrīparvata is Nīla.
The shrine named Dharmavajra is dark green.
In these cremation grounds, practitioners must perform the fourfold conduct of the vetāla, such as wandering through the cemetery, lying down, and remaining stationary.
Therefore, there is a purpose for drawing the cremation grounds all around the mandala.
The procedure for the generation of the deity who is the supported (*āśrita-deva*). Regarding the generation of the deity, there are two primary methods:
generation by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*) and generation by means of the exhortation through the four songs (*caturgīti-saṃcodana*).

The meditative cultivation procedure for the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) by means of the five awakenings is according to the chapter on the *Nairātmyāsādhana* in the *Sampuṭatantra*, and according to the seventeenth chapter of the *Ṭīkāratnāvalī* on the *Kṛṣṇayamāritantra*.
This has already been largely stated.
Here, by describing its essential nature, the procedure of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) will be clarified.
It is said in the *Sampuṭatantra*: "The vowels reside in the form of the moon, and the consonants in the form of the sun" (3.3).

In accordance with this, first of all, it is essential for the practitioner to abide in the bodhicitta of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bodhicitta*). Immediately thereafter, having performed the meditation on the sixteen vowels—the meaning of the *āli*—they should be transformed into a moon; here, the moon symbolizes semen (*śukra*). In the *Sampuṭa-tantra* and the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, the vowels are doubled: one is rotated clockwise from the right and the second is rotated counter-clockwise (to the left).
While performing that, one should practice its cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The intention behind doubling the number [of recitations] for the practice of cultivation is that this serves as an indicator of thirty-two [deities]. It is stated in the *Hevajra*: "The Blessed One takes the form of semen; its bliss is known as the Kāminī."
Here, through the division of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), there are sixteen vowels, which become thirty-two.
The *Āli* (vowel series), however, resides in its entirety within the body in the form of the sixteen vowels among the seminal fluids (*śukra*) and so forth.

During the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), expanding upward from the left side of the body, it gradually reaches the form ‘a’ in the big toe, the form ‘ā’ in the shank, the form ‘i’ in the chest, and the form ‘ī’ in the womb.
She resides in the form of the letter *u* at the navel and in the form of the letter *ū* and so forth at the heart.

It is stated in the *Saṃvarodayatantra*: "In the same manner, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight until the new moon, there occurs a transition; on the left side is the Moon, which is *Āli* and subtle by nature."

In the *Hevajra* as well, it is stated that the thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and eighty minor signs (*vyañjana*) of the Tathāgata exist within the body in the form of semen and blood, as it has been said: "The Teacher possesses the thirty-two marks; the Lord possesses the eighty signs.
He is established in the female organ within Sukhāvatī under the name of semen."

It is stated in the *Āmnāyamañjarī* that the sixteen limbs, which have been described above, are occupied by semen (*śukra*) and bliss (*sukha*). Within those two locations, the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the vowels is performed as doubled, being divided according to the distinction between the white and black fortnights.

Above the lunar orb, the Sun is visualized in the form of Kālī; having combined the six consonants *ḍa, dha, ya, ra, la, va* in the form of the secondary ornaments (*upavyañjana*), the meditative cultivation of the forty consonants is performed in their blood-red color.
Regarding the six syllables that are combined within the thirty-four syllables, a difference of opinion is observed.
In the *Ratnāvalī*, a commentary on the *Kṛṣṇayamāri-tantra*, "ta da dha va ya la" are assembled.
Having doubled the consonants, the intention behind creating eighty is indeed the clarification of the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*).
Furthermore, those [seeds] which reside within the body in the form of blood—
thereafter, one should perform the visualization of the weapon amidst the seed-syllables between the moon and the sun.
In the *Hevajra-sādhanopāyikā*, Śāntipāda states that one should perform the visualization of the two types of weapons for the father and mother.

Generally, in all the ritual means (*sādhana*), after imitating the methods of the radiation and withdrawal of rays through the visualization of a single weapon, one should perform the visualization of either the Weapon-Vajrasattva or whichever [deity] is appropriate; therein,
one should meditate upon that which has been transformed.

Because one performs the cultivation by means of the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*), the cultivation of everything from the mandalas of emptiness, moon, and sun to the ritual weapons and so forth is called the "cultivation of Vajrasattva.
When there is the state of perfection within the Vajrasattva of the fifth awakening, it is called the "resultant Vajrasattva" (*phalavajrasattva*).

If one should perform the cultivation of Vajrasattva through the exhortation of the four songs, for the sake of the perfection of Vajrasattva via the five awakenings, [one meditates on] the parents within the Vajrasattva.

Likewise, having entered into those three seed-syllables— Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ— which resemble the intermediate state being within the *yuganaddha* body of that Vajrasattva, the very Vajrasattva who arises from them is called the "Causal Vajrasattva.

When the Causal Vajrasattva has been perfected through the five awakenings (*pañcābhisambodhi*), the goddesses beginning with Carcikā urge him to arise for the sake of the welfare of living beings by means of song.

Indeed, the intention behind the name of the goddess Carcikā was established by the Buddhas in the past, at the time of their accumulation of merit; impelled by the power of the four divine abodes—loving-kindness and the rest—and the cultivation of selflessness, they brought forth a deity endowed with passion for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
By means of song, one should rouse and manifest the deity through the method of purifying the womb-born, which is performed by means of the meditation on the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

If one were to combine the procedure for the arrival of the Causal Vajrasattva within the Resultant Vajrasattva with the purification [of the continuum], then virtuous karma must indeed be performed for the sake of taking birth in the human realm. For the sake of perfecting that virtuous karma, there exists the path of preliminary action—consisting of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*), the worship of the assembly (*gaṇapūjā*), and so forth—as well as the path of accumulation (*saṃbhāramārga*).
The meditation on emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) is like death itself.

That which is equivalent to the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) is the state of mind facing toward rebirth for the sake of a new birth; it is the "ultimate dharma" (*agradharma*) at the final stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
This very act of linking [to a new existence] is the entry into the womb, the first [moment of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)].

It exists as equal to the stage of the Joyous (pramuditā-bhūmi). The attainment of growth through the ninefold seat of rawness (āmāsana) is equivalent to following the yoga of the ninefold cultivation.
Its state of having arisen is the means for attaining perfect enlightenment (sambodhi).
This ritual act is similar to the production of a lineage through the attainment of a son;
this very thing is the nature of the resultant Vajrasattva. All of this constitutes the external conduct of the resultant Vajrasattva.
The abiding of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), such as loving-kindness and compassion, as well as the protection wheels and so forth, exists as one’s own previously undertaken karma.
The songs of the four goddesses and others are the analogies, while the four divine abodes constitute the nature of the object of comparison.
Through this practice, the expansion of the four elements, the *tilaka*, or the *bodhicitta* is performed within the internal practices.
Vajrasattva is considered the being (*sattva*) of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), who is the cause of the union (*yuganaddha*).

These seed-syllables—*oṃ*, *āḥ*, and *hūṃ*—enter into the form of the bodhicitta at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) or the secret place; having entered therein, they generate compassion and passion within that body of union. Likewise, from them [arises] the principal deity (the fruit).

The arising of Vajrasattva occurs. Furthermore, this process of dissolution and cultivation constitutes the actual state of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*); that is to say, it consists of the correct realization and practice of the method for beings to arise. Indeed, it exists for the purpose of understanding the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of both the causal Vajrasattva and the resultant Vajrasattva.

The process of repeated dissolution and likewise arising, as well as the realization of the momentary destruction of origination and the realization of suchness (*tathatā*), are understood as the objective focus of this procedure. It is also stated in the *Samvarodayatantra*: "Birth is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*); having known birth as the generation stage, one shall attain perfect Buddhahood. Just so: "Having known birth as the generation stage, one shall attain perfect Buddhahood."
This thorough knowledge of the aggregates has been taught by the Speaker of Reality.

The realization of the path for the practitioner according to the generation stage (utpattikrama) was categorized by the venerable Ācārya Koṅtul into four types of practitioners, following the meditations of the generation stage:
1. the beginner (ādikarmika), 2. one with slight entry into knowledge (svalpajñānāveśa).
3. Limited engagement with knowledge; 4. Perfect engagement with knowledge.

1. A beginner practitioner, at the outset during the time of practice, is unable to perform the visualization of the complete gross deities in a single moment through the four means of accomplishment, such as service (*sevā*).

Therefore, gradually visualizing the divine mandala as the form of the Buddha, [one should understand] that "Vajrasattva" and "the Wielder of the Vajra" refer to the principal deity in the form of one's chosen divinity, as prompted by the four songs; thus he says, "Carcikā and the others," and so forth.
One should understand that those very deities previously visualized as Nairātmyā and the rest are intended here.
He speaks [the following] to explain the purpose of the song:

"Just as... and so forth. This is the meaning: immediately after [the mind] has melted through a mind of compassionate passion (*karuṇārāga*), there is an exhortation; following that, one should understand that the bodhicitta, having transferred to the *tāraka* [syllable], enters. Such a practitioner is called a beginner (*ādikarmika*).

2. *Svalpajñānāveśa* (Limited Knowledge-Entry): Although this practitioner is capable of performing the visualization (*bhāvanā*) of the gross divine mandalas, he is called one who possesses limited knowledge-entry because he is unable to do so for the deities of the abodes (*āyatanika-devas*) in a single moment. 3. *Jñāne svalpādhikāralābhi-sādhaka* (Practitioner Attaining Limited Authority in Knowledge): This practitioner attains the fitness to perform the visualization of the deities of the abodes in a single moment.
In this context, there occurs the meditation on the generation stage alone for as long as it takes.
Immediately thereafter, the practitioner must perform meditation by joining the two stages—the generation stage and the completion stage.
At that time, the practitioner gains the capacity for the emanation and reabsorption of mandalas within the subtle drops.

In this regard, although through the practitioner's effort the unity of the beginning, middle, and end of the watch (yāma) is attained, nevertheless the practitioner remains incapable of entering into the infinite accumulation of karma— into karmas that exist in countless forms— and of attaining the necessary capacity. It is precisely here that the practitioner is considered to have acquired only a slight degree of authority in knowledge.

4. The achiever of the perfect attainment of authority regarding gnosis: in each and every moment of this [state], there occurs a clear manifestation of infinite meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). By mere recollection, one is able to bring about the welfare of infinite sentient beings. This constitutes the final and most excellent stage of the generation process (*utpattikrama*).
In this state, the practitioner also proceeds upon the path of "heat" (*uṣmamārga*) of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).

The fourfold classification of practitioners was also stated by the venerable Ānandamati: that practitioners should perform meditation according to the procedure of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) as it pertains to their respective means of accomplishment (*sādhanopāya*).
According to their view, a beginner (*ādikarmika*) is a practitioner who is unable to perform the meditation of all the maṇḍalas in a single moment.

Thus, in that celestial mansion (*vimāna*), although the practitioner is incapable of performing the visualization of the gross deities (*sthūladeva*) who have been installed there, he is capable of performing the clear visualization of the heart-mantras and so forth of the subtle deities of the abodes (*āyatanadeva*). Consequently, a difference arises in the method of visualization between the first and second types of practitioners: the first performs the visualization of the entire mandala sequentially, whereas the second performs meditation on the gross deity in a single moment and performs the sequential visualization of the subtle deities of the abodes.
And he performs it.
The third practitioner meditates upon not only the gross deities, but also the subtle deities, in a single moment.
For the practitioner who has reached the third stage, the non-dual state of the generation and completion stages arises.

Immediately thereafter, even the meditation of the practitioner during the intervals between the watches of the night becomes indivisible. In this state, the practitioner must perform the recitation of the complete generation stage (*abhisamaya*) once in a single day.
But not so with *pratibhāna* (inspired intuition).
Even for a practitioner who has attained this state, the final stage of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) is not yet reached.
Only when the fourth stage is attained does the practitioner reach perfection in the generation stage and become proficient in the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) as well.
It is also stated in the *Saṃvarodayatantra*: "A yogi of dull or middling capacity should meditate on the generation [stage] through the cultivation of the maṇḍala;
one of superior capacity [should realize] the maṇḍala instantaneously as mere mind."
The meditation on the stage of completion is performed through the yoga of the instantaneous mode.

That is to say, one performs the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the mandalas of the deities with dull, medium, and sharp faculties respectively; likewise, even during the cultivation of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), one effects the visualization of the deity’s body instantaneously.

While commenting on this verse, the venerable master Sera Chökyi Gocha stated that this represents the progressive stages of development for a single practitioner within the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

In the first stage, the practitioner gradually performs the visualization of the gross mandala of deities; this is the mild [level]. In the second stage—that is, when some practice has been developed—he simultaneously visualizes the gross mandala of deities in a single moment and gradually visualizes the subtle mandala of deities;
this is the middling [level].

In the third stage, one performs the meditation on the entire mandala of deities, both gross and subtle, in a single instant; likewise, the practitioner of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) also accomplishes the visualization of the deity with instantaneous ease. Regarding a general introduction to the completion stage: the basis of the completion stage is *bodhicitta* (the mind of awakening), which—in the tantric scriptures—is used as a synonym for one's own innate mind (*nijacitta*), the subtle wind-mind (*sūkṣmaprāṇacitta*), and so forth.
There is a great difference between the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and the mind of awakening (*bodhi-citta*).
The thought of awakening is that which abides for the sake of all sentient beings, whereas the mind of awakening is the continuum of awakening.
For this is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) and is adventitious (*āgantuka*).
This alone distinguishes the bodhisattva from the vehicles of the śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha.
Once the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) has arisen, the practitioner becomes a bodhisattva and is called one belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle (bodhisattvayānī).

Clarifying this characteristic of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), Haribhadra stated: "The production of the thought of awakening is the desire for perfect awakening for the sake of others. For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, the very longing for awakening is the mind directed toward awakening.
The desire for the welfare of others and the desire for perfect awakening for that purpose are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*)."
Since the mind (*citta*) apprehends all phenomena through a general state of evenness,
whereas aspiration is directed toward a specific phenomenon as its object,
it is possible for there to be a mental factor (*caitasika*) called the "mind of awakening" (*bodhicitta*), but not a [separate] "mind" (*citta*).

Therefore, the desire for both can be described by the term "mental perception" (*cittasaṃjñā*), because as long as there is intensity in these two types of desire, the practitioner will attain proximity to enlightenment (*bodhi*) and the bodhicitta will blossom. In the treatises, two types of bodhicitta are explained: 1. *saṃvṛti-bodhicitta* (conventional bodhicitta),...
2. And the ultimate bodhicitta.
Regarding conventional bodhicitta, there are two divisions by way of its essential nature.
Thus, it is said in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "That bodhicitta should be understood, in brief, as being of two kinds."
The mind of aspiration for enlightenment, and the mind of setting out for enlightenment itself.

The aspiration for the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of every living being is the *praṇidhānacitta* (the mind of aspiration), and the practice of the ten perfections for that purpose is the *prasthānacitta* (the mind of application).
These two distinctions are described there by means of a simile as follows: "Just as the difference between one who desires to go and one who is actually going is perceived..."
Likewise, the distinction between these two should be understood by the wise according to their respective order.

In the Vajrayāna, that which is the stabilization of the *bodhicitta*, therein *bodhi* is the *citta*, yet it is indeed only the *bodhicitta*. That which is rooted in the means (*sādhana*) is the reality itself, and not merely that which is rooted in the goal (*sādhya*).
In the *Guhyasamāja*, the nature of the tantra is described through the distinctions of basis (*āśraya*), path (*mārga*), and fruit (*phala*).
The path is precisely the unshakeable basis; the fruit is precisely the path; and the distinction is merely a difference in state.
That very same [reality] is also the *bodhicitta*.
Regarding the essential nature of *bodhicitta*, it is established in the *Guhyasamāja* that *bodhicitta* exists as the inseparable form of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).

In the system of the Pāramitā-naya, twenty varieties of emptiness are formulated, such as external emptiness, internal emptiness, the emptiness of both the external and internal, and the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
When phenomena have been analyzed through logical arguments, their lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) ultimately remains as their final state.
Furthermore, due to the differentiation of the subjects (dharmin), there are also various distinctions in emptiness (śūnyatā).
Those who know the system of the Pāramitās consider the essential nature of emptiness to be of the character of a simple negation (prasajyapratiṣedha).

Some consider the nature of [emptiness] to be that of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*) and luminosity; furthermore, in the Vajrayāna, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which is the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*), is understood as having the very nature of a relative negation.

This is because, in the texts of the Father Tantras (*pitṛtantra*), the fourfold division of emptiness—namely, emptiness (*śūnya*), extreme emptiness (*atiśūnya*), great emptiness (*mahāśūnya*), and total emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*)—is sequentially established by means of the third [stage], light (*āloka*), and the fourth gnosis called luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Direct realization was considered equal [to the previous stages].

In the knowledge of the first light (*ālokajñāna*), following the direct realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is the exhaustion of forty conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) associated with attachment (*rāga*). When there is the awakening to extreme emptiness (*atiśūnyatā*) through the knowledge of the second appearance of light (*ālokābhāsajñāna*), there is the exhaustion of thirty conceptual constructions. And at the time of awakening to extreme emptiness through the knowledge of the attainment of light (*ālokopalabdhi-jñāna*), there occurs the exhaustion of seven conceptual constructions associated with delusion (*moha*).
Through the knowledge of these three, a subtle duality remains upon the awakening to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Only when the awakening to the emptiness of all things arises by means of the knowledge of the final luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) is the non-dual ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) directly realized.
Furthermore, it is taught in the Mother Tantras that the fourfold emptiness is progressively realized through the four joys (*ānanda*) associated with the four objects.
And this state is divided into four moments, beginning with the moment of maturation (*vipāka*).

By this, it is made perfectly clear that when conceptualizations and extremely subtle forms have dissolved into the luminous mind (*prabhāsvara-citta*), the final state of the luminosity is indeed its non-dual state, which can only exist as a state of absolute negation (*paryudāsa-svarūpa*).
This indeed is the very nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in the Vajrayāna;
moreover, it must certainly be understood that there is no difference between this state of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*) and the Pāramitānaya or the Vajrayāna.
In the nondual tantric treatises, such as the *Kālacakra*, the *Sekoddeśa*, and others, emptiness is described as being endowed with all supreme aspects (*sarvākāravaropetā*).
Since emptiness is form, for it is from within the wind that mirages, smoke, fireflies, lamps, and so forth appear;
and all these arise in the form of the deities of Kālacakra.
Because the emptiness of the objects arises by the power of the self-nature luminosity, it exists as non-different from that luminosity.
Therefore, luminosity (*prabhāsvaratva*) here consists of both the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and the conventional form of the deity’s body as an object.
Within this conventional form, there is non-difference from luminosity by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, it can be said that even the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) is the supreme conventional joy (*saṃvṛtirati*).
Since this has arisen and become manifest through the cultivation of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and so forth—
whatever it may be—
the fruit is nonetheless the very nature of the union (*yuganaddha*) of the illusory body and luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Compassion, luminosity, immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), and so forth are synonyms.
In the Pāramitā system, just as emptiness is merely emptiness, so too is compassion merely compassion.
In the *Buddhakapāla-tantra*, the emptiness of the Pāramitā system is explained as follows: "In the absence of gnosis, emptiness is devoid of continuity; it is like that of a householder."
In reality, however, the non-dual state of emptiness and compassion is required, because compassion and immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) are synonymous.
Only when emptiness is manifested through great bliss or through compassion does it accomplish the welfare of sentient beings.
Compassion itself is indeed the great passion (*mahārāga*).
The very non-differentiation of great passion (*mahārāga*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitutes the form of compassion (*karuṇā*) in the Vajrayāna.
For the sake of awakening to the bodhicitta, which is the non-dual nature of emptiness and compassion, numerous methods have been extolled in both the Pāramitā and Mantra systems.

Among these, in the Unsurpassed Tantras (*anuttaratantra*), the realization of the vital points (*marman*) of the channels (*nāḍī*), winds (*vāyu*), and drops (*tilaka*) as taught therein is the most excellent method of all.
Therefore, this triad (the reality) is here examined.

Regarding the methods of cultivation for the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) within the Father Tantras, Mother Tantras, and Non-dual Tantras—concerning the adamantine body (*vajradeha*)—there are many different opinions and variations; however, the defining characteristic of the means for attaining the inseparable union (*yuganaddha*), in which the conventional, self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), and ultimate clear light (*paramārthaprabhāsvara*) are of one nature, is common to all of them.

In that very context, the attainment of mastery over the vajra-body, the channels (*nāḍī*), the winds (*vāyu*), the drops (*tilaka*), and so forth—which serve as the basis for the practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*)—is also to be respected as being of the same nature.
What, then, is the vajra-body?
The vajra-body is precisely the aggregate of the thirty-six constituents (*skandha*).
This is possible only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and not in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*).
For in the form realm, the elements of space, air, fire, earth, and water exist only in a slight degree.

Therefore, a practitioner of the Unsurpassed Tantra (*anuttaratantra*) must be a being of the desire realm alone, and not of the form or formless realms; because it is only in the desire realm that the thirty-six aggregates (*skandha*) and the six elements (*dhātu*) [are fully present].
That fullness is conceived as being complete.
In the *Saṃvarodayatantra*, regarding the six constituents (*ṣaḍdhātu*), it is stated: "Skin, flesh, and blood are said to be born of the mother;
sinews, marrow, and semen [are born of the father]."
It is said to be "born of the father."
Thus, O Kuśika, the six [verses] are according to the words of Piṇḍavajrasattva.
This body, composed of the six elements—skin, flesh, blood, sinews, marrow, and semen—is purified through the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
This is also called the "impure emanation body" (*samalanirmāṇakāya*).
Just as a cloth is a collection of threads, so too our body is a network of channels (*nāḍī*).
In the *Saṃvarodayatantra*, the arrangement of the seventy-two thousand channels within the body is described.
Among them, there is a cluster of fifty-two channels at the *uṣṇīṣa* (the crown), sixteen at the throat-cakra (*kaṇṭhacakra*), eight in the heart-lotus (*hṛdayakamala*),
and sixty-four principal channels in the navel-lotus (*nābhikamala*).
In the *Saṃvarodayatantra* as well: "Now, therefore, I shall explain the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) in its proper order.
There are seventy-two thousand channels that pervade the body;
the primary channels (*nāḍikā*) and secondary channels (*upanāḍī*) are situated based upon their respective locations."
The one hundred and twenty names are said to be the predominance of the channels (nāḍī).
Furthermore, the twenty-four channels, such as the *uṣṇīṣa* and others, which nourish the nails, teeth, and body, also hold preeminence.
Regarding this, it is stated therein: "The channels, the locations, and the seats are twenty-four in number."
Among them, three channels are all-pervading and serve as the primary supports.
In this context, there are three principal channels (nāḍīs), beginning with Avadhūtī, Lalanā, and Rasanā.
Avadhūtī has synonyms such as Avadhūtī, Madhyamā, Brahmadaṇḍa, Rāhu, and Śaṅkhinī.
Some teachers consider the channel Avadhūtī to be conceptual and exceedingly subtle.

In some places, the *avadhūtī* channel is described as pervading the entire body; in others, it is said to extend from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) down to the backbone, starting from the navel-center four finger-widths below; and in yet other places, it is discussed as being from the tip of the secret organ down to the soles of the feet. Furthermore, the number of channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*) is found to be either four or three in various accounts.
The opinion of the great scholar Raṅ’byuṅ rdo rje is as follows: just as the central channel (*madhyamā*) is the root of gnosis, so too is the *mahāprāṇa* channel the root of phenomenal existence.

It is said: "The channel that carries semen, known as *lalanā*, consists of twenty-four thousand lunar channels; the channel that carries blood, known as *rasanā*, consists of twenty-four thousand solar channels;
and the channel that carries the twenty-four winds is the *madhyamā*."
In the *Hevajra*, the *avadhūtī* is described thus: "The *avadhūtī* is in the central region, devoid of subject and object.

It is the ultimate existence of all phenomena, the very luminosity free from the conceptual proliferation of the four extremes. By dissolving discursive thoughts, one enters the middle; it is merely the attainment of stability. How can the central channel be described?"
In the same way, it is impossible to speak of *lalanā* and *rasanā* as being in a state of duality.
Is there actually a subtle channel (*nāḍī*) situated within our body?

If the channels such as the *madhyamā* and the *cakras* exist merely according to description, then is this simply a matter of mental visualization, performed immediately after one's own body has been transformed into that of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*)?
And that which is to be investigated:

furthermore, in the *Saṃvarodaya Tantra*, *Hevajra Tantra*, *Saṃpuṭodbhava Tantra*, *Kālacakra Tantra*, *Vajravārāhīrahasya Tantra*, *Jñānodaya Tantra*, and others, the essential nature of the channels *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī* is clarified as follows: "The *rasanā* and *lalanā* channels [are on either side of] the *avadhūtī*; the *rasanā* is to the right of the *avadhūtī*."

To the left is the *lalanā*; these two channels originate from the navel, diverging four finger-breadths below it. In the region of the navel, they are connected to the great channel (*mahānāḍī*) at the seat of the heart (*hṛdayāśaya*, i.e., the *gurdā*). From this point onward, the *rasanā* is connected to the right side of the heart and the *lalanā* to the left.
Then, from the great channel of the heart, they descend into the throat-cakra (kaṇṭhacakra) located below the ears;

proceeding from the channel of the occiput (kūkāṭikā), they emerge through the openings at the lower part of the ears and, together with the tree-channel (vṛkṣanāḍī), reach the brain, where they are joined at the Brahma-aperture (brahyarandhra) of the head.
Thus, this pair of channels pervades all the gateways of the sense organs.
Specifically, these two channels from the two nostrils of the nose extend upward to the crest.

At their lower end, they diverge from a crossroads formed by the junction of three channels; the right channel, by means of its downward-pointing tip at the base of the tongue, facilitates the discharge of blood from the female uterus and performs the functions of retaining and expelling waste for both males and females.

Regarding the essential nature of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, it is stated in the *Hevajratantra-pañjikā-ratnāvalī*, the *Sampuṭodayatantra*, the *Saṃvarodayatantra*, and other texts: *lalanā* carries semen (*śukra*), while *rasanā* carries blood (*rakta*).
From the wheel at the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣacakra*) down to the wheel of the secret organ, *lalanā* and *rasanā* remain embraced by the *avadhūtī*.
In the twelfth chapter of the *Vajramālā*, the explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*) of the *Guhyasamāja*, one hundred and eight winds (*vāyu*) are described.

Among them, those known as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, *samāna*, and *vyāna* are called the primary winds; likewise, the winds known as *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya* are said to be their subsidiary limbs.
In the *Kālacakra*, the functions of such winds are described as follows: "The *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, and *udāna* winds reside in the petals of the lotus of the earth."
Vyāna, Nāga, Kūrma, the wind Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
Thus, these ten types of winds, which are the various functions [of the breath], reside within the wheel of channels (nāḍicakra),
from the Śaṅkhinī down to the entire navel-wheel and the lotus of one's own heart, beginning with the syllable *ti*.
The *prāṇa* carries the breath and all food and drink along the paths of the sun and the moon;
the *apāna* leads them downward; and the *samāna* distributes all the essences equally throughout the body.
The udāna wind vibrates the body and performs singing and dancing with the face, hands, and feet;
the vyāna wind likewise causes disease and the breaking of limbs through the influence of the qualities of nature.
In our body, the great prāṇa-vāyu alone is the foundational support for all other vāyus;
without it, life is impossible.
This resides within the heart-lotus.
Every day, one healthy person takes six hundred and two hundred—that is, eight hundred—exhalations and inhalations.

Regarding this, Āryadeva, clearly explaining the different locations and functions of the other winds arising from the *mahāprāṇa*, stated: "The *apāna* wind resides below the navel at the place where the three channels are gathered together."
And this [vāyu] expels the impurities of feces, urine, semen, blood, and the acidic tastes of the bodily constituents (dhātus), while performing the functions of evacuation and collection.
The samāna-vāyu resides in the region of the navel;
just as a gardener waters the roots of trees with water from a well, [so does it distribute the essence].
In the same way, it separates all food into its constituent tastes, such as astringent and the others, and having brought all these tastes to the location of the channels, it nourishes the body.
The udāna-vāyu resides in the throat-cakra.
This [vāyu] also effects the separation of what has been swallowed and drunk; even the activity of digestion occurs by means of this very wind.
The vyāna-vāyu resides in all the limbs and in the joints.
The primary function of this wind, however, is the distribution of energy throughout the body.
A description of its locations and functions is also found in the *Vimalaprabhā*.

In the following verse, a very brief description of these locations is obtained: "The *prāṇa* is in the heart, the *apāna* in the anus, the *samāna* is situated in the navel, and the *udāna* resides in the region of the throat."
Vyāna is that which pervades the entire body.
The winds of the limbs, such as the *nāga* and *kūrma*, are also designated by names such as *cara*, *vicara*, *samyakcara*, *pracarana*, and *nicara*.
They produce the cognitions of the five sense faculties.
Furthermore, in the *Pañcakrama*, it is stated that consciousness has become mixed with the wind in its subtle form.
Having emerged from the paths of the sense-faculties, it does not take objects as its support.
The locations, functions, and other details of these five subsidiary winds are briefly as follows: The *nāga* wind reaches the channel-petal at the base of the right arm and circulates there;
it connects one peak of this channel to the eye, and its function is the perception of form.
The tortoise wind (kūrmavāyu) moves along with the petal of the jayā-nāḍī situated at the posterior part of the heart. This very [wind] places the crest upon the ears;
moreover, the primary function of this wind is the perception of sound, as well as the trembling of the hands and feet.
The *kṛkara* wind moves through the channel *ambuṣā*, which is situated at the base of the left arm and the shoulder;
it resides in one part of the nose,
and its primary function is the perception of smell.
The Devadatta-vāyu moves through the lalanā-nāḍī on the left side of the heart and through the nāḍī of the Aries-lagna.
One of its peaks resides at the tip of the tongue.
Its primary functions are the taking up of taste and yawning.
The Dhananjaya-vayu circulates through the Kuhū-nadi of the left breast.
Through this channel, it resides at the peak [of the head], in the middle of the sub-tongue (upajihvā), in the hair, and in all the apertures.
Its primary function is the perception of touch, and it remains for some time even in a dead body.
All the winds described above are merely limbs of the great vital wind (mahāprāṇavāyu).
They are given distinct names according to their locations and functions.
Apart from the time of inhalation and exhalation, these four winds flow separately through the right and left apertures of the nose.

In the *Vyākhyātantravajramālā*, this description was set forth in this manner along with the five Tathāgatas, the five colors, and the five elements: "On the tip of the nose is that which is called 'all'; this is the visualization of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Abiding in breath control are the five rays [of light] through the state of the Buddhas."
When [the breath] issues forth from the *prāṇa* upwards through the pair of left and right,
and downwards as well, it is known as the fourfold internal strength (*bala*).
One should point out the coming and going [of the breath] at the lotuses of the throat, heart, navel, and secret place.
This wind, which follows the entire body and initiates all movements, has Vairocana as its intrinsic nature; it departs from the dead body in two ways.

Thus, here, along with the description of the five principal winds (*pradhānavāyu*) and the five limb-winds (*pañcāṅgavāyu*), this has been established: all these are limbs of a single principal life-force wind (*prāṇavāyu*). The method for meditating upon this will be explained later in the section on Vāyuyoga or Caṇḍālīyoga. *Tilaka* means the essence (*tilaka*), which is great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and its cause.
Its threefold division consists of: 1. the *mūlaniṣprapañcatilaka*, 2. the *bhrāntyavidyātilaka*, and 3.
the *bandhakārakadravya*.
And the tilaka of the mantra-wind:
1. Innate gnosis itself is the root-tilaka free from conceptual proliferation.
The nature of the mind is that which awakens as the Dharmakāya.
The very luminosity of the mind (*cittaprabhāsvaratā*) arises as its manifestation through the contemplation of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Just as when the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is disjoined, the attainment of the emptiness of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāvaśūnyatā*) is the characteristic of the *dharmakāya*,

so too, while abiding in luminosity, the manifestations of external and internal smoke, fireflies, the moon, and so forth, which constitute the luminous nature of all phenomena, characterize the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The characteristic of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the unimpeded grasping of the intrinsic nature of its own objects by means of the six sense faculties.

In the state of the *tilaka* of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), through the union of semen, blood, and wind, semen arises as the grasper and blood as the grasped; thus it assumes the relationship of object and subject, which is produced by the ignorance of delusion.
For although this is non-dual by its very nature, it nevertheless perceives duality.

By purifying the substance that causes bondage, the mantra, and the *vāyutilaka*, and by dividing them into the forms of the purified and the purifier, the sixfold division is accomplished. Having conceptualized [the factors] through ignorance (*avidyā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and having substituted the names "feeling" (*vedanā*), "mental formations" (*saṃskāra*), "perception" (*saṃjñā*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) for [their opposites], there exists the *adhāramantratilaka* which grasps both the name and its object, once they have been purified.
The purification of this basis, as well as its name and meaning, occurs through the cultivation of the deity, the recitation of mantras, and so forth.
For this very reason, this is called the "purifying mantra-mark" (*pariśodhaka-mantra-tilaka*).

By means of the three conditions—the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—the dependent mind becomes restless and grasps at sense objects.
This wind-tilaka is that which is purified by the wind;
