it is the wind-tilaka that serves as the cause for its cessation and purifies the yoga of the wind.
The substance-tilaka is that which purifies the five elements—the semen and blood comprised within the aggregates of sound, form, and so forth, appearing as the objects of the five sense faculties.
Among those who purify the *dravya-tilaka* through the *pratipakṣa-tilakas*, there are twelve *rasas* and twenty-four *kaṣāyas*, totaling thirty-six primary elements; furthermore,
through the association with the five principal vital airs (*vāyu*), there are five *tilakas*.

Through the conjunction of the five-limbed winds, the *tilakas* located in the moon and sun situated in the upper and lower parts meet, and thus twelve *rasa-tilakas* and the *kaṣāya-tilaka* residing in the twenty-four *pīṭha* locations remain.
As it is said in the *Saṃvarodayatantra*: "In Pulliramalaya, at the head, resides that which carries the nails and teeth."
At the location of the Jālandhara-śikhā, she carries the hair and body hair;
residing in both knees as Kulatā, she carries the young lion.
Beyond this, within all the channels (*nāḍīs*) that exist throughout the body, even in every single pore, the *tilaka* of substance (*dravya-tilaka*) is present.
Among these, for the yogin of the *Anuttara-tantra*, the center of practice is the *tilaka* of blood obtained from the Mother (*mātṛ-labdha-rakta-tilaka*).

This is located four finger-breadths below the region of the navel, at the junction of the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels, in the lower part of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), situated in the form of the letter *A-pluta* and residing in the lotus of the upper *uṣṇīṣa*.
And also in the *Jñānodayatantra*: "Residing in the center of the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), she whose form is the supreme color of wisdom (*prajñā*),
shaken by the wind of karma, blazing and having the nature of the innate (*sahaja*),
appearing like a flash of lightning, extremely subtle like the tip of a hair, and like a thread of poison."
Having meditated upon it, the mantra-practitioner should cause it to arise; the true guru should thus instruct.

In terms of their essential nature (*sāra*), however, the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), the unstruck wind (*anāhata-vāyu*), and the mark of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca-tilaka*)— these three— are described separately due to the diversity of their functions.
In reality, however, all of these are one's own mind, innate gnosis (*sahaja-jñāna*), or luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), which is devoid of beginning and end.
This channel is described for this purpose: that it is the support of the Great Vital Breath (mahāprāṇa) for all living beings.
In its absence, the very existence of the channels—namely the Madhyamā, Lalanā, and Rasanā—would be impossible.
It is precisely from this [Great Vital Breath] that the central channel, whose nature is emptiness (śūnya), manifests, embraced by the Lalanā, Rasanā, and the others.
This very [state] is also the unstruck sound (*anāhata-vāyu*),
because the vital air (*vāyu*) becomes non-different from the mind,
and the mind is devoid of beginning and end.
These are devoid of permanence, decay, and annihilation;
therefore, the wind, being non-different from them, is also like the mind.
For this very reason, it is also called the unstruck wind (*anāhata-vāyu*).
It is stated in the *Mahāmūrtilaka* that the wind possessing five rays exists in an inseparable form with the luminous mind (*prabhāsvara-citta*).
From this very [mind], the elements of wind, fire, water, earth, and so forth, arise in succession.
The five rays are perceived as being like the constituents of the five elements.
Creation arises from the luminosity and the unstruck wind (*anāhatavāyu*).

Through the non-differentiation of the wind from the luminosity that is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), movement occurs therein; it is precisely through this movement that the world is created.
Today, within the scope of scientists' analysis of subatomic matter, it is known that even protons, neutrons, electrons, and waves reach a state of "great emptiness" (mahāśūnyatva).
This great emptiness is not a mere non-existence, for existence can never arise from non-existence.
Therefore, this consciousness of great emptiness is also inseparable from subtle air (*sūkṣma-vāyu*), since it provides movement to this [air] and brings forth the universe.
In this way, the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) of the world is indeed non-different [from it].
In the absence of this, the very existence of the *tantra* scriptures would be impossible.
In the *Nāmasaṃgīti* as well, it is stated that this wind—the inhalation and exhalation—is the stream of all syllables, including vowels and consonants, attached to the staff of the *samaya*-bell.
It is not merely this much; rather, it is described that even perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) arises from this very wind.
This is the source of all things, and while it is the basis for verbal expression, it itself remains inexpressible and unborn.
Just as it is said: "The Blessed One, the Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the syllable *A*."
The letter A is the foremost of all letters, of great significance, and the supreme syllable.
For the Great Vital Breath is indeed non-arising, devoid of verbal expression;
it is the foremost cause of all designations, and all speech is its brilliant radiance.

In the *Rahasyadīpikā*, a commentary on the *Vasantatilaka*, it is likewise stated regarding the praise of the syllable ‘A’: "The letter ‘A’" and so forth, [is called] "of great significance" (*mahārtha*) because it indicates the primordial, unarisen reality (*tattva*).
It is the "leader of the phonemes" (*varṇanāyaka*), for by this alone they are animated.
Furthermore, whatever mantras or statements there are for embodied beings or practitioners that are authoritative, they have arisen from that very source.
Thus, it is established that all sentient beings are by their very nature devoted to mantra.
As long as the actual state of reality of the three [bodies]—spoken of as having an indivisible nature—is not correctly understood, the practice of the completion stage cannot possibly occur.

For this very reason, this brief introduction has been provided. Regarding the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) of the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), even within the method of cultivation for the meditation on the completion stage, some differences are observed according to the distinctions between the Father Tantra, Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), and Non-dual Tantra (*advayatantra*).

Furthermore, within the Father Tantra, even according to the distinction of the spiritual families (*kula*) of those to be trained, slight variations are seen in the practice of the means of achievement (*sādhana*).

Although there are numerous methods of practice (*sādhana*) and lineages for the *Guhyasamāja*, the primary scripture of the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), among them the Ārya tradition and the Jñānapāda tradition are the most prominent.
According to the Ārya tradition, in the sixth chapter of the root *Guhyasamāja* tantra, [it is stated]: "By means of the body of mantra-realization..."
Impelled by speech within the mind,
one shall accomplish the most excellent siddhi,
which is dear because it brings satisfaction to the mind.

Based on this verse, from the point of "mantranidhyapti" onwards, the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*)—which serves as the basis for the practice of vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) through the isolation of speech—is understood.

Therefore, by means of this, one performs the isolation of body (*kāyaviveka*) and, through the door of the body, carries out vajra-recitation; then, by attaining the isolation of speech and stimulating the Vajrasattva residing in the heart, the four supreme accomplishments (*siddhi*) beginning with "pravara" are obtained within the continuum of the yogi’s mind.
Through the recitation of the supreme vajra, there is the turning [of the mantra] and the solitude of the mind;
the accomplishment is self-consecration;
and the satisfaction of the mind is the purification of the illusory body, which is the ultimate clear light.
"Priya" refers to the body of the Vajradhara of the yuganaddha [union].
In the *Caryāmelāpaka*, Āryadeva considers the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) to be contained within the six stages.

Master Nāgārjuna, citing a passage from the *Vajramālā*, the explanatory tantra of the *Guhyasamāja*, subsumes the practice of the completion stage for all Anuttarayoga tantras within the five stages.
And he composed a separate summary of the meaning for the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
However, he considers certain portions of both physical isolation (*kāyaviveka*) and vajra-recitation as verbal isolation (*vāgviveka*) to be limbs of the generation stage.
Therefore, in the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), there is the sequence of verbal isolation and the sequence of mental isolation (*cittaviveka*).
Self-consecration is the conventional truth; it is the stage of the illusory body,
and the stage of the clear light of ultimate reality through manifest enlightenment.
Non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) and, by implication, the sequence of the two truths in union (*yuganaddha*); these are counted as the five stages (*pañcakrama*).
It is also stated in the *Pañcakrama*: "One should enter the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*) through the successive stages of the reality of wind (*vāyutattva*);
having attained mastery over mantra..."
The vajra-recitation is well-mastered.
The mantra-practitioner, established in vajra-recitation, shall attain the profound realization of the mind;
abiding in the illusion-like samādhi, he shall enter into the limit of reality.
Arising from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), one attains non-dual gnosis;
established in the samādhi of union (yuganaddha),
one no longer has anything further to train in.

Scholars such as Candrakīrti and others, considering that the two stages of the Unsurpassed Tantra— the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*)— are subsumed within the Five Stages (*pañcakrama*), regard the isolation of speech (*vāgviveka*) along with the isolation of body (*kāyaviveka*),

as well as the stage of vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpakrama*), to be merely preliminary states for the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*), which is the actual focal point of the mind. According to this view, in the root practice of the completion stage, the isolation of mind occupies the very first position.
And here, vajrajāpa is subsumed within the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*).

Thus, there are five stages (*pañcakrama*) here: the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), the stage of isolation of mind (*cittavivekakrama*), the stage of the conventional illusory body (*saṃvṛtimāyākāyakrama*), the stage of ultimate clear light (*paramārthaprabhāsvarakrama*), and the stage of the union of the two truths (*yuganaddhasatyadvayakrama*).

According to the systems of Munidatta, Abhayākaragupta, and others, vajrajāpa is the basis for the practice of focusing on the mind; therefore, with respect to the isolation of mind, the isolation of speech (*vāgviveka*)—which is vajrajāpa—is primary here.
Therefore, in place of mental isolation (*cittaviveka*), the opportunity for verbal isolation (*vāgviveka*) has been provided.
This is merely an engagement in expansion and summary based on the root of this inequality;
in reality, there is no contradiction with the intended tenet here.
Furthermore, the practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is also subsumed within the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

Regarding the topic in the twelfth chapter of the *Mūlatantra*: "Now, the service (*sevā*) should be performed within the four-cornered vajra by those of firm vows," it is described in the *Uttaratantra* as follows: "Having performed the service through the six-limbed yoga, one should accomplish the supreme practice;
otherwise, the supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) will never arise."
Withdrawal, meditation, breath control,
retention, recollection, and concentration— this is called the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*).
By their essential nature, these six yogas are also subsumed within the *Pañcakrama*.
Just as withdrawal and meditative concentration pertain to isolation of the body,
breath control to isolation of speech, and retention, coupled yoga, recollection, and meditative absorption to the clear light;
so too is their sequence fixed.
For indeed, in the absence of the preceding means, they do not arise in successive order.
Just as the prior establishment of the Śaikṣa-yuganaddha is required for the attainment of the Aśaikṣa-yuganaddha,
so too the Illusory Body (māyākāya) and the Ultimate Clear Light (paramārthaprabhāsvara) are required for the attainment of the Śaikṣa-yuganaddha.
The practitioner who strives for the attainment of the fourth [body], the ultimate luminosity, shall partake in infinite merit.
However, the direct realization of emptiness arises only immediately after the acquisition of the common illusory body;
therefore, the attainment of the illusory body is required.

To attain this, one should dissolve the wind—which is like the time of death—into the unstruck bindu (*anāhata-bindu*) located in the heart-lotus, thereby effecting the attainment of the exemplary clear light (*upamā-prabhāsvara*).
For this purpose, the knots of the channels (*nāḍī-granthi*) of the heart-lotus must be pierced through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and vajra-recitation (*vajra-jāpa*).

For that end, by means of the yoga of the separation of the subtle body (*sūkṣma-kāya-viveka*), one performs the procedure for gathering the winds and so forth within the wheel of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) situated at the lower part of the central channel (*avadhūtī*).
Prior practice is required.
For one who has completed the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), the practice of the full stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) is required in order to attain physical isolation (*kāyaviveka*).
Thus, in the absence of the preceding means, the accomplishment of each subsequent means is not possible.

The fivefold stage (*pañcakrama*) is divided into five parts through the methods of cultivation beginning with isolation of body (*kāyaviveka*), the analysis of its characteristics, and the methods of accomplishment; these include distinctions such as the procedures for descending and ascending, and the process of transformation.
Isolation of body (*kāyaviveka*) is the very body of the deity that arises in the mind—which is by nature great bliss and emptiness—as something unarisen through conceptual construction.

Body isolation (*kāyaviveka*) is fourfold: the body isolation sealed by one hundred families, the body isolation sealed by five families, the great secret sealed by three families, and that sealed by one family.
Body isolation is twofold, distinguished as being either innate (*svarūpagata*) or obtained subsequent to meditative equipoise (*samāhita-pṛṣṭhalabdha*).

Through internal subdivisions such as the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four elements (*dhātu*), the six sense faculties (*indriya*), and the five objects (*viṣaya*), there are one hundred varieties.

And just as it was established in the *Guhyasamāja Mūlatantra* regarding the subject of physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*) by relying upon the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*): "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed to be the five Buddhas."
Furthermore, by way of distinctions of color—such as external and internal, light and long, white, red, and so forth—even a single aggregate (*skandha*) has five divisions.
Likewise, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and the others are also divided into five types through the distinctions of pleasure, pain, equanimity, wind, bile, and so on.
In the context of explaining the analysis of the body consisting of the four elements, it is stated in that very same place: "Earth is known as Locanā; the water element is remembered as Māmakī."
That which is called Pāṇḍarā is fire, and Tārā is proclaimed to be wind.
It is proclaimed that even the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) is to be meditated upon as the form of the Goddess by dividing it into its various parts, such as hair, bones, body hair, and nails.

In the same way, the aggregates (*skandha*) beginning with perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), as well as the elements of fire, water, and so forth, are to be understood [in this manner].

In the *Guhyasamāja*, at the occasion of explaining the method for meditating on the discernment (*viveka*) of the six sense-faculties and the body, it is stated: "The adamantine bases (*vajrāyatana*) themselves are the supreme maṇḍala of the Bodhisattvas."
Regarding the six sense faculties, which serve as the basis for physical seclusion:
the eye is Kṣitigarbha;
the ear is Vajrapāṇi; the nose is Ākāśagarbha; the tongue is Lokeśvara; and the body element, the aggregate of the three gnoses, and the mind are known as Sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin or Mañjuśrī.
Thus, the six sense faculties are the forms of the Bodhisattvas.
In that very context, the cultivation of physical seclusion regarding the five objects is clarified as follows:
"The mantra practitioner should always visualize the deity through touch, sound, and so forth."
That is to say, the very meditation upon Rūpavajrī, Śabdavajrī, Gandhavajrī, Sparśavajrī, and so forth, constitutes the isolation of the objects and the body.
In this manner, through the fivefold division of each of the aggregates, elements, and so on, there are one hundred families (*kula*).
Therefore, it is taught in the *Uttaratantra* that "the family is further [divided] into a hundred ways."
When there is inclusion, they are included within twenty-five, three, or even one;
it is described in that very context: "The reality is said to be the five families (*pañcakula*); the secret is called the three families (*trikula*).
Within the single family lies the great secret of the deities.
Physical isolation (*kāyaviveka*) is precisely the contemplation of this body, either moment by moment or having transformed it entirely into the form of Vajradhara.

As for the etymology of "body" (*kāya*), it is a term that indicates a collection; where there is a collection of various factors such as the physical frame, flesh, bones, and blood, therein also resides the mind as a collection of preceding and succeeding moments.
Therefore, this is called "body."

Through the meditation on the aforementioned assembly of deities by means of the general body-view (*sāmānyakāyadṛṣṭi*), there arises a general appearance and the exhaustion of attachment (*abhiniveśa*). Therefore, this is declared to be "discrimination" (*viveka*).
In this manner, the cultivation of the discrimination of the body was described in the scriptures.
The practitioner who accomplishes physical isolation (kāyaviveka) should sit upon the Dharma-seat of Vairocana.
On this seat: 1. the feet are in the vajra-posture (vajrāsana), and 2.
the hands are in the gesture of meditative equipoise (samāhitamudrā).
3. The backbone (the vertebrae) is straight;
4. the chest is broad; 5.
the neck is slightly inclined forward.
6. The tongue should touch the palate; 7. the lips should be parted;
8. and the eyes should look straight ahead through the region of the nose.
These seven stations are the seven dharma-thrones of Vairocana.
By means of performing the vajra-posture (*vajrāsana*), the downward-voiding wind (*apānavāyu*) comes under one's own control.
When one is established in the meditative gesture (*samāhitamudrā*) and the navel has been activated, the fire becomes pacified.
By the straightness of the *kaśerūkā* (vertebral column), the *vyāna-vāyu* is governed; by the straightness of the two arms and the expansion of the chest, the *prāṇa-vāyu* becomes governed.
When the neck is bent and the tongue is directed toward the palate, the *udāna-vāyu* comes under control.

Here, having performed the vajrāsana, one should fix the mind with one-pointed concentration upon either a weapon or a subtle tilaka-mark in the center of the jewel-wheel (*maṇicakra*) located in the lower part of the *avadhūtī*.

By practicing in this manner, through the simultaneous entry of wind and mind and their non-differentiation, all the winds are gathered into the channel-wheel (*nāḍīcakra*) situated in the lower part of the *avadhūtī*.
And the wind, having entered the central channel (*madhyamā*) in due order, attains its goal.
By transformation, the air flows equally through both nostrils.
When the air is situated in the middle channel (madhyamā-nāḍī), inhalation and exhalation are obstructed,
and signs such as rays of light and so forth appear.

Regarding the sequence of ascending from the state of realization, the method of reversal consists of the entry, stabilization, and arousal of the vital wind (*vāyu*) into the central channel (*madhyamā*). By means of the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, relying upon the self-resounding nature of the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*), when the channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*) situated in the upper and lower parts of the heart have become relaxed, all the winds located above and below dissolve into the *avadhūtī*.
At that time, the primordial wisdom of *āloka* (light) arises.

In that state, a transformation of physical isolation (*kāyaviveka*) and vocal isolation (*vāgviveka*) occurs. Vocal isolation depends upon breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); it is the yogic application of the student's mental continuum which, through the inseparable union of the vital air (*vāyu*) and the mantra, destroys the conceptualization of subject and object. Having realized the true nature of the vital air and the fixed meaning of the mantra, the entry, abiding, and emergence of the principal vital airs along with the *prāṇa* into the central channel (*madhyamā*)—this very yoga is vocal isolation.

The threefold division of the purification of speech (*vāgviveka*) according to the distinction of locations is as follows: the meditation on the *anāhata* tilaka at the tip of the heart-nose; the meditation on the ray-tilaka at the tip of the mouth-nose; and the meditation on the substance-tilaka at the tip of the secret-nose.

Regarding the practice, within the limit of meditating on the subtle tilaka at the heart-nose, there are twelve white syllables that illuminate the light, situated outside the channel-wheel (*nāḍīcakra*) of the eight-petaled heart-lotus.
In the center, having omitted the letter *ma*, one should visualize the consonants that indicate the manifestation of light (*ālokābhāsa*) as red in color,
and the four vowels beginning with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* as black in color.
Having adorned all the letters with a *tilaka*, one should abide in the nature of the mind in the form of the short vowel situated in the middle of that [arrangement] as the *anāhata-tilaka*.
The mind itself is the mandala of syllables conjoined with the unstruck bindu;
having thus established one-pointedness, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
After attaining the state of the mantra-tilaka, one should visualize the unstruck tilaka at the tips of the mouth and nose, and recite the vajra through the gateway of breath control.
At that time, the sound of the three syllables arises spontaneously;
thus, listening with the mind, one should perform the *vajrajapa*.

By the power of *haṭhayoga*, that wind which previously could not be gathered within the heart-lotus by the two methods of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is drawn down into the *avadhūtī* at the tip of the nose.
Having performed the meditation on the subtle *tilaka* as the object of focus, it can be mastered through the means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
In brief, as the primary practice of *vajrajāpa*, breath control is performed by establishing the winds consisting of the five wisdoms in the form of a single mass within the nose;
this alone is the principal task.
The cultivation of this [speech] is performed through a distinction of locations and not in a single place.
Thus, the purification of speech (*vāgviveka*) is an auxiliary limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) itself.
With its assistance, the *karmavāyu* flowing in the *lalanā* and *rasanā* enters into the *madhyamā*.

And in the *Guhyasamājottara-tantra* it is also said: "One should emanate the breath, which consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements, in the form of a sphere at the tip of the nose;
this great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*."

By means of the mind’s abiding in the *anāhata-bindu* within the heart, the elements beginning with earth, water, fire, and so forth, gradually dissolve away. Finally, even the mind comes to rest in the non-dual.
Through that power, characteristics such as mirages, smoke, the flame of a lamp, and the clear sky arise.

The method for the reversal of the upward movement of consciousness (*avagati*)—through the assistance of external and internal mudrās, vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*), and other means—causes the knots in the channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*) of the heart to burst open. When this occurs, the pervasive wind (*vyānavāyu*) dissolves entirely into the unstruck point (*anāhatabindu*) situated within the heart-lotus; at that time, the knowledge of light (*ālokajñāna*) shines forth, and the discernment of speech (*vāgviveka*) transitions into the discernment of mind (*cittaviveka*). Through the power of the external mudrā and the internal breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), all ten winds, together with the root-wind, remain exactly as they are within the unstruck point at the heart-center.
And at the time of death, the elements dissolve.
While these remain, the knowledge of light arises;
this very yoga of the continuum of training is the seclusion of the mind.

Alternatively, mental isolation (*cittaviveka*) is simply the stabilization of the mind in great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is like a sesame seed, once all the winds of conceptualization within the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) have been dissolved into the unstruck drop (*anāhatavindu*) through the power of meditative cultivation.
This consists of two aspects: the means of achieving mental isolation and the actual state of mental isolation.

The means occurs during the ordinary state as the arising of the three cognitions, such as light (*āloka*); it arises during the state of meditative union (*samāpatti*), the state of deep sleep, and the state of unconsciousness.
This is realized during the practice of the path, specifically in vajra-recitation and the third consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*).
The accomplishment of the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*) and the attainment of the stage of Supreme Dharma (*dharmāgrabhūmi*) on the path of application (*prayogamārga*) occur simultaneously.
Some scholars have maintained that the service of a consort (*mudrāsevana*) is indispensable for the means of accomplishing the isolation of mind.
They cite this statement from the *Pañcakrama*: "Of all illusions (*māyā*), the illusion of woman is preeminent;
this differentiation of the three types of gnosis is clearly perceived right here."
That is to say, by practicing vajra-japa and the external mudrā as the internal means for the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*), the [three lights] such as *āloka* are to be directly realized.
What is the knowledge of *āloka* and so forth?
This thorough understanding is necessary.
Otherwise, the means of accomplishment cannot be conceived.
This is presented in brief.
And so it is said in the *Pañcakrama*: "Knowledge consists of mere awareness; it is without defining characteristics, like space."
However, it has a division consisting of twilight, night, and day; likewise,
there is light, the appearance of light, and the attainment of light.
Although self-cognizing gnosis (*svasaṃvedyajñāna*) alone is the sole gnosis, which we must realize and abide in;

this realization is straightforward in one respect, yet in another it is difficult, because it is precisely due to the non-realization of this luminous self-cognizing gnosis that this [world] is partitioned and bound by chains.
The wheel of existence turns;
sentient beings remain suffering and unpeaceful.
Here, for the sake of direct realization during the stage of practice, these classifications have been established based on the characteristics that will be revealed.
This subject becomes very clear when combined with that which is to be purified and its corresponding explanation:
just as there is the perception of arising and the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), so too are death and the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) considered to be the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
As stated above, the three cognitions of light and so forth, which exist in the ordinary state, manifest spontaneously at the time of death.
How so? Generally, at the outset, the birth of living beings occurs by depending upon the five elements, and in the end, they perish through the dissolution of these very elements.

Regarding the signs that manifest at the time of death, practitioners have declared as follows: when the constituent elements such as earth and the rest have dissolved, the physical body reaches its end;
and due to the exhaustion of the *samāna* vital air, food is no longer assimilated by the self.
The body becomes warm throughout and gradually wastes away.
When the prāṇa-vāyu is diminished, one is unable to perceive objects due to the weakness of the eyes. Upon the depletion (or destruction) of the apāna-vāyu—
Excrement, urine, and so forth become obstructed.
When the vyāna-vāyu is diminished, the limbs and minor members of the body become devoid of sensation.
When the udāna-vāyu is destroyed, there occurs lightness of inhalation and lengthening of exhalation.

In that sequence, the network of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) will perish; because the earth element dissolves into the water element, the body undergoes a state of decay compared to its former condition, and the throat, head, and feet will become incapable of supporting the body.
There will be an incapacity to grasp objects with the hand.
A person lying on the bed of death will say, in order to divert himself,
"The mind is like the appearance of a mirage.
It will come to be so.
Immediately after this, the wheel of the heart-channels will waste away;
there will be the dissolution of the water-element into the fire-element. The mouth, tongue, and other parts, having become parched, will turn black.
He himself will become unable even to touch the tip of his own nose.

At that time, there will be an appearance of smoke within the internal mind; thereafter, the destruction of the throat-channel-wheel (*kaṇṭhanāḍīcakra*) and the dissolution of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) into the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*) will occur.
Cool wind will flow through both the mouth and the nostrils.
At the end, the vital heat will exit from the body.
In this state, there is an internal radiance resembling a firefly,
and there will be an incapacity for the external discernment of objects.
Thereupon, the secret wheel of channels will perish, and the vital air (vāyu) will dissolve into consciousness.
At that time, the external sign will manifest in the form of long inhalation and exhalation; moreover, the exhalation will become more pronounced while the inhalation will become lighter.
There will be a harsh, rasping sound;
an internal radiance like the blazing of a lamp will be perceived,
and thus the bodily winds, together with the five principal winds, will dissolve into consciousness.
And the sense faculties will become incapable of performing their functions;
this is the method of dissolution for the external gross elements. Thereafter follows the dissolution of the internal subtle [elements].

This indeed is the time of the dissolution of the three consciousnesses, and the sequence of its essential nature is as follows: the consciousness of light dissolves into the mind situated in the heart-lotus, wherein all the vital winds have dissolved.
Subsequently, the white semen received from the father, located in the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), enters the heart-lotus by way of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*).
At that time, the mind shines like the sky pervaded by the light of an autumn moon; the thirty-two conceptualizations associated with aversion are suppressed.
At that moment, there is no appearance whatsoever other than the manifestation of light (*ālokābhāsa*).
This very manifestation of light is the non-dual abiding of light and the emptiness of cognition.

The knowledge of the appearance of light (*ālokābhāsa-jñāna*), which is red and obtained from the mother via the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), is increased from the lower part upward and reaches the heart-lotus.
Then, within the mind, there arises the knowledge of the appearance of light— red and equal to space pervaded by the radiance of the sun—
which establishes a state of non-duality with extreme emptiness (*atiśūnyatā*).
At that time, nothing whatsoever remains in the mind other than the appearance of the light of passion;
this itself is the knowledge of the appearance of light.
Now, all forty conceptualizations associated with passion perish.

When the knowledge of the attainment of light occurs upon the dissolution of the semen and blood into the unstruck drop (*anāhatavindu*)— that is, the clear light (*prabhāsvara*)— a momentary, indistinct appearance of an object arises in the mind of the practitioner directly before the manifestation of the clear light.
In this state, there is only an indistinct appearance of the mind itself.
And together with great emptiness, it attains that state of non-duality.
This very state is the abiding of the wisdom of the apprehension of light.
In this condition, conceptual constructions bound to delusion are brought to cessation.

Regarding the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) described above—the nature of the three gnoses and their sequence—once the realization of those three gnoses is accomplished, the path for attaining the state of luminosity unfolds.
The very meaning of "attainment" (*upalabdha*) in the term "attainment of light" (*ālokopalabdha*) is the reaching of proximity to luminosity.
Immediately following the moment of attainment, in the second moment, the gnosis of luminosity arises as non-dual through the emptiness of all phenomena, both object and subject.
This is the luminosity of the Mother (*mātṛ-prabhāsvara*); by means of it, the practitioner effects the direct realization of the state of luminosity, which functions like the Mother.

During his lifetime, the practitioner, by means of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), performs the entry, abiding, and emergence of the vital winds (*vāyu*), thereby manifesting the three gnoses (*trijñāna*) and through that, directly realizing emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
At the time of death, he becomes established in the *dharmakāya* by gradually discerning the signs of the impending [dissolution].
In this context, the wind itself is the support for the mind whose nature is emptiness.
The self-support of light is the emptiness accompanied by wind;
this indeed is emptiness.
This itself is the non-dual knowledge of illumination (*ālokajñāna*). Likewise, there exists the non-dual appearance of illumination (*ālokābhāsādvaya*),
and the luminous knowledge of the all-empty luminosity (*prabhāsvarajñāna*), which is the non-duality of luminosity and total emptiness.

This luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) is twofold, distinguished by the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). For total emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*) is the luminosity of the object, while the knowledge that establishes its own object—total emptiness—is the luminosity of the subject.
The mudrā is the external limb for the means of accomplishing the isolation of the mind (*cittaviveka*).
The intended meaning of the word *mudrā* is stated in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "It is called *mudrā* because one is sealed (*mudrayate*) by means of the *vajra*."
Mudrā is of two kinds: 1. *karmamudrā* and 2. *jñānamudrā*.
That which, through action, possesses hair, breasts, and so forth, is the *karmamudrā*.
And as for the *jñānamudrā*, she is one who is manifested by mere gnosis (*jñāna*) alone. The internal means of accomplishment consists precisely of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*);
beyond that, the meditation on the sequence of the *piṇḍakrama* and the sequence of penetration (*anubhedanakrama*) is performed.
This is clarified in the *Pañcakrama*: "The disciple who has received the instruction should then practice yoga in two ways:
by means of the sequence of grasping the mass (*piṇḍagrāhakrama*) and likewise by means of the sequence of penetration (*anubhedakrama*)."
Whether from the head or from the feet, as long as [the mind] has reached the heart, the yogi enters the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi); this is known as the "grasping of the mass" (piṇḍagrāha).
Having first rendered both the stationary and the moving world luminous, one should subsequently do the same for oneself; for this is the sequence of non-differentiation.
Just as the wind of the breath dissolves entirely within a mirror,
so too should the yogi repeatedly enter the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
In the meditation on the sequence of the *piṇḍa*, the practitioner himself visualizes his chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).
Therein, he meditates upon the chosen deity as dissolving from the crown of the head down to the heart-luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

In the sequence of the *anubheda*, when there is a desire to visualize the deities, one first [dissolves] the external maṇḍala and the individual deities within one's own body; therein, each one is dissolved into the luminosity of the mind (*cittaprabhāsvara*) residing in the heart, whether stationary or moving.
One gradually dissolves the moving world into one's own self,
and likewise dissolves the self into its own luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), just as water poured onto warm dregs dissolves and, having merged into a single drop, evaporates.
This process of dissolution within the luminosity is the sequence of non-differentiation (*anubheda*).
Although this is the method of practice for the fourth stage, this manual is nevertheless applied here as well.
Through this practice of the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*), there arises only a general understanding of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This very realization constitutes both the path of application (*prayogamārga*) and the supreme mundane dharma stage (*dharmāgramārga*).
Therefore, the luminosity of the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*) is also described as the "luminosity of the simile" (*upamāprabhāsvara*).

Upon the cessation of the downward movement, there occurs a reversal until the limit of the isolation of mind; for the practitioner who has perfected the luminosity of the simile, through the vibration caused by the karma-wind, this [luminosity] is aroused during the reverse-order perception of light.
This time is said to be the transition and transference from the isolation of mind into the illusory body (*māyākāya*).

When the knots within the entire network of channels—including the central channel situated in the heart-lotus—have been unraveled, the complete process reaches its culmination in the isolation of the mind (*cittaviveka*) up until the state of arising within the illusory body (*māyākāya*).
Once it has arisen within the illusory body, that sequence of practice is called the "illusory body.
At the stage culminating in the isolation of the mind, the illusory body manifests as the exemplary clear light (*upamā-prabhāsvara*).
The auxiliary condition for this is the subtle vital air (sūkṣma-prāṇavāyu). The material cause is the mind (citta),
which is produced within a divine body adorned with the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana).
This very [body] is called the illusory body (*māyākāya*).
This is the body of the knowledge of the outflows (*āsravajñānakāya*).

It has four divisions, known as: the illusory body of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-māyākāya*), the illusory body obtained subsequent to meditative equipoise (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-māyākāya*), the illusory body of dreams (*svapna-māyākāya*), and the illusory body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava-māyākāya*).

Immediately following the isolation of the mind (*cittaviveka*), the body perceived as an illusion (*māyākāya*) can be categorized into three distinct types according to the stages of practice: the illusory body of practice (*abhyāsakrama-māyākāya*) and the ultimate illusory body (*paryantamāyākāya*).

The etymological derivation is as follows: the very body of the knowledge of the outflows (*āsravajñānakāya*), characterized by the twelve similes such as the "illusory body" and so forth, is called the *māyākāya*.
These twelve similes are: 1. This [body] is like an illusion because it arises from nothing more than vital breath and mind (*prāṇacitta*);...
2. This is all-pervading, resembling the reflection of the moon;
3. this is like an appearance devoid of flesh, bone, blood, and so forth;
4. vibrating at every moment, it is like a mirage.
5. Endowed with the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), it is distinct from the gross body and resembles the subtle dream-body;
6. although connected to the body of karmic maturation (*vipākakāya*), it appears elsewhere and is thus like an echo-body (*pratiśrutkāya*);
7. this body is like a city of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*).
8. When there is one, it appears as many, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*);
9. the five colors of this body are unmixed and resemble a rainbow;
10. the maturation body (*vipākakāya*) is like a cloud, and the illusory body (*māyākāya*) exists like lightning emerging from the midst of a cloud.

11. This [body] has emptiness as its intrinsic nature (*śūnyatā-svabhāva*), being like a bubble that arises from water and dissolves; 12. it is like the form of Vajradhara reflected in a mirror, appearing with the complete perfection of major and minor limbs.
Among these similes, the simile of a dream is considered superior in comparison to the others.
For indeed, twenty-five percent of one's life is spent at night merely in the observation of dreams;
and just as sleep is indispensable for dreaming, so too is the prior movement of consciousness necessary here for the arising of the illusory body (*māyākāya*).
The occurrence of dreams during sleep is equal to the illusory body (*māyākāya*).
The practitioner of the illusory body, having emanated a subtle body from his gross body, moves about;
this activity is exactly like the separate existence of the subtle body from the gross body during the state of dreaming.
In accordance with dreams, three aspects of the body are observed: 1.

The *vipākakāya* (ripening body), which carries pleasure and pain arising from the ripening (*vipāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome [karma]. 2. The *svapnakāya* (dream body), which is manifested and appears due to various latent predispositions (*saṃskāravāsanā*). 3. The *manomayakāya* (mind-made body) in the impure state, and the *jñānakāya* (gnosis body) in the pure state.
That which remains inseparable from luminosity is precisely this innate body (*nijakāya*).
Among these three, it is the subtle innate body alone that serves as the basis for the practice of the illusory body (*māyākāya*), abiding in the nature of one's own continuum.
Even the dream body cannot serve as the support for the practice of the illusory body, because it is merely temporary.
Therefore, one's own body—that is, the subtle vital energy (*prāṇa*) and mind alone—is the basis for the practice of the illusory body (*māyākāya*). The gross body is merely like its dwelling place.
Among the five root winds, the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) is present.
The vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) is also twofold, distinguished as gross and subtle.

One is that upon the cessation of which death occurs; the second is that which does not depend on the sense faculties but depends on mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and it is this that constitutes the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
After death, it is by means of this very [subtle breath] that there is rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
On the path, it is by the power of spiritual practice alone that this very illusory body (māyākāya) is brought forth.

And when, under the sway of karma and afflictions, this [body] is born, then the sentient being appears in various forms within the wheel of existence and wanders in the cycle of saṃsāra. The root of this as well is precisely this mind of sentient beings.
It is also stated in the *Pañcakrama*: "The entire world is dependent; it does not arise as independent.
Its cause is the Clear Light, which is the Clear Light of universal emptiness."
By that very mind through which fools have fallen into bondage within saṃsāra,
by that same mind yogins have gone to the destination of the Sugatas.
The entire world arises from the subtle vital breath and mind (*prāṇacitta*), and not through a succession of the existence of their respective individual phenomena.
The universal cause is the luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara*), which is the nature of the great emptiness and the non-dual form of the mind and the five-colored light-wind.

Just as water has moisture and fire has heat, so too is the core of the Tantric vision revealed through the non-duality of the mind and the subtle wind; this very [realization] regarding the illusory body (*māyākāya*) is the secret of Tantra. This experience cannot be achieved without a Guru.

In this regard, it should be understood that there are two types of bodies: the coarse and the subtle. Generally, the nourishment of these occurs through practice; otherwise, it is said that the subtle body arises at the time of death. If one realizes the illusory body (*māyākāya*) during one's lifetime and masters it, then upon the dissolution of the three consciousnesses in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), having arisen in the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), one is liberated.

Since the physical body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) consists of nothing but a subtle vital breath and a subtle mental body, and furthermore, because for the sake of accomplishing the illusory body (*māyākāya*) when all winds have become unstruck (*anāhata*) through the power of practice, knowledge of these two bodies is necessary;
here it must be considered: when the practitioner is raised up into the subtle body, is there then a severance of connection from the coarse body or not?
Some disputants considered it to be a cessation,
while others accepted that even without cessation, there is an arising within the subtle body;
both views may be appropriate.

What is not possible? As long as the practitioner has been raised up in an illusory body (*māyākāya*) by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he will remain separate from his coarse body (*sthūlakāya*).
When the power of meditative concentration is exhausted, he will again return to the coarse body.

In reality, as long as the practitioner has not attained the ultimate clear light (*paramārthaprabhāsvara*) and the first bhūmi, there can be no complete severance of the connection with the coarse body according to the will of the subtle body.
It is not understood how this might be so.
To accomplish the sādhana, one who accomplishes the *māyākāya* sādhana must generally be endowed with four qualities:

1. He should attain firm mastery over both the coarse and subtle aspects of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*); 2. He should be a knower of the meaning of the four classes of tantra; 3. [He should possess] the correct accomplishment of the isolations of body, speech, and mind...
One should perform [the practice]; one who desires the cultivation of the *yuganaddha* (united) stage should become [intent upon it].

The realization of the illusory body (*māyākāya*) cannot be achieved without the instruction of a guru, due to its extreme secrecy and fullness of mystery. For this purpose, along with devotion: "There is no solidity in your body; there is neither flesh nor blood."
You have displayed a body in the sky like a rainbow.
Thus, in the *Sarvajñānayānasaṃdoha*, having praised the Guru according to the method taught in the *Pañcakrama*, one should entreat him to reveal the secret of the illusory body (*māyākāya*).
What are the causes and conditions for the illusory body?
Even with mind alone, in the absence of wind, form is not established.
When only air exists and the mind is absent, knowledge is not possible.
Like the proponents of materialism (*bhautikavādin*), it cannot be maintained that all things arise from the elements alone.
In the field of experience, this is not possible without the mind assuming form.
If the arising of consciousness from mere insentient matter is asserted, questions such as "How is there unity?
and "In what manner?

arise; these are indicated by the marks of inquiry. Conversely, if we were proponents of consciousness [as the primary reality], then to deny that which is directly perceived through the impact of manifest objects would be a repudiation of what is evident.
This is impossible.
If such were the case, how could one conceive of the existence of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as mutually dependent yet possessing an undifferentiated nature?
Furthermore, how could an explanation of external objects such as pots and cloths as being of the nature of pure consciousness (*śuddhacetanā*) ever be made?
And how might the mutual relationship between these [factors] be well-established?
Should we accept a slight predominance of wind over consciousness, considering all phenomena to be subtle portions of the luminous vital breath and mind?
Just as the Vaibhāṣika, who asserts external objects, considers even a subtle atom to be a composite of the four elemental constituents.

In its gross form, this becomes the nature of fire, water, and so forth; and from subtle consciousness, the fifty gross mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*)—such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), anger (*krodha*), and the rest—arise.

Thus, it is considered that these are mutually dependent. However, if one intends to describe the expansion of pure consciousness alone, what possible connection could there be between that and the minds of specific individuals such as Rāma or Śyāma?
If one person is liberated, why are all not liberated?
If this [doctrine of] individual existence were accepted, how could all things described in the scriptural treatises be luminous?
When a person attains awakening and gains Buddhahood, how does that omniscience—possessing the knowledge of all-knowingness—pervade all objects of knowledge?
To the extent that knowledge is pervasive, to that same extent the pervasion of the body of knowledge (*jñānakāya*) is intended.
How will this be established?

If it does not pervade all objects of knowledge and all living beings, then how could the high resolve, latent tendencies, desires, and so forth of all those to be trained (*vineyajana*) be known? If this is not possible, then—
What is the goal of the science of spirituality (adhyātma-śāstra)?

If its goal is merely peace and freedom from dualities in this life, then what indeed is the necessity for the science of spirituality? It is possible to achieve a state of non-duality for the mind through some form of mental diversion at any time.
In that case, would the great *adhyātma* (inner science) itself become fragmented?
In this way, many questions are liable to arise. The subtle vital breath and mind (*prāṇa-citta*) alone provide the solution to these problems.
This essential nature cannot be understood without a guru;
therefore, our guru alone is our refuge. As it is said in the *Pañcakrama*: "The so-called process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna-krama*)," and so forth.
The vision of truth through the conventional is obtained by the grace of the Guru’s feet; it is not attained otherwise.

Regarding the specific means of accomplishment for the illusory body (*māyākāya*), there are three divisions: the beginner’s illusory body, the purified illusory body, and the illusory body of the unified pair (*yuganaddha*). When all phenomena have been analyzed within the beginner’s means of accomplishment, emptiness is established through the reason of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and its conditions; furthermore, this is demonstrated by the arguments of the *Vajra-kaṇa* and other texts regarding both causes and conditions arising from causes and conditions.
Moreover, these possess existence on the level of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
And that which is dependent origination:
thus, within conventional reality, there exists for entities only the nature of phenomena produced through dependent origination, which is the illusory body (*māyākāya*).
This illusory body is demonstrated by means of examples.

And just as, even in the absence of external objects, one should investigate the immutability, stability, and so forth of things by examining the body manifested in a dream through cognition, the echo manifested [from sound], the reflection, the bubble-like appearances in water, the essence-less mirage, the rainbow of Indra, and so on.
This is the very method of practice for beginner practitioners.
He preserves a written image of Vajrasattva facing a mirror,
positioned so that it appears upright in the mirror.
In the same way, let them behold with a single mind,
and also in the Five Stages: form, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness as the fifth.
Likewise, there are four elements.
The eyes, the objects, and the fivefold cognition—whether internal or external—all are non-differentiated; everything is indeed illusion (māyā) and nothing else.
And by means of a reflection in a mirror, the illusory body is characterized.
From this point forward, all things, both stationary and moving, are purified within the playful manifestation of the mantra-knowledge of the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*).
Generally speaking, this is precisely the pure *māyākāya*.

Regarding the distinction between the ordinary illusory body (*māyākāya*) and the pure illusory body (*viśuddhamāyākāya*), there are two primary types: the former being the conventional aspect of the illusory body revealed immediately after the third stage of mental isolation (*cittaviveka*), which is the pure illusory body. Due to differences in conventional usage, some scholars consider the first to be impure and the second to be the pure illusory body.
They cite the form reflected in the mirror as the first [example], and they consider the second to be the unobscured aggregate (*skandha*).

This practice is accomplished through the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*) alone, by means of the dissolution of the elements beginning with earth into the *ānāhata* bindu residing in the heart, together with the assistance of the three gnoses (*jñāna*).

The very reality that arises from the illusory body (*māyākāya*) in reverse order from the exemplary luminosity (*upamā-prabhāsvara*) is the practice of the illusory body of union (*yuganaddha-māyākāya*).

The transformation of the state of realization, relying upon external and internal means together with the practice of the illusory body (*māyākāya*), occurs at the point of directly perceiving total emptiness through the innate luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) accompanied by the three gnoses; at that time, the practitioner’s state shifts from the illusory body to the fourth stage, the ultimate luminosity (*paramārthaprabhāsvara*). Then, the practitioner enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The luminous (*prabhāsvara*) is precisely the realization of truth (*satyābhisamaya*) that is non-different from the object—the emptiness—which arises solely from the knowledge of the great bliss of the subject; this alone is the continuum-yoga (*santatiyoga*) of one in training.
This very thing is, by implication, the characteristic of the ultimate luminosity (*paramārthaprabhāsvara*), which is the luminosity of the fourth stage.
Its etymological derivation is that the innate knowledge of great bliss itself is the ultimate luminosity.
When one becomes oriented toward that [reality], the end of the phenomenal world (*saṃvṛti*)—that is, the entire manifold of dualistic appearances—comes about.
This very state of non-duality is the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

Although numerous internal distinctions can be established, such as the luminosity of the subject (*viṣayin*), the luminosity of the object (*viṣaya*), the luminosity of the illustration (*upamā*), and the luminosity of the thing illustrated (*upameya*), they remain non-dual in their essential nature.
The nature of the mind, which is luminous from the very beginning, is itself the luminosity of the basis. Appearance is the mind,
and the mind is self-cognizable.
Great bliss exists as self-cognizable;
great bliss is inseparable from emptiness. This realization can be accomplished through the yoga of the winds and through the stabilization of the natural state.
In accordance with this, it is possible to establish two types of practice for the realization of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*):
1. The direct realization of this [luminosity] is impossible through the churning of analytical investigation;
just as by one afflicted with jaundice, conch shells and other such objects appear yellow, even though their actual color is white.
Even through a hundred thousand explanations, yellowness cannot be perceived as whiteness;
therefore, the treatment of people must be conducted solely by means of medicine for these diseases.

The venerable Ācārya Rangjung Dorje also states that the direct realization of the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is not possible through the intellect—just as, although fire resides within wood, it does not manifest even by rubbing two pieces of wood together.
That can be produced,
but not by means of an extremely subtle fragment.
In the same way, the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is directly realized precisely through the union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, which is the entry of the wind into the *avadhūtī*.
The explanation of which has been set forth in the *Vajrajāpa*, *Cittaviveka*, and other [works], that practice of the yoga of the winds (*vāyuyoga*) must also be performed here.

2. Regarding the second method for the direct realization of the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) abiding with its own nature (*saprakṛtistha*), for the sake of accomplishing this, one should [visualize] the illusory body (*māyākāya*) naturally produced, starting from the soles of the feet up to the head, in all directions—right, left, and so forth.
The meditation on the "mass" (*piṇḍadhyāna*) consists of stabilizing the mind within the heart-lotus along with the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Just as when breath is exhaled into a mirror, it gradually dissolves into a drop and then into emptiness, so too should one meditate here.
The "vessel" is the world of sentient beings.
Having again withdrawn the world of sentient beings into one’s own body of light,
and that body of light as before, the act of causing it to abide in the clear light is called "penetrating meditation" (*anubhedadhyāna*).
This is stated in the *Caturthadevīparipṛcchāvyākhyātantra* for the purpose of performing the meditation by joining [the mind] with the wind.
And because at the time of the meditation on the *piṇḍa*, all the winds and the *bodhicitta* are to be gathered within the heart—
for which purpose even the yoga of the winds is required—
the intention of *bodhicitta* here is precisely the mind of clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
Through the repeated cultivation of both meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the ultimate luminosity (*paramārtha-prabhāsvara*) becomes manifest.

It is understood that when one abides in these two, even the support-body (*āśraya-kāya*) of ultimate luminosity, being a non-fruitional body (*avipāka-kāya*), is indeed an illusory body (*māyā-kāya*).
Furthermore, this illusory body is not perceived as something separate from the fruitional body (*vipāka-kāya*), having abandoned it.
That very body and its state realize the ultimate luminosity.
In the innate state, the method for realizing luminosity is that all phenomena are mind,
and mind itself is like the empty sky within one's own self.
Therefore, the mind should become equal to space, abiding in its own natural state.

And it is said in the *Guhyasamāja*: "In the contemplation of one's own mind, all phenomena are established. For these phenomena abide in the space-vajra; they are neither phenomena nor the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
When the mind abides in its own natural state, then all phenomena perceived as external forms are merely appearances, and at that time, no superimposed phenomenon exists whatsoever.
It is like a child in a garden filled with various beautiful flowering trees who does not perceive either beauty or ugliness.

Śabarīpāda also says: "Just as the water of all rivers becomes one upon falling into the ocean, so too, through the observation of the mind (*cittāvalokana*), all conceptual minds and mental factors (*prajñapticitta-caitasika*) subside within the luminous mind (*prabhāsvaracitta*). Tilopāda also speaks thus: "Just as when looking at the celestial Gaṅgā, the very act of seeing itself ceases."

In the same way, by observing the state of the natural condition of one’s own mind, all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) would be restrained. Just as mist, clouds, and the like arise in space and dissolve back into that very space, so too do conceptual constructions and mental factors (*caitasika*) arise within the luminous mind and subside right there.

This has also been established in the *Jñānasiddhi*: "Just as a reckless dog abandons a stone and runs after the person who threw it," [so does the mind pursue its objects while neglecting its own source].

In the same way, without observing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one should seek that mind which is its source, so that there may never again be the casting of conceptual construction, which is like a stone. Just as when a clod of earth is thrown, it runs away, yet it is not the thrower.
Thus, whatever is cultivated by the mind, that comes to be; it is not merely mental.
Siddha Viravāpāda also declares that, like an ocean devoid of waves,

like the flame of a lamp sheltered from the wind, or like a garuḍa soaring high in the sky, one should remain solely in the illumination of present awareness, free from conceptualization of the past and deliberation on the future.
By remaining thus, the clear light manifests of its own accord.

Sārapāda also says: "By restraining the activities of the mind and mental factors, the vital wind (*vāyu*) is stilled; and through the stilling of the wind, the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*) will be directly realized.
Thus, it is observed that there is even a simple path for the realization of the Clear Light.
Had all spiritual contemplatives followed this very path, then this present society would have attained a state of supreme excellence.
Furthermore, this is the fault of people: they do not desire to obtain that which is easily attained,
but consider only that which must be obtained with difficulty as their own true gain.
One does not investigate that which is near for the sake of attaining it;

for this very reason, because it has been produced together with oneself since beginningless births and is thus close at hand, one fails to perceive it, and so this wheel of existence remains bound by the chains of the cessation of suffering.

As stated in the *Śaṅpākargyud*, the treatise titled *Mahāmudrāmañjūṣā*: "There are four causes for non-realization: 1. Our mind is inseparable from the *dharmakāya*, yet because it is so extremely close, it cannot be recognized as such.
2. Although this [mind] remains in a state of constant arising, it is impossible to know due to its extreme profundity."
3. For the direct realization of this, only mindfulness and alertness are required;
however, due to extreme simplicity, we do not trust it.
4. Even though the three bodies are self-manifested, because of its excellence, the intellect does not grasp them.
From the very beginning, our own mind is empty of appearances;
this itself is the Dharmakāya. For appearance-ness belongs to the Nirmāṇakāya.
The union is the enjoyment body; these constitute the three bodies.
By avoiding the four aforementioned defects, we are able to directly realize the clear light.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Gyeyakośa* that for the realization of the luminosity of the mind (*cittaprabhāsvara*), the wind moving through the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels will dissolve into the *madhyamā* by virtue of the sense faculties— the mind, eyes, and so forth— abiding in their natural state. Therefore, the relaxation of the mind is one of the unsurpassed instructions.
This [practice] is also the limb of *dhāraṇā* within the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).

Here, the sense organs, such as the eyes, which have form and so forth as their objects, dissolve; having become of a single flavor within the luminosities of perfect internal cessation, they arise as non-dual.
It is also said in the *Guhyasamāja*: "When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the sign arises."
That sign of the five elements was spoken by Bodhivajra.

The reversal of the ascent of realization, which is the ultimate luminosity (*paramārthaprabhāsvara*), occurs within this stage of union (*yuganaddhakrama*) once the fourth ultimate luminosity has been manifested through the reverse process during the attainment of light.
The characteristic of the stage of union is the non-dual, single-flavored gnosis of the two truths— known as the unstruck vajra-body and ultimate luminosity— which are inseparable.
This twofold division is established by way of abandonment and the subject matter to be expressed.
This is the nature of the union of the ultimate and the conventional;
therefore, it is called the stage of union (*yuganaddha*).

And it is also stated in the *Pañcakrama*: "Having understood conventionality and ultimate reality separately through their distinctions, that wherein their union occurs is called 'yuganaddha' (the yoked pair)."

Regarding the question of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): why is this not appropriate, that while in the *Āgamas* (the words of the Buddha) the qualities of the successive stages and so forth of practitioners beyond the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) are described,
whereas in the [tantric] *Śāstras* this is only set forth up until the attainment of the first stage?
For immediately after attaining the vision of reality and the first stage (*bhūmi*), the practitioner establishes a connection with the Tathāgatas and hears the Dharma.
From them, he does not derive a specific understanding of the scriptures' particular purpose;
rather, he is able to effect his own purification through the chosen deities such as Vajradhara.

Furthermore, for those who have not directly realized non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*), it is entirely inappropriate to attempt a refutation by means of their own conceptual constructions (*svavikalpa*).

The limit of determination through conceptualization extends only as far as the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*). Moreover, this [refutation] is established as a mere succession; for even when Bodhisattvas established in non-conceptuality reach the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and proceed to act, they must still eliminate the positions and counter-positions regarding the obscurations and the stages.
It is being established:
this much is appropriate, and this remains to be investigated.

Regarding the connection with the arousal of the yuganaddha, Āryadeva, having raised five questions in the *Caryāmelāpaka*, clarifies their refutation: first, regarding the meaning of the third stage...

Immediately following the isolation of mind (*cittaviveka*), when the illusory body (*māyākāya*) is directly realized within the fourth luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), will there be an end to the contaminated illusory body or not? In response to this, the end of the contaminated illusory body is accepted; immediately after the fourth stage, the body of union (*yuganaddhakāya*) consisting of uncontaminated vital wind (*anāsravaprāṇavāyu*) will manifest.
2. When asked regarding the sequence of traversing the path, it is explained in detail therein in connection with the five paths and the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

3. When will the turning away from existence (bhava-vyāvṛtti) be accomplished, and what is its extent? The answer to this is: when the afflictions (kleśa), along with their latent tendencies (savāsana), have been destroyed, existence turns away immediately following the attainment of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
What is the intention regarding liberation?
Liberation is the eradication of the afflictive obscurations along with their roots and the attainment of the "yoked pair" (yuganaddha) by those in training (śaikṣa).
What is the cause for attaining liberation?
For this is the reason why the attainment of the path of seeing occurs through a common form in both the Pāramitā-naya and the Mantra-naya;
however, there is a difference regarding the nature and qualities of that path of seeing.
Just as in the Śrāvaka-yāna, even after the direct realization of emptiness, the arising of existence through karma and afflictions does not persist until the attainment of the state of an Arhat.

In the Pāramitā system, when the path of seeing is attained, although birth in existence through the power of karma and afflictions is prevented by the direct realization of emptiness— which destroys the view of a designated self— the innate grasping at a self is not yet eliminated. In the Mantra system, however, the destruction of both the views of the designated and the innate self is accomplished precisely upon the path of seeing.
And these distinctions [of the object] are considered to arise from the distinctions in the cognizing consciousness that directly perceives the emptiness of the object.
However, this must be further investigated: is it not the case that the cognition of the object does not depend at all upon the intensity or specific quality of the cognizing consciousness?
When there is a distinction in the cognizer, is there no distinction in the nature and other attributes of the object?
What is this being suggested? Is it that the very nature of object-cognizing consciousness, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), does not exist as emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Or that those qualities which arise in the mind do not arise from the knowledge of emptiness?
Is it not the case that the slight increase in qualities among practitioners who have ascended the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) does not arise from the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*)?
Likewise, is it not improper to differentiate between the profundity, pervasiveness, and clarity of the object and the subject?
Whatever may be the case, immediately after the first stage (*bhūmi*), the outflows (*āsrava*) perish and uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) arises.
From this very [practice], the non-differentiation of body and mind arises;
this is called the path of the learner’s unified body (*yuganaddhakāya*).
When fully refined, this gradually attains the unified body of the non-learner (*aśaikṣika-yuganaddhakāya*).

The Tradition of Jñānapāda: According to the tradition of Jñānapāda for the *Guhyasamāja*, the four meditations of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) are performed through the four joys and the four awakenings in the four stages.
This was obtained by Jñānapāda through the oral transmission from the mouth of Mañjuśrī.
At the command of Mañjuśrī, Jñānapāda composed the *Muktitilaka*, which is the foundational text for the completion stage procedure of the Jñānapāda tradition.

In accordance with this, following the meditation on the mandalas of the five families centered on Akṣobhya in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), one meditates in the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) upon the Unstruck Tilaka (*anāhatatilaka*) in the heart, the Jewel Tilaka (*maṇicakra*) in the secret place, and the Emanation Tilaka (*nirmāṇatilaka*) at the tip of the nose. Through the gradual experience of the four joys, beginning with joy (*ānanda*) and supreme joy (*paramānanda*), the completion stage is accomplished. Regarding the method of practice: having visualized the entire mandala within the unstruck drop (*bindu*) in the heart-lotus according to the procedure similar to that of the generation stage, and having performed the rite of gathering and dissolution, one attains one-pointed concentration upon the tilaka.
There is a method for attaining the first bliss:

by churning the *tilaka* located in the heart within the *maṇicakra* through the application of breath (*vāyu*), and having meditated thereon upon the complete mandala of deities as before, and having visualized the *tilaka* residing in the heart of the principal deity,
supreme bliss is obtained simply through the practice of meditation on their gathering and dissolution.

3. Having meditated on the *tilaka* of the sign at the tip of the upper nose, one focuses on the subtle wind-*tilaka* through the power of the *vajra-jāpa* and other winds; this cultivation of all phenomena as being like an illusion is *viramānanda*.
4. The cultivation of the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is prescribed.
Through the yoga of meditation on the analysis of the mass (*piṇḍa-anubheda-dhyāna*) and by repeated practice, the signs of the three gnoses—such as mirages, smoke, and so forth—arise.
The Mother Tantra completion stage includes texts such as the *Hevajra*, *Cakrasaṃvara*, *Catuṣpīṭha*, *Mahāmāyā*, and *Buddhakapāla*.

Nāgārjuna, taking the *Guhyasamāja*—a Father Tantra text—as his basis, composed the *Piṇḍīkṛta* for the generation stage and the *Pañcakrama* for the completion stage, thereby establishing a very clear procedure for practice;
however, this was not written in the Mother Tantra texts.
The Mother Tantra texts alone are extensive and widespread; it is difficult to include any single one of them within specific systems.
Siddhas have composed commentaries on Hevajra alone in numerous methods.
For instance, Ḍombīpāda strongly exhorted [the practitioner] to perform the *caṇḍālī* sādhana together with the *vasantatilaka* in the *Amṛtasādhanā*.

Saroruhapāda also taught that through the application of the six syllables (*ṣaḍvarṇayoga*) in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), and furthermore by means of the method for the sequential dissolution of those syllables, one attains the direct realization of the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
Samayavajra associated this with the subtle *tilaka*.

This [text], having bestowed its power upon both the yoga of the analysis of the alms-gathering (*piṇḍānubhedana*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), proclaims the method for the manifestation of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*).
The intention of the *Hevajra* and other Mother Tantras is known by the name "Six Yogas" (*ṣaḍyoga*).
Its dissemination was carried out by the Tibetan translator Marpa Dharmamati, the founder of the Kagyu (*kargyuda*) tradition.

The six yogas of Nāḍapāda consist precisely of Caṇḍālī, the illusory body (*māyākāya*), dream, clear light (*prabhāsvara*), the transference of consciousness at the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and so forth.
This system generally follows the fourfold tradition of the Tibetan schools.
A brief introduction is presented here, as this is primarily the method for the practice of Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*).
The Caṇḍālī is indeed the Caṇḍālī herself, the essence-filled practice of the Unsurpassed Tantra.
It is said that the Caṇḍālī is the foundation-stone of this path;
without her, no other practice of the Unsurpassed [Tantra] is possible.
For the cultivation of Caṇḍālī, the actual state of body and mind must be understood.
This has been explained in detail above in relation to the body.
Without realizing the state of the mind, [the practice] cannot be directly realized; therefore—
Just as milk exists within the body of a cow, yet it is impossible to milk the milk from her horns;
rather, the milk is drawn only from her udders—so too it is said in the *Hevajra*: "The great gnosis resides within the body, free from all conceptual constructions."
Pervading all things, it resides in the body yet is not born of the body.
A question arises: "Great gnosis exists within the body, yet how is it directly perceived?
It is stated in the *Samyagvāk* treatise that it resides thus in the navel-center (*nābhikṣetra*) of the body.
Due to the differentiation of the network of channels (*nāḍicakra*), there are four divisions of the navel.
Regarding the fields of the crown,

throat, heart, and navel: while explaining this, the master Kṛṣṇapāda says that the king of mind resides at the navel during the waking state, in the throat-cakra during the dream state, in the heart during the state of deep sleep, and in the crown during the state of meditative absorption.
In the waking state, the mind is crowded with various conceptual forms and perceptions within the field of the navel.
In the dream state, the mind resides at the throat center (*kaṇṭhacakra*), characterized by existence and non-existence as it is stirred by the vital wind (*vāyu*).
In the state of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), the mind resides in the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Therefore, this state of being turned away from that [defilement] is extremely difficult to achieve;
for this mind, stained by passion, persists in a defiled form and forgets its own inherently stainless nature.
This is called the fourth stage, the stage of transition.

Having understood the stability of the mind in these four states, the practice is undertaken. In the waking state, having ignited the fire of gnosis in the form of the letter *A* at the junction of the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *avadhūtī*, the mind is purified through the practice of *caṇḍālī*. In the dream state, by relying on the throat-cakra through the practice of dreaming; in deep sleep, through the practice of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); and even in the state of meditative absorption, through the practice of *caṇḍālī*, the mind is thoroughly cleansed.
For here, at the moment when the senses engage with their objects, on the one hand, meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) proceeds,
and on the other hand, Caṇḍālī causes the *bodhicitta* to flow from the location of the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Thus, Caṇḍālī is the purifier of both the states of waking and meditative absorption.

Although the accomplishment of Caṇḍālī grants the attainment of all fruits, she primarily bestows the Dharmakāya. Through the practice of dream yoga, the Saṃbhogakāya is accomplished; through the illusory body, the Nirmāṇakāya; and through the clear light, the Mahāsukhakāya. The meaning of "Caṇḍālī" is as follows: she is the one who rejects and devours all phenomena—the aggregates, sense-bases, elements, and so forth; she is of the nature of non-conceptuality, the mother of all Victors, and indeed Vajrabhaṭṭārikā herself is Caṇḍālī.

It is as follows. In the *Hevajratantra-ṭīkā*, regarding Caṇḍālī, it is stated: “Caṇḍā is Prajñā because she has the nature of being fierce (*caṇḍa*) in cutting through the primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*); Āli is Vajrasattva. Thus, by the word ‘Caṇḍālī,’ [this union] is expressed,” and so forth.
