As for its divisions, there are four divisions of this Caṇḍālī: 1. The Hot Caṇḍālī, ignited by the fire of gnosis in the form of the letter *A*.
2. Tilaka-śrāvikā Mahāsukha-caṇḍālī;
3. Caṇḍālī who, after entering the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī) from the midst of the wind, moves upward and is free from conceptual construction; 4.
Phala-caṇḍālī, who, by means of blazing, awakens the four joys and brings about the state of union (yuganaddha).

The practice of Caṇḍālī consists of two methods of practice: the preliminary ritual (*pūrvakarmavidhi*) and the principal ritual (*maulavidhi*). Through the preliminary ritual, the channels (*nāḍī*), winds (*vāyu*), and vital drops (*tilaka*) are purified.
Various yogic postures (*āsana*) are prescribed for the purification of the channels, winds, and vital drops.
Having first visualized one's own body before it as one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the networks of channels (*nāḍīcakras*) are meditated upon in their distinct forms.

For the sake of practice, by forming a visualization of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) as being like an extremely fine hair and then like the massive Mount Sumeru, knowledge of the network of channels is attained.
To purify the pathways of the channels, meditation is performed on *lalanā* and *rasanā*—that is, on *Ālikāli*—as they enter sequentially at the tip of the nose and exit from the secret organ.
In the purification of the winds, meditation upon the color of the wind and the breath-control practices known as *recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka* are practiced.
Having thoroughly understood the location of the semen and blood and their connection to those winds, the fundamental *caṇḍālī* is accomplished.
This fundamental *caṇḍālī* is not performed as a visualization within this body of maturation (*vipākakāya*).
Furthermore, for this purpose, one should perform the transformation of oneself into some chosen deity cultivated through the method of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

In this regard, having transformed oneself into Hevajra, the channel-wheel (*nāḍīcakra*) located four finger-widths below the navel is to be visualized, starting from the lotus of the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Father-deity.
The procedure for visualization is described in this manner in the *Sampuṭodbhava*, which is an explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*) of the *Hevajratantra*.
A lotus with sixty-four petals is situated in the center of the navel;
a lotus with thirty-two petals is established in the center of the head.
Furthermore, there is a sixteen-petaled lotus situated in the middle of the throat,
and likewise, an eight-petaled lotus is taught to be in the heart.
The practice of Caṇḍālī-bhāvanā is generally performed by first practicing the meditation on the short and prolated form of the syllable ‘A,’ as described in the *Hevajra-tantra*.
Here, it is explained according to the *Padyākarapa*:

one performs the self-meditation on Hevajra in union (*yuganaddha*), wherein at the center of the sixty-four-petaled lotus located at the navel is the seed-syllable ‘A,’ which is black and yellow with upward-pointing rays; and at the center of the eight-petaled lotus located at the heart—
The meditation is performed upon the syllable ‘HŪṂ’, which has the nature of the blue-colored Vajra-Rāhu;
upon the syllables ‘Bhraṃ Āṃ Jrīṃ Khaṃ’ within the four-petaled lotuses of the channels;
and upon the syllable ‘Evam mayā’ facing downwards on the petals of the four channels at the boundary.

In the center of the sixteen-petaled wheel located at the throat, one performs the meditation on the syllable *haṃ*, which has the nature of a red-colored sun, is adorned in its four directions by the downward-facing, red-colored *tilaka-nāda* of the syllable *oṃ*,
and is present during the time of exhalation (*praśvāsa*, i.e., the occasion of the *recaka* breath control).
From each letter, five rays of light issue forth and pervade the entire universe;
and at the time of exhalation (during the *recaka* breath control),
the wind consisting of all those lights dissolves therein.
At the time of the *kumbhaka* breath-retention, the wheels of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) of identical color should be visualized very clearly, like reflections in a mirror.

Thereafter, when the moon has dissolved into the radiance of the Mother-deity within the syllable ‘Aṃ’, and that [moon] has then dissolved into the seed-syllable ‘Aṃ’ at the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*), one kindles the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*).
This fire, increasing upward and reaching the heart wheel (*hṛdayacakra*), [consumes] the five Tathāgatas...
It kindles the fifth [cakra], such as that of Māmakī, and causes great bliss (*mahāsukha*) to flow.
As it is said in the *Hevajratantra*: "The Caṇḍālī, ignited at the navel, burns the five Tathāgatas."
And Locanā and the others burn; when I am burnt, Śaśin flows forth.

In the *Abhidhānottara-tantra*, Caṇḍālī is described as the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*); in the *Vajramālā*, as fire; in the *Mahāmudrā-tilaka*, as the wind of karma (*karmavāyu*); and in the *Cakrasaṃvara*, she is designated as a *tilaka*.
A *tilaka* can only be spoken of in terms of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), for its essential nature is like fire.

Regarding the preliminary practice of Caṇḍālī: having established a focused visualization on the long vowel "Ā" at the point where the *lalanā*, *rasanā*, and *madhyamā* channels meet, four finger-breadths below the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), one performs the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) of *kumbhaka*.
Having meditated upon this as being like a blazing fire at the navel, one performs fifty *kumbhakas*.
Gradually moving upward, the fire reaches the heart, the throat, and finally the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Having reached the *uṣṇīṣa*, all the limbs and minor members are filled with the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*), and the *bodhicitta* becomes inseparable from the semen.
It is meditated upon as the manifestation of untainted great bliss (*anāsrava-mahāsukha*).
According to the non-dual tantric scriptures such as the *Kālacakra*, when the entire body is pervaded by untainted bliss, it destroys the "taint" (*āsrava*) that resides within the body,
just as mercury situated within iron destroys the iron by setting it ablaze.
In that very way, having ignited the lamp of undefiled great bliss— the tilaka of the substance of the outflows— it destroys [the ordinary body];
this body of the practitioner, composed of the six elements, becomes like a rainbow and attains the illusory body (māyākāya),
and by means of this very body, one attains the saṃbhogakāya.

Through the gradual upward movement from the navel-cakra up to the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), and again from the crown-cakra down to the navel-cakra, the practice of downward movement constitutes the method for attaining the [four joys]: *ānanda*, *paramānanda*, *viramānanda*, and *sahajānanda*. Thus, the experience of the four joys through meditation is only possible when all the vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*) enter and remain within the central channel (*madhyamā*) by the power of the practice of *caṇḍālī*. And because...

The fire of gnosis, entering through the middle [channel] and penetrating the cakras, pierces them. All the channels enter the central channel; all the vital winds become the subtle *praṇava*; and all the *tilakas* (mystical marks) are purified within the stainless and unstruck (*anāhata*) *tilaka*.

Upon reaching the area from the secret organ up to the navel, there is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) of the object; upon reaching the area from the navel up to the heart, there is the supreme emptiness of the object and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) of the subject; and at the time of reaching the area from the throat up to the *uṣṇīṣa*, the innate joy (*sahajānanda*) of both subject and object is obtained.
These are called the four moments (*kṣaṇa*): the moment of variety (*vicitra-kṣaṇa*),...
[The moments are] the moment of maturation (*vipāka*), the moment of dissolution (*vimarda*), and the moment of the absence of characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*).

As for bliss (*ānanda*), it is called the "moment of variety" (*vicitra*); for this is directly realized by relying upon either an external condition, namely a consort (*mudrā*), or an internal condition, namely the yoga of the winds (*vāyu*) or the yoga of the *caṇḍālī*.
Since this arises from the gathering of the collection of varieties, it is therefore designated as the "moment of variety."
The second, however, is the moment of maturation (*vipākakṣaṇa*), because here, due to its variegated nature, no further effort is required;
the third, then, is the moment of destruction (*vimarda*).
After the accomplishment of the transformation, and even after the attainment of that perfect bliss, will there be some further bliss beyond it?
This is not perceived.
This alone is the supreme bliss.
The yogin attains that which is thus established in investigation;
for this very reason, this fourth moment is called the moment of dissolution (*vimardakṣaṇa*).
It is devoid of characteristics; it is to be established in the realization that is free from conceptual proliferation and devoid of defining marks. This alone is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
In the *Hevajra*, it is stated that the four moments (*catuḥkṣaṇa*) are to be joined with an external consort (*bāhyamudrā*).
In the *Pañcakrama* as well, this very state of attaining the fourth ultimate clear light (*paramārthaprabhāsvara*) constitutes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Mantra system.
A detailed exposition of the virtues and faults arising from the practice of *caṇḍālī* is found in the *Caṇḍālībhāvanāvidhi* composed by Tilopa, Samyagvāk, Kapeḍachī, Jamapala, and Pāao.
And in the *Padyākaraposepha*, it is stated:
"The illusory body (*māyākāya*) is taught in the *Hevajra*: 'Self, life-force, being, time, and the person—this is the nature of all things, and it exists in the form of illusion.'"
One should cultivate the meditation on all phenomena as being like an illusion.

There are many varieties of the illusory body (*māyākāya*) according to its own tradition; specifically, there is the variety of the procedure for arising from the illusory body according to the method of cultivation of the Five Stages (*pañcakrama*).

For instance, in the *Pañcakrama*, immediately after the three cognitions, the illusory body is raised by means of the exemplary clear light (*upamā-prabhāsvara*), and through the impure illusory body and the fourth clear light joined with wind, [it is established] in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*).

Having entered [the central channel], immediately after the direct realization of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*), when the subtle wind begins to vibrate in reverse order, that is called the pure illusory body (*viśuddhamāyākāya*). Furthermore, in the Mother Tantra, by meditating on Caṇḍālī, causing the wind to enter the central channel (*madhyamā*), and emitting the bodhicitta, one realizes emptiness through the four joys; subsequently, following innate joy (*sahajānanda*), the arising of the illusory body occurs.
This very [body] is called the pure illusory body (*śuddhamāyākāya*).

In this context, a manual for the practice (*sādhanapaddhati*) of the illusory body produced by means of the exemplary luminosity (*upamāprabhāsvara*) is not found within the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
However, it is indeed within the generation stage (*utpattikrama*)—in the maṇḍala of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) as the receptacle world—that [it occurs].

For the world of sentient beings, it is the appearance of their chosen deity; for sound, it is the appearance of the chosen deity in the form of divine mantras; and for the mind and mental factors, it is the appearance of the chosen deity—this indeed is the pure *māyākāya*.
The realization that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, belonging to the illusory body of union manifested immediately after luminosity—the purified illusory body—is the impure *mahākāya*.

In the *Pañcakrama*, following ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the impure illusory body, which arises even prior to the exemplary luminosity (*upamā-prabhāsvara*) from the purified illusory body, is considered the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).

In the Father Tantras (*pitṛtantra*), having caused the wind to enter the central channel (*madhyamā*), the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) is directly realized through the three cognitions (*trijñāna*). However, in the Mother Tantras (*mātṛtantra*), while the entry of the wind into the central channel is indeed respected, the independent sequence (*svatantrakrama*)—taught as distinct from the clear light, the illusory body (*māyakāya*), and so forth—is not indispensable; rather, it is established by means of apprehending the *caṇḍālī* in the form of an object of focus, or the *bindu*. According to this method of practice, the *bindu*, which is the focal point of the practice, becomes the clear light itself.
Furthermore, there is also a separate method of practice found for quickly recognizing the state of the mind during sleep and its general illusory nature.
Since the king of the mind dwells in the throat center (kaṇṭhacakra) during dreams, the practice of dream yoga is performed at the throat center.
The nature of dream is to be known as the emptiness of coemergent gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) itself;
this is stated in the *Guhyasamāja-pradīpoddyotana-ṭīkā*: "All phenomena are luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Whether in the state of dreaming or the state of waking, everything exists only within the mind of phenomena (*dharmacitta*)."
There is nothing distinct from the mind;
therefore, the dream is described as the innate gnosis (sahajajñāna) that is empty of [conceptual] knowledge (vidyā).
And just as—so too, in this very state where the two types of gnosis are perfectly integrated within the elements, sense-bases, faculties, and so forth.
When the state of emptiness is great, he who is asleep may indeed see a dream due to the influence of the wind-element (*vāta*).

Whether while sleeping or having awakened, he does not conceive of any difference [between them], yet he still longs for the fruits of the dream. Indeed, all phenomena (*dharma*) are like dreams; they are both false and non-false, and there is an absence of both.

This very luminosity (*prabhāsvaratva*) belongs to all phenomena, both objects and subjects, which is perceived in the waking state as external objects and in sleep through the movement of the vital wind (*vāyu*) in the form of dreams.
Therefore, just like the meditation on Caṇḍālī in the waking state, the practice for accomplishing dreams is performed in order to recognize the mind within a dream.
Here, this meditation on dreams is intended for beginners (*ādikarmika*).
Through the mastery of the bodies of Caṇḍālī and Māyā, equanimity arises both in the waking state and in dreams;

therefore, formal practice (*sādhana*) is not strictly necessary. Nevertheless, at the time of sleep, the practitioner should contemplate the chosen deity within his own body, which is composed of the complete network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*).

One should focus the mind one-pointedly and contemplate that within the syllable ‘Aḥ’ at the throat-cakra resides the nature of the speech of all Tathāgatas, consisting of five-colored light; then, thinking, "In the dream state, there is the realization of the dream," one should fall asleep so that even in the dream, the dream is fully recognized as such.

Since even a dream is but a form of the mind itself, one should likewise meditate on the *vajrajāpa* within the throat-cakra (*kaṇṭhacakra*), and having dissolved that into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), remain firmly established in the state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). This is indeed the practice for accomplishing dreams.

Having fully recognized that "a dream occurs within a dream," one should cultivate [the practice] in the dream state exactly as meditation, yoga, and other practices are performed during the waking state.

Thus, for one who has practiced the dream accomplishment (*svapnasādhana*), there is no distinction between night and day. Regarding the subject of dream accomplishment, the *Saṃvarodayatantra* and the *Vajraḍākārṇavatantra* should be paid special attention.

As for the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), the procedure for accomplishing the clear light in the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*) is exactly like that in the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), as was previously stated.
In general, Nāḍapāda’s *Ṣaḍdharmayoga* is considered to be a compendium of the *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage) practices of all the Unsurpassed Tantras (*anuttarayoga-tantras*).
Within this work, the yoga of the illusory body (*māyākāya*), clear light (*prabhāsvara*), vital winds (*vāyu*), and so forth, are taken from the Father Tantra, such as the *Guhyasamāja*;
while the yogas of the candālī, the channels (*nāḍī*), and the drops (*tilaka*) are established respectively according to the Mother Tantras, such as the *Hevajra* and *Cakrasaṃvara*.

The dream state and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are taken from the *Vajraḍākārṇava* and the *Saṃvarodaya*, while the transition [between states] is extracted from the *Sampuṭodbhava* and the *Catuṣpīṭha*.
Furthermore, the method for the yoga with the action seal (*karmamudrā*) within the *caṇḍālī* is upheld from the *Advayatantra*, the *Kālacakra*, and other such works.
Thus, this is called the method for accomplishing the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) of the entire Unsurpassed Tantra.
For this very reason, the method for accomplishing the Six Yogas (*ṣaḍyogasādhanāvidhi*) is found, in some form or another, within the four traditions of Tibet.

Although this is the method for accomplishing all the Unsurpassed Tantras (*anuttaratantra*), it is called the "Yoga of Caṇḍālī" as the central point or the vital core (*marma*) of the Six Yogas; and since this is the extraordinary method of accomplishment for the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), scholars have primarily accepted it as a practice of the Mother Tantra.

In the Father Tantra (*pitṛtantra*), the winds, the three knowledges, the ultimate reality, and the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) are specifically analyzed; and in the Mother Tantra (*mātṛtantra*), the *caṇḍālī*, the four joys (*caturānanda*), and so forth are explained.
This alone is the difference between these two.
As for the practice, the practice of the clear light through the dissolution of the body (*piṇḍānubhedana*) should be understood here as being exactly like that in the Father Tantra.
In this context, a method of practice similar to dreaming has been set forth for the direct realization of the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) within sleep.

Just as prior to falling asleep at the time of lying down, one should pray to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*) so that, upon entering deep sleep, one may fully recognize the clear light; while transforming oneself into the chosen deity, one should meditate on the four-syllable mantra "Anuttara"—which consists of the five wisdoms and the nature of the five Buddhas—within the center of the four petals of the heart-lotus, with the syllable *hūṃ* being dark blue in color and the syllables on the lotus petals being blue.
Having inhaled the air through the breath, one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention).
During exhalation, one should meditate repeatedly that the entire Brahmāṇḍa is pervaded by the five rays [of light], and at the conclusion of the inhalation, these dissolve back into the mantras.

At times during exhalation, one should meditate that all the worlds of the vessel (*bhājanaloka*) and the worlds of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) are pervaded by the five rays; and at the time of inhalation, may all these mantras produce an even greater radiance of light.
Such a meditation as this should be performed:
for each individual syllable of the mantra, [starting] with the letter *a* (in the sequence *a-nu*) within this phoneme *nu*,...
In that very same sequence, *nu-ta*, *ta-ra*,
and *ra-hu*.
Having caused the resonance of the syllable *hūṃ* and the *tilaka* of resonance to dissolve into that very state, one should remain concentrated therein.
By thus meditating on the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), having fallen asleep, the clear light can be directly realized through the force of its continuity during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

As for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): generally, it is the period from when a sentient being, due to ignorance, wanders within the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) until they are able to emerge from above it and attain knowledge. This duration constitutes the intermediate state.

It is possible to establish three divisions: 1) the intermediate state of the arising of nature (*prakṛtyutpatti-antarābhava*), 2) the intermediate state of the suffering of death (*mṛtyuduḥkhāntarābhava*), and 3) the intermediate state of the *dharmadhātu* (*dharmadhātu-antarābhava*).
In reality, however, the intermediate state is simply the ignorance of the innate wisdom (*sahajajñāna*) that exists throughout the three times;
according to its various states, many divisions of this can be established.

Those [beings] which arise in various forms through the movement of the wind—though grossly speaking, the intermediate state itself is called the *antarābhava* (intermediate existence) because it exists between death and birth. As it is said in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "That which exists here between the state of death and the state of rebirth is the *antarābhava*."
The proof of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which severs the path of the six yogas, has been explained.
It is precisely in the intermediate state that awakening arises in an inseparable form as the body of union—that is, the illusory body (*māyākāya*) which is the ultimate clear light.
Therefore, this is called the "severer of the path."

According to the system of the three bodies (*trikāya*), if perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is to be attained while still alive, then it must be possible within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and not during the state of being alive;
for without the relinquishing of this body of maturation (*vipākakāya*), the arising of the subtle illusory body (*māyākāya*) and the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) in union is never possible.
This body, having arisen from the elements, cannot be the body of clear light.

The reason for this is precisely that both followers of the Pāramitāyāna and followers of the Mantrayāna consider the Buddha to have attained enlightenment at the very beginning in the Akaniṣṭha realm;

they regard Śākyamuni and others as being merely emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). However, in the non-dual *Tantra-kālacakra*, it is held that by consuming the contaminated aggregates (*sāsravaskandha*) of this ripening body (*vipākadeha*) through the gateway of the stainless great bliss-mark (*anāsravamahāsukhatilaka*), one attains a new body resembling a rainbow.
In this context, it is not considered that the attainment of perfect enlightenment occurs through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

It is stated in the *Kālacakra*: "Therefore, the Dharmadhātu bestows here the moment of innate bliss that is motionless; having drawn in by means of the vital breath all the Māras of the afflictions who have entered the paths of the [six] flavors, and having struck them down, the yogi—having entered the path—attains in this very life supernatural powers, the stage of omniscience, and the status of a teacher of the three worlds, bypassing death and any other subsequent birth."
That is to say, if one was unable to attain the supreme state during one's lifetime, what will one obtain in a future birth?
In the Mother Tantras, there lies the inherent greatness of the practice for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because this very state is extremely subtle and powerful.
As it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*: "He possesses a body of the same kind [as his future birth], is visible to the pure divine eye, and moves with the speed of the supernatural power of karma."
Possessing all the sense-faculties, resistant, irreversible, and endowed with fragrance.
By this very reason, there is ease in arising within the body of union (*yuganaddha*).
This practice consists of these three divisions: the taking of the *dharmakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya*, and the *nirmāṇakāya* as the path.

In the general practice of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), at the time of death, the practitioner [contemplates] the five aggregates, the four elements, the six sense bases, the five objects, the five supporting consciousnesses, and the twenty-five principles.

In the procedure for the state of absorption (*layavidhi*), the characteristics that are about to arise should be understood according to the manual of the *Pitṛtantra*. For instance, immediately after the exhaustion of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) based on the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), as well as the earth element, the eye faculty, and objects such as visible forms, a mirage-like appearance arises within the mind, and an external bodily radiance is seen to be both vanished and indistinct.

The realization of the *dharmakāya* occurs after the exhaustion of the external gross elements and internal subtle conceptualizations. Following the sequence of *āloka*, *ālokābhāsa*, and *ālokopalabdhi*, the white semen obtained from the father—emerging from the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus—and the red blood obtained from the mother—which moves upward below the navel-center—unite into a single flavor within the heart-lotus. Therein, they become non-dual with the *prabhāsvara* (clear light) along with the *sarvaśūnya* (total emptiness).

At that moment, by relying on a similar cultivation performed during one's lifetime and through its power, having fully realized it, the very abiding of that [nature] is the single state of the *dharmakāya*.
This state, in which the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) abides in non-dual form, is called the "union" (*melana*) of the son-practitioner with the mere luminosity.
For one's own mind, abiding in its natural state, is the mother.
And by the power of spiritual practice (*sādhana*), that which has been fully realized exists as the Son (*putra*).
The basis (*āśraya*) itself is the path (*mārga*), and the path itself is the fruit (*phala*), which remains indestructible.

Here, this must certainly be understood: although the basis, the path, and the fruit exist separately according to their different states (*avasthābheda*), suchness (*tathatā*) is indeed one; likewise, in this very state, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is itself the Enjoyment-body (*sambhogakāya*).
The enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are, in fact, mutually non-different.
It should not be understood that because [the Buddha] abides in the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), the enjoyment body would not be required therein.
For the enjoyment body (sambhogakāya) does not possess the nature of the dharma-body;
rather, the enjoyment body itself is called the dharma-body. In this context, the non-duality of body and gnosis exists by virtue of its being the embodiment of gnosis.
Gnosis alone is the Tathāgata;
gnosis itself is the nature of the Tathāgata.
In that state, distinctions such as "possessing the thought of awakening," "possessing compassion," or "possessing many forms" are not applicable.
These states are said to belong to the *dharmakāya*, the *bodhicitta*, and compassion.

Therefore, it was previously established in the context of the general meaning of the *niṣpannakrama* that in the Vajrayāna, *bodhicitta*—which is merely the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)—attains the status of the goal (*sādhya*). This is precisely the excellence of the Vajrayāna.

If the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is not able to abide in the *dharmakāya*, then, having been aroused within the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), he will manifest as a being in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) immediately after the appearance of light.
And that which is called the subtle body will,

at that time, be raised up within the *saṃbhogakāya* by the power of the accomplished means, just as a fish rises from water. Thus, this very rising from the *saṃbhogakāya* is liberation from the *saṃbhogakāya*.
If the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) were not to arise within the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*), then it would become a sentient being in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The duration of a sentient being's intermediate state is at least seven days and at most forty-nine days.
After forty-nine days, the sentient being will certainly take birth.
Therefore, the funeral rites and other ceremonies for the deceased are performed for up to forty-nine days.

By the power of his previous merit, the being attains birth in a pure realm such as Sukhāvatī; or, entering the womb of a mother at will, he takes birth and gradually attains perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

This very [attainment] is liberation from the perspective of the *nirmāṇakāya*. In terms of its essential nature, however, the method for attaining the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya* consists precisely in the further cultivation of the method for attaining the *dharmakāya*. This is done by integrating that attainment with the circumstances of one's own life—at this very time of life or at the time of death—and by taking as a basis the signs manifested when the winds have entered the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*). This process is called "taking the *dharmakāya* as the path."
Thus, in order to take the three bodies (*trikāya*) as the path, one must first understand the method for manifesting the three bodies at the actual time of death.
For the purpose of spiritual practice (*sādhana*) is indeed said to be liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), by recognizing death during one's lifetime.
Here, a question may arise: such recognition will not be possible at the time of death, because death—
In reality, there is not merely one state of intense sleep, but rather various distinct states within the continuous flow of one’s own mind.
Therefore, even during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is possible to take birth at will in the *saṃbhogakāya* or in realms such as Sukhāvatī.
Just as verses we remembered in childhood are recalled even in old age, [so too are these states retained].
In the past, we did not become acquainted with a wicked person or a place until after many years had passed.
Just as a potter’s wheel, once set in motion, continues to spin rapidly on its own momentum while the potter fashions the jars,
so too a practitioner who recognizes the signs arising at the time of death is able to attain the fruit of bringing [the mind] onto the path.

We are able to describe transition (*saṃkramaṇa*), transference (*saṃkramaṇa*), or even emergence (*utkrānti*) through general terms as being characterized by a constant flow and a nature of movement. Therefore, although the momentariness of the luminous mind consists of a continuous stream and is subject to transformation at every instant—like the flame of a lamp—it nevertheless possesses an uninterrupted quality of movement.
Even while existing in this way, it remains inexpressible within its own luminous nature and arises as the essence of suchness (*tathatā*).
The thorough knowledge of its true nature is itself the transition from ignorance to knowledge. Although it is indeed one,

just as a bird flying through the air by means of a wind-vehicle over the middle of the great ocean will, after wandering about, return to that very same place, so too we, having relied upon various different methods, [return] in the end to that very same [reality].
We shall abide in the center.
Regarding this distinction, in the treatises there is mention of the transition into the *dharmakāya* and the transition into the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Methods of accomplishment such as the powerful and principal transference, the transference of consciousness into a pure field, and the transference into another's body are found; among these,
the transference into the three bodies and so forth, which occurs within the practice of the intermediate state, is precisely the taking of the three bodies as the path.

This practice of transference (*saṃkramaṇa-sādhanā*) exists for the purpose of benefiting those to be trained and leading them correctly onto the path, as well as for one's own entry into another’s body and for transference into a pure realm such as that of a king. The practice of the upward departure (*utkrānti*) and the practice of transference are explained in detail in the third chapter of the eighth kalpa of the *Sampuṭodbhava Tantra*.

In the nineteenth chapter of the *Saṃvarodayatantra*, titled "The Yoga of the Vision of the Signs of Death and the Transference of Consciousness," after demonstrating the preliminary signs of death, [the text describes] the procedure for unifying one's own mind—the subtle vital wind and mind located within the heart-lotus—at the time of death.

By means of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), it is led upward and expelled from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*); then, through the mind of the Buddha Amitābha residing in a pure land, or of the meditated Vajradhara, it is joined in a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
It was thus established:
"When the time of death has arrived, one should employ the supreme yoga of departure;
one should fill the channels leading to the nine gates by means of inhalation (pūraka)."
One should block the gateway by means of *kumbhaka* (retention),
purifying the cavity of the gateway;
one should expel the universe by means of *recaka* (exhalation) and bring about the state that is tranquil and peaceful.

Thus, at the time of death, having closed the other openings such as the eyes, ears, mouth, and nostrils, and having placed the mind itself within the seed-syllable along with the force of the vital breath (vāyu),
one effects the transition by propelling it upward. If it exits through another opening instead of the [intended] aperture, then the practitioner who has met death will obtain birth in various wombs.

And as it is stated in the Saṃvarodayatantra: "Listen, O Guhyaka! According to the distinction between superior and inferior, the navel is for those desiring heaven, and by means of the *bindu*, for those possessing a body of form."
Above that is the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and the pure [state] is divided according to those destinies;
from the two nostrils one becomes a yakṣa, and likewise from the two ears a kiṃnara.
O Goddess, if [the seed] enters through the two eyes, one will become a king of men;
if through the mouth, a preta; and likewise, if through the urine, a lower animal.

By exhaling [the breath] downwards, they go to hell; otherwise is the path to liberation. To perform the ritual slaughter of a deity at an improper time when the moment for transcendence has not arrived leads to hell.

Therefore, during his lifetime, the practitioner, having visualized himself as the chosen deity (*iṣṭadeva*), should fix the mind together with the breath upon the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*. While reciting that syllable, he should lead [the mind] from the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) up to the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Then, while reciting the letter *ka*, he should bring the wheel of channels (*nāḍī-cakra*) down to the base of the heart and establish it in stability.
This is the very method for the practice of transference (*saṃkramaṇa*).

If the practitioner attains proficiency in the egress of the mind (*cittotkrānti*), then he is capable of entering even another's body. Even when the gross body of another person has died, if their internal triple-consciousness (*trivijñāna*) has not perished, then by the power of his own practice, he is able to transfer the consciousness of the deceased to pure lands and other such realms.
For this very reason, the practitioner established this path to liberation even without [the usual] meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Since the subtle body of the deceased attains birth in realms such as Sukhāvatī and from there achieves perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*),
this very path for accomplishing the welfare of others has been taught.
Thus, although this *Ṣaḍdharmayoga* of Nāḍapāda is the essence of all Anuttara Tantras, its primary basis for the practice of the six yogas is indeed the *Caṇḍālīyoga*.
Therefore, this has been set forth here for the practice of Mātṛtantra.

It includes the method for the practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) of the non-dual tantra (*advayatantra*, namely Kālacakra), a general introduction to the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), and a general basis for the Kālacakra completion stage; like other Unsurpassed Tantras (*anuttaratantra*), its foundation is likewise the vajra-body (*vajradeha*).
Among the channels (*nāḍī*), the three that are preeminent— Lalanā, Rasanā, and Avadhūtī— are known by the names Sun, Moon, and Rāhu.
They consist of the three elements of water,
fire, and space, and they facilitate the movement of semen, blood, and wind within the white, red, and dark-colored [channels].
In this [work], a description of the six chakras is found:
a channel-wheel (nāḍicakra) with four petals in the uṣṇīṣa,
sixteen petals in the forehead, and thirty-two petals in the throat.
The channel-petal wheels are described as having eight petals at the heart, sixty-four petals at the navel, and thirty-two at the secret places.
The practice of the Kālacakra is performed through the four types of service or by means of the system of six-limbed yoga.
In the Kālacakra, service is performed with the five nectars and so forth, with the oceans and vajras, and with the recitation of mantras and other such rites.
Through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs], there is "near-attainment" (*upasiddhi*) by means of the nectar born from the vajra-lotus.
Meditation on the state of the single flavor of the three vajras and the lotus, beginning with bliss (*ānanda*), constitutes the "practice" (*sādhana*).
That which becomes truly unfailing through the union of wisdom and means, by virtue of the subtle yoga, is indeed the "great practice" (*mahāsādhana*).

The practice of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is fixed within the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), for the state to be attained consists of the three vajras: Body-Vajra, Speech-Vajra, and Mind-Vajra.
Through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one brings about the accomplishment of the major and minor marks for that body whose perfection has not yet occurred.

By means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and retention (*dhāraṇā*), the practitioner, with respect to the wind which is the root cause of speech, accomplishes either the speech of the Omniscient One or the sixty-four Brahma-voices.
Thus, through two of the limbs of yoga, the vajras of body, speech, and mind are attained.

The great master Tsongkhapa, elucidating the procedure for the sequence of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), stated: "The attainment of the form of non-dual identity, in which the fruit—great bliss—is inseparable from emptiness, is produced by a cause of the same class (*sajātīyahetu*) alone, and not by one of a different class."

Therefore, the very abiding of one’s own mind— filled with passion for the Mother-deity manifested in the form of the union of mother and father within the visualized form of the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) which is empty by its own nature— is itself the attainment of the bliss of the unchanging (akṣara-sukha), or rather, the yoga of meditative concentration (dhyāna-yoga). Furthermore, at the time of the practice of recollection (anusmṛti), by swallowing the bodhicitta through Caṇḍālī and bringing it as far as the jewel-wheel of the crown of the head, the attainment of the four joys occurs.
In this context, meditation is precisely the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) of the fourth syllable.
At that very moment, when the *caṇḍālī* blazes within the navel, the yogi directly perceives the divine image (*devabimba*), and therein the bliss of passion arises.
This is indeed *anusmṛti*.

For the arising of recollection (*anusmṛti*), one should stabilize the wind within the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) by means of retention (*dhāraṇā*) so that it becomes motionless, and thereby ignite the *caṇḍālī*.
Thus, the very stabilization of the two winds within the central channel is designated as "retention.
To attain the state of retention, the wind flowing through the *lalanā* and *rasanā* must be made to enter the central channel by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

That which is called the yoga of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the cultivation of the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), which is possible only immediately after the accomplishment of the eleven characteristics that are about to arise day and night through the method of the yoga of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
When the eleven characteristics have been directly realized through withdrawal, they attain firmness by means of the yoga of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Thus, the sequence of the six-limbed yoga is established.
The sequence of the six-limbed yoga in the *Kālacakra* is as follows: withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the non-engagement of the ten objects and sense-faculties within the body;
discernment (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), analysis (*vicāra*), joy (*rati*), and immovable bliss (*acalasukha*) constitute meditation (*dhyāna*), which is also one-pointedness of mind.

Prāṇāyāma has two paths; there may also be a stumbling into the central channel. The entry of the vital breath (prāṇa) into the *bindu* occurs when both movements are destroyed; and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is one-pointedness of mind.

When the vision of Caṇḍālī truly occurs within the body, that is recollection (*anusmṛti*) in space. Samādhi is the non-emission of bliss by means of the nature of wisdom and method, within the image of gnosis (*jñānabimba*).

This means of accomplishment of the Sustainer of the Universe may be of three kinds according to the distinctions of "soft" (mṛdu) and so forth; there are three mudrās with three measures, corresponding to the threefold movement: the physical action, the mental resolve, and the divine.

A detailed exposition of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) was previously presented here in brief as the *Ṣaḍaṅgayogavidhi*; now, its specific practice is introduced in due order. First is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). This is divided into four sections known as the nature of the object, the means, the method, and the result.

The visual and other cognitions of ordinary beings proceed toward their respective objects—forms, smells, tastes, and so forth—through the doors of their own sense organs, just as honey-bees experience the nectar of flowers.
The word *prati* in *pratyāhāra* is employed in eleven senses;
however, in this context, it has only the sense of negation (*niṣedha*).
The word *āhāra*, on the other hand, signifies "abandonment" (*tyāga*).

Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is precisely the severing of the connection between the five sense-faculties and the five objects, withdrawing them into consciousness, and causing the five sense-faculties—which are of the nature of gnosis—to enter into the fivefold object that is the nature of luminosity. This is the intended meaning: having abandoned the appearance of generality, the state of abiding in the appearance of gnosis is indeed pratyāhāra.

And it is stated in the *Guhyasamājottaratantra*: "The withdrawal of the ten sense faculties from all their respective objects of activity for the sake of attaining the [true] food is called *pratyāhāra*.
Vajrapāṇi, in his commentary on the *Cakrasaṃvara*, established that the very cultivation of the characteristic of space is the practice of *pratyāhāra*.
The abiding of the non-manifesting mind has the characteristic of space;
this very cultivation of space is considered the cultivation of emptiness.
Through the practice of this, the power to integrate the non-conceptual wind (*nirvikalpa-vāyu*) within the central channel (*madhyamā*) is attained.

Regarding the method of practice, the *Kālacakra Tantra* states: "Withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the tenfold Lord of Victors. And likewise: "Withdrawal is the non-engagement of the ten objects and their perceiving subjects within the body;
by means of withdrawal, the yogi, being devoid of sense-objects, is empowered by all mantras. Through such statements, the method for practicing withdrawal was established.

In brief, the practice for accomplishing withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is simply the turning of the mind toward emptiness after severing the connection between the object and the subject, such as the grasping of forms and so forth.
As it is said: "Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added.
Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated."

In accordance with these words, the means of accomplishing withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is simply the mind’s abiding in its true state as it is, free from both that which is to be removed and that which is to be added.

Alternatively, just as a person sees their own true form in a mirror, so too, by meditating on the form of one's chosen deity within the mirror of one's own mind, the means of accomplishing withdrawal is the state of the mind being restrained from engaging with external objects.

For those who abide in the aforementioned states, the four signs beginning with smoke appear during the night, and the six characteristics beginning with flame appear during the day, as explained in the *Kālacakra*: "By those whose minds are unattached to space, whose eyes are unblinking, and who have entered the vajra-path, from emptiness there arise smoke, a mirage, a clearly visible pure firefly, and a lamp;
then flame, moon, sun, and vajra, as well as the supreme digit and the drop. In the midst of that, the Buddha-image is seen—the manifold Saṃbhogakāya, free from sense objects."
In this regard, it has also been established within the definition that the *saṃbhogakāya* reflected therein is not some external object, but rather one's own mind itself.

Within that [mind], the image of the Omniscient One is like the sun in water—unclouded, possessing all colors, and manifesting in every form; one's own mind is devoid of objects, and there is no other mind but this very mind.
When the characteristics of the objects and so forth of emptiness have been revealed, one meditates on the divine image according to the instructions of the Guru.

By this, the channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and other practices attain firmness; and finally, even the bodhicitta gradually becomes well-stabilized, which becomes the cause for attaining great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

It is also stated in the *Kālacakra*: "In emptiness, one should meditate on the path of smoke and so forth by means of the Guru’s restrictive rules until the limit of the universe; therefore, one makes the prāṇa and apāna winds stable within the channel-wheels."
Afterwards, the yogi brings about the cessation of the bodhicitta, just as a planet [eclipses] the moon; therefore, whatever is desired here in this life may be attained within a few days.
Dhyāna is simply the steadiness of the mind upon its object;
and dhyāna is the foundation of yoga.
Through its firmness, other yogas based upon it become stable.

In the characteristics illuminated by luminosity, the very natures of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) consist of one-pointedness characterized by the joy and bliss of the reversal of conceptual construction through wisdom.
Furthermore, in the *Guhyasamāja-uttara-tantra*: "Conceptual construction is said to be meditation; that meditation is fivefold:
vitarka and vicāra..."
Joy as well as bliss, and likewise one-pointedness of mind— these five are the constituents of dhyāna.

It is also stated in the *Kālacakra*: "Wisdom (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), passion (*rati*), immovable bliss (*acalasukha*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and one-pointed mind (*ekacitta*)."
That is to say, the contemplation of the eleven characteristics of the luminosity is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Conceptualization (*kalpanā*) grasps phenomena;
and here, conceptualization consists in the knowledge of the characteristic of form as being empty of the notion of a phenomenon.

Vitarka (investigation) is not merely the mental deliberation upon the knowledge of the characteristics of the nature of emptiness, but rather the direct experience of it— that is, the production of an experience consisting of certainty that is free from both object and subject.
(Mīmāṃsā) Prīti (joy) is the experience of bliss that occurs when the external body and the internal mind are sustained by dhyāna (meditative absorption).
The second [dhyāna] is the very mind whose nature consists of bliss (*sukhātmaka-svarūpa-citta*); this is called "bliss" (*sukha*), which is immutable bliss (*akṣara-sukha*).
And by means of this, pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) is obtained.

In this context, according to the *Kālacakra*, by the statement "in the center of that, the Buddha-image, the manifold Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) devoid of objects," it is shown that through this [practice], the Enjoyment Body—which constitutes the extraordinary characteristic of meditative absorption—manifests, and the knowledges such as the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) are attained.
As stated in the *Kālacakra*: "O Lord of Men, through the yoga of meditation, one becomes pure and attains the five superknowledges."

Prāṇāyāma is the meaning of the term *prāṇāyāma*, which refers to the drawing out (*āyāma*), restraint (*nirodha*), and so forth of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), or its expansion. By obstructing the movement of the vital breath, the nectar of immortality—that is, long life—is attained;
and simultaneously with prāṇāyāma, great bliss is experienced.
In the Kālacakra, having accomplished the nāgas and so forth, the excellent gods and humans are to be accomplished by the yogin;
having accomplished the smoke-signs and so forth, the middling ones who cause fear of death are to be accomplished.
Having accomplished the vital breaths and so forth, the drops (bindus) in which the moon has melted must be accomplished;
having accomplished true bliss, the all-pervading body of the coemergent Victor (Sahaja-jina) must be accomplished.

Through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), immediately upon the manifestation of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) in the form of emptiness, death is conquered by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),

and the attainment of the vajra-body occurs. Within the vajra-body, the primary purpose of breath control is precisely the attainment of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) by means of the *tilaka* [the seminal drop], in due order.
Without attaining a vajra-body and long life, it is impossible to reach the supreme state in this life;
therefore, first, the attainment of immeasurable longevity must be achieved.

At the outset, the body of all the Victors must be protected by the practitioner for the sake of accomplishment, because without a body there is no accomplishment, nor is the supreme bliss attained in this birth.

Therefore, for the sake of the body's purpose, one should practice the yoga of the channels every day; once the body is perfected, all other perfections within the abode of the three worlds come under one's service.

The practice of *prāṇāyāma* is essential for the purpose of protecting the body. As it is stated in the *Kālacakra*: "Prāṇāyāma has two paths; when there is a faltering, the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs in the central channel.
The path of the *lalanā* and *rasanā* on the left and right dissolves into the central channel."

Because the five elements beginning with earth and the five sense objects flowing within the *rasanā* have dissolved, they become tenfold in form. As stated in the *Sekoddeśaṭīkā*: "One should recite [the mantra] by means of the undivided central channel (*madhyamā*), which possesses the nature of the five mandalas of the *lalanā*. Regarding the procedure for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) in the *Kālacakra*: "When the mouth is closed, the entire external wind is drawn in with force by the *prāṇa* through both nostrils; then the *apāna* wind is struck, resembling lightning and fire."
Through the practice of yoga over time, one attains a state of equilibrium within the midst of the moon, sun, and fire; it removes hunger and thirst from the body and bestows immortality.

Nāgārjuna clarified the practice of *prāṇāyāma* by extracting it from the *Pañcakrama*, the *Caturdevīparipṛcchāvyākhyātantra*, the *Samājottaratantra*, the *Vajramālā*, and other tantras; the practice of *prāṇāyāma* is also analyzed in the *Hevajra* and *Saṃvarodayatantra*.
The intention of these texts is precisely this: one should draw the five light-filled winds from twelve finger-breadths up to sixteen finger-breadths and place them at the tip of the nose.
When the breath is situated in the navel region, one should forcefully draw the outgoing air upward, unify it with the inhaled breath during *prāṇāyāma*, and perform *kumbhaka*.
A long duration for the retention of *kumbhaka* is required;
the exhalation must not be taken up simultaneously.
Having relinquished something, that bondage should be performed.

Due to the complete abandonment of exhalation (*praśvāsa*), the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) cannot remain for a long time. The mind should be fixed upon these syllables: *oṃ* during inhalation (*śvāsa*), *hūṃ* during retention (*kumbhaka*), and *āḥ* during exhalation (*praśvāsa*).

Therefore, *oṃ hūṃ āḥ* is a constituent part of *prāṇāyāma*. In some traditions, *āḥ* is applied during retention (*kumbhaka*), *hūṃ* during exhalation (*praśvāsa*), and *oṃ* during inhalation (*śvāsa*); alternatively, according to the *Mahāmāyātantra*, *oṃ* is for exhalation, *hūṃ* for retention, and *āḥ* for inhalation—the mind should be focused upon these syllables.
During the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, the movement of the breath gradually becomes increasingly subtle.
Within the limit of inhalation and exhalation, mindfulness remains fixed upon its own object by placing a light cloth or the hand at the nose.
This method is also taught even without the recitation of a mantra from a rosary.
Even in the ordinary state, the inhalation should be perceived with intensity, while the exhalation should be perceived with slowness alone.

The method for the practice of *prāṇāyāma* is thus clearly elucidated in the *Kālacakra*: "When the [inner] image (*bimba*) is perceived, one should perform the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) at every daily occasion, until the wheel of rays, revolving and encircling one's own body, is seen. Within six months, the mind of the yogis, which has reached the path of equanimity, becomes devoid of touch; from the end of passion and non-passion, even for a single moment, the number of breaths of the All-pervading Lord increases."

After the manifestation of the reflection of the divine form through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) until a wheel of light-filled wind is perceived revolving within one's own body. Through this practice and the integration of breath control, fire is generated; there occurs a clear vision of the subtle channels throughout the entire body, as well as of the wind moving therein and of the semen, blood, and other constituents.
Thus, immediately after the emergence of these appearances, by the practice of *prāṇāyāma* for a period of six months, semen, blood, and other such elements become clearly visible;
and by this, the emission of semen is restrained.
Thereafter, even without the embrace of the two organs, the yogi should enter by way of the path of immutable great bliss in the form of emptiness.

As it is stated in the *Kālacakra Tantra*: "That power which proceeds from the center of the navel to the supreme state, the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], the end of the digits—that [power] is completely restrained at the navel, resembling lightning and fire, and arisen in the form of a staff."
Moving with a soft and playful gait, she indeed caused the wheel to rotate within the central channel until, by force, it touched the external skin at the aperture of the *uṣṇīṣa* like a needle.
At that time, one should forcefully propel the downward-voiding wind (āpāna) upward;
when the pair of winds is restrained, it pierces the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) and proceeds to the supreme city.
Thus, through the mental cultivation of the various vajras together with their objects, one attains the state of moving through space;
furthermore, this Viśvamātā becomes the very nature of the five superknowledges for yogins.
Power (*śakti*) arises from the element of breath (*prāṇavāyu*); from the element of earth, it extends over twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);

the water element over thirteen finger-breadths; the fire element over fourteen finger-breadths; from the element of air, it extends over fifteen finger-breadths; and the space element extends over sixteen finger-breadths.

Through the medium of one’s own nose, when the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—flowing through the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels respectively—enter into the *madhyamā*, they become as stainless as lightning, taking on the very nature of the syllable *huṃ*.
By means of Haṭhayoga, gradually causing [the vital energy] to ascend from the navel-cakra, one pierces the knots of all the channels and reaches as far as the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa).
Then, having emerged externally, the practitioner is capable of attaining accomplishments such as entering the bodies of others, becoming a Khecarī, and proceeding to the pure stages.
In the Ṣaḍyoga of Nāḍapāda, this is described as "descending" (saṃkramaṇa) and "ascending" (utkramaṇa).
The practitioner, having caused the great bliss to flow upward as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahyarandhra*) and then directing it downward, enters the center of the jewel-wheel (*maṇicakra*).

This is clearly stated in the *Kālacakra Tantra*: "By means of the winds striking together, the crest of fire like lightning melts the moon at the crown. Whichever drop (*bindu*) is melted from this flows down to the throat and heart, and then to the navel and secret place.

That vibration and fluidity of the drop which reaches the tip of the vajra-jewel, when restrained, bestows the moment of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*) at the tip of the banner, provided that the stream of drops is not emitted."
This procedure for the downward and upward movements is assisted by the terminology of the four joys (*ānanda*) and the four moments (*kṣaṇa*) found in other texts.
By expelling the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) to the outside, the practitioner may even encounter death;
therefore, one must practice the downward and upward movements continuously.
In the Mother Tantra, this very method is the procedure for the practice of Caṇḍālī.

In the Kālacakra: "Breath control (*praṇāyāma*) bestows the fruit of universal equanimous bliss as far as it reaches the crown of the head; beyond that, it is undesirable, causing the fear of death and being the cause of the destruction of the aggregates (*skandha*).

Having pierced the *uṣṇīṣa*, the yogi who proceeds toward the state of supreme bliss should indeed be applied [to that path]; even in the absence of the aggregates, he enters into equanimous bliss, though he remains renowned in the world."
This practice is also performed through the service of *mudrā*.

Regarding this subject, it is said in that very same work: "The entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the center; the binding of the movements of the sun and moon in the right and left channels; the mind absorbed in supreme bliss during the application of *mudrā*; the awakening of the *vajra*;

or the sound of the *vajra* [in the form of] the splashing of water from one's own hands; the non-emission of the seed for the sake of bliss—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru, which brings about bliss and removes the fear of death."

When breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been mastered, the practitioner will be honored by the Bodhisattvas; having been prophesied by the Buddhas, he will attain great accomplishment (mahāsiddhi). Here, the definitive meaning (nītārtha) of the term "Bodhisattva" refers to the sense faculties (indriya).

That is to say, the accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as the divine eye, the divine ear, and so forth, will be attained. Regarding this point in the *Kālacakra*, it is also said: "Therefore, the motionless bliss, the innate (*sahaja*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), bestows here even for a moment;
having drawn in all the afflictions and Māras that have entered the courses of the [six] flavors by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."

If a yogi who has entered the path should die here in this very birth, he then proceeds to supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the stage of omniscience, and the status of being the teacher of the three worlds; yet, due to that [death], he undergoes another birth through the grasping of that [intermediate state].

Regarding *dhāraṇā*: although the word *dhāraṭā* is employed in the sense of both the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), here the intended meaning of *dhāraṇā* is the stabilization of the bodhicitta within the *tilaka* (spot) of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*). Generally, this limb of yoga called *dhāraṇā* consists of the abiding of the wind—which flows through the left and right channels, as well as above and below—in the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) at the *tilaka*, or alternatively, within the five or six channel-wheels (*nāḍī-cakra*).
In reality, *dhāraṇā* is precisely the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) upon the *tilaka* located at the wheel of the forehead through the practice of specific [concentration].
In the *Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā* it is also stated: "Having meditated on one's own mantra in the heart, one should place it within the *bindu* of the vital breath.
One should hold that jewel which is restrained and beyond the senses; this is known as *dhāraṇā*."

As long as the mixing of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths has not occurred at the navel-center (*nābhicakra*), the cultivation of *kumbhaka* (retention) in other centers such as the heart is not possible.
Therefore, by means of *prāṇāyāma*, once the secret signs have manifested through the union of *prāṇa* and *apāna* in the field of the navel, one must accomplish *dhāraṇā* (concentration).

Through *prāṇāyāma*, having gradually rendered the air free from coming and going within the navel-center, the heart-center, and the throat-center, the very act of dissolving it into the tilaka located on the forehead is *dhāraṇā*.

It is also stated in the *Kālacakra Tantra*: "Having assumed the cross-legged posture, with the mouth wide open, one should not touch the teeth against one another. The external wind, drawn in, enters the center of the navel as the cool nectar.
It removes heat, hunger, and thirst in the excellent body when it is properly restrained. Furthermore, the white drop, encircled by its own retinue on the forehead, releases nectar."
It is also stated in the *Guhyasamājottaratantra*: "Having meditated on one's own mantra in the heart, one should place it within the vital drop (*prāṇabindu*).
Having restrained the jewel of the senses and maintaining [the focus], this is known as 'retention' (*dhāraṇā*)."
The empty form (*śūnyarūpa*), which has been cultivated through the limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), is further nourished by the limb of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Having restrained the channels, winds, and the *tilaka* by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the *tilaka* is stabilized in the central channel (*madhyamā*) through the limb of retention (*dhāraṇā*).
This very process of bringing about the recollection of that empty form—which has been made firm by withdrawal and concentration and is like space—is the yoga-limb known as recollection (*anusmṛti*).
In the *Guhyasamājottaratantra*: "Having meditated upon that which is to be recollected, one should then clearly recollect its form;
this is to be known as 'recollection' (*anusmṛti*), for a mental image arises therein."

In the *Sekoddeśaṭīkā* as well, this view is made very clear: "Recollection" (*anusmṛti*) is the expansion—that is, the pervasion throughout the entire expanse of space—of the relative truth, which consists of the manifestations of the three realms, once it has been stabilized through the practices of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Buston, clarifying the definition of recollection, stated: "By the power of accomplishing the limb of retention (*dhāraṇā*), one ignites the *caṇḍālī* within the navel center; [recollection is] the manifestation of one’s chosen deity, who is non-conceptual and consists of the three realms, resembling a reflected image, within the nature of that *caṇḍālī*."
The state of appearance itself is *anusmṛti*.
And in the *Kālacakra Tantra* it is also said: "The vision of Caṇḍālī that occurs within the body and in space is indeed *anusmṛti*.
For the practitioner, there are three divisions according to the distinction of weak, middling, and superior faculties."

The superior practitioner is one who practices meditative absorption together with infinite great mudrās that are like particles of Mount Sumeru; the middling practitioner is one who is absorbed together with the great mudrā consisting of gnosis; and the inferior practitioner is one who is absorbed together with the action great mudrā. As it is said in the *Kālacakra*: "This practice of the Lord of the Universe may also be of three kinds, according to the divisions of 'soft' and so forth."
The three mudrās, consisting of three measures, are the divine [states] of karma, saṃkalpa, and divya, by virtue of the threefold movement.

The place of practice (*sādhanāsthala*) is thus clearly elucidated in the *Kālacakra*: "These four mudrās, which grant the fruit of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), should be meditated upon by the yogi at all times and in all places—
whether in a village, a forest, a cremation ground, an impure or pure dwelling, a brothel, or a temple."
Through the practice of incantations for those of high and low caste, and through the enjoyment of food, drink, and other such things that bestow physical strength and happiness.

In general, just as the practice of the Vajra Body is performed through the branch of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), firmness therein is attained through the branch of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and just as the practice of the Vajra Speech is carried out by controlling the vital winds (*prāṇa*) through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and stability therein is achieved through retention (*dhāraṇā*), in the same way, the Vajra Mind is accomplished through recollection (*anusmṛti*) and through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
And having attained that firmness, the supreme state is reached.

In the *Kālacakra*, distinct from the Father Tantra and Mother Tantra, the existence of four drops (*bindu*) is individually accepted within the channel-wheels (*nāḍīcakra*) of the crown, throat, and heart.
These drops, when set in motion by the vital wind (*vāyu*) during the four states beginning with waking, produce various delusions.
Just as in the waking state, all the upward-moving winds are gathered in the crown wheel (uṣṇīṣacakra) and all the downward-moving winds are gathered in the navel wheel (nābhicakra),
producing merely a diverse appearance and an appearance of delusion.
Even in the state of dreaming, the upward-moving winds are gathered at the throat-cakra and the downward-moving winds at the secret organ; these produce mere sound and the delusion of speech.

In deep sleep, all the upward-moving winds gather at the heart-cakra and the downward-moving winds at the jewel-cakra (maṇicakra); becoming unified, non-conceptual, and indistinct, they produce delusion.

When a man and woman reach the state of union, all the upward-moving winds (*ūrdhvabhāgīyavāyu*) are gathered at the navel wheel (*nābhicakra*), and the downward-moving winds (*adhovāyu*) are gathered at the tip of the secret organ; these produce the experience of bliss and emission.

Through the purification of this very process, one gradually attains, in an extensive manner, the mere appearance, the mere sound, and the mere non-conceptuality, whereby the body, speech, and mind, as well as the gnosis-vajra (*jñānavajra*), are realized.

Having established meditative equipoise together with the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), the practice is performed through the yoga of Caṇḍālī.

In the Kālacakra, by means of the winds striking together, the crest of fire from the lightning strikes the wheel at the crown; whichever drop is melted by this, having descended through the throat and heart, it is restrained at the navel and the secret place.

That vibration and flow of the drop which reaches the jewel of the vajra and is firmly restrained at the tip of the banner—if it bestows the moment of the wisdom of Prajñā through the non-emission of the stream of drops, that is bliss.
By the entry of the vital wind into the central channel, the Caṇḍālī blazes forth.
The practitioner, being of three types according to his own capacity, becomes absorbed together with the Mudrā;
cultivating the recollection of the chosen deity through withdrawal and meditation, he performs dhyāna by establishing non-difference from that great bliss.

When the *tilaka* (drop) resides sequentially within the four wheels (*cakras*), then there occurs the attainment of bliss (*ānanda*), supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), cessation-bliss (*viramānanda*), and innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), which is immutable pleasure (*akṣarasukha*). For the three types of practitioners, the method for accomplishing recollection (*anusmṛti*) is said to be precisely this attainment of immutable pleasure, according to their respective capacities. The superior practitioner, being composed in meditative absorption together with the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) consisting of his own conceptualized element, cultivates recollection.

It is also stated in the *Kālacakra*: "Neither meditation, nor mantra recitation, nor ritual implements, nor the seats of the great maṇḍalas; neither fire-offerings, nor mantra-consecrations, nor the invocation and dispatching of the families of the Victors within the menstrual flow [of the consort];
it is only through the application of all mudrās that the accomplishment of mudrā bestows the supreme bliss of the Lord."
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, that should be meditated upon by the yogi at every daily occasion.

O Lord of Men, one's own mind enters into a state of swoon or sleep and becomes devoid of intrinsic nature; yet in the waking state, it manifests as having an intrinsic nature. This does not reveal the path of liberation for living beings.
Indeed, the Vajra-mind of yogins, when differentiated by existence and non-existence, does not bestow equal bliss.
One's own mind is that which is embraced by its own wisdom, which has entered into innate bliss, and which bestows liberation.

Having abandoned all artificial means, that practitioner who, by means of his own wisdom whose nature is the three realms and the body, embraces the chosen deity—the essence of mind whose nature is innate bliss—and experiences the four joys, for him this is the method of practice (*sādhanāvidhi*).

A practitioner of middling faculties performs the meditation in the form of the deity of the Kālacakra union; likewise, [he meditates] upon the white-colored moon on the forehead of the parents consisting of gnosis (*jñānamaya*).

One places the syllables as follows: *Oṃ* at the throat upon the sun, red in color; *Āḥ* in the mind upon Rāhu, black in color; *Haṃ* at the navel upon fire, yellow in color; *Ho* at the secret organ upon gnosis (*jñāna*), blue in color; and *Svā* at the head upon space, dark green in color.
This very practice is the means for achieving recollection (*anusmṛti*) by the practitioner through the central faculty.

A practitioner with inferior faculties, having directly realized the fourfold bliss through the yoga of the *caṇḍālī* and having experienced great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is unable to attain its firmness;
therefore, he must resort to the action-seal (*karmamudrā*). As stated in the *Kālacakra*: "First, the action-seal is to be resorted to for the purpose of increasing this innate bliss of the Victor."

The entry of the vital breath into the center, the binding of the courses of the sun and moon in the right and left channels, the mind reaching supreme bliss during the application of the mudrā, and the awakening of the vajra;

the sound of the vajra in the lotus, or the splashing of water from one's own hands for the sake of pleasure, the non-emission of the seed-syllable accompanied by bliss—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru, which removes the fear of death.

Therefore, this practitioner, having served the *karmamudrā* and bound the vital wind (*vāyu*) within the central channel (*madhyamā*), again attains the experience of bliss through the application of the *mudrā*. The emission of the seminal essence (*śukra*) reaching as far as the forehead from the crown of the head is *ānanda* (joy).

Its arrival from the forehead to the throat and the heart is *paramānanda* (supreme joy). From there, its arrival as far as the secret organ is *viramānanda* (cessation-bliss), and its arrival at the tip of that, reaching the *vajramaṇi*, is *sahajānanda* (innate bliss).

The attainment of great bliss consists precisely in the cessation of the movement of the seminal essence (*śukra*) within its respective locations; in other words, it is the practice for attaining the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*).
Samādhi is indeed perfect stability; thus, the very act of perfect retention is samādhi.
The meaning of samādhi is precisely abiding in that nature which is non-differentiated between subject and object, being devoid of the grasped and the grasper.
The purpose of the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is the expansion of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
Having purified the resultant body within the *dharmadhātu*, it effects the attainment of the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) which is the non-duality of object and subject.

The very nature of meditative concentration is the experience of the union (*yuganaddha*)—free from the appearance of duality—of wisdom-great-bliss and the gnosis endowed with the excellence of all aspects.

And it is said in the *Guhyasamājottaratantra*: "By means of the meditative absorption of wisdom and method, having condensed all phenomena in brief through the yoga of the mass, one visualizes [the deity] within the central image.
The instantaneous perfection of gnosis is designated as 'samādhi'."
Through concentration (*samādhi*) and recollection (*anusmṛti*), the expansion of the realized immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) and its attainment of stability arise.
Therefore, just as there are three types of practitioners of recollection, there are likewise three types of concentration.

By remaining in meditative union (*samāpatti*) with the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), and the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), the practitioner attains the expansion of the realized immutable bliss through the yoga of recollection.
Just as the attainment of firmness in the bliss of the syllable (*akṣarasukha*) and its expansion are reached, so too does the destruction of subtle conceptualizations arise;
and finally, the practitioner attains non-duality (*advaya*).

From this very process, the impurity-stain (*aśuddhatilaka*) is destroyed, and through the complete purification of the maturation-body (*vipākakāya*), this very body is transformed into the desired deity, the Wheel of Time (*Kālacakra*), which consists of gnosis (*jñānamaya*).
And this indeed is the fruit of the six-limbed yoga of samādhi.
Samādhi, like anusmṛti, is also threefold.
Here too, having cultivated the action-seal (karmamudrā) and the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā), the practice is performed by becoming absorbed in the great seal (mahāmudrā).

The firmness that is attained through the yoga of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) regarding the great bliss which the practitioner obtains by means of recollection (*anusmṛti*) is explained in the *Uttarakālacakra* concerning the accomplishment of meditative concentration through the service of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*): "In half a year, leprosy is removed from the excellent body of practitioners; what else [could it not do] when in union with Wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Even if one's own mind falters, [it is purified] always through the cessation of the vital winds (*prāṇavāyu*)."

It indeed removes old age for seven years, including gray hair, when half a year has passed (or when two years have passed); thereafter, the accomplishment of the mudrā occurs within a few days through the application of the path and the mind.

The practice of serving the *jñānamudrā* is described in the *Sādhanāpaṭala* as follows: The *mudrā* is like an illusion; she appears in the mind and in space as if possessing form, like a reflection in a mirror. Illuminating the three worlds, she flashes with many rays resembling lightning and wind. Undivided from external bodies, yet devoid of sense objects, she abides for a month within the sky. Consisting of consciousness, she alone embraces the mind of the world in its manifold forms.

The method for practice together with the Mahāmudrā is also taught in that very same place: "Abandoning this defiled heart of the *karmamudrā* and the imagined *jñānamudrā*, one should meditate upon the *divyamudrā*, the mother of the supreme Victors,

for the sake of perfect enlightenment— she who is untainted, changeless, equal to space, all-pervading, accessible through yoga, immutable, born of primordial wisdom, the remover of the impurities of existence, and conjoined with Kālacakra."
The procedure for accomplishing the factors of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is essentially identical to that of recollection (*anusmṛti*).
Its distinction lies in this: once the state of "yoked union" (*yuganaddha*) has been fully realized through the factor of recollection, firmness must be attained therein.
As it is also stated in the *Guhyasamāja*: "Merely by being perfumed by meditative concentration, one becomes free from obscurations."
In this way, three limbs of the six-limbed yoga cause the body, speech, and mind to attain the vajra-body,
while the other three limbs cause that [vajra-body] to attain firmness.
Having matured within the Wheel of Time in the state of union (*yuganaddha*), the practitioner of the non-dual tantra abides in the supreme state within this very body.
This has been described by taking as its basis this very method for accomplishing the non-dual reality (*advayatattva*).

By the aforementioned authorities, it is clear that Buston drew extensively from the *Kālacakra-tantra*, the *Samājottara-tantra*, and the *Sekoddeśa-ṭīkā* in support of his own system of yoga practice;
