thus, the description here is primarily based on the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*) method propounded by Buston.
The detailed exposition of this, however, was composed in the *Sādhanāpaṭala* and the *Jñānapaṭala* of the *Vimalaprabhā*, the commentary on the *Kālacakra*.

The Sixth Chapter: The Two Distinct Traditions of the Non-dual Tantra in Tibet. (1) The Tradition of Śāmakapa. The initial layout of the practice manual (*sādhanāpaddhati*) for this tradition was performed by Āryadeva.

Furthermore, the primary credit for the propagation of this [tradition] belongs first and foremost to Narasiṃha (Jedima Pāgyagaravā), born in the region of Vidarbha-Carasimha in South India, who received instruction from fifty-four gurus;
he, moreover, traveled to Tibet at the age of fifty.
From the Christian year 1966 until 1987 CE (for twenty-one years), he resided in Tibet, where his center for the propagation of the Dharma was located precisely in the region of Dingri.
Even at the time of his death, while addressing the inhabitants of Dingri, he taught one hundred verses.
Furthermore, there are two lineages of the tradition of peace that serve as particularly powerful sources of inspiration:
1. the Indian tradition of peace, and 2.
the Tibetan lineage of the Yoginī Machig Labdrön.

The first [lineage] here was presided over by Āryadeva. The second lineage proceeded from Macig, having originated in the place called Labchi in Tibet; because it arose there, it received its name from the name of its own field as *Labchi-pradīpa* (Maciga Labdön).
Thus he was born.
At the age of twenty-three, Macig Labdrön traveled from the Kosal region of India to Tibet,
where she was married by the master Guru Bhadra, who was a practitioner of Buddhakapāla.
A detailed biography of him can be found in the work titled *Aṣṭasaptaticchedakavivṛtti*. The method of practice is the *Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra*, a foundational text of the Śamaka lineage.
In it, it says: "Therefore, one should know that the Great Mantra of the Perfection of Wisdom is a mantra of knowledge, a supreme mantra," and so forth.

In the passage, “The mantra unequalled and peerless; the mantra that pacifies all suffering,” the lineage of those who bring about pacification (*śamaka*) was firmly established through the very word *praśamana*.
Āryadeva, taking the *Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra* as his basis, composed the *Āryaprajñāpāramitopadeśakārikā* in fifty verses and propagated this lineage of pacifiers.
In this work, regarding the method of cultivation (*bhāvanāvidhi*), it is made very clear that the sense faculties, such as the eyes, should not be forcibly restrained.
One should remain in the nature of non-conceptuality, without grasping that resembles the engagement of direct perception toward objects.
One must cut through the Māras of attachment, aversion, anger, and so forth, using the axe of mindfulness and clear comprehension.

The attainment of the Perfection of Wisdom does not lie outside; rather, it is one's own mind, devoid of existence and non-existence, without characteristics, naturally luminous, and of the very nature of one’s own mind.
One’s own mind should be established pervading exactly as much of empty space as it extends.
When there is the realization of the true nature of one's own mind, there is no necessity for the abandonment of mental factors such as attachment and aversion, which take the form of its waves;
rather, they subside of their own accord.
Just as when the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) have ceased, the necessity for the cessation of the other sense faculties does not arise;

so too it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "The pacifier of the suffering of the three types of suffering, the infinite one who has attained the three liberations, liberated from all obscurations, he has reached equality with space."
One should abide in one's own mind, which is like the cloudless sky and free from obscurations, for the sake of striking down and pacifying the three types of suffering.

Although by its very nature the entire world is, from the beginning, unarisen and of a luminous nature, a sentient being becomes a partaker of suffering because it is whirled about by the wind of ignorance.
Therefore, the dissolution of the flow of the wind of ignorance into the luminosity and the firm abiding in the non-dual reality is the very essence of the meditation on peace.
The Yoginī Macī Galabaḍona said: "Having regarded the body as equal to a corpse, reality (*tattva*) is directly realized simply by establishing the mind in a state like the unobstructed sky.
In the lineage of tranquility (*śamaka-paramparā*), the realization of reality is performed through three systems: the Pāramitā-naya, the Mantra-naya, and the Sahaja.
Just as those who consider themselves Bodhisattvas manifest the power of the *bodhicitta*, so too their investigation, view, and conventional conduct are impelled by that *bodhicitta*."
In the same way, even within this lineage of tranquility (*śamaka-paramparā*), the necessity of abiding in a state free from dualities and conceptual constructions (*nirdvandva-nirvikalpa*) is urged.
These two limbs of practice follow the method of "cutting" (*chedaka*).
And what is this "cutting"?
The intention of "cutting" (chedaka), however, is the breaking of the grasping at a self, which effectively means its abandonment.
Grasping at a self alone is the cause of existence (bhava).
For it is through the arising of the cultivation of egoism (ahaṅkāra) that there suddenly occurs the expansion of attachments toward "my house," "my family," and so forth.
For that purpose, one performs various ritual actions and is bound within the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*).

As an antidote to this, in the *Pāramitānaya*, the teaching of the non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*) is carried out through the application of reasoning; likewise, in the *Mantranaya*, having transformed the forms of both the stationary and the moving, the stages of generation (*utpattikrama*) and completion (*niṣpannakrama*) are cultivated.
In the lineage of the Śamaka tradition, the practice of both systems is undertaken;

simultaneously, through meditative cultivation, practitioners offer their own body— conceiving its skin as the Golden Island (Svarṇadvīpa), its hands and feet as the [other] limbs, its blood as the water endowed with eight qualities, its flesh as the eighth auspicious mark, its backbone as Mount Sumeru,
and its two eyes as the sun and moon— to the chosen deity, along with the four continents beginning with Jambudvīpa.

In this very chain of the infinite wheel of existence (*ananta-bhavacakra*), there remains no living being whatsoever who has not himself, at some time, served as mother or father to someone. We thus stand under a debt to all beings; to discharge that debt, the *Chedaka* (the Liberating One) effects a separation between the subtle body (*cetana-śarīra*) and this gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*). Having then nourished it with substances—whether with or without outflows (*sāsrava-anāsrava-dravya*)—such as flesh, blood, and so forth, according to the desires of living beings, he offers it back to them.
The practitioner of the lineage of cutting (*chedakaparamparā*) goes to a cremation ground, a stream of water, or elsewhere, and performs the practice.

In order to abandon attachment to the body, he goes to a cremation ground, meditates on his own body as a mass of flesh and blood, and offers it to the *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth. The accomplished master Ilārasapāmahodaya, explaining the lineage of cutting very clearly, says: "The practice performed in places such as cremation grounds, solitary locations, and streams of water is the external cutting (*bāhyachedikā*) of the limbs and members of the body."
Offering oneself to living beings in the form of food is the internal severing practice; furthermore,
the total eradication of the grasping at a self is said to be the ultimate severing practice.
This can be stated by way of analogy: the enemy does not exist outside; rather, it is the enmity of one's own mind itself.

Regarding the passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth existing within oneself, the very perception of them as "good" or "bad" is Māra. The destruction of all that, through a state of complete equanimity—by seeing everything as non-dual and free from conceptual construction—is the sole objective of all spiritual practices.
The Śamaka lineage also leads one toward this very view as its means of realization.

(2) As for the Ñingma lineage: if the development of all vehicles of the Buddha’s Dharma—namely the Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Bodhisattvayāna (comprising the Pāramitāyāna and Vajrayāna)—occurred anywhere apart from the Noble Land [of India], it was precisely in the land of Tibet.
The first entry of the Buddhist religion into Tibet occurred during the time of Emperor Srong-btsan-sgam-po (615 CE);
however, one year later, Glaṅ-dar-ma destroyed the Buddha's teaching.

At that time, many seekers of knowledge, such as Ratnabhadra, Marapa, Dharmamati, and others, came to Bhāratavarṣa; having engaged in study and teaching there, they subsequently propagated the Buddhist Dharma once again. Thus, two lineages of the Buddhist Dharma became established in the land of Tibet. The first lineage is the Early Translation (Nyingma).
The second is called the Later Tradition (Sarma).
Within the second lineage, four schools—namely Kagyu, Sakya, Kadampa, and Gelug—flourished. In the Earlier Tradition (Nyingma)...

The Vajrayāna was propagated. In this way, there are numerous tantric texts whose circulation occurred solely within the Nyingma tradition, and which are found in forty-six volumes within the compendium titled *rNying ma rgyud ’bum*.
Among these, the *Sarvadharmamahāśāntibodhicittakulayarājagarbhaguhya-herūkalīlātantra-jñānaguhyapradīpa* and others are preeminent;
yet they have no inclusion within the Kargyu tradition.
Therefore, it is essential to provide an introduction to the Nyingma tradition and its literature.
In this tradition, there have been many renowned translators and accomplished masters (*siddhapuruṣa*).
In particular, the master of Oḍḍiyāna, Padmasambhava, and the Great Professor Śāntarakṣita were invited to Tibet by the Tibetan King Khri-srong-lde-btsan (815 CE).
Upon seeing the path for these two, the Emperor established the monastery named Samye; it was here that the words of the Buddha were translated into the Tibetan language.
Śāntarakṣita ordained young men and established the Vinaya teachings in the land of Tibet.
Ācārya Padmasambhava consecrated twenty-five individuals, including Je-vaṅ, Ñe-raṅ, and Mahodaya, in the Vajrayāna; they were the first to attain spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Within that very lineage, many practitioners and masters emerged who received the Dharma scriptures from secret locations; one hundred and eight accomplished ones (*siddha*) appeared.
Following them, within this same lineage, the omniscient Lochen Pā was born.
And he made this tradition exceedingly prosperous.
This lineage specifically emphasizes the primacy of spiritual practice (*sādhana*).
In the land of Tibet, the vast majority of accomplished beings (*siddhapuruṣa*) arose within this very tradition.
In the Nyingma tradition, nine vehicles (yānas) are revered: 1. the Śrāvakayāna, 2. the Pratyekabuddhayāna, 3.
the Bodhisattvayāna, [4. the Kriyāyāna, 5. the Caryāyāna, 6. the Yogayāna, 7. the Mahāyoga, 8. the Anuyoga, and 9. the Atiyoga].
4. the vehicle of Kriyātantra, 5. the vehicle of Upāya, 6. the vehicle of Yogatantra.
7. the Mahāyoga Tantra Vehicle, 8. the Anuttarayoga Tantra Vehicle, and 9. the Atiyoga Tantra Vehicle.
Here, these vehicles (yānas) are briefly examined so that the ancient Tibetan tradition regarding their proof may be elucidated.
An introduction to the nine vehicles mentioned herein is presented in their proper order. Generally, the etymological meaning of the word *yāna* is "ascending" (*ārohaṇa*).
The vehicles explained herein lead us progressively upward;
therefore, they are called "vehicles" (*yāna*).

1. The Śrāvaka-yāna: having analyzed the ultimate reality of the subject and object as being of the nature of phenomena (*dharmātmaka*), and with the aspiration to personally attain liberation, one adopts some form of ethical discipline (*śīla*) from among the eight types of *prātimokṣa*.

Having abandoned misconduct and rendered the mind serviceable through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one who realizes the Four Noble Truths through the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*) in their sixteen aspects attains the path leading from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*) up to the state of an Arhat;
this is declared to be the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

2. Regarding the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle: here, having perceived consciousness for a mere moment as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths in their sixteen aspects is performed in the same manner as in the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

Furthermore, in this context, the cultivation of profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which is of the nature of its thorough integration with that [cultivation], confers a distinct excellence of its own.

Thus, in the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha, having attained the state of an Arhat as the fruit of that vehicle, teaches the Dharma through physical gestures (*kāyasaṃketa*). 3. This Bodhisattva Vehicle is the means for accomplishing this vehicle: having analyzed selflessness (*nairātmya*) in all phenomena, one practices the cultivation of altruism by engaging in the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Having cultivated the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) on the path of training (*śaikṣamārga*) by means of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*), one attains the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣamārga*), which is effectively the stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhābhūmi*).

4. The practitioner of this Kriyātantra vehicle, following the vase and crown initiations, realizes that the nature of self is ultimately pure and free from the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭirahita*), through the six principles such as the nature of the deity (*devatātathatā*).
Having personally summoned the deity of gnosis (jñānadeva) into the presence of the deity of the arising of the commitment (samayotpattideva), he beholds them in the form of both master and servant.

Having entered into the supports of sound and mind, he meditates in samādhi upon the suchness (tathatā) abiding as fire which is the mantra, and upon the suchness that is the end of sound which abides as sound.
By means of external bathing and pure conduct, this person primarily attains the stage of the Vajradhara of the three families.
5. This practitioner of the Means Vehicle—that is, the Vehicle of Conduct Tantra—receives, along with the vase and crown initiations, the name initiation marked by the eight auspicious signs.
[This pertains to] the Yoga Tantra of vision.

And according to the *Caryā* [Tantra] (*Kriyātantra*), the master himself, regarding the deity of the arising of the commitment (*samayotpatti-deva*) as being face-to-face with the wisdom-being deity (*jñānasattva-deva*), and considering them as a kinsman or a friend, cultivates recitation (*japa*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), thereby attaining the stage of the Vajradhara of the fourth family.

6. In the vehicle of *Yogatantra*, the practitioner receives both the master initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) along with the vajra-disciple initiation (*vajraśiṣyābhiṣeka*); and in the ultimate sense, there is the empowerment of the signless nature of phenomena (*animitta-dharmatā*) by way of the conventional Vajradhātu deity.

Having visualized himself as a deity through the five modes of perfect awakening (*pañcābhisambodhi*) and the four miraculous displays (*pratihārya*), and having simultaneously invoked the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) deity, he dissolves that [wisdom-being] into himself; then, having bound the four seals (*caturmudrā*), performed the offerings and worship, and completed the dismissal (*visarjana*), he attains the supreme state on the Akaniṣṭha level—the form of the fruit—by practicing both internal meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and external conduct such as ritual purity.

7. This is the Mahāyoga Tantra Vehicle. A practitioner of this vehicle, having fortified the capacity for the benefits derived from the four types of empowerment through the profound empowerment (*gambhīrābhiṣeka*), realizes—in the fundamental vision (the actual practice)—all phenomena as the Great Dharmakāya, which is inseparable from the luminosity and emptiness of the mind. Having attained the secret empowerment within the path of the generation stage and the completion stage, and practicing the yoga of the wind-bindu (*vāyutilaka*) and the stage of union (*yuganaddhakrama*), one attains unsurpassed enlightenment in a single lifetime.
8. In the Atiyoga Tantrayāna, the practitioner is primarily consecrated here by the fourth empowerment (*caturthābhiṣeka*).

Having perceived all states of existence and the phenomena of nirvāṇa from the very beginning as being of the nature of the Buddha, he undertakes the conduct established through the instructions on the mental categories.
Being superior to all affirmations and negations, as well as to all abandonments and adoptions, he practices the path and attains the state of the Buddha Samantabhadra.
If these nine vehicles are determined to be included within the stages of the path, they are then subsumed within the three vehicles alone:
1. the Hīnayāna (Śrāvakayāna), 2. the Bodhisattvayāna, [and 3. the Buddhayāna].
3. And the Mantra Vehicle.
These three vehicles must not be abandoned for the sake of the progressive increase of realization.
An exposition of this has been set forth elsewhere.

Conclusion: If the investigators of all other philosophical systems (*darśana*) are not distinct from those who investigate the nature of reality (*vastuvādin*), then, provided they do not fall into mere verbal disputes, they will all arrive at a single consensus regarding the ultimate truth (*tattva*).

For example, the Buddhist Vijñānavādins, considering the universe to be an expansion of their own mind, regard the very nature of the mind as such; why then should this mind itself not have been the creator of the world?
Do the Mādhyamikas not, in fact, accept the oneness of all principles? Is it not precisely this mind that is conceived as the substratum of creation?
In the Vajrayāna, however, one’s own body is the complete Brahmāṇḍa;
even the arrangement of the twenty-four pīṭha sites and the ten bhūmis occurs within this very body, which itself arises as the cause of creation.
Whether one is a proponent of Īśvara (theism) who is Hindu, Christian, or Muslim,
all of them explain this very reality— this luminous mind that is free from the four extremes and devoid of conceptual proliferation— through their own respective systems under different names.
In this state of mental tranquility, no distinction whatsoever can be established.
Therefore, we observe that it is precisely through this that Great Beings (mahāpuruṣas) are found to have realized all phenomena.
As the Lord Maitreya stated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*: "Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added."
Reality must be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.

If each individual, carrying out their respective distinct principles attained through their own capacity and effort, were to follow the meaning of this verse in both worldly affairs and the field of meditation, then they would be able to become happy. If individuals are happy, then the nation and the world as well can become happy.
The future is the fruit of the present;

when the present is auspicious, the future will also be excellent. There is not even a trace of doubt in this matter: if this life were filled with happiness and its course were likewise full of happiness, then what necessity would there be for Nirvana hereafter?

This indeed is essential: that one should not make that reality—which is limitless, indivisible, and beyond the scope of the senses—an object of one's own intellect, nor should one create distinctions therein by relying on external arrangements.
Only by proceeding with indivisibility, equanimity, neutrality, and a state free from conceptual construction can the actual vision and reality of the Vajrayāna be known; not otherwise.
In this regard, those belonging to the Vajrayāna tradition have striven for a long time and have achieved direct realization.
Not only that, but having experienced this very state within this very life, they have manifested the method for accomplishing their own ultimate excellence.
If its evaluation were to be conducted with an impartial attitude, setting aside sectarian notions regarding the tradition, then it will certainly bring about the welfare of humanity.

It is evident that today there is an absolute necessity for the methods of practice (*sādhana*) according to the Tantric systems of philosophy, which bring fear to the world. I hope that humanity will realize this subject in its own life.

I perform this dedication so that, through the power of the merit born from composing this work, all living beings may attain perfect enlightenment. I pay homage to those bodies in which that jewel of the excellent mind has arisen;
I go for refuge to those mines of happiness, in whom even an injury results in a succession of bliss.
This work entitled *Vajrayānadarśanamīmāṃsā*, composed by the monk Vaṅchuk Dorje Negi and edited by the Indian Sanskrit scholar Dharmadatta Caturveda, has reached completion.
May there be auspiciousness for all beings!
